=== NOTES 3:42 | Urban Development – Urbanisation Trends, Challenges (housing, Slums, Transport, Waste, Finance)
## SUB 0 | State Extremes of Urbanisation (Census 2011)
[42:0:0] # Urban share (level of urbanisation)
[42:0:1] TABLE head: Rank | States (Census 2011)
  [42:0:1.0] Most urbanised State | Goa 62.2% (49.8% in 2001 – also first in 2001); then Mizoram 52.1%, Tamil Nadu 48.4%, Kerala 47.7%, Maharashtra 45.2%, Gujarat 42.6%
  [42:0:1.1] Least urbanised State | Himachal Pradesh 10.0%; then Bihar 11.3%, Assam 14.1%, Odisha 16.7%, Jharkhand 24.0%, Rajasthan 24.9%
  [42:0:1.2] Low-urban NE / hill States | Arunachal 22.9%, Sikkim 25.2%, Tripura 26.2%, Nagaland 28.9%
  [42:0:1.3] Middle group | Punjab 37.5% (highest among land-locked Punjab, Haryana 34.9, MP 27.6, J&K 27.4); AP (undivided) 33.4%; West Bengal 31.9% (lowest of AP, Haryana, Mizoram, WB)
  [42:0:1.4] Descending 2001 | Tamil Nadu 44.0 > Maharashtra 42.4 > Gujarat 37.4 > Andhra Pradesh 27.3
  [42:0:1.5] Descending 2011 | Maharashtra 45.2 > Gujarat 42.6 > Andhra Pradesh 33.4 > West Bengal 31.9
  [42:0:1.6] Least urbanised southern State | Andhra Pradesh (undivided, 33.4%); Karnataka ~38.7%, Kerala 47.7%, TN 48.4%
  [42:0:1.7] MP districts, highest urban % | Bhopal 80.9%; Indore 74.1, Gwalior 62.7, Jabalpur 58.5

## SUB 1 | Urbanisation Trends in India – Census Figures
[42:1:0] TABLE head: Item | Census 2001 | Census 2011
  [42:1:0.0] Urban population | 28.6 crore (27.81%) | 37.71 crore (377.1 million) = 31.16%
  [42:1:0.1] Rural population | 74.3 crore (72.19%) | 83.3 crore (68.84%)
  [42:1:0.2] Total towns | 5,161 | 7,935
  [42:1:0.3] Statutory towns | 3,799 | 4,041
  [42:1:0.4] Census towns | 1,362 | 3,894 provisional (3,892 final)
  [42:1:0.5] Million-plus cities / UAs | 35 | 53
[42:1:1] - Increase 2001-11: urban **+91.0 million**, rural +90.4 million – first decade with a larger urban than rural increase.
[42:1:2] # Phases
[42:1:3] TABLE head: Phase | Period | Urban share
  [42:1:3.0] Slow | 1901-31 | 10.8% → 12%
  [42:1:3.1] Moderate / medium | 1931-61 | 12.2% → 18.3% (urban population +45.46 million)
  [42:1:3.2] Rapid | 1961 onward | 18% → 31.16%
[42:1:4] - Urban share: **11% (1901) → 31.1% (2011)**; growth is fuelled by a steady **village-city flow**.
[42:1:5] - India's urban population (2001: 28.6 crore) exceeded the **USA's total population** (28.1 crore); the USA has a far higher **level** of urbanisation, which does not explain India's larger numbers.
[42:1:6] - India's level of urbanisation is **lower than China's**; poor planning of Indian cities is true but is not the reason.
[42:1:7] - Rapid urbanisation after 2001 (million cities 35 → 53) is true; the mobile revolution is true but unrelated.
[42:1:8] - India is **not over-urbanised** (31.1%), though large cities lack infrastructure.
[42:1:9] - **Urban growth** = rise in urban population and in the number of urban centres (UPPSC key: also rise in total population and urban income – "all").
[42:1:10] - Roots of **urban poverty lie in rural areas** – low rural literacy pushes migrants into low-paid city work (UPPSC A-R key: R explains A).
[42:1:11] - Most urban religious group (2011): **Jains (~80%)**; Buddhists 43%; Muslims, Christians ~40%; Hindus 29%; Sikhs 28%.
[42:1:12] - India **2nd** in absolute urban population, after China; cities ~**3% of land**, ~**60% of GDP**.
[42:1:13] - **Hidden urbanisation**: satellite **DEGURBA** estimate (EAC-PM) about **63% urban**; under-counting starves peri-urban areas of municipal funds.
[42:1:14] > Number traps: 31.16% (not 31.36 or 33.16); 27.81% in 2001; 53 million cities; 3,894 census towns; 7,935 towns.
[42:1:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC 15 p.20-21 (31.16%, 27.81%, 7,935 towns, 53 million cities, 3,894 census towns, +91.0 m urban); Rocket Indian Geography p.66 (31.16%); app notes 3:42 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Cities – Million-plus Cities and Megacities
[42:2:0] - **1901: Kolkata** the only million city (~15 lakh). Million cities: 12 (1981), 23 (1991), **35 (2001)**, **53 (2011)**.
[42:2:1] - Million-plus share of urban population: 37.8% (2001), 42.6% (2011).
[42:2:2] - **2001:** most million cities in **Uttar Pradesh (6)** – Kanpur, Lucknow, Agra, Varanasi, Meerut, Allahabad (so "only 5 in UP" is false); Maharashtra 4, TN 3, WB 2. **Ludhiana, Kochi, Surat and Nagpur** were all million-plus.
[42:2:3] - **KAVAL towns** (Kanpur, Agra, Varanasi, Allahabad, Lucknow) are NOT the only million cities; the **North-East** had no million city (2001 and 2011).
[42:2:4] - **2011:** most million-plus UAs – **UP and Kerala (7 each)**, Maharashtra 6. **No million-plus city in Odisha**; Haryana – Faridabad; J&K – Srinagar; Jharkhand – Jamshedpur, Dhanbad, Ranchi.
[42:2:5] - **2001 megacities (6)**: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru – **not Ahmedabad**. 2011: nine UAs above 40 lakh (adds Ahmedabad, Pune, Surat).
[42:2:6] TABLE head: Year | Order by population
  [42:2:6.0] 1991 | Bombay (13.7 m) – Calcutta (10.9) – Delhi (9.4) – Madras (3.8)
  [42:2:6.1] 2001 (city proper) | Greater Mumbai 11.98 m – Delhi 9.88 – Kolkata 4.57 – Chennai 4.34 – Bangalore 4.30 (by UA Kolkata 13.2 m was ahead of Delhi 12.9 m)
  [42:2:6.2] 2011 UAs | Greater Mumbai 18.41 m, Delhi 16.31 m, Kolkata 14.11 m, Chennai 8.70 m, Bengaluru 8.50 m, Hyderabad 7.74 m
[42:2:7] - Highest population pair (2011): **Mumbai and Delhi**. UP UAs (2011): **Ghaziabad > Agra > Varanasi > Meerut**.
[42:2:8] - **Urban corridors** = urban functions **expanding along transport routes**.
[42:2:9] - **Oxford Economics (2016, 2015 data):** Delhi NCR (GDP at PPP $370 bn) moved to **30th** among global metro economies, ahead of Mumbai (31st, $368 bn) – "Delhi displaces Mumbai as economic capital".
[42:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC 15 p.20 (53 million cities 2011); indiatvnews.com / businessinsider.in reports on Oxford Economics 2016 (fetched via web search); Census 2001-2011 city tables as quoted in PYQ explanations; app notes 3:42 sub 3
## SUB 3 | Census Definitions – Urban Area, Towns and Size Classes
[42:3:0] TABLE head: Type | Criteria
  [42:3:0.0] Statutory town | Any place with a municipal corporation, municipality, nagar panchayat, cantonment board or notified town area – notified by the State by law
  [42:3:0.1] Census town (= urban area test, Census 2001/2011) | All 3: population ≥5,000; ≥75% of male main workers in non-agricultural work; density ≥400 per sq km
[42:3:1] - **No minimum area** and **no electricity criterion** (e.g. "60% households electrified" is not a test; "60% males" is wrong – it is 75%).
[42:3:2] - Rural area = all areas not urban; 3/4 or more engaged in primary activities.
[42:3:3] - **Census 2027** keeps the 1981 census-town criteria; RGI retained them despite **MoHUA's** objection before the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Housing and Urban Affairs (chair **Magunta Sreenivasulu Reddy**).
[42:3:4] # Size classes (six)
[42:3:5] TABLE head: Class | Population
  [42:3:5.0] Class I | 1 lakh and above (468 UAs/towns in 2011, about 70% of urban population)
  [42:3:5.1] Class II | 50,000-99,999
  [42:3:5.2] Class III | 20,000-49,999
  [42:3:5.3] Class IV | 10,000-19,999
  [42:3:5.4] Class V | 5,000-9,999
  [42:3:5.5] Class VI | below 5,000
[42:3:6] - **Small towns = Class IV, V and VI** (under 20,000).
[42:3:7] - Class I share of urban population: 65.2% (1991); **2001: 62.32% in UPPSC keys** (other compilations about 68-69%); ~70% (2011).
[42:3:8] - Highest growth: **Class I** towns (Census 1991); **Class III** (Census 2001). Class IV had the largest number of towns in 2001.
[42:3:9] - **Slum (Census)**: a compact area of at least **300 population or about 60-70 households** of poorly built, congested tenements in unhygienic conditions.
[42:3:10] - A village turns into a town when **traders and manufacturers** appear – they depend on village resources, but not wholly.
[42:3:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC 15 p.20 (3/4 rule, census towns); ies.gov.in Arthapedia "Cities and Towns" (size classes, 70% in Class I, 394 → 468); app notes 3:42 sub 0
## SUB 4 | Global Urbanisation and Projections
[42:4:0] - **UN World Urbanization Prospects**: about **68%** of the world urban by **2050** (WUP 2018; earlier estimates said ~70% by 2050).
[42:4:1] - World urban share: **54.5% (2016)**; **56.2% (2020)** (World Cities Report 2024).
[42:4:2] - **Urban overtook rural**: commonly dated **2009** (WUP 2009 Revision: 3.42 bn urban vs 3.41 bn rural); later UN revisions put the crossover in 2007-08.
[42:4:3] TABLE head: Region (2020, WCR 2024) | Urban %
  [42:4:3.0] Australia/New Zealand (most urbanised) | 86.3
  [42:4:3.1] North America | 82.6
  [42:4:3.2] Europe | 74.9
  [42:4:3.3] Oceania (whole) | 68.2
  [42:4:3.4] East Asia | 64.8
  [42:4:3.5] Africa | 43.5
  [42:4:3.6] South Asia | 36.6
[42:4:4] - Fastest urbanisation in the last three decades: **Asia** (UN-Habitat Global Report on Human Settlements 2009).
[42:4:5] - Largest urban agglomeration of the world: **Tokyo(-Yokohama)** in every UN list from the 1960s to WUP 2018 (Mexico City and New York below it); WUP 2025 (new method) puts **Jakarta** first, Dhaka second, Tokyo third, **New Delhi fourth**.
[42:4:6] - **SDG 11 (UN)**: cities occupy **3% of land** but use **60-80% of energy** and produce **75% of carbon emissions**.
[42:4:7] - India: ~**60 crore** urban by **2031**.
[42:4:8] ~~ Sources: un.org SDG 11 fact sheet as quoted in the PYQ explanation; UN press and wall-chart pages on WUP 2009 Revision (via web search); World Cities Report 2024 figures as quoted in the PYQ explanations; app notes 3:42 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Causes and Social Effects of Urbanisation
[42:5:0] - Main component: **migration** (natural increase similar in rural and urban areas).
[42:5:1] - **Push**: monsoon failure, rural unemployment, **lack of rural jobs**, non-growing farm land, **rural-urban imbalance**.
[42:5:2] - **Pull**: **magnetic features of cities** – jobs, public facilities (health, education), transport, industrial growth.
[42:5:3] - **Philip M. Hauser** – "**Population Implosion**" = rural-urban concentration of people. "**New Population Bomb**" = rapidly growing **Third World urban population**.
[42:5:4] - **Crime rises with urbanisation and industrialisation** – industrial-urban life causes family and cultural disorganisation (UPPSC A-R: R explains A).
[42:5:5] > Statement sets mixing push and pull factors are usually **all correct**.
[42:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society - Group 2 Prelims 01 p.93 (factors behind urbanisation) and 02 p.1 (urban crime); app notes 3:42 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Urban Challenges – Slums, Housing, Heat, Governance
[42:6:0] # Slums
[42:6:1] - **Mumbai**: slums **41.3% of urban households** – highest share among metros (Census 2011); Kolkata 29.6%, Chennai 28.5%, Delhi 14.6%.
[42:6:2] - Among **million-plus cities**: **Greater Visakhapatnam ~44%** of population in slums; Greater Mumbai and Vijayawada ~41%.
[42:6:3] - Slum population 2001: Greater Mumbai 6.5 m, **Delhi 1.9 m** (more than Chennai 0.8 m, Bangalore, Surat).
[42:6:4] - 2011: 6.55 crore slum dwellers = 17.4% of urban population; World Bank estimate ~**177 million**.
[42:6:5] # Housing, waste, heat, governance
[42:6:6] - Urban housing shortage ~**18.78 million units** (2012 Technical Group); costs exceed middle-class incomes → cramped, unserviced housing (NextGen).
[42:6:7] - Sewerage, solid waste and public-transport gaps; private vehicles cause congestion.
[42:6:8] - **Urban heat island** = a city much **warmer than nearby rural areas** (3-5°C).
[42:6:9] - Governance: **fragmented authority**, little **fiscal autonomy** (ES 2025-26 ch.15); urbanising areas left under panchayats.
[42:6:10] - **Urban design** = the arrangement and design of buildings, **streets and public spaces**; urban (city) planning = wider land-use regulation (master plans, **zoning**).
[42:6:11] - **India Urban Observatory** – **New Delhi** (MoHUA office); data hub for evidence-based planning.
[42:6:12] - **MoHUA (2017)** = merger of Ministry of Urban Development + **Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation** (MoHUPA – earlier nodal ministry for identifying urban BPL families).
[42:6:13] - **e-lala** – e-commerce portal for small traders (CAIT); Ministry of Urban Development, Nov 2015.
[42:6:14] - Social Forestry is NOT under the Minimum Needs Programme.
[42:6:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society - Group 2 Prelims 01 p.93 and 02 p.1-2 (housing, transport, sewerage, master plans, zoning); en.wikipedia.org "Urban design" (via web search); app notes 3:42 sub 6
## SUB 7 | Municipal Finance
[42:7:0] - **Property tax** = most important own revenue; also advertisement tax, professional tax, **octroi** (levied and collected by **local bodies**; now subsumed in GST), fees, fines; plus State grants.
[42:7:1] - **Property tax gap:** Economic Survey 2016-17 used **satellite imagery** of Bengaluru; cities collect only **5-20%** of potential.
[42:7:2] - **74th Amendment – Twelfth Schedule: 18 functions** – urban planning, water supply, public health and sanitation, slum improvement, urban poverty alleviation, fire services, urban forestry, vital statistics (not police).
[42:7:3] TABLE head: First | Fact
  [42:7:3.0] First municipal bond | Bangalore Mahanagara Palike, 1997
  [42:7:3.1] First without State guarantee | Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, 1998
[42:7:4] - Budget 2026-27: **City Economic Regions** – ₹5,000 crore per CER over 5 years.
[42:7:5] TABLE head: Body | Urban grant
  [42:7:5.0] 15th FC | ULBs 36% of local body grants
  [42:7:5.1] 16th FC (2026-31) | ULBs ₹3.6 lakh crore (45%) vs RLBs ₹4.4 lakh crore; 80% basic / 20% performance
[42:7:6] - **Local Finance Enquiry Committee (1963) – K. Santhanam**; A.D. Gorwala (1951) – rural credit; Balwantrai Mehta (1957), Ashok Mehta (1977-78) – panchayati raj.
[42:7:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:42 sub 7 (property tax, bonds, FC grants, committees)
## SUB 8 | UN-Habitat and Urban Forums
[42:8:0] TABLE head: Body / idea | Fact
  [42:8:0.0] UN-Habitat | Set up 1978 after Habitat I (Vancouver, 1976); HQ Nairobi; publishes World Cities Report
  [42:8:0.1] Right to the City | Henri Lefebvre (1968); adopted in the New Urban Agenda (Habitat III, Quito, 2016)
  [42:8:0.2] SDG 11 | Sustainable Cities and Communities – UN-Habitat's mandate
  [42:8:0.3] APMCHUD | Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Housing and Urban Development; first meet New Delhi, 2006
  [42:8:0.4] World Cities Day (31 Oct) | General theme "Better City, Better Life"; 2019 sub-theme "Changing the World: Innovations and Better Life for Future Generations"
[42:8:1] - UN-Habitat city prosperity criteria: productivity, infrastructure, **quality of life, equity**, sustainability – **not optimum population**.
[42:8:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:42 sub 8 and 3:43 sub 2 (World Cities Day)
## SUB 9 | Andhra Pradesh Urbanisation
[42:9:0] - Undivided AP (2011): **33.4%** urban, 2.82 crore urban people; least urbanised southern State.
[42:9:1] - Residuary AP (2011 base): **29.6%** urban (1.49 crore).
[42:9:2] - **123 ULBs = 17 municipal corporations + 79 municipalities + 27 nagar panchayats** (SES 2024-25); an older APPSC paper keyed **71** municipalities.
[42:9:3] - **Greater Visakhapatnam** – highest slum share among million-plus cities; **Vijayawada** ~41%.
[42:9:4] - Capital: **Amaravati** – **AP–UN-Habitat MoU**: Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs.
[42:9:5] - "One Water, One City, One Future" urban water vision at **IFAT India 2026**.
[42:9:6] - **Nigama Sabha (Satavahana period):** the body that ran town administration.
[42:9:7] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.263-264 (123 ULBs, 17/79/27, 1.49 crore urban); app notes 3:42 sub 9

=== NOTES 3:43 | Urban Programmes – Amrut, Smart Cities Mission, Sbm-urban, Pmay-u, Nulm
## SUB 0 | Swachh Bharat Mission and Swachh Survekshan
[43:0:0] # SBM basics
[43:0:1] - Launched **2 October 2014** (**Gandhi Jayanti**) – October 2014; goal **ODF and Clean India by 2 October 2019** (Gandhi's **150th** birth anniversary) – the only one of Jan Dhan, BBBP, Janshree Bima and SBM with that deadline.
[43:0:2] - Two components: **Rural (Grameen)** and **Urban (Shahari)**; SBM-Gramin also targeted an ODF rural India by **2 October 2019**.
[43:0:3] - Focus on **collective behavioural change** of the whole community; open defecation is part of the usual early-morning walk, crop check and socialising for many (mainly rural India).
[43:0:4] - **Swachh Yug** (2016): to make **villages along the Ganga ODF**.
[43:0:5] - **SBM-U 2.0** launched **1 October 2021**: garbage-free cities.
[43:0:6] # Swachh Survekshan
[43:0:7] - **2017 assessment areas**: waste collection, sweeping and transportation; processing and disposal; ODF; **capacity building (SBM e-learning portal)**; **IEC and behaviour change** – **not "level of micro particles"** in the air.
[43:0:8] TABLE head: Garbage Free City star | Prerequisite certification
  [43:0:8.0] 1 Star | ODF
  [43:0:8.1] 3 Star | ODF+
  [43:0:8.2] 5 Star | ODF++
  [43:0:8.3] 7 Star | Water+
[43:0:9] - **Water+ (Aug 2021)**: AP became the first State with more than one Water+ city – **three: Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Tirupati**.
[43:0:10] - GFC vision: no garbage or litter visible in the city at any time of day.
[43:0:11] - **Indore**: cleanest city (10 lakh+), year after year; **Swachh Survekshan 2024-25 (July 2025)**: Indore top for the **8th year in a row**; new **Super Swachh League** of 23 cities.
[43:0:12] - Super Swachh League, 10 lakh+ group: **Indore, Surat, Navi Mumbai, Vijayawada (AP)**.
[43:0:13] - Ranked "cleanest big city" (10 lakh+) in 2024-25: **Ahmedabad**, then Bhopal, Lucknow.
[43:0:14] - Visakhapatnam: SafaiMitra Surakshit Shehar award (sanitation worker safety).
[43:0:15] - **Swachh Vayu Survekshan** (MoEFCC, under the **National Clean Air Programme**): ranks cities on clean-air actions; million-plus top city **Indore** (2023, announced by Bhupender Yadav; also 2025); **2026** (5th edition): **Lucknow** 1st, Indore 2nd, Jabalpur 3rd.
[43:0:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 (Swachh Bharat logo and slogan section); app notes 3:43 sub 2; pib.gov.in releases on Water+ (Aug 2021) and Swachh Vayu Survekshan as quoted in the app notes
## SUB 1 | Smart Cities Mission
[43:1:0] # Selection
[43:1:1] - Launched **25 June 2015** by MoHUA; **100 cities** – a holistic city rejuvenation programme via competitive challenge.
[43:1:2] - Two-stage; rounds: Round 1 (Jan 2016) 20, fast track 13, Round 2 27, **Round 3 (June 2017) 30** (incl. **Amaravati**), **Round 4 (Jan 2018) 9** + Shillong (June 2018) = 100.
[43:1:3] - City shares among States: **equal weight to urban population and number of statutory towns** (not districts).
[43:1:4] - **Uttar Pradesh: 10 smart cities** – Lucknow, Kanpur, Agra, Varanasi, Prayagraj, Aligarh, Jhansi, Moradabad, Bareilly, Saharanpur.
[43:1:5] - **Logo text**: "Smart City – **MISSION TRANSFORM-NATION**".
[43:1:6] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [43:1:6.0] Area-Based Development | Retrofitting/redevelopment of at least 50 acres
  [43:1:6.1] Pan-City | Tech solutions; Integrated Command and Control Centres
  [43:1:6.2] SPV | One per city; company under Companies Act, 2013; 50:50 equity of State/UT and ULB
  [43:1:6.3] CITIIS 2.0 (2023) | 18 smart cities; integrated waste management; partners AFD, KfW, EU, NIUA
[43:1:7] # Financing
[43:1:8] - Centre **Rs 48,000 crore** – **Rs 100 crore per city per year, about Rs 500 crore per city** over the mission – matched by State/ULB.
[43:1:9] - Other sources: ULB own funds, Finance Commission grants, municipal bonds, PPP, loans, convergence.
[43:1:10] - **Water and sewage financed through property tax**.
[43:1:11] - Progress (11 Jul 2025): Rs 47,459 crore (**99%**) of central share claimed; mission extended to **2025-26**.
[43:1:12] - **BRICS Smart Cities Conference**: **Jaipur, 17-19 August 2016** (MEA with ORF).
[43:1:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society - Group 2 Prelims 02 p.3 (Smart Cities aim); orfonline.org event report "BRICS Cities Require Smart Policy Solutions" (via web search); app notes 3:43 sub 4

  [43:2:0.7] 8 | AMRUT 2.0 / SBM-U 2.0 | 1 October 2021
  [43:2:0.8] 9 | PMAY-U 2.0 | 2024
[43:2:1] - Order asked in PYQ: **JNNURM → NUHHP → AMRUT → Jal Jeevan Mission**.
[43:2:2] TABLE head: Programme | Objective | Focus
  [43:2:2.0] AMRUT | Basic civic amenities – water supply, sewerage, drains, parks, non-motorised transport; renewing urban infrastructure | Urban
  [43:2:2.1] HRIDAY | Preserve heritage character of heritage cities – accessibility, safety, livelihood, cleanliness | Urban
  [43:2:2.2] Smart Cities Mission | Citizen-friendly, tech-enabled cities by retrofitting/redevelopment | Urban
  [43:2:2.3] SBM-Urban | ODF and scientific solid waste management | Urban
  [43:2:2.4] Rurban Mission (SPMRM, 2016) | Rural-urban clusters with urban amenities | Rural
  [43:2:2.5] DAY-NULM | Self-employment, skilling, shelters, street vendors among the urban poor | Urban
  [43:2:2.6] Rajiv Awas Yojana | Slum-free India | Urban
  [43:2:2.7] Atal Bhujal Yojana (ABY) | Groundwater recharge with community participation | Rural
  [43:2:2.8] UDAY | Discom finances – tariff rises, interest cut, coal rationalisation, loss reduction | Power
[43:2:3] - New urban infrastructure schemes: **Swachh Bharat Mission, HRIDAY, Smart City**; **Digital India is NOT** one.
[43:2:4] - Odd one out among urban rejuvenation missions = **Rurban Mission** (rural focus).
[43:2:5] - **AMRUT** – **Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation**.
[43:2:6] - **HRIDAY** – (National) **Heritage City Development and Augmentation Yojana**.
[43:2:7] - **SEHAT** – Social Endeavour for Health and Telemedicine.
[43:2:8] - **GHTC-India** – **Global Housing Technology Challenge**.

## SUB 3 | Urban Housing – PMAY-U, RAY, VAMBAY, GHTC-India
[43:3:0] TABLE head: PMAY-U (2015-2022) vertical | Type
  [43:3:0.0] ISSR – In-situ Slum Redevelopment (land as resource) | CSS
  [43:3:0.1] CLSS – Credit Linked Subsidy | Central Sector
  [43:3:0.2] AHP – Affordable Housing in Partnership | CSS
  [43:3:0.3] BLC – Beneficiary-Led individual house construction/enhancement – central assistance Rs 1.5 lakh per house | CSS
[43:3:1] - PMAY-U 2.0 (2024): **1 crore more** urban houses; verticals BLC, AHP, Affordable Rental Housing, Interest Subsidy Scheme; **ISSR not in 2.0**; 1.25 crore+ houses sanctioned under PMAY-U and 2.0.
[43:3:2] - **GHTC-India** (MoHUA, 2021): innovative, sustainable, eco-friendly, **disaster-resilient** construction technologies from across the globe; **Light House Projects** (foundation Jan 2021): Indore, Rajkot, Chennai, Ranchi, Agartala, Lucknow.
[43:3:3] - **Rajiv Awas Yojana (RAY)**: mission of **"Slum-free India / slum-free cities"** – not free houses or interest-free loans.
[43:3:4] - **Rajiv Rinn Yojana (RRY, 2013)**: interest subsidy for housing of **EWS and LIG in urban areas**.
[43:3:5] - **VAMBAY** (Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana, **Dec 2001**): housing for **urban slum dwellers below the poverty line without adequate shelter**; merged into JNNURM's **BSUP**; rural counterpart **Indira Awaas Yojana**.
[43:3:6] - **PMAY-NTR Nagar** (AP, 2017): **1.93 lakh** houses for the urban poor (built by L&T, Shapoorji Pallonji and others); **APTIDCO** is the State nodal agency for PMAY-U (TIDCO houses).
[43:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 18 p.6 (PMAY 2015-2022, four components, CLSS central sector); NextGen Society - Group 2 Prelims 02 p.3; deccanchronicle.com "1.93 lakh houses in urban areas across Andhra Pradesh" (via web search); app notes 3:43 sub 6
## SUB 4 | JNNURM and Earlier Urban Schemes
[43:4:0] - Announced in Budget 2005-06; launched **3 December 2005**; a **7-year** **urban renewal programme**.
[43:4:1] - Urban infrastructure and basic services in **63 mission cities** – mainly the **million-plus cities** (over 60), State capitals and heritage cities; succeeded by AMRUT and Smart Cities (2015).
[43:4:2] - Objectives: urban infrastructure (water supply, sewerage, solid waste, roads, **urban transport**, renewal of old city/**heritage areas**), houses and basic services for the poor; **urban electrification was NOT an objective**; not rural housing or employment.
[43:4:3] - Components: **UIG** (Urban Infrastructure and Governance) + **BSUP** (Basic Services to Urban Poor); smaller towns via **UIDSSMT** + **IHSDP** (Integrated Housing and Slum Development Programme).
[43:4:4] - Reforms: **25% of municipal budget** for the urban poor; **25% of developed land** for EWS/LIG; **7-point charter** – tenure, housing, water, sanitation, education, health, social security.
[43:4:5] - **ILCS** (Integrated Low Cost Sanitation), **1980-81**: end dry latrines and manual scavenging; funded on **sharing basis – Centre 75%, State 15%, beneficiary 10%**.
[43:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 18 p.6 (JNNURM BSUP, IHSDP, 25% budget, 7-point charter, 25% land); app notes 3:43 sub 1
## SUB 5 | AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0
[43:5:0] - Launched **25 June 2015**; revamps **urban infrastructure** (basic services) – initially **500 cities** (15 merged → 485) covering about **60% of urban population** (so "400 cities" is wrong).
[43:5:1] - Mission cities: all ULBs with **1 lakh+** population; other State/UT capitals; all **HRIDAY cities**; cities on stems of main rivers; hill-State, island and tourist cities. **Dausa was NOT** a Rajasthan mission city (till March 2024); Jaipur, Ajmer, Alwar, Tonk qualified.
[43:5:2] - Outlay: **Rs 1 lakh crore**, incl. Rs 50,000 crore central (2015-16 to 2019-20); delivered through **State Annual Action Plans**.
[43:5:3] - **Thrust areas**: **water supply**; **sewerage and septage**; **storm-water drains to reduce flooding**; **public / non-motorised urban transport**; **green spaces and parks with recreation centres for children**; capacity building. NOT: high-rise buildings, Wi-Fi, uninterrupted power, crop procurement.
[43:5:4] - **AMRUT 2.0** (1 Oct 2021 to 2025-26): **universal water supply in all statutory towns**; 100% sewerage/septage in the 500 AMRUT cities; Rs 2.79 lakh crore projects sanctioned.
[43:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society - Group 2 Prelims 02 p.3 (AMRUT civic amenities); app notes 3:43 sub 3
## SUB 6 | HRIDAY – Heritage Cities
[43:6:0] - **National Heritage City Development and Augmentation Yojana**, started **21 January 2015** by **MoHUA**: urban planning, economic development and heritage conservation.
[43:6:1] - **12 cities**: Ajmer, **Amaravati (AP)**, Amritsar, Badami, Dwarka, **Gaya**, Kanchipuram, Mathura, **Puri**, Varanasi, Velankanni, **Warangal**.
[43:6:2] > **Agra is NOT** among the 12 HRIDAY cities. Telugu-state HRIDAY cities = Amaravati and Warangal.
[43:6:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society - Group 2 Prelims 02 p.3; app notes 3:43 sub 5
## SUB 7 | Andhra Pradesh Angle
[43:7:0] - **Four Smart Cities**: **Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Tirupati, Amaravati** (not Guntur or Vijayawada); Amaravati came in Round 3 (30 cities, June 2017).
[43:7:1] - **Kakinada**: second most populous city of (old) East Godavari, near the 82.5°E IST meridian, a Smart City.
[43:7:2] - Apr 2026: Vizag, Kakinada and Tirupati reported progress under the extension; Vizag – integrated command centre + intelligent traffic system.
[43:7:3] - **Swachh Andhra** (2024-25): waste segregation **96.07%**; 6,890 TPD; 104 STPs (690.90 MLD). AP's **Black Spot Monitoring and Management App** tracks **garbage vulnerable points** and sanitation issues.
[43:7:4] - Urban funding (Jul 2026): ~**Rs 19,561 crore** mobilised (AMRUT 2.0, AIIB, Urban Challenge Fund, UIDF, SBM 2.0).
[43:7:5] - **Anna Canteens**: meals at **Rs 5** for the urban poor; reopened **Aug 2024**.
[43:7:6] - Urban-affairs MoU with **UN-Habitat** (not UNESCO), Jul 2026; parliamentary panel wants a High-Level Expert Committee on urban infrastructure to 2047.
[43:7:7] - **APTIDCO**: State nodal agency for PMAY-Urban (TIDCO houses).

=== NOTES 3:44 | Human Capital – Education and Health Expenditure; Nep 2020; Ayushman Bharat and Health Financing
## SUB 0 | Human Capital Formation – Meaning, Means and Indicators
[44:0:0] - **Human capital** = the **stock of skill and productive knowledge** (and health) embodied in people; population becomes human capital when there is investment in **education, training and medical care**.
[44:0:1] - **Human capital formation** = a process of **increasing the knowledge, skill levels and capacities** of the people – **intangible wealth** (UPSC 2018 key: "2 and 4"); it is not accumulation of tangible wealth or of more (physical) capital.
[44:0:2] - **Means:** investment in **education, health, on-the-job training, migration and information**. **Skill development** programmes enhance **human capital** (not physical, working or fixed capital). **Purchase of machinery** = physical capital; **irrigation** has no direct impact on human capital.
[44:0:3] - **Returns:** investment in human capital **yields returns in the future** because **education and health make people more productive** (UPPSC 2025 A-R: both true, R explains A). India's IT revolution shows human capital ranking above plant and machinery.
[44:0:4] - **Kerala:** low **infant mortality rate** because of **adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities** (APPSC 2025).
[44:0:5] - **Economic Survey 2025-26** (ch. 11): shift from **access to quality**, learning outcomes and **preventive care**; new concerns obesity and digital addiction.
[44:0:6] - Indicators cited: **MMR 88** per lakh live births; **stunting 29.3%**, wasting 19%.
[44:0:7] > Human capital = people (education, health, skills); physical capital = machines, buildings. Statement items test "intangible" and "process of raising knowledge and skills".
[44:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.2-3 (human capital, human capital formation, IT revolution, SSA, IMR); UPSC CSE 2018 official key; Economic Survey 2025-26 ch. 11; app notes 3:44 sub 0
## SUB 1 | School, Literacy and Higher Education Programmes
[44:1:0] TABLE head: Programme / law | Year | Fact
  [44:1:0.0] Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) | 2001 (2000-01) | Flagship for Universal Elementary Education, ages 6-14 – "universalising access to (elementary) education, education for all"
  [44:1:0.1] Education for All (UNESCO, Dakar Framework 2000) | target 2015 | Global EFA goals
  [44:1:0.2] Kalp Yojana (UP Government) | 1998 | Primary education
  [44:1:0.3] Saakshar Bharat | Sept 2009 | Restructured National Literacy Mission; adult literacy with focus on female literacy
  [44:1:0.4] RTE Act 2009 | in force 1 April 2010 | Free and compulsory elementary education, ages 6-14 (Art. 21A)
  [44:1:0.5] Unnat Bharat Abhiyan | 2014 (MHRD) | Connects higher education institutions with rural communities to solve development challenges
  [44:1:0.6] Jeevan Kaushal | 2019 (UGC) | Life-skills curriculum for higher education
  [44:1:0.7] National Testing Agency (NTA) | 2017 | Autonomous body to conduct entrance examinations for higher education institutions (JEE Main, NEET-UG, UGC-NET)
[44:1:1] - **Class X board exam made optional:** announced by HRD Minister **Kapil Sibal** (2009), with grading/CCE – optional from **2011** (the March 2010 batch still sat it). ⚠ Reversed: compulsory again from 2017-18; CBSE holds Class X boards **twice a year from 2026**.
[44:1:2] - **GER in higher education:** **18.8%** for **2010-11** (provisional AISHE, released by MHRD Sept 2012) – the "till now" answer of APPSC papers of that time. ⚠ Now **28.4%** (AISHE 2021-22, 18-23 age group); NEP 2020 target **50% by 2035**.
[44:1:3] - **Online credits:** students can earn credits through **MOOCs on SWAYAM** provided by the Ministry of Education (UGC credit framework) – A-R: both true, R explains A.
[44:1:4] - **GATE:** conducted jointly by **IISc Bengaluru** and **seven IITs** (Bombay, Delhi, Guwahati, Kanpur, Kharagpur, Madras, Roorkee).
[44:1:5] - **IGNOU** (1985): the **only national (central) open university**; called the **world's biggest university** by enrolment.
[44:1:6] - **First Yoga university:** **Bihar Yoga Bharati, Munger** (Bihar), 1994.
[44:1:7] - **Spending per student:** **Himachal Pradesh** spends far more per student than AP, UP or Bihar (Bihar lowest).
[44:1:8] > Traps: SSA = elementary (not secondary/higher); RTE = elementary 6-14; Saakshar Bharat = women's literacy; NTA (not "National Testing Service").

[44:1:10] - **Technical education:** a small share of public education spending (well under 10%); India Development Report 2004-05 figure for 1992-93 not verified.

## SUB 3 | NEP 2020 – Structure, Targets and Linked Schemes
[44:3:0] - Approved by the Union Cabinet on **29 July 2020**; drafting committee **K. Kasturirangan**.
[44:3:1] TABLE head: Stage | Ages | Classes
  [44:3:1.0] Foundational | 3-8 | 3 years pre-school / Balvatika + Classes 1-2
  [44:3:1.1] Preparatory | 8-11 | Classes 3-5
  [44:3:1.2] Middle | 11-14 | Classes 6-8
  [44:3:1.3] Secondary | 14-18 | Classes 9-12
[44:3:2] - New structure **5+3+3+4** (replaces 10+2); **vocational education from Grade 6**; GER **100% from pre-school to secondary by 2030**; higher-education GER 50% by 2035; public education spending **6% of GDP**.
[44:3:3] - **First State to initiate implementing NEP:** **Uttarakhand** – Balvatikas in 4,457 anganwadis, **12 July 2022**.
[44:3:4] TABLE head: Scheme | Purpose
  [44:3:4.0] Samagra Shiksha | Integrated school education, pre-school to Class 12
  [44:3:4.1] ULLAS | Adult literacy – New India Literacy Programme
  [44:3:4.2] DIKSHA | Digital e-content platform (NCERT)
  [44:3:4.3] NIPUN Bharat | Foundational literacy and numeracy
  [44:3:4.4] PM POSHAN | School meals, Balvatika to Class 8
  [44:3:4.5] PM-SHRI | Model schools
  [44:3:4.6] Vidya Pravesh | School readiness
  [44:3:4.7] PARAKH | Assessment (not school meals)
[44:3:5] - **Bharat Nirman** (2005, rural infrastructure) is **NOT** an NEP scheme (UPPSC 2025).
[44:3:6] - **Padhe Bharat:** **100-day** reading campaign (1 Jan 2022), joyful reading in mother tongue/local languages, in line with NEP.
[44:3:7] - **National Curriculum Frameworks** (by **NCERT**): Foundational Stage (**Oct 2022**); School Education (**2023**). The **Citizen Centric Survey** for the NCF was launched in **August 2022** (10 questions, 23 languages).
[44:3:8] > Ages: Foundational 3-8, Middle 11-14. ULLAS = adults, NIPUN = FLN, PARAKH = assessment.

## SUB 4 | Health Policy and Financing – NHP and National Health Accounts
[44:4:0] - **First National Health Policy:** **1983**. Later NHP **2002** and **NHP 2017**.
[44:4:1] - **NHP 2017:** public health spending **2.5% of GDP by 2025**; shift from curative to **preventive and primary care**; **universal health coverage** (not restricting services to tertiary hospitals).
[44:4:2] - **Seven priority areas** (NHP 2017, environment for health): **Swachh Bharat Abhiyan**, balanced healthy diets and exercise, tobacco/alcohol/substance abuse, **Yatri Suraksha**, **Nirbhaya Nari**, reduced stress and safety at the workplace, reducing indoor and outdoor air pollution. **Annapurna Scheme is NOT** among them.
[44:4:3] - **National Health Accounts 2019-20:** released **25 April 2023** by **Dr V.K. Paul, Member (Health), NITI Aayog** (prepared by NHSRC); OOPE share fell from **62.6% (2014-15) to 47.1% (2019-20)**; government health expenditure 1.35% of GDP.
[44:4:4] TABLE head: Indicator (176th Report, Standing Committee on Health) | Figure
  [44:4:4.0] Government health expenditure | 1.43% of GDP (target 2.5%)
  [44:4:4.1] Household OOPE | 43.4% of total health expenditure (2022-23)
  [44:4:4.2] Health share of government spending | 6.12% (2021-22) → 4.89% (2022-23)
  [44:4:4.3] Medicines | ~21% of current health expenditure
[44:4:5] - **Missing middle:** **40 crore+** Indians outside full subsidy cover who cannot afford private care.
[44:4:6] > Targets: health **2.5%** of GDP (NHP 2017) vs education **6%** (NEP 2020).
[44:4:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Sheets Indian Society p.9 (first NHP 1983); tribuneindia.com 26 Apr 2023 (NHA 2019-20, V.K. Paul); app notes 3:44 sub 1

## SUB 7 | Educational Thinkers, Philosophies and Teaching Methods
[44:7:0] TABLE head: Thinker / school | Contribution
  [44:7:0.0] Rousseau | Naturalism; learning by doing, heuristic discovery, observation – the project method (Kilpatrick, 1918) is not his
  [44:7:0.1] John Dewey | Pragmatism – "learning by doing"; father of the progressive education movement (Laboratory School, 1896)
  [44:7:0.2] A.S. Neill | Summerhill (1921) – keyed as the initiator of progressive schools
  [44:7:0.3] Froebel | Kindergarten – school as a play garden for primary learners ("gifts and occupations")
  [44:7:0.4] Maria Montessori | Didactic (self-correcting) apparatus
  [44:7:0.5] Ivan Illich | Deschooling ("Deschooling Society", 1971)
  [44:7:0.6] J. Krishnamurti | Founder of "The School" (KFI, Chennai); "a school is a sacred place where all are learning about the complexity of life and its simplicity"
  [44:7:0.7] Robert Glaser (1962) | Basic teaching model – 4 components: instructional objectives, entering behaviour, instructional procedures, performance assessment
  [44:7:0.8] Derek Unwin | Educational technology = "application of modern skills and techniques to the requirements of education and training"
[44:7:1] - **Methods:** **laboratory method** uses the **maximum senses**; **role play** best lets one **re-examine one's own and others' views, feelings and behaviour**; **learner-controlled instruction** = learner decides when, where, with what to study and when to be tested.
[44:7:2] - **Functions of education:** adjustment function = **social adjustment**.
[44:7:3] - **Guidance services:** **follow-up service** is on the weakest footing for vocational courses.
[44:7:4] - **Group dynamics** (Kurt Lewin) = **adjustment consequences in small groups**.
[44:7:5] - **Obstacles to educational change:** cultural lag, traditionalism, vested interests and lack of resources are usually listed as obstacles.
[44:7:6] - **Mobile schools** concept – printed key **McDonald** (not verified).
[44:7:7] > Most items come from the APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer paper (education and psychology portion).
[44:7:8] ~~ Sources: general education-theory knowledge, not checked (no NextGen/Rocket coverage); newworldencyclopedia.org (A.S. Neill, Summerhill 1921)
## SUB 8 | Educational Psychology – Intelligence, Needs, Learning, Development, Personality
[44:8:0] TABLE head: Theory / term | Given by / meaning
  [44:8:0.0] Two-factor theory of intelligence (g and s) | Charles Spearman
  [44:8:0.1] Hierarchical theory of intelligence | Cyril Burt and Philip Vernon
  [44:8:0.2] Multifactor theory | Thorndike – level (difficulty), range (number of tasks at a level), area, speed
  [44:8:0.3] Hierarchy of needs | Abraham Maslow – self-actualisation is the highest need
  [44:8:0.4] Word association test | Jung (1910, Clark University lectures)
  [44:8:0.5] Projective test | Unstructured stimuli – ink-blots (Rorschach), pictures (TAT)
  [44:8:0.6] Law of exercise (Thorndike) | Repetition forms habits and strengthens the S-R bond
  [44:8:0.7] Gestalt law of Prägnanz | Keyed as closure (strictly the master law of "good figure")
[44:8:1] - **Learning:** a response is strengthened through **reward** (reinforcement).
[44:8:2] - **Piaget:** **sensorimotor 0-2 years**; **conservation** appears at about **6 years** (concrete operational).
[44:8:3] - **Conflicts (Lewin):** two positive goals = **approach-approach**; two motives not in accord = **conflict**.
[44:8:4] - **Defence mechanism:** raising self-worth by identifying with illustrious persons or institutions = **identification**.
[44:8:5] - **Percept** = organisation of sensory experiences about an object; **giftedness** = early language, abstract thinking, strong memory, intellectual curiosity.
[44:8:6] - **Parten's play:** **parallel play** – each child plays alone but watches what others do.
[44:8:7] - **Statistics basics:** **tally marks** give the **class frequency**; separate vertical/horizontal rectangles = **bar graph** (a histogram has adjoining rectangles).
[44:8:8] ~~ Sources: general psychology knowledge, not checked (no NextGen/Rocket coverage)

  *1 only | 2 only | Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2
  x: Statement 1 is correct: human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge and health in people. Statement 2 is wrong: human capital is formed through investment in education, health, on-the-job training, migration and information. So '1 only'.

=== NOTES 3:45 | Indian Agriculture – Importance, Land Use Classification, Cropping Seasons and Cropping Pattern
## SUB 0 | Cropping Seasons – Kharif, Rabi and Zaid
[45:0:0] # Three crop seasons
[45:0:1] TABLE head: Season | Sowing | Harvest | Major crops
  [45:0:1.0] Kharif | June-July (SW monsoon onset) | Sep-Oct / Oct-Nov | Rice (paddy), maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, groundnut, soybean, jute, sugarcane, tur/arhar
  [45:0:1.1] Rabi | Oct-Dec (after monsoon) | March-April | Wheat (the most important rabi crop), barley, gram, mustard, peas, linseed, potato
  [45:0:1.2] Zaid | March-June (summer) | June-July | Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder
[45:0:2] - **Crop seasons:** Kharif, Rabi, Zaid-Kharif and Zaid-Rabi together denote the **crop seasons** of India; besides Rabi and Kharif the **third season is Zaid** ("Track", Barsati, Sharad, Jhum are not seasons).
[45:0:3] - **Rabi** depends on winter rain from **western disturbances** + irrigation; mustard is sown Oct-Nov and harvested Feb-Mar.
[45:0:4] - **Zaid:** short, irrigation-dependent summer window **between rabi and kharif**; products are mainly **vegetables and fruits** (watermelon). Sub-seasons: Zaid Kharif (Aug-Sep sowing), Zaid Rabi (Feb-Mar sowing).
[45:0:5] - **Sugarcane:** annual/long-duration crop, placed on the **Kharif** side in exam keys (barley, gram, wheat are Rabi).
[45:0:6] - **Jowar** is mainly a kharif crop (also some rabi jowar in the Deccan) – the usual "NOT a major rabi crop" answer against linseed, gram, wheat.
[45:0:7] - **Pulses:** **tur/arhar = kharif**; **gram/chana = rabi**. Millets mainly kharif.
[45:0:8] - **Kharif set (UPSC 2004):** cotton, groundnut, maize = kharif; mustard = rabi.
[45:0:9] - **Monsoon season:** the SW monsoon season runs from about **mid-June to mid-September** (kharif sowing window).
[45:0:10] # Crops grown in both seasons (AP)
[45:0:11] - AP: **paddy, maize, jowar, bajra and pulses** are grown in both kharif and rabi; AP 2024-25 paddy: 14.04 lakh ha kharif + 6.93 lakh ha rabi.
[45:0:12] > Match pattern: Rabi – wheat; Kharif – paddy; Zaid – watermelon; sunshine = a natural resource. Jute and cotton are Kharif, never Rabi.
[45:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 20 p.8 (Zaid Kharif / Zaid Rabi); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 05 p.1; app notes 3:45
## SUB 1 | Crop Classification – Food, Cash and Mixed Farming
[45:1:0] TABLE head: Group | Crops
  [45:1:0.0] Foodgrains = cereals + pulses | Rice, wheat, coarse cereals/millets (Shree Anna), pulses
  [45:1:0.1] Oilseeds | Groundnut, mustard, soybean, sunflower, sesame
  [45:1:0.2] Cash / commercial | Cotton, jute, sugarcane, tobacco, rubber, plantation crops, groundnut
[45:1:1] - **Cash crop:** grown for sale, not self-consumption – **cotton** (textiles), jute, groundnut, sugarcane, tobacco, rubber. **Jowar** is a food crop, not a cash crop; in the UPPSC key **soyabean** is also treated as "not a cash crop" (oilseed/pulse-type food crop).
[45:1:2] - Rice, maize, wheat = **food crops**.
[45:1:3] - AP traditional food crops: paddy, jowar, bajra, ragi, pulses; traditional commercial: **groundnut, cotton, tobacco, sugarcane**.
[45:1:4] - **Commercialisation of agriculture:** producing crops **for sale** (market) rather than for **own consumption**; shown when non-food crop area grows faster than food-crop area.
[45:1:5] - **Mixed farming:** **cultivation of crops together with rearing of animals** (milch cattle); raising several crops together is mixed/multiple cropping, not mixed farming.
[45:1:6] - **GM mustard** (DMH-11) was cleared by GEAC as safe (2017 recommendation; environmental release nod 2022, matter in the Supreme Court); **Bt cotton (2002)** is the only commercial GM crop; Bt brinjal under moratorium since 2010.
[45:1:7] ~~ Sources: G.C. Leong (src/geography/gc-leong-geography-18.2) p.2 (mixed farming); app notes 3:45
## SUB 2 | Operational Holdings – Agriculture Census
[45:2:0] # Definition and size classes
[45:2:1] - **Operational holding**: all land used for farm production and operated as **one technical unit** by one person, alone or with others, **regardless of title, size or location**.
[45:2:2] - Size of an operational holding = **owned land + leased-in land – leased-out land**.
[45:2:3] - Agriculture Census uses **five size classes**:
[45:2:4] TABLE head: Class | Size
  [45:2:4.0] Marginal | Below 1 ha
  [45:2:4.1] Small | 1-2 ha
  [45:2:4.2] Semi-medium | 2-4 ha
  [45:2:4.3] Medium | 4-10 ha
  [45:2:4.4] Large | 10 ha and above
[45:2:5] - "Small and marginal farmers" = holdings up to 2 ha.
[45:2:6] # All-India data
[45:2:7] TABLE head: Item | 2010-11 (9th) | 2015-16 (10th)
  [45:2:7.0] Small + marginal share of holdings | ~85% | 86.2%
  [45:2:7.1] Small + marginal share of area | ~44% | 47.3%
  [45:2:7.2] Women-operated holdings | 12.8% | 13.9%
  [45:2:7.3] Average holding | 1.15 ha | 1.08 ha
[45:2:8] - **2010-11 average holding:** all groups **1.15 ha**; **SCs 0.80 ha**; **STs 1.52 ha**.
[45:2:9] - 10th Census: **146 million** holdings; average down from **2.28 ha (1971)** → fragmentation. **Largest average holding: Nagaland** (2015-16).
[45:2:10] # Andhra Pradesh
[45:2:11] TABLE head: AP (residual State) | 2010-11 | 2015-16 | 2021-22 (prov.)
  [45:2:11.0] Holdings (lakh) | 76.21 | 85.24 | 96.90
  [45:2:11.1] Average holding | 1.06 ha (undivided AP: 1.08 ha) | 0.94 ha | 0.86 ha
[45:2:12] - Area operated by class (AP 2015-16): **marginal 29.18%, small 29.16%**, semi-medium 25.24%, medium 12.97%, large 3.45%; in 2010-11 the **small** class held the largest share of area; by 2021-22 marginal 32.29%.
[45:2:13] - 2021-22: largest average **Ananthapuram (1.62 ha)**; smallest **Visakhapatnam (0.40 ha)**.
[45:2:14] > Number vs area: small-marginal = ~86% of holdings but only ~47% of area.
[45:2:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 21 p.3 (definition, five classes); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.366 (Annexure 5.4); AP SES 2016-17 / 2018-19 via web search (1.06 ha, 76.21 lakh); app notes 3:45
## SUB 3 | Land Use – Terms, Nine-fold Classification and AP Data
[45:3:0] # Terms
[45:3:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [45:3:1.0] NSA (Net Sown Area) | Counts a plot once
  [45:3:1.1] GCA (Gross Cropped Area) | Counts a plot once per crop
  [45:3:1.2] Cropping intensity | GCA ÷ NSA × 100
[45:3:2] - "Area sown more than once" included = **GCA**, so GCA > NSA.
[45:3:3] # India, 2021-22
[45:3:4] TABLE head: Item | Figure
  [45:3:4.0] Geographical area | 328.7 Mha
  [45:3:4.1] Agricultural land | ~54.8%
  [45:3:4.2] Net sown area | 141 Mha (42.8%)
  [45:3:4.3] Gross cropped area | 219.16 Mha
  [45:3:4.4] Cropping intensity | 219.16 ÷ 141 × 100 ≈ 155.4%
  [45:3:4.5] Forest cover (ISFR 2021) | 21.71% of geographical area
[45:3:5] # Nine-fold classification
[45:3:6] - 1 Forests; 2 Area under non-agricultural uses; 3 Barren and unculturable land; 4 Permanent pastures and grazing land; 5 Land under miscellaneous tree crops; 6 Culturable waste land; 7 Current fallows; 8 Fallows other than current fallows; 9 Net sown area. **Net irrigated area is NOT** a category.
[45:3:7] - **Land use pattern** (deforestation, hill-slope cultivation) is a man-made factor behind landslides; steep slope is natural.
[45:3:8] # Andhra Pradesh land use
[45:3:9] TABLE head: AP item | Figure
  [45:3:9.0] Geographical area (present AP) | 162.97 lakh ha (undivided AP: 275.04 lakh ha)
  [45:3:9.1] Forests (land-use share) | 36.88 lakh ha = 22.63% (ISFR 2021 forest cover only 18.28%)
  [45:3:9.2] NSA 2016-17 | 60.77 lakh ha = 37.29%; 2015-16: 62.08 = 38.1% (ES 2016-17: ~38%)
  [45:3:9.3] NSA 2017-18 | 60.48 lakh ha = 37.1%
  [45:3:9.4] NSA undivided AP 2006-07 | ~37.2% of geographical area
  [45:3:9.5] NSA 2023-24 | 49.55 lakh ha = 30.40% (current fallows jumped to 24.29 lakh ha)
  [45:3:9.6] Cropping intensity | 1.25 (2016-17); 1.21 (2023-24)
[45:3:10] - Largest AP category = **NSA**, then **Forests**; smallest = miscellaneous tree crops (0.95%).
[45:3:11] - **Lateritic soils** occupy only about **1%** of AP (coastal patches – East Godavari, Kadapa, Nellore).
[45:3:12] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.6, p.49, p.53, p.331, p.358 (Annexure 5.1); NextGen AP Geography - APPSC 03 p.23 (laterite ~1%); app notes 3:45
## SUB 4 | Importance of Agriculture and Growth
[45:4:0] TABLE head: Indicator | Figure
  [45:4:0.0] Share in GVA | ~18% (ES 2025-26) – Ministry of Agriculture 2021: between 15% and 25% (~20%)
  [45:4:0.1] Employment | 46.1% of workforce (PLFS 2023-24); 54.6% in Census 2011
  [45:4:0.2] Growth | Average 4.4% (FY16-FY25); volatility of agricultural growth has declined
  [45:4:0.3] Agri exports | Record $51.91 billion = 11.86% of merchandise exports
  [45:4:0.4] Horticulture | ~One-third of agri GVA; 2024-25 output 367.72 MT passed foodgrains 357.73 MT
  [45:4:0.5] Foodgrains 2016-17 (3rd AE) | 273.38 million tonnes
[45:4:1] - Roles: GVA and employment, exports, **raw material** for industry, **food security**.
[45:4:2] - Output rose mainly through **improved methods and technology** (HYV seeds, irrigation, fertiliser – Green Revolution), not area expansion.
[45:4:3] - **Rain-fed farming:** sustainability depends most on the **frequency and adequacy of rainfall**.
[45:4:4] - After **1991**: **decline in public investment** in agriculture; **WTO AoA (1995)**: market access, domestic support, export subsidies.
[45:4:5] - **Agricultural Renewal Action Plan** (AP, Group-II 2017): soil health; irrigation/water augmentation and demand management; credit and insurance – **not "boosting capital formation"**.
[45:4:6] - 2009-10 (drought year): kharif area fell, but **rabi rice area was higher** than the previous year.
[45:4:7] > Contrast: GVA share ~18% vs employment 46.1% – Statement "agriculture still has a large employment share" true; "no decline in volatility" false.
[45:4:8] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 (app notes 3:45 sub 0); general knowledge (foodgrains 2016-17, 2009-10 rabi)
## SUB 5 | Cropping Pattern – India and Andhra Pradesh
[45:5:0] # India
[45:5:1] - Long-run shift: **food crops → commercial and high-value crops**.
[45:5:2] - **Factors of cropping pattern:** natural (soil, rainfall), historical, social, economic and **government policy** (MSP, procurement, subsidies).
[45:5:3] - **Rice: largest cropped area** in India (~51-52 Mha); pulses and oilseeds: stagnant yields.
[45:5:4] - Rice-wheat expansion (2015-2025): Punjab, Telangana, MP – assured **MSP procurement**; policy to shift **~20% of rice area to pulses** to cut urea use and save groundwater.
[45:5:5] - **Soyabean:** largest area **Madhya Pradesh** (5.35 Mha, 2009-10), then Maharashtra.
[45:5:6] # Andhra Pradesh
[45:5:7] - **Rice** = largest crop (about **one-third of GCA** in 2004-05); 2024-25: **paddy 20.97 of 37.51 lakh ha** of foodgrains.
[45:5:8] - **West Godavari** = largest area under food crops (rice bowl, Godavari delta).
[45:5:9] TABLE head: AP crop | Main region
  [45:5:9.0] Rice | Krishna-Godavari delta
  [45:5:9.1] Maize | Guntur (Godavari-Krishna belt)
  [45:5:9.2] Sorghum (jowar) | Kurnool
  [45:5:9.3] Groundnut | Anantapuramu
[45:5:10] - **Cotton = "white gold"** of AP, expanding; groundnut shrinking (11.36 → 3.46 lakh ha, 2011-12 → 2024-25); oilseeds 15.46 → 5.35 lakh ha.
[45:5:11] - Expanding: maize (poultry feed), horticulture, **oil palm (East Godavari, Eluru, West Godavari)**, aquaculture; shrinking: ragi, jowar.
[45:5:12] TABLE head: AP foodgrains area (lakh ha) | 2021-22 | 2023-24 | 2024-25 | 2025-26 (2nd AE)
  [45:5:12.0] Area | 41.44 | 33.24 | 37.51 | 42.74
[45:5:13] - 2024-25: pulses 11.66 lakh ha, maize 3.20 lakh ha; production 161.86 lakh t. 2025-26 (2nd AE): paddy 24.68 lakh ha.
[45:5:14] - **Kharif 2026** (El Niño): AP rainfall **51% below normal** (1 June-25 Aug); sown 20.35 vs 25.63 lakh ha; shift to pulses and drought-resilient crops (as of 2026).
[45:5:15] - AP problems: monsoon dependence (~50% NSA rainfed), holdings below 1 ha, soil-fertility loss.
[45:5:16] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.49-53; app notes 3:45 (AP 2025-26 data); general knowledge (district patterns)
## SUB 6 | Irrigated Area
[45:6:0] - India 2021-22: **net irrigated area 77.9 Mha**; **gross irrigated area 120.3 Mha**.
[45:6:1] TABLE head: Source of net irrigated area | Share
  [45:6:1.0] Tubewells | 47.3%
  [45:6:1.1] Canals | 24.7%
  [45:6:1.2] Other wells | 13.2%
  [45:6:1.3] Other sources | 12%
  [45:6:1.4] Tanks | 2.8%
[45:6:2] - **Wells (tubewells + other wells) irrigate the largest area** – about 60% of NIA.
[45:6:3] - **Largest irrigated area (absolute): Uttar Pradesh**.
[45:6:4] - Irrigation covers ~67% of rice area but only ~26% of pulses; ~51-52% of NSA is **rainfed**.
[45:6:5] - **AP:** gross irrigated area ≈ **52% of GCA** (AP Economy in Brief 2020); GIA 32.71 lakh ha, NIA 26.03 lakh ha (2023-24).
[45:6:6] - **Canals in the north:** Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed) and can feed canals all year; peninsular areas rely more on tanks.
[45:6:7] ~~ Sources: Land Use Statistics 2021-22 (app notes 3:45 sub 3); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.53
## SUB 7 | Agro-climatic Zones
[45:7:0] - **Agro-climatic zones:** regions delineated by climate, soil, topography and other factors that decide suitable cropping; soil formation itself depends on climate, altitude and bedrock – both statements true but unrelated.
[45:7:1] - **AP: six zones** (APSES 2024-25, on 13 pre-2022 districts); older material and 2017 Group-II key: seven; undivided AP: nine.
[45:7:2] TABLE head: Zone (pre-2022) | Districts
  [45:7:2.0] North Coastal | Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam
  [45:7:2.1] Godavari ("Rice Bowl") | East and West Godavari
  [45:7:2.2] Krishna | Krishna, Guntur, Prakasam
  [45:7:2.3] Southern | Chittoor, YSR Kadapa, SPS Nellore
  [45:7:2.4] Scarce Rainfall | Kurnool, Anantapuramu
  [45:7:2.5] High Altitude and Tribal | Agency areas
  [45:7:2.6] All-India body | Zones
  [45:7:2.7] Planning Commission (1989) | 15 regions, 72 sub-zones
  [45:7:2.8] ICAR – NARP | 127 zones
[45:7:3] - AP coastal districts → East Coast Plains and Hills; Rayalaseema → Southern Plateau and Hills.
[45:7:4] - AP has **22 soil categories**; **10** of them cover over **88%** of the State.
[45:7:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:45 sub 9 (APSES 2024-25)

=== NOTES 3:46 | Irrigation – Sources, Projects, Groundwater, Micro-irrigation, Pmksy and Watershed Development
## SUB 0 | Sources of Irrigation – India and States
[46:0:0] TABLE head: Source of net irrigated area (India, 2021-22) | Share
  [46:0:0.0] Tubewells | 47.3% (2022-23: 49.34%)
  [46:0:0.1] Canals | 24.7% (2022-23: 22.85%)
  [46:0:0.2] Other wells | 13.2%
  [46:0:0.3] Other sources | 12%
  [46:0:0.4] Tanks | 2.8%
[46:0:1] - **Dominant source = wells/tubewells (groundwater)**, not canals; groundwater meets about **64%** of irrigation needs; India ≈ **25% of global extraction** and has the **largest groundwater-irrigated area in the world**.
[46:0:2] - **Uttar Pradesh**: largest **tubewell-irrigated area** and largest irrigated area overall.
[46:0:3] TABLE head: State | Irrigation fact
  [46:0:3.0] Punjab | Highest percentage of cropped area irrigated (~98%)
  [46:0:3.1] Haryana | Highest % among Haryana, UP, MP, Maharashtra (2011: 83.9%)
  [46:0:3.2] UP, Haryana, Rajasthan, AP | Four States with the largest canal-irrigated area
[46:0:4] - **Canals in North India:** fed by **perennial (snow-fed) rivers** – Ganga, Sutlej, Beas – so they flow all year.
[46:0:5] - **Tanks** matter in **AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu** – undulating **hard-rock**, impervious terrain with poor groundwater, where wells fail; hence tank and well maps are **negatively related**.
[46:0:6] - **Bamboo drip irrigation:** 200-year-old tribal system of **Meghalaya (North-East India)**.
[46:0:7] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 10 p.1 (bamboo drip); Land Use Statistics 2021-22 and 2022-23 (app notes 3:46 sub 0); general knowledge (State ranks)
## SUB 1 | Canals and Projects – State and Source
[46:1:0] TABLE head: Canal / project | State | Fact
  [46:1:0.0] Indira Gandhi Canal | Rajasthan | Longest canal of India (~650 km); from Harike Barrage (Sutlej-Beas), not Ghaggar; turned part of the Thar Desert into irrigated land
  [46:1:0.1] Sirhind Canal | Punjab | Sutlej at Ropar
  [46:1:0.2] Upper Ganga Canal | Uttar Pradesh | Ganga at Haridwar
  [46:1:0.3] Nagarjuna Sagar | AP/Telangana | Krishna: Right = Jawahar Canal, Left = Lal Bahadur Shastri Canal
  [46:1:0.4] Tawa Project | Madhya Pradesh | Tawa (Narmada tributary), Narmadapuram
  [46:1:0.5] Kalpasar | Gujarat | Proposed freshwater reservoir across the Gulf of Khambhat
  [46:1:0.6] Kelo | Chhattisgarh | Among the 99 AIBP priority projects under PMKSY
  [46:1:0.7] Parwan | Rajasthan | Multipurpose project
  [46:1:0.8] Renukaji Dam | Himachal Pradesh | National project on the Giri (Yamuna basin)
  [46:1:0.9] Lakhwar | Uttarakhand | Multipurpose project on the Yamuna
  [46:1:0.10] Ken-Betwa link | MP and UP | First river-link project
[46:1:1] - Other facts in the same UPSC 2000 item: Narmada rises at Amarkantak; Nizam Sagar is on the Manjira; Penganga joins the Godavari system.
[46:1:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 02 p.48 (Indira Gandhi Canal command); Rocket Indian Geography p.97 (Kelo); PMF Lens 2026-05-09 p.6 (Kalpasar); general knowledge (project locations)
## SUB 2 | PMKSY and Watershed Development
[46:2:0] # PMKSY
[46:2:1] - Launched **1 July 2015**; umbrella irrigation scheme; motto: **"Har Khet Ko Pani"** and **"More crop per drop"** – raise **water-use efficiency**.
[46:2:2] - Components: **AIBP**, **Har Khet Ko Pani** (assured irrigation; CAD and water management), **Per Drop More Crop** (micro-irrigation; now under PM-RKVY), **Watershed Development**. **National Water Grid is NOT** a component.
[46:2:3] - Objectives: **convergence of investment** in irrigation at field level, **expand cultivable area under irrigation**, **improve on-farm water-use efficiency**; works: renovate water bodies, rainwater-harvesting structures, **recharge of aquifers**. **Not** an objective: protecting farmers against crop failure (that is crop insurance – PMFBY); "construction of wells" is the item keyed as incorrect.
[46:2:4] - **PMKSY planning:** District Irrigation Plans → State Irrigation Plans; **State Level Sanctioning Committee chaired by the Chief Secretary**.
[46:2:5] - **Micro Irrigation Fund**: corpus **Rs 5,000 crore** with **NABARD**.
[46:2:6] # Watershed
[46:2:7] - **Hariyali** (launched January 2003; guidelines from **1 April 2003**): watershed / rainwater-harvesting scheme = **water management**.
[46:2:8] - Hariyali, **IWDP** (Integrated Wasteland Development Programme, 1989-90 nationally; 100% central assistance) and NWDPRA merged into **IWMP** (2008); IWMP subsumed in PMKSY as **WDC-PMKSY** (2015); funding **90:10 → 60:40**; **WDC 2.0** adds springsheds.
[46:2:9] - **Neeranchal National Watershed Project**: **World Bank**; **nine States incl. AP and Telangana**.
[46:2:10] - **Watershed Development Fund:** NABARD, 1999-2000, corpus Rs 200 crore.
[46:2:11] - **Tarun Bharat Sangh**: **Rajasthan** NGO of **Dr Rajendra Singh** ("Waterman", johads).
[46:2:12] - **Four Waters Concept** (T. Hanumantha Rao): **rain water, surface water, ground water and soil moisture** – "river water" is not one of the four.
[46:2:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 07 p.51 (Har Khet Ko Pani, Per Drop More Crop); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.128; app notes 3:46 sub 3; general knowledge (IWDP, four waters)
## SUB 3 | Groundwater – CGWB, Aquifers and Atal Bhujal
[46:3:0] - **Aquifers:** clay holds water but its pores are tiny and poorly connected → **poor aquifer**; sand and gravel are good aquifers.
[46:3:1] - **CGWA** was constituted under **Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**.
[46:3:2] - CGWB categories (stage of extraction): **Safe, Semi-critical, Critical, Over-exploited**, + Saline.
[46:3:3] - India stage: **60.63% (2025)**; high utilisation in **Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu**, Delhi; low in high-rainfall Odisha.
[46:3:4] - **Uttar Pradesh** has the largest **replenishable groundwater** resource (Ganga alluvium).
[46:3:5] - **GRACE** satellite studies: severe depletion in **north-west India** – Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and **Delhi** (epicentre named in the APPSC 2019 key).
[46:3:6] - **Atal Bhujal Yojana**: **December 2019**; **World Bank**-aided **Central Sector**; **Ministry of Jal Shakti**; 7 States – Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, UP; **AP NOT included**; **demand-side** community management via GP Water Security Plans.
[46:3:7] - **Piezometers** (digital water-level recorders with telemetry) give real-time groundwater levels (AP: 1,810 piezometers).
[46:3:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 07 p.54 (CGWB mandate); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.132 (piezometers); app notes 3:46 sub 4
## SUB 4 | PM-KUSUM and Micro-irrigation
[46:4:0] - **KUSUM = Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan** (2019, **MNRE**).
[46:4:1] TABLE head: PM-KUSUM | Content
  [46:4:1.0] A | 10,000 MW decentralised grid-connected solar plants (0.5-2 MW)
  [46:4:1.1] B | 14 lakh standalone solar pumps (up to 7.5 HP)
  [46:4:1.2] C | Solarisation of grid-connected pumps, incl. feeder-level
[46:4:2] - Objective: **remove farmers' dependence on diesel and kerosene** – an **agricultural solar pump** scheme; concern: may encourage **over-drawing of groundwater**.
[46:4:3] - **Drip irrigation:** water straight to the root zone; fertiliser through the same lines (fertigation).
[46:4:4] - **APMIP** (since **2003**): AP ranks **1st** in micro-irrigation; **Rayalaseema 64%** of area; AP has **converged MGNREGA with the AP Micro Irrigation Project**.
[46:4:5] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary 02 p.19 (PM-KUSUM); app notes 3:46 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Andhra Pradesh – Irrigation, Groundwater and APWALTA
[46:5:0] TABLE head: Project | River | Facts
  [46:5:0.0] Polavaram | Godavari | National Project (APRA 2014); 960 MW; diverts 80 TMC to Krishna; Left Main Canal → East Godavari and Visakhapatnam (Yeleru, Vizag water); 89% complete; dedication by March 2027
  [46:5:0.1] Galeru-Nagari | Krishna | 38 TMC; 2.60 lakh acres
  [46:5:0.2] Veligonda (Poola Subbaiah) | Krishna | 43.5 TMC; 4.47 lakh acres
[46:5:1] - AP 2024-25: GIA 36.77 lakh ha; groundwater **41% of GIA** (~19 lakh borewells).
[46:5:2] TABLE head: AP net irrigated area by source (lakh ha) | Canals | Tanks | Wells | Total
  [46:5:2.0] 2016-17 | 12.25 | 2.36 | 11.62 | 27.19
  [46:5:2.1] 2023-24 | 10.08 | 2.55 | 12.42 | 26.03
[46:5:3] - After bifurcation **groundwater (wells)** has become the major source, overtaking canals.
[46:5:4] - **38,862 tanks**; groundwater stage **31.5% (Safe)**; **12 of 679** mandals over-exploited; **Anantapur** district has had the most over-exploited mandals.
[46:5:5] - **APWALTA 2002** (AP Water, Land and Trees Act): against indiscriminate **borewell** digging; controls groundwater; promotes tree planting; **rainwater harvesting compulsory on plots of 200 sq m and above**; drinking-water norm in the exam key: one tube well per **250 population** (not verified in the library); over-exploited villages notified (300 villages, GEC 2023-24).
[46:5:6] - **HNSS:** lift canal taking Krishna flood water from **Srisailam** to Rayalaseema; **Neeru-Chettu** (2015): drought-free AP via tank desilting.
[46:5:7] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.127, p.132-134, p.381 (Annexure 5.14); Rocket AP Geography p.36 (Polavaram Left Main Canal); app notes 3:46 sub 5, 7
## SUB 6 | Project Classes and AIBP
[46:6:0] TABLE head: Class | Culturable Command Area (CCA)
  [46:6:0.0] Minor | Up to 2,000 ha
  [46:6:0.1] Medium | 2,000-10,000 ha
  [46:6:0.2] Major | Above 10,000 ha
[46:6:1] - **Minor irrigation**: about **65%** of irrigated area; the **maximum irrigation potential** is created through **minor projects** (groundwater + small surface works).
[46:6:2] - **AIBP**: speeds up **ongoing major and medium** projects; **99** prioritised projects through **NABARD's LTIF** since 2016 (**8 in AP**).
[46:6:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:46 sub 1

=== NOTES 3:47 | Water Resources and River-linking; Water Use Efficiency and Command Area Development
## SUB 0 | Water Resources, Water Stress and State Firsts
[47:0:0] TABLE head: Per capita water per year | Status
  [47:0:0.0] Below 1,700 m³ | Water-stressed
  [47:0:0.1] Below 1,000 m³ | Water-scarce
[47:0:1] - India has about **4% of the world's water resources** (and ~18% of its population); already **below 1,700 m³** (water-stressed).
[47:0:2] - **Cauvery** is the most exploited (most fully utilised) river in terms of abstraction of available water.
[47:0:3] - **Water** is the **universal solvent** (it dissolves more substances than any other liquid).
[47:0:4] - **Meghalaya**: first State to approve a **draft State Water Policy** (2019).
[47:0:5] - **Tamil Nadu**: first to make **rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory** for all buildings; AP's APWALTA 2002 covers plots 200 sq m+.
[47:0:6] - Water = **Entry 17, State List**; inter-State rivers = **Entry 56, Union List**.
[47:0:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:47 sub 0; general knowledge (4% share, Cauvery, universal solvent)

## SUB 2 | Water-use Efficiency and Conservation
[47:2:0] TABLE head: Method | Efficiency
  [47:2:0.0] Drip | ~90% (highest)
  [47:2:0.1] Sprinkler | ~70-80%
  [47:2:0.2] Flood/basin/canal surface | 30-50% (lowest)
[47:2:1] - **PMKSY** aims at enhancing **water-use efficiency** ("More crop per drop"), not organic, hybrid or GM seeds.
[47:2:2] - **Micro-irrigation**: water straight to the root zone; cuts evaporation and runoff. **DSR** and **SRI**: save up to 50% water.
[47:2:3] - **Zero / minimum tillage**: lower evaporation, better soil moisture. **Crop-residue mulch** keeps soil moisture.
[47:2:4] - **Conservation Agriculture** (FAO): minimum soil disturbance, **permanent soil cover (at least 30%)**, crop diversification.
[47:2:5] - **Bench terracing**: most widely adopted mechanical soil and water conservation measure on **hill slopes**.
[47:2:6] - **Virtual water** (Tony Allan): water **consumed in producing a product**; exporting rice exports virtual water.
[47:2:7] - **Flow duration curve:** plots discharge against the **percentage of time it is equalled or exceeded**.
[47:2:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:47 sub 1; general knowledge (bench terracing, flow duration curve)
## SUB 3 | National River Linking Project
[47:3:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [47:3:0.0] National Perspective Plan | 1980
  [47:3:0.1] NWDA | Set up July 1982 as a society (not 1970, 1980 or 1992); carries out NPP
  [47:3:0.2] Links | 16 Peninsular + 14 Himalayan = 30
  [47:3:0.3] Progress | PFRs all 30; FRs 26; DPRs 14
[47:3:1] - **Arthur Cotton**: first proposed (19th century); **K.L. Rao**: Ganga-Cauvery link; **Suresh Prabhu**: 2002 Task Force.
[47:3:2] - **Ken-Betwa**: **first NPP link implemented**; MP-UP; MoA March 2021; **Daudhan Dam inside Panna Tiger Reserve**.
[47:3:3] TABLE head: Godavari-Cauvery link | From | To
  [47:3:3.0] Godavari-Krishna | Inchampalli | Nagarjunasagar
  [47:3:3.1] Krishna-Pennar | Nagarjunasagar | Somasila
  [47:3:3.2] Pennar-Cauvery | Somasila | Grand Anicut
[47:3:4] - **AP drought-proofing:** **Godavari** surplus water is moved to the Krishna basin – **Pattiseema lift** (Polavaram → Prakasam barrage) and Polavaram's 80 TMC diversion feeding **HNSS and GNSS**.
[47:3:5] - Criticism: "surplus" basins unreliable under **climate change**; displacement; ecological loss.
[47:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.67 (NWDA 1982); Praveen CA360 2026-04 magazine p.27 (NWDA 1982); app notes 3:47 sub 4

=== NOTES 3:48 | Agricultural Inputs – Seeds, Fertilisers and Subsidy Regime, Pesticides, Mechanisation, Extension Services
## SUB 0 | Fertilisers – Urea, NBS, Neem Coating, Nano and DBT
[48:0:0] # Urea and the subsidy regime
[48:0:1] - **Urea:** white, highly water-soluble, **46% nitrogen** (closest exam option: 47%); loses N quickly by **volatilisation and leaching**, hence slow-release forms (**urea briquettes**, neem coating).
[48:0:2] - **Urea = most subsidised fertiliser**; stays under **statutory price control** (fixed MRP); **not** covered by NBS. Budget 2026-27: urea subsidy Rs 1,16,805 crore vs NBS Rs 54,000 crore.
[48:0:3] - **Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS), 2010:** the policy now followed for **P&K fertilisers** – a **fixed per-kg subsidy on N, P, K and S**, announced yearly; covers **22 grades** of decontrolled P&K; **manufacturers set the MRPs**.
[48:0:4] - Fertiliser subsidy = **second largest subsidy after food**; Budget 2026-27 **Rs 1.71 lakh crore** (RE 2025-26: Rs 1.86 lakh crore).
[48:0:5] - India: **2nd largest consumer, 3rd largest producer** of fertilisers. National Investment Policy for Urea-2026 adds **10 MT** urea capacity.
[48:0:6] TABLE head: Reform | Year | Provision
  [48:0:6.0] NBS | 2010 | Fixed per-nutrient subsidy on P&K (and S)
  [48:0:6.1] Neem-coated urea | Notified May 2015; all domestic urea from 1 Sep 2015, imported from 1 Dec 2015 | Neem coating slows the release/dissolution of urea (nitrogen) in soil and stops diversion of farm urea to industry
  [48:0:6.2] DBT in fertilisers | Pilot from October 2016 | Subsidy paid to fertiliser companies after sale at PoS devices (Aadhaar-linked), not to farmers
  [48:0:6.3] PM-PRANAM | Approved 28 June 2023 | States keep 50% of the subsidy saved by cutting chemical fertiliser use
  [48:0:6.4] Nano DAP (liquid) | Launched by Amit Shah, April 2023 | IFFCO; 8% N, 16% P
[48:0:7] - **IFFCO Nano Urea:** one **500 ml bottle = one 45 kg bag**; foliar spray.
[48:0:8] # Balance and efficiency
[48:0:9] - **N:P:K = 10.9 : 4.1 : 1 (2023-24)** vs ideal **4:2:1** – the urea-centred subsidy **distorts the NPK ratio**.
[48:0:10] - **Balanced fertiliser use** = nutrients in the right proportion as per soil test → **corrects all deficiencies** (not just "adds NPK").
[48:0:11] - **Efficient fertiliser use** = **more crop per kg of fertiliser**; the grain response per kg NPK fell from 13.4 kg (1970) to 3.7 kg (2005).
[48:0:12] - **Indiscriminate use of urea** is the main human disturbance of the **nitrogen cycle** (nitrate leaching, N2O emission).
[48:0:13] # Fertiliser types and use by State
[48:0:14] - Nitrogenous: **ammonium sulphate**, ammonium nitrate, **urea**; phosphatic: **ammonium phosphate (DAP/MAP)**, superphosphate.
[48:0:15] - **Largest consumer by quantity: Uttar Pradesh**; in 2009 the top two were **UP and (undivided) Andhra Pradesh**; Punjab is high per hectare.
[48:0:16] ~~ Sources: Union Budget 2026-27 at a Glance p.20; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 04 p.177; PMF Environment 07 p.2-3, p.13-14; app notes 3:48 sub 2

## SUB 2 | Seeds – Seed Village, SRR, GM Crops and Seed Systems
[48:2:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [48:2:0.0] Seed Replacement Rate | % of a crop's area sown with certified/quality seed (not farm-saved seed)
  [48:2:0.1] Varietal Replacement Rate | % of area under varieties released in the last 3-5 years
  [48:2:0.2] Seed Village | Farmers given foundation seed and trained in quality seed production → produce certified seed locally and make it available to others at the right time and affordable cost
[48:2:1] - **Seed Village Programme:** ensures timely supply of quality certified seed of notified varieties at farmers' places at affordable prices and quick multiplication of new varieties in the mandal/district; **6.85 lakh seed villages** under the Sub-Mission on Seeds and Planting Materials (ES 2025-26).
[48:2:2] - **SRR constraint (UPSC 2014):** a **demand-supply gap in quality seed of low-value, high-volume crops**; India **has** a National Seed Policy (2002) and private firms **do** supply vegetable/horticulture seed.
[48:2:3] - Seed accounts for **20-25%** of productivity; problems: high cost of hybrids for small farmers, shortage of quality seed, unresolved GM seed issues.
[48:2:4] - **SATHI portal** (Seed Traceability, Authentication and Holistic Inventory): **Phase 1 launched 19 April 2023 by Narendra Singh Tomar** (Union Agriculture Minister).
[48:2:5] - **Indian Seed Congress 2017** (Kolkata) theme: **"Seed of Joy"**.
[48:2:6] - ICAR **2019-21: 562** new HYVs; **3,236 HYVs since 2014**; Jan 2026: **184 varieties of 25 crops**.
[48:2:7] - **Genome-edited rice (May 2025):** **DRR Dhan 100 Kamala** (from **Samba Mahsuri**) + **Pusa DST Rice 1** (from **MTU 1010**); SDN-1 edits **carry no foreign DNA** → outside GMO rules.
[48:2:8] TABLE head: Act / body | Provision
  [48:2:8.0] Seeds Act 1966 | Quality of notified seeds
  [48:2:8.1] PPV&FR Act 2001 | Farmers may save, use, exchange and sell farm-saved seed only unbranded
  [48:2:8.2] GEAC | Approves GM crops; Rules 1989 under EPA 1986; MoEFCC; cleared GM mustard DMH-11 in 2022
[48:2:9] - **GM crops with built-in toxins (Bt):** risk of pest resistance and of **encouraging more use of agricultural chemicals**; **Bt cotton** is GM, not a green manure.
[48:2:10] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary 01 p.51 (seed villages); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.176; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.56 (Seed Village Programme); app notes 3:48 sub 4; general knowledge (SATHI, Seed Congress theme)

## SUB 4 | Soil Health Card, Manures and Organic Farming
[48:4:0] - **Soil Health Card Scheme:** launched **19 February 2015, Suratgarh (Rajasthan)**; part of NMSA (Soil Health Management); card shows nutrient status and fertiliser advice.
[48:4:1] - **Interval:** the 2015 scheme said a card **once in every 3 years** (AEE 2016 key); in practice cards are now issued **free every two years** (cycles 2015-17, 2017-19).
[48:4:2] - Impact: fertiliser use cut **8-10%**; over **25 crore** cards issued.
[48:4:3] - **Glyricidia = green leaf manure**; green manure crops: **sunn hemp, dhaincha, green gram** (Bt cotton is GM, not a green manure). **Vermicompost:** earthworms turn organic waste into manure.
[48:4:4] - **Organic farming = eco-friendly:** compost, green manure, bone meal; crop rotation, companion planting (HYV cultivation, glass houses and shifting cultivation are not).
[48:4:5] TABLE head: Scheme | Year | Feature
  [48:4:5.0] NPOP | 2001 | Commerce Ministry / APEDA certification
  [48:4:5.1] PKVY | 2015 | Cluster of 50 farmers / 50 acres; certified by PGS-India or NPOP
  [48:4:5.2] National Mission on Natural Farming | Nov 2024 | Stand-alone mission
  [48:4:5.3] NMSA | – | Merged into PM-RKVY from 2022-23; agroforestry "Har Medh Par Ped"
[48:4:6] - **Zero Budget Natural Farming:** **Subhash Palekar**.
[48:4:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.125 (SHC every two years, 8-10% cut); web: PIB factsheet PDF Aug 2025 static.pib.gov.in doc2025816613501 (both "once every 3 years" and "every two years"); app notes 3:48 sub 3, sub 6
[48:4:8] - **Soil Health Cards in AP:** about 22.24 lakh cards issued by mid-2016 (cycle I); 2017-18 target 21 lakh.
## SUB 5 | Mechanisation and Pesticides
[48:5:0] - Private investment in agriculture goes mostly to **labour-saving mechanisation** – a response to **rising wages and a tighter labour market** (migration, non-farm jobs).
[48:5:1] - Mechanisation level: India **40-45%** (below 50% vs >90% in developed countries).
[48:5:2] - **Zero Till Seed-cum-Fertiliser Drill:** developed at **G.B. Pant University of Agriculture and Technology, Pantnagar**.
[48:5:3] - **Cage wheel:** fitted to tractors/power tillers for puddling in **wetland (paddy)** fields.
[48:5:4] - **SMAM** (Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation): subsidises machines, **custom hiring centres**, farm machinery banks; 25,689 CHCs (2014-15 to 2025-26).
[48:5:5] - **Namo Drone Didi:** drones to **women SHGs**; **Rs 1,261 crore** (2023-24 to 2025-26); target **15,000** drones; **80%** central assistance up to Rs 8 lakh.
[48:5:6] # Pesticides
[48:5:7] - **Chemical pesticides:** advantage = **high efficacy**, quick action; drawbacks = residues, harm to friendly insects, resistance.
[48:5:8] - **Biological control** (natural enemies, bio-pesticides such as **neem-based** products): **low cost**, eco-friendly.
[48:5:9] - **IPM:** biological, cultural and need-based chemical control.
[48:5:10] TABLE head: Law / event | Provision
  [48:5:10.0] Insecticides Act 1968 + Rules 1971 | Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee
  [48:5:10.1] Draft Pesticides Management Bill 2025 | Replaces the 1968 Act
  [48:5:10.2] Endosulfan | Banned by Supreme Court, 2011
  [48:5:10.3] Aldrin (banned) | Killed mugger crocodiles in Kota
[48:5:11] - India still uses at least **66** pesticides banned elsewhere.
[48:5:12] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.175-176 (mechanisation), p.178 (pesticides, IPM); Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary 01 p.51 (CHCs); app notes 3:48 sub 5, sub 8; general knowledge (zero-till drill, cage wheel)

## SUB 7 | Andhra Pradesh – Inputs and Extension
[48:7:0] - **Tenant farmers' cards:** **Loan Eligibility Cards / Certificates of Cultivation (COC)** earlier; now **Crop Cultivator Rights Cards (CCRCs)** under the **AP Crop Cultivators Rights Act 2019** (11-month agreement; **9,13,283** CCRCs by 3 Jan 2025) – give access to bank credit, insurance, input subsidy.
[48:7:1] - **D-Krishi:** Aadhaar-enabled **seed** distribution system of AP.
[48:7:2] - **ATMA in AP:** all **26 districts**, **60:40** funding; disseminates latest technologies and fills adoption gaps through **bottom-up planning (SREP)**.
[48:7:3] - **APCNF:** run by **Rythu Sadhikara Samstha (RySS)**; **jeevamrutham, ghanajeevamrutham**; **10.20 lakh farmers** (2025-26); **Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity 2024**.
[48:7:4] - **Rythu Seva Kendras** (formerly Rythu Bharosa Kendras): village one-stop centres for inputs, soil testing, e-Panta, CCRCs, insurance; **8,489** functional after rationalisation; buildings under **MGNREGS**.
[48:7:5] - Fertiliser consumption **39.39 LMT** (2024-25); 2015-16 actual use **80.78%** of allotment; pesticide use **2,650 MT → 1,716 MT** (2014-15 → 2024-25).
[48:7:6] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.8, p.55-58; app notes 3:48 sub 12; general knowledge (COC cards, D-Krishi)
