=== NOTES 3:49 | Green Revolution – Components, Achievements and Criticism; White, Yellow, Blue and Rainbow Revolutions
## SUB 0 | Green Revolution – Meaning, Package and Nature
[49:0:0] - **Green Revolution** = large rise in foodgrain output (mainly **wheat and rice**) through **High Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds** – **increasing output through HYVs**, not "making land green" or forest canopy.
[49:0:1] - **Scientific core / focus: HYV seeds**; nature = **Seed-Fertiliser-Water technology** (a package; HYVs are only its core) – the best description of the late-1960s Green Revolution (BPSC 2018).
[49:0:2] - HYVs need **assured irrigation**, so the benefits stayed confined to **areas with irrigation facilities** (Punjab, Haryana, western UP).
[49:0:3] TABLE head: Component | Note
  [49:0:3.0] HYV seeds | Dwarf varieties; the core
  [49:0:3.1] Chemical fertilisers | Urea (N), phosphate (P), potash (K)
  [49:0:3.2] Irrigation | Controlled water supply
  [49:0:3.3] Pesticides, herbicides | New seeds not acclimatised to local pests
  [49:0:3.4] Mechanisation | Pump sets, tractors
  [49:0:3.5] Credit, storage, marketing, MSP | Supporting – credit is not one of the "most important" components (HYV, fertiliser, irrigation)
[49:0:4] - **Not** part of it: **traditional seed varieties**, **crossbreeding of indigenous cows with European breeds** (that is the White Revolution), expansion of forests, three crop seasons.
[49:0:5] - **HYV traits:** **short stature (dwarf)** resists lodging; **quicker maturity** allows **double cropping**.
[49:0:6] - **Pioneer State: Punjab** – "**Granary of India**"; first crop transformed: **wheat**.
[49:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 20 p.5-6; NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 03 p.32; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.152-153; NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 04 p.25
## SUB 1 | Persons – Borlaug, Swaminathan, Subramaniam
[49:1:0] TABLE head: Person | Contribution
  [49:1:0.0] Norman E. Borlaug | Father of the Green Revolution in the world; American (USA) agronomist; Mexican dwarf wheats (CIMMYT, Mexico); Nobel Peace Prize 1970; "the man who saved a billion lives"
  [49:1:0.1] M.S. Swaminathan | Father of the Green Revolution in India; coined "Evergreen Revolution"
  [49:1:0.2] C. Subramaniam | Union Minister for Food and Agriculture (1964-66) who led the policy push; Bharat Ratna 1998
  [49:1:0.3] Indira Gandhi | Prime Minister; released the "Wheat Revolution" stamp, July 1968
  [49:1:0.4] Verghese Kurien | White Revolution (not Green)
[49:1:1] - **Not associated** with the Green Revolution: **Sardar Swaran Singh** (External Affairs/Defence Minister), **Rafi Ahmed Kidwai** (Food Minister, died 1954).
[49:1:2] - Trap: Borlaug worked in **Mexico** but was **from the USA**; his HYVs were **wheat**, not paddy.
[49:1:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 04 p.25; NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 03 p.8; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.152; app notes 3:48 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Second Green Revolution, Evergreen Revolution and BGREI
[49:2:0] - **Second Green Revolution:** called for by **PM Manmohan Singh** (**3 Jan 2006, 93rd Indian Science Congress, Hyderabad**): first GR technologies had "run their course".
[49:2:1] - Aims: extend **seed-water-fertiliser technology to areas left out** (eastern, rainfed, dryland), crops beyond wheat-rice (**pulses, oilseeds, horticulture, non-food crops**), **integrate cropping with animal husbandry, social forestry and fishing**; based on **biotechnology**, not more HYVs of wheat/rice or more chemical pesticides.
[49:2:2] - **May 2006 programme** for the Second Green Revolution: a **seven-point strategy**.
[49:2:3] - **Dry zone:** agrarian economy, and has large potential for the Second Green Revolution – both true, but the potential does not explain why it is agrarian.
[49:2:4] - **Evergreen Revolution:** concept of **M.S. Swaminathan** – raise productivity **in perpetuity without ecological harm**; Aug 2025 centenary conference theme "**Evergreen Revolution, The Pathway to Biohappiness**".
[49:2:5] TABLE head: BGREI | Fact
  [49:2:5.0] Full name | Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India
  [49:2:5.1] Launched | 2010-11
  [49:2:5.2] Parent | Sub-scheme of RKVY
  [49:2:5.3] Aim | Rice-based productivity in eastern India
  [49:2:5.4] States (7) | Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, Eastern UP, West Bengal (Punjab is not one)
[49:2:6] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.154 (evergreen / second green revolution); app notes 3:49 sub 6; general knowledge (seven-point strategy, BGREI)
## SUB 3 | Yellow Revolution – Oilseeds
[49:3:0] - **Yellow Revolution = oilseeds** (edible oil production): began **1986** with the **Technology Mission on Oilseeds**; linked with **Sam Pitroda**; **rapeseed-mustard** is its emblem crop.
[49:3:1] - Not pulses, millets, cereals, turmeric, poultry or sunflower alone.
[49:3:2] - Now: **National Mission on Edible Oils** – **NMEO-Oilseeds** and **NMEO-Oil Palm**.
[49:3:3] - **Soybean** = the "**miracle crop**" (golden bean) – an oilseed rich in protein and oil.
[49:3:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Geography p.53 (Yellow Revolution oilseeds); app notes 3:49 sub 8; general knowledge (soybean miracle crop)
## SUB 4 | White Revolution – Operation Flood
[49:4:0] - **Operation Flood (1970)** by the **NDDB** = **milk production**; national milk grid on the **Anand (Amul) three-tier cooperative** model; world's largest dairy development programme.
[49:4:1] - White Revolution **started in Gujarat**; **Anand** is a district of **Gujarat**.
[49:4:2] - **GCMMF (1946)** markets milk (**AMUL**); **NDDB set up 1965** to copy the AMUL model.
[49:4:3] - **Dr Verghese Kurien** – **Father of the White Revolution**, with **Tribhuvandas Patel**; also behind the **Institute of Rural Management, Anand (IRMA)**.
[49:4:4] TABLE head: Phase | Years | Achievement
  [49:4:4.0] I | 1970-80 | Financed by the World Food Programme; 18 milk sheds linked to 4 metros
  [49:4:4.1] II | 1981-85 | Milk sheds 18 → 136
  [49:4:4.2] III | 1985-96 | 30,000 new dairy cooperatives
[49:4:5] - **White Revolution 2.0** (Sept 2024, **Ministry of Cooperation**): **75,000** new dairy cooperatives. Milk output **239.3 MT (2023-24)**; India = world's largest producer.
[49:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 21 p.2; NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 04 p.25; app notes 3:49 sub 7
## SUB 5 | Background and Timeline
[49:5:0] - 1950s-60s food shortages → imports from the USA under **PL-480**; droughts **1965-66 and 1966-67** (foodgrains 72.3 and 74.2 MT) forced a new strategy.
[49:5:1] TABLE head: Programme | Year | Coverage
  [49:5:1.0] IADP (Intensive Agricultural District Programme) | 1960-61 | Pilot in 7 districts of 7 States; AP's district = West Godavari
  [49:5:1.1] IAAP (Intensive Agricultural Area Programme) | 1964-65 (1965) | IADP extended to 114 districts; 117 blocks in AP
  [49:5:1.2] HYV programme | Rabi 1966-67 | Full-fledged from 1966, during the Plan Holiday (1966-69)
[49:5:2] - **G.B. Pant University of Agriculture and Technology, Pantnagar** – **India's first agricultural university (1960)**; the Indian Green Revolution **started from Pantnagar**.
[49:5:3] - 1966: **18,000 t** Mexican wheat seed imported.
[49:5:4] TABLE head: Phase | Years
  [49:5:4.0] Pre-Green Revolution | 1951-68
  [49:5:4.1] Early Green Revolution | 1968-81
  [49:5:4.2] Later Green Revolution | 1981-92 (spread to new areas)
[49:5:5] - Order (APPSC 2023): **IADP (1960) → end of first Green Revolution period → MSSRF (1988)**.
[49:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 20 p.2, p.5-6; NextGen AP Economy Static-1 01 p.6 (IAAP 114 districts, 117 AP blocks, West Godavari); Rocket Indian Economy p.3 (Pantnagar 1960; first HYV 1966-67)
## SUB 6 | Outcomes and Criticism
[49:6:0] - **Gains:** wheat (most), then rice; Punjab, Haryana, western UP; end of PL-480 dependence; foodgrains **72 MT (1965-66) → 357.73 MT (2024-25)**.
[49:6:1] - **Inequality:** **inter-regional, inter-personal (inter-class) and inter-crop** – farmers with **more than 10 ha** benefited most.
[49:6:2] - **Crop bias:** **pulses** (and oilseeds, coarse cereals) gained little.
[49:6:3] - **No true self-sufficiency (UPSC 1994):** GR **restricted to small pockets**, **food costly relative to the earnings of the poor**, **too much emphasis on wheat and paddy** over coarse grains (statements 1, 2, 3).
[49:6:4] - **Ecological cost:** soil fertility loss, falling water table, salinity, toxic residues – so "it did not involve much social and environmental cost" is **false**, though GR did modernise agriculture.
[49:6:5] - Groundwater: Punjab and Haryana extract **35-57% more than recharge**; nutrient use skewed at **N:P:K 10.9:4.1:1** (not balanced); rice-wheat monoculture.
[49:6:6] - **Johl Committee:** shift **20% of paddy area** (diversification).
[49:6:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 20 p.6; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.153-154; app notes 3:49 sub 5

  [49:8:0.0] IR-8 | Dwarf rice from IRRI, Philippines; "miracle rice", released 1966 – Golden Jubilee Nov 2016
  [49:8:0.1] Jaya | First dwarf rice variety developed in India (1968)
  [49:8:0.2] Taichung Native-1 (TN-1) | First semi-dwarf rice introduced in India (1965)

  [49:8:0.4] MTU / BPT series | RARS Maruteru / Bapatla (AP); BPT 5204 = Samba Mahsuri; MTU 1010 parent of Pusa DST Rice 1

## SUB 4 | Yield Gaps, Inter-State Variation and Pathways
[50:4:0] # Yields
[50:4:1] TABLE head: Crop | India | Benchmark / leader
  [50:4:1.0] Rice | about 2,929 kg/ha | China about 7,100 – India less than half; Punjab highest
  [50:4:1.1] Wheat | – | Punjab highest (about 50 q/ha)
  [50:4:1.2] Cotton | about 440 kg/ha | world about 770; Kapas Kanti target 755
  [50:4:1.3] Oilseeds | 1,398 kg/ha | groundnut is the exception (above world average)
[50:4:2] - **Rice yield above national average:** AP, Telangana, TN; **below:** Odisha, UP, Bihar.
[50:4:3] - **Pulses yield:** highest in **MP and Gujarat**.
[50:4:4] - **Cotton yield (UPPSC 2008):** among **West Bengal**, Bihar, Assam and AP, **West Bengal** is highest (about 510 kg/ha in 2005-06 vs AP 347, Assam 73); Gujarat and Haryana are higher still. **Black (regur) soil** is best for cotton.
[50:4:5] # Concepts and causes
[50:4:6] - **Intensive cultivation:** more **labour and capital** per hectare to raise output from the same land; extensive = more land under the plough.
[50:4:7] - **Cereal yield:** kg per hectare of **harvested** land under cereals. **TFP:** output growth not explained by input growth.
[50:4:8] - **Causes of low productivity:** small holdings, monsoon dependence and inadequate irrigation (rice ~67% irrigated vs pulses ~26%), skewed NPK, low seed replacement, ~30% cold-chain losses, climate (~8% yield fall per 1°C).
[50:4:9] - **Pathways:** irrigation, quality seed (SRR/VRR, genome editing), balanced fertiliser (Soil Health Card), plant protection, mechanisation (Custom Hiring Centres).
[50:4:10] - Growth has come **more from area than yield**; now led by livestock and fisheries.
[50:4:11] - **TFP drivers:** agricultural research and new varieties, irrigation, rural roads and markets, extension, education.
[50:4:12] - **El Niño and pulses:** acreage −2 to −9%, yield −5 to −25%, output −6 to −30%. Universal cold-chain access is NOT a cause of the yield gap – its lack is.
[50:4:13] - **Area trends:** cotton area down 18 lakh ha, output **290.91 lakh bales (2025-26)** from about 350 – India became a **net importer of raw cotton**; soybean area in MP fell about **10%** (2023 to 2024); Telangana's cultivated area 1.31 crore acres (2014) → **2.2 crore acres** (FY23).
[50:4:14] > A "which one is the pathway" stem with irrigation, seed, pesticides and fertilisers as options has no single answer – all four raise productivity.
[50:4:15] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:50 sub 5-7; RBI Handbook of Statistics on Indian States, state-wise cotton yield table (via web search)
## SUB 5 | Crop Production Missions
[50:5:0] TABLE head: Mission | Launch | Crops / feature
  [50:5:0.0] Technology Mission on Oilseeds | 1986 | Yellow Revolution (Sam Pitroda); pulses, maize added later
  [50:5:0.1] NFSM | Oct 2007 (2007-08) | rice, wheat, pulses, coarse cereals; HYV seed distribution, demonstrations, new varieties – credit is NOT an objective; renamed NFSNM in FY25
  [50:5:0.2] BGREI (RKVY) | 2010-11 | rice in the eastern States
  [50:5:0.3] INSIMP (RKVY) | 2011-12 | millets: cluster demonstrations of production and post-harvest technology and value addition; poor, small, marginal and tribal farmers have the larger stake; no free kits to shift commercial-crop farmers
  [50:5:0.4] NMOOP | 2014 | oilseeds + oil palm
  [50:5:0.5] NMEO-Oil Palm / NMEO-Oilseeds | 2021 / 2024 | about 70 MT oilseeds by 2030-31
  [50:5:0.6] Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses | 2025-26 to 2030-31, ₹11,440 crore | 100% MSP procurement of tur, urad, masoor
  [50:5:0.7] PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana | 2025-26 to 2030-31 | 100 low-productivity districts
[50:5:1] - **"Tilhan Mission" (Feb 2020):** **oilseed** production.
[50:5:2] - **Green Revolution outcome:** wheat first, then rice; Punjab, Haryana, western UP; widened regional disparity (hence BGREI).
[50:5:3] - **Committees:** NCA 1970 (N.R. Mirdha, report 1976); Doubling Farmers' Income – **Ashok Dalwai** (not Swaminathan).
[50:5:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:50 sub 9-10; UPSC Prelims 2016 (INSIMP) statement analysis
[50:5:5] - **NCA final report (1976):** 15 parts, including one on rural employment.

=== NOTES 3:51 | Agricultural Strategy and Policy – National Agriculture Policy, Doubling Farmers' Income, National Missions
## SUB 0 | National Missions and Schemes
[51:0:0] TABLE head: Mission / scheme | Launch | Focus | Key facts
  [51:0:0.0] NMSA | operational 2014-15 | climate-resilient, rainfed farming | one of the 8 NAPCC missions; RAD, Soil Health Management, Per Drop More Crop (to 2015), agroforestry; Krishonnati sub-mission from 2018-19; under PM-RKVY since 2022-23
  [51:0:0.1] NMSA – Rainfed Area Development (RAD) | – | Integrated Farming System models | Centrally Sponsored: 60:40 Centre-State (AP and other general States), 90:10 NE/Himalayan
  [51:0:0.2] RADP | 2011-12 | rainfed areas | sub-scheme of RKVY, Department of Agriculture and Cooperation
  [51:0:0.3] NICRA (ICAR) | 2011 | climate-resilient agriculture | the actual 2011 climate-resilience programme
  [51:0:0.4] RKVY (National Agricultural Development Yojana) | 2007-08 | State-led plans | grants to raise State farm spending; soil-test, fertiliser and tool-testing labs funded – Agricultural Engineering is not a listed component (CGPSC)
  [51:0:0.5] NFSM | Oct 2007 | foodgrains | renamed NFSNM in FY25
  [51:0:0.6] MIDH | 2014-15 | horticulture | 60:40 (90:10 NE/Himalayan)
  [51:0:0.7] NMEO-Oil Palm / NMEO-Oilseeds | Aug 2021 / 3 Oct 2024 | oil palm (NE, A&N) / oilseeds | ₹11,040 crore / ₹10,103 crore; 39 → 69.7 MT by 2030-31
  [51:0:0.8] PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana | 2025-26 | 100 low-performing districts | Central Sector, six years
[51:0:1] - **12th Plan farm missions:** **NFSM**, **National Mission on Agricultural Extension and Technology**, **National Mission on Oilseeds and Oil Palm** – "all the above".
[51:0:2] - **"Started in 2011-12 to enhance food security and make agriculture resilient to climate change"** – APPSC keys: **NMSA** (strictly, NMSA became operational in 2014-15; the 2011 climate programme is ICAR's NICRA).
[51:0:3] - **NMSA components:** Soil Health Cards free every **two years**; micro-irrigation subsidy up to **55%**; e-NAM is NOT an NMSA component.
[51:0:4] - **Scheme-feature match:** **KCC** – credit for crops and animal husbandry; **PMKSY** – water-use efficiency; **RKVY** – diversification, value addition, marketing support; **AIF** – infrastructure such as cold storage.
[51:0:5] - **Price-realisation schemes:** PM-AASHA (2018: PSS via NAFED/NCCF, PDPS 40%, MIS 25%); e-NAM (April 2016, **SFAC – Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium**; 1,656 mandis); Operation Greens (Budget 2018-19, TOP → 22 perishables); Krishi UDAN (air transport of perishables).
[51:0:6] - **AgriStack pilot:** on **13 April 2021** the Department of Agriculture signed an MoU with **Microsoft** for a pilot in **100 villages** of UP, MP, Gujarat, Haryana, Rajasthan and AP.
[51:0:7] > Mission-year PYQs (APPSC G1 2019, G2): NMSA 2014-15 vs RADP 2011-12; NMSA RAD funding 60:40.
[51:0:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:51 sub 5-7; app notes 3:50 sub 9
## SUB 1 | National Agriculture Policy 2000 and Earlier Commissions
[51:1:0] - **NAP 2000** (July 2000): growth target **over 4% per annum**.
[51:1:1] - **Thrusts:** private participation via **contract farming** and **land leasing**; price protection; national agricultural insurance; **Rainbow Revolution** across all farm sub-sectors.
[51:1:2] - **Land reform in NAP 2000:** consolidation of holdings all over the country, redistribution of ceiling-surplus and waste land, tenancy reform, updating land records; APPSC key: **consolidation of holdings**.
[51:1:3] TABLE head: Colour | Sector
  [51:1:3.0] Yellow | Oilseeds
  [51:1:3.1] Blue | Fisheries
  [51:1:3.2] Golden | Horticulture / honey
  [51:1:3.3] Silver | Eggs
  [51:1:3.4] Grey | Fertilisers
[51:1:4] - **ICAR Drishti (Vision) 2025:** increase in **food production**.
[51:1:5] - **National Commission on Agriculture (NCA):** 1970-76, **Nathu Ram Mirdha**; coined "social forestry".
[51:1:6] - **National Commission on Farmers (NCF):** constituted **18 Nov 2004**, **M.S. Swaminathan**; MSP at **C2 + 50%** (government pays **1.5 × A2+FL**, 22 mandated crops); Agricultural Renewal Action Plan – 2006-07 the Year of Agricultural Renewal.
[51:1:7] - **Agricultural Renewal Action Plan packages:** soil health enhancement, water harvesting and efficient use, credit and insurance reform, technology dissemination, market reform – phasing out MSP is not one of them.
[51:1:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:51 sub 1-2; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.59 (NCF, 18 Nov 2004)
## SUB 2 | Policy Since 1991 and the WTO Boxes
[51:2:0] TABLE head: Change after 1991 | Fact
  [51:2:0.0] Public investment | Declined with liberalisation
  [51:2:0.1] Technology | new technologies and contract farming helped productivity
  [51:2:0.2] MSP | not abolished – still in force
  [51:2:0.3] WTO (1995) | import competition rose; subsidies fell as a share of farm income
  [51:2:0.4] GM crops | Bt cotton (2002) – only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation
[51:2:1] TABLE head: Box | Nature | Examples
  [51:2:1.0] Green | minimal or no trade distortion – permitted without limit | decoupled direct income payments, research, training, extension, pest control, infrastructure, food security stocks
  [51:2:1.1] Amber | trade-distorting – reduction commitments expressed as Total AMS (product-specific + non-product-specific support in one figure); de minimis 5% developed / 10% developing | MSP, input subsidies
  [51:2:1.2] Blue | Amber support that requires farmers to limit production – placed in the Blue Box | direct payments tied to production limits
[51:2:2] - **Peace Clause (Bali 2013):** shields developing countries' public stockholding from challenge **even if** they breach the 10% ceiling – it does not tell them "not to exceed" it.
[51:2:3] - **Agriculture Orientation Index (SDG 2.a.1):** agriculture's share of government spending ÷ agriculture's share of GDP; tracks **SDG 2**; compiled by **FAO**, not IFPRI.
[51:2:4] - Dunkel Draft: **Sharad Joshi** backed it; **Tikait (BKU)** and **Nanjundaswamy (KRRS)** opposed. Budget 2020-21: 16 action points for farmers.
[51:2:5] > APPSC G1 2024 WTO statements: only the Total AMS statement is right.
[51:2:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:51 sub 3; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 20 p.10 (Amber Box); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 04 p.187 (boxes)
## SUB 3 | Sustainable Agriculture and Rainfed Areas
[51:3:0] - **Meaning:** use of land so that its quality remains intact – meeting present needs without harming future generations.
[51:3:1] - **Ultimate goal:** conservation of natural resources, environmental protection **and** human health and safety – "**all of these**"; pillars = environmental health, economic profitability, social and economic equity.
[51:3:2] - **Rainfed farming:** 50-60% of net sown area, about 40% of food output.
[51:3:3] - **National Rainfed Area Authority (NRAA, 2006):** the **single platform** for holistic, sustainable development of rainfed areas; knowledge inputs and watershed approach.
[51:3:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:51 sub 5
## SUB 4 | Doubling Farmers' Income
[51:4:0] - **Ashok Dalwai Committee (2016-18):** 14 volumes; base year **2015-16**, target **2022**.
[51:4:1] - Shift from production to **income**: value addition, e-NAM/APMC reform, post-harvest infrastructure, land-leasing laws.
[51:4:2] - **Seven sources:** crop productivity, livestock productivity, resource-use efficiency, cropping intensity, diversification to high-value crops, better price realisation, shift to non-farm jobs. Dependence only on traditional low-value crops is NOT a source.
[51:4:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:51 sub 4

## SUB 6 | Phases of Agricultural Development
[51:6:0] TABLE head: Phase | Period | Defining feature
  [51:6:0.0] Pre-Green Revolution | 1951-68 | land reforms, irrigation, Community Development; PL-480 imports; droughts 1965-67
  [51:6:0.1] Early Green Revolution | 1968-81 | New Agricultural Strategy – HYV seeds (wheat first), fertiliser, irrigation
  [51:6:0.2] Later Green Revolution | 1987-92 | spread to rice and other regions
  [51:6:0.3] Income phase | 2016 onwards | Doubling Farmers' Income – from production to income
[51:6:1] - Foodgrains: 72.3 MT (1965-66) → record 357.73 MT (2024-25).

  The spread of the Green Revolution to rice and other regions marks which phase?
  Pre-Green Revolution (1951-68) | Early Green Revolution (1968-81) | *Later Green Revolution (1987-92) | Income phase (2016 onwards)
  x: The Later Green Revolution (1987-92) spread the new technology to rice and other regions; the early phase began with wheat.
[fa6d8366fb495] sub6
  PL-480 imports and the droughts of 1965-67 belong to which phase of Indian agriculture?
  Early Green Revolution | *Pre-Green Revolution | Later Green Revolution | Income phase
  x: The Pre-Green Revolution phase (1951-68) saw land reforms, irrigation, PL-480 imports and the 1965-67 droughts.
[g317be8088c41] sub6
  What is the HYV-seed, fertiliser and irrigation strategy of the Early Green Revolution phase (1968-81) known as?
  *New Agricultural Strategy | Package Programme for Rainfed Areas | Agricultural Renewal Action Plan | Rainbow Revolution
  x: The Early Green Revolution phase (1968-81), with HYV seeds, fertiliser and irrigation, is called the New Agricultural Strategy.

=== NOTES 3:52 | Agrarian Crisis – Causes, Farmer Distress and Suicides, Loan Waivers, Small-holding Viability
## SUB 0 | Crop Insurance – CCIS to PMFBY and AP Schemes
[52:0:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Year | Fact
  [52:0:0.0] CCIS (Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme) | 1 April 1985 (kharif) | first national crop insurance scheme
  [52:0:0.1] NAIS | Rabi 1999-2000 | replaced CCIS
  [52:0:0.2] Varsha Bima (rainfall insurance) | SW monsoon 2004 | run by Agriculture Insurance Company of India (AICIL); piloted in 20 areas of AP, UP, Karnataka, Rajasthan – not 2007
  [52:0:0.3] WBCIS | Kharif 2007, first in Karnataka | extended to 10 States from Kharif 2008
  [52:0:0.4] MNAIS | 2010-11 | –
  [52:0:0.5] PMFBY | 2016 | replaced NAIS and MNAIS (not WBCIS); premium 2% kharif, 1.5% rabi, 5% commercial/horticulture – not a uniform 2%; covers post-harvest losses from cyclones and unseasonal rain; voluntary from 2020; YES-TECH (yield), WINDS (weather), DigiClaim
  [52:0:0.6] RWBCIS | 2016 | protects insured farmers (all categories) against loss from adverse weather; pays when weather deviates from triggers
[52:0:1] - **Not a claim ground:** low yield from **poor-quality seed**. Cover is for natural calamities (drought, flood), pests and diseases.
[52:0:2] - **AP:** PMFBY, WBCIS/RWBCIS and the Unified Package Insurance Scheme have run in AP; there is **no** special scheme for GM crops. **Dr YSR Free Crop Insurance (2019-24):** State paid the whole premium; covered **22 notified crops** (2022); voluntary from **Rabi 2024-25** (farmer pays a small fixed share, State and Centre share the rest); Kharif 2026 – every crop insured, Collectors accountable.
[52:0:3] - **PMFBY slogans:** "One Nation – One Scheme"; "One Nation, One Crop, One Premium".
[52:0:4] > Most-asked angle (13 PYQs): scheme years – CCIS 1985, NAIS 1999, Varsha Bima 2004, WBCIS 2007 Karnataka; PMFBY premium statements (UPSC 2016).
[52:0:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:52 sub 6; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.54 (NAIS 1999 replacing CCIS); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 04 p.181 (PMFBY replaced NAIS of 1999 and MNAIS 2010-11)
## SUB 1 | Causes of Agrarian Crisis and Farmer Suicides
[52:1:0] TABLE head: Cause | Data point
  [52:1:0.0] Small holdings | 86% small and marginal
  [52:1:0.1] Rain-fed | about 50% of NSA; groundwater = 64% of irrigation; 17% blocks over-exploited
  [52:1:0.2] Post-harvest | cold-chain deficit 30% → up to 40% fruit/vegetable loss
  [52:1:0.3] Soil | NPK 10.9:4.1:1 vs ideal 4:2:1
[52:1:1] - **Indian agriculture is still ailing due to** under-investment, low productivity **and** post-harvest losses – "all the above".
[52:1:2] - **Rural poverty** is the effective reason for slow agricultural development (no capital for inputs and technology).
[52:1:3] - **Debt cycle:** high input cost → borrowing → crop failure or low price → inability to repay → fresh borrowing → debt trap.
[52:1:4] - **Suicides:** main reasons – **crop failure** and **bankruptcy/indebtedness** (NCRB ADSI 2015); concentrated in **rain-fed** belts. ADSI 2023: farm sector 10,786; Maharashtra 38.5%, Karnataka 22.5%, AP 8.6%.
[52:1:5] - **Swaminathan Commission** = National Commission on Farmers, constituted **2004** (18 Nov), after farmer suicides; MSP = **C2 + 50%** (C2 = A2 + imputed family labour + rent and interest on owned land and capital); National Agricultural Risk Fund.
[52:1:6] - **Farm protests:** Sharad Joshi (Shetkari Sangathan) backed globalisation; Nanjundaswamy (KRRS), Tikait (BKU) opposed; 2020-21 farm laws repealed 2021.
[52:1:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:52 sub 0, 3, 4, 8; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.59 (NCF on 18 Nov 2004, farmer suicides)
[52:1:8] - **Delhi-border protests 2020-21 – demands:** repeal of the three farm laws, a legal guarantee of MSP, withdrawal of the Electricity (Amendment) Bill.
## SUB 2 | Small Holdings and Agricultural Households
[52:2:0] TABLE head: Agriculture Census | Small + marginal holdings | Their area
  [52:2:0.0] 2010-11 | about 85% (84.97%) | about 44% – 44.58% in the APPSC key; 44.31% in the census figures quoted by Ramesh Singh
  [52:2:0.1] 2015-16 | 86.2% | 47.3%
[52:2:1] - **2015-16 States:** by number of holdings **UP 1st, Bihar 2nd, Maharashtra 3rd**; by operated area **Rajasthan 1st**. Semi-medium + medium: 13.2% of holdings, 43.6% of area.
[52:2:2] - **NSSO 70th Round (2013) SAS:** **Rajasthan** – highest share of agricultural households among rural households (about 78%); **Kerala** – over 60% earned most income from non-farm sources; OBCs are about **45%** of agricultural households (not "over 60%").
[52:2:3] - **NSS 77th Round (2019):** about half indebted; debt ₹74,121; income wages → crops → livestock; most indebted **AP 93.2%**, Telangana 91.7%.
[52:2:4] - **Bullock capitalists:** **Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph** ("In Pursuit of Lakshmi", 1987) – self-employed small-to-medium farmers with **some resources but not rich**.
[52:2:5] - Remedies: 10,000 FPOs (2020, ₹6,865 crore), Custom Hiring Centres, cluster and joint farming. Other: Guntur study (tenants' debt ₹2,07,444; informal 51.5%); R. Radhakrishna Expert Group on indebtedness (2007); AP Microfinance Act 2011 (3 lenders, ₹2 lakh cap); 7.72 crore KCCs vs 146 million holdings.
[52:2:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:52 sub 1-2; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 04 p.151 (Agriculture Census 2010-11), p.179 (NSSO 70th Round)
## SUB 3 | Loan Waivers and Debt Redemption
[52:3:0] TABLE head: Waiver | Facts
  [52:3:0.0] ADWDRS 2008 | small/marginal: full waiver; others: 25% OTS relief on paying 75%
  [52:3:0.1] AP Agricultural Debt Redemption Scheme 2014 (Runa Mafi / Runa Upasamana) | implemented by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha; ceiling ₹1.5 lakh/family; horticulture ₹10,000/acre; balance paid in annual instalments – 2nd instalment released from 22 June 2016 (Runa Upasamana Arhatha Patralu)
[52:3:1] - **Effect on aggregate demand (all four channels):** private consumption (net wealth up), public-sector spending/taxes, crowding-out via higher State borrowing, crowding-in as bank NPAs fall.
[52:3:2] - **RBI critique:** moral hazard; hurts credit culture.
[52:3:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:52 sub 5; apagrisnet.gov.in GO dated 22-6-2016 (2nd instalment drive, via web search)
## SUB 4 | Income Support and AP Tenant Farmers
[52:4:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Fact
  [52:4:0.0] PM-KISAN | ₹6,000/yr in 3 instalments of ₹2,000; at launch only small and marginal families with up to 2 hectares – extended to all landholding families from June 2019
  [52:4:0.1] Annadata Sukhibhava (AP) | ₹20,000; tenants covered
  [52:4:0.2] KALIA / Rythu Bandhu | Odisha / Telangana (₹12,000 per acre)
  [52:4:0.3] PM Kisan Maandhan | pension for small farmers
[52:4:1] - **First State to give loans to tenant farmers:** **Andhra Pradesh** – AP Land Licensed Cultivators Act, **2011** (Loan Eligibility Cards).
[52:4:2] - **CCRC = Crop Cultivator Rights Card** (AP Crop Cultivator Rights Act, **2019**): for lease-holders/tenants, valid 11 months; no ownership transfer; hurdle – landowner's signature. AP pioneered RMGs and JLGs.
[52:4:3] - **2011 crop holiday (Konaseema paddy farmers):** special committee chaired by **Mohan Kanda** (not Jayati Ghosh, not Koneru Ranga Rao).
[52:4:4] - Tenants often lack passbook, KCC and insurance; those missing from **e-crop** data miss insurance and relief.
[52:4:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:52 sub 7

=== NOTES 3:54 | Land Records and Titling – Digital India Land Records Modernisation, Svamitva
## SUB 0 | Andhra Pradesh Land Records, Registration and Resurvey
[54:0:0] # Portals and records
[54:0:1] TABLE head: Platform | Fact
  [54:0:1.0] Bhudhaar (Bhudaar) | Web portal (with Bhuseva) launched by CM N. Chandrababu Naidu on 20 Nov 2018; gives every land parcel an 11-digit unique number; people view land records online
  [54:0:1.1] Meebhoomi | Earlier portal (13 June 2015) to view Adangal / 1-B records
  [54:0:1.2] Webland | AP's digitised land records platform
  [54:0:1.3] Bhu Bharathi | Computerisation of land records, united AP, 1992; pilot Nizamabad
  [54:0:1.4] CARD | Computer-aided registration: anywhere registration, auto-mutation, at Grama Sachivalayams – a registration system, not a court
  [54:0:1.5] Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain | Pilot 24 July 2026, 7 mandals
[54:0:2] - **Encumbrance Certificate (EC):** issued by the **Sub-Registrar's (Registration) office** where the property documents are registered; shows the charges/transactions on a property.
[54:0:3] - **Village secretariat land-record staff:** AP proposed a **Survey Assistant** in each village secretariat for **100% verification of land records**; the post was filled in 2019 as **Village Surveyor (Grade-III)**.
[54:0:4] # Resurvey and passbooks
[54:0:5] - **Resurvey** (Jagananna Saswatha Bhu Hakku and Bhu Raksha) from **December 2020**: drones, CORS, GIS; **6,901 villages, 81 lakh parcels**.
[54:0:6] - **QR-coded pattadar passbooks** (January 2026) carry the **State emblem**: 36 lakh issued; 56 lakh more by March 2027.
[54:0:7] - **N-LRSI** (NCAER Land Records and Services Index) grades States on **digitisation and quality of land records**: AP **10th (2020) → 6th (2021)**; **Madhya Pradesh** topped.
[54:0:8] - **Karnataka Bhoomi (2000):** first to computerise **RTCs** (Records of Rights, Tenancy and Crops).
[54:0:9] ~~ Sources: web – Hans India 20 Nov 2018 and Wikipedia "Bhudhaar" (search results); app notes 3:54 sub 5
## SUB 1 | SVAMITVA – Drone Mapping of Village Abadi
[54:1:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [54:1:0.0] Full form | Survey of Villages and Mapping with Improvised Technology in Village Areas
  [54:1:0.1] Launch | 24 April 2020 (National Panchayati Raj Day); nationwide 2021
  [54:1:0.2] Ministry / type | Panchayati Raj (not Mines); Central Sector
  [54:1:0.3] Agencies | Survey of India (implementing); NICSI (technology)
  [54:1:0.4] Technology | Drones + CORS (Continuously Operating Reference Stations) – an integrated property validation solution for rural India
  [54:1:0.5] Coverage | Abadi (inhabited village) areas only – not agricultural land
  [54:1:0.6] Output | Property Cards (Records of Rights, also in DigiLocker): 3.06 crore in 1.86 lakh villages (Jan 2026; earlier 2.76 crore)
  [54:1:0.7] Target | 6.62 lakh villages; drone survey done in 3.28 lakh of 3.44 lakh notified villages (Dec 2025)
[54:1:1] > Exam angle: drones + CORS + property cards = SVAMITVA; ULPIN and DILRMP are land-record programmes, PMGSY is roads.
[54:1:2] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary part 2 p.41; Rocket CA 2026-01 p.153, p.186; app notes 3:54 sub 3
## SUB 2 | DILRMP, ULPIN and NGDRS
[54:2:0] - Began as **NLRMP in 2008** (UPPSC 2016) = merger of **CLR** (Computerisation of Land Records) + **SRA&ULR** (Strengthening of Revenue Administration and Updating of Land Records); renamed **Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme**.
[54:2:1] - **Central Sector, 100% central funding** from **1 April 2016** (earlier centrally sponsored); extended to **2025-26** with two new components – **consent-based Aadhaar seeding** and **computerisation of revenue courts**; mandatory **gender column** in the RoR.
[54:2:2] - Components: modern record rooms, survey/resurvey, **digitised cadastral maps**, computerised registration, State data centre (Property Cards for abadi are **SVAMITVA's**, not DILRMP's).
[54:2:3] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [54:2:3.0] ULPIN (Bhu-Aadhaar) | 14-digit alphanumeric parcel ID from the geo-coordinates of the parcel's vertices; 36.67 crore parcels
  [54:2:3.1] NGDRS | "One Nation One Registration Software" – common, configurable registration application for sub-registrars and citizens
  [54:2:3.2] Land Stack (National Digital Land Initiative) | Cloud GIS; a Bhu-Aadhaar for every parcel
  [54:2:3.3] Phase (DILRMP 3.0) | 1 (2008-16) digitisation, resurvey; 2 (2016-26) ULPIN, NGDRS, e-Court integration; 3 (2026-31) GIS Land Stack
[54:2:4] - Progress: **RoR digitised 99.8%**; cadastral maps 97.24%; SROs computerised **95.73%**.
[54:2:5] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 04 p.146 (NLRMP 2008); Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary part 2 p.41; app notes 3:54 sub 0, 2
## SUB 3 | Land Titling – Presumptive vs Conclusive
[54:3:0] TABLE head: Presumptive (present) | Conclusive
  [54:3:0.0] Registration only records a transaction; title can be challenged | State guarantees the title; cannot be disputed once issued
  [54:3:0.1] Registration, survey and revenue records kept separately | Single title register
[54:3:1] - **Clear titles** → land usable as **collateral**, less litigation.
[54:3:2] - **NITI Aayog Model Conclusive Land Titling Act, 2020:** adoption is **each State's choice**.
[54:3:3] - **SC (1 January 2026):** **registration of a transfer deed is distinct from title**.
[54:3:4] - **AP Land Titling Act, 2022:** presumptive → **conclusive**, State as guarantor; criticised for limiting disputes to the **High Court**; **repealed 2024**.
[54:3:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:54 sub 1, 4

=== NOTES 3:55 | Agricultural Credit – Institutional Structure, Nabard, Kcc, Priority Sector Lending, Interest Subvention
## SUB 0 | NABARD – Establishment, Role, Refinance and RIDF
[55:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [55:0:0.0] Full form | National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (traps: Nation, Real, Net, Research)
  [55:0:0.1] Recommended by | CRAFICARD (1979-81), B. Sivaraman
  [55:0:0.2] Act | NABARD Act, 1981 (Act 61 of 1981 of Parliament)
  [55:0:0.3] Established | 12 July 1982 (Sixth Five Year Plan)
  [55:0:0.4] Headquarters | Mumbai; initial corpus Rs 100 crore
  [55:0:0.5] Ownership | RBI sold its stake in 2019 → fully owned by the Government of India
[55:0:1] - **Merged/replaced at birth:** RBI's **Agricultural Credit Department (ACD)**, **Rural Planning and Credit Cell (RPCC)** and the **Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation (ARDC)** – NOT IFCI, IDBI or SIDBI.
[55:0:2] - **Apex development finance institution** for **agriculture AND rural development** (not agriculture alone; also cottage, small and village industries) – the **apex bank for rural / agricultural credit** and the **only body catering to all types of rural credit**; set up as an apex body to **coordinate all institutions in the rural financing system**.
[55:0:3] - **Primary role = refinance**: refinances **Scheduled Commercial Banks, RRBs, State Cooperative Banks, State Land Development Banks** – **not EXIM Bank**; does not lend directly to farmers (lends to **States** via RIDF). Refinance only for agriculture and rural development (not export or industrial finance).
[55:0:4] - **Supervises RRBs and State/District cooperative banks**; launched **SHG-Bank Linkage (1992)**.
[55:0:5] - **Credit planning:** NABARD prepares district-wise **Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs)** → roll up into the **State Focus Paper** → base of the State's **Annual Credit Plan**. AP 2026-27 plan: **Rs 5.11 lakh crore**.
[55:0:6] - **NABARD Award for Rural Innovations** instituted in **2012** to mark NABARD's **30 years**.
[55:0:7] TABLE head: NABARD fund | Year / size | Purpose
  [55:0:7.0] RIDF (Rural Infrastructure Development Fund) | 1995-96; funded by banks' PSL shortfall deposits | Loans to States for rural roads, bridges, godowns, irrigation, fisheries, forests
  [55:0:7.1] LTIF (PMKSY) | – | Irrigation
  [55:0:7.2] Warehouse Infrastructure Fund | 2013-14, Rs 5,000 crore | Warehousing
  [55:0:7.3] Food Processing Fund | 2014-15, Rs 2,000 crore | Food processing
[55:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 02 p.37; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.10; Rocket Indian Economy p.22-23, p.88; web – YourStory Oct 2012 (search result: NABARD Award 2012 for 30 years); app notes 3:55 sub 2, 3
## SUB 1 | Cooperative Credit Structure and Land Development Banks
[55:1:0] TABLE head: Tier / body | Level | Credit
  [55:1:0.0] PACS | Village | Short-term, direct to farmers
  [55:1:0.1] DCCB | District | Short-term; main function finances PACS
  [55:1:0.2] State Cooperative Bank (e.g. APCOB) | State apex | Short-term; refinanced by NABARD
  [55:1:0.3] Land Development Banks (now Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks) | State/primary | Long-term – land development, wells, machinery
  [55:1:0.4] RRBs | Region | Direct to small farmers, labourers, artisans
[55:1:1] - Short-term cooperative chain: **StCB → DCCB → PACS** (3-tier); long-term: **LDBs / CARDBs**. LDBs are part of the **Cooperative Credit Structure** (quasi-commercial), not commercial banks, IDBI or FCI.
[55:1:2] - **First Land Development Bank: Jhang (Punjab), 1920.**
[55:1:3] - Cooperative banks work on the **"No Profit No Loss"** model and "one member one vote"; they lend beyond agriculture; **NABARD is not a cooperative bank**.
[55:1:4] - **Direct credit to rural households:** **RRBs and Land Development Banks**; **NABARD only refinances** (UPSC 2013: 1 and 3).
[55:1:5] - UPSC 2020: **Scheduled Commercial Banks**, not DCCBs, deliver the most short-term farm credit; financing PACS is a key DCCB function.
[55:1:6] - Institutional sources: **cooperative societies/banks, commercial banks, RRBs**, government (**taccavi** loans); non-institutional: moneylenders, relatives, traders.
[55:1:7] - **SIDBI** = main institution for **MSMEs**, not agriculture.
[55:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.9-10; Rocket Indian Economy p.22; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 05 p.85; web – TNAU Agritech "Land Development Bank" (search result: Jhang 1920); app notes 3:55 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Regional Rural Banks
[55:2:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [55:2:0.0] Recommended by | Working Group on Rural Banks (1975), M. Narasimham – RRBs as part of the multi-agency approach
  [55:2:0.1] Set up | Ordinance 26 Sept 1975 → RRB Act 1976; 5 RRBs on 2 October 1975 (Gandhi Jayanti)
  [55:2:0.2] First RRB | Prathama (Grameen) Bank, Moradabad (UP), sponsored by Syndicate Bank
  [55:2:0.3] Sponsor | A Scheduled Commercial Bank (not RBI, not NABARD)
  [55:2:0.4] Share capital | Centre 50% : Sponsor bank 35% : State Government 15%
  [55:2:0.5] Regulation | NABARD supervises; sponsor bank supports
[55:2:1] - Functions: banking in rural and semi-urban areas; mobilise rural resources; loans mainly to **small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, rural artisans** (not large industry); **supplement Scheduled Commercial Banks**; participate in institutional farm credit. RRBs did **not take over agricultural refinance** (that is NABARD's).
[55:2:2] - **Bhandari Committee (1994):** **RRB restructuring**; identified 49 RRBs; more powers to RRB Boards.
[55:2:3] - **One State, One RRB:** 26 RRBs amalgamated, effective **1 May 2025** → **28 RRBs**.
[55:2:4] - RRBs and SFBs have a **75%** PSL target.
[55:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 02 p.40; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.8; Rocket Indian Economy p.43; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 05 p.84; app notes 3:55 sub 1
## SUB 3 | Kisan Credit Card
[55:3:0] - Launched **August 1998 (1998-99)** – not 2001 – as a **NABARD model scheme** (with RBI), on the **R.V. Gupta Committee** recommendation; aim: **adequate and timely credit** for cultivation needs.
[55:3:1] - **Issuers:** **commercial banks, RRBs, cooperative banks/credit societies (PACS)**, small finance banks – not NABARD, EXIM Bank, payment banks or local area banks.
[55:3:2] - **Short-term purposes (UPSC 2020: 1, 3, 4):** crop cultivation, **post-harvest expenses**, marketing loans, **consumption requirements** of farm households, **working capital for maintenance of farm assets**; also investment credit for allied activities → KCC covers **consumption and investment credit**.
[55:3:3] - **Not** short-term KCC credit: **combine harvesters, tractors, mini trucks**, family house, village cold storage.
[55:3:4] - Extended to allied/non-farm activities **2004**; **animal husbandry and fisheries 2019**; electronic KCC per **T.M. Bhasin** Working Group.
[55:3:5] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [55:3:5.0] Collateral-free | Up to Rs 2 lakh; Rs 3 lakh with hypothecation tie-up
  [55:3:5.1] Operative KCCs (31 March 2025) | 7.72 crore
  [55:3:5.2] RBI KCC Directions (19 June 2026) | Tenure 6 years for loans from 1 January 2027
[55:3:6] - **Pashu Kisan Credit Card:** **Haryana (2020)**; first cards to 101 animal farmers at Bhiwani (6 December).
[55:3:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.23 (KCC Plan 1998); app notes 3:55 sub 4; general knowledge (KCC purposes, UPSC 2020 key), not checked
## SUB 4 | Sources and Shares of Agricultural Credit
[55:4:0] - **Largest source:** **commercial banks** – about **three-fourths** of institutional farm credit (2010-11: 73.86%; cooperatives 16.68%).
[55:4:1] - **Agency order:** **commercial banks > cooperative banks > RRBs** (3, 1, 2); **least: foreign private banks**.
[55:4:2] - After the **1991 reforms**, credit flow to **agriculture** rose notably.
[55:4:3] - **Rural branches** of SCBs incl. RRBs ≈ **37%** of all branches (RBI, 30 June 2012).
[55:4:4] - Non-institutional share in rural credit: ~90% (1950) → **23.4%** (2021-22).
[55:4:5] - **Ground Level Credit FY25 Rs 28.69 lakh crore** vs target **Rs 27.50 lakh crore**; **South** gets ~48% of credit with ~17% of cropped area.
[55:4:6] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Highlights part 1 p.23 (GLC FY25); app notes 3:55 sub 7; general knowledge (RBI branch share 2012), not checked
## SUB 5 | Types of Credit and Rural Credit Terms
[55:5:0] TABLE head: Credit | Duration | Purpose
  [55:5:0.0] Short-term (crop loans) | Up to 15 months | Seeds, fertiliser, wages
  [55:5:0.1] Medium-term | 15 months – 5 years | Bullocks, pumps, implements
  [55:5:0.2] Long-term | Over 5 years | Land development, wells, machinery (LDBs)
[55:5:1] - **Taccavi (taqavi)** = government **agricultural loans** to cultivators (Muhammad bin Tughluq's taqavi written off by Firoz Shah).
[55:5:2] - **Bank-linked SHG** lending is the "**modern**" rural lending channel (cooperatives, RRBs, commercial banks = conventional).
[55:5:3] - **All India Rural Credit Review Committee (1969)** recommended **entry of commercial banks** into rural credit (multi-agency approach).
[55:5:4] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 04 p.179 (crop loans <15 months, long-term >5 years); NextGen Indian History - APPSC 03 p.67 (taqavi loans); app notes 3:55 sub 0

  [55:6:0.0] Lending rate on short-term crop/KCC loans | 7%
  [55:6:0.1] Subvention to lenders | 1.5%
  [55:6:0.2] Prompt repayment incentive | 3%
  [55:6:0.3] Effective rate for prompt repayers | 4%
[55:6:1] - **Modified Interest Subvention Scheme (MISS):** **Central Sector**, run through **RBI and NABARD**; limit Rs 3 lakh → **Rs 5 lakh (Aug 2026)**.
[55:6:2] - Post-harvest loans at 7% for up to **6 months** against **WDRA negotiable warehouse receipts**.
[55:6:3] - **Kisan Rin Portal (September 2023):** joins **KCC data with interest-subvention claims**; before it, banks filed ISS/PRI claims **manually with RBI and NABARD**.

=== NOTES 3:56 | Agricultural Marketing – Apmc, E-nam, Contract Farming, Model Acts, Fpos, Warehousing
## SUB 0 | Grading and Standardisation – AGMARK
[56:0:0] - **AGMARK** = **quality** certification mark for **agricultural goods**, under the **Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937** (trap: not "Grading and Marketing").
[56:0:1] - Issued by the **Directorate of Marketing and Inspection (DMI)**, Ministry of Agriculture – **not FAO, not FCI, not BIS**.
[56:0:2] TABLE head: Laboratory | Place
  [56:0:2.0] Central Agmark Laboratory (apex lab of DMI) | Nagpur
  [56:0:2.1] Central Quality Control Laboratory (APPSC) | Nagpur
[56:0:3] - **BIS Standard Mark is mandatory for automotive tyres and tubes** (UPSC 2017: only I correct).
[56:0:4] - **AGMARKNET** (2000) = market-price portal. **One Nation, One Regulator** = end dual certification under **BIS and AGMARK**.
[56:0:5] ~~ Sources: web – Wikipedia "AGMARK" and agmarknet archive (search result: CAL Nagpur, apex lab of DMI); OnlyIAS NCERT Economy part 03 p.23 (Agmark quality logo); app notes 3:56 sub 2
## SUB 1 | e-NAM – National Agriculture Market
[56:1:0] - Launched **April 2016**; "**One Nation, One Market**"; online platform **linking APMC mandis and other yards** – a virtual market backed by physical mandis (does not replace them).
[56:1:1] - Lead agency **SFAC**; Central Sector, funded via **Agri-Tech Infrastructure Fund** (2015); up to **Rs 75 lakh per mandi**.
[56:1:2] - **Reforms required of States:** **electronic trading / e-auction** for price discovery, **single licence valid across the State**, **single-point levy** of market fee – NOT abolition of market trading or State price regulation.
[56:1:3] - **E-auction** = bidding through an **electronic trading portal**.
[56:1:4] - **Direct payment** to the farmer's bank account; warehouse trading with **e-NWRs**.
[56:1:5] - **Economic Survey 2022-23:** online, competitive, transparent bidding with **1.74 crore farmers and 2.39 lakh traders** = e-NAM. Mar 2026: **1,656 mandis**.
[56:1:6] - **AP:** **33 markets** on e-NAM; **11 mandis** in inter-mandi trade (2024-25).
[56:1:7] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 04 p.168; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.95; app notes 3:56 sub 5
## SUB 2 | APMC Acts, Model Acts and the Farm Laws 2020
[56:2:0] - Agricultural markets = **State List**; markets are regulated under **APMC Acts enacted by States** (UPSC 2015) – not the Essential Commodities Act or the Grading and Marking Act.
[56:2:1] - AP law: **AP (Agricultural Produce and Livestock) Markets Act, 1966**. Set-up order: **area notified** → Market Committee → market yard.
[56:2:2] - Regulated markets ensure **open auction, standard weights, recorded prices, licensed buyers**; ~**2,477** regulated markets; market fee **1%**.
[56:2:3] - APMC problems: market/licence fees, commission charges, **cartels of licensed traders**, too few mandis; **price spread** = **consumer price − farmer's price**; NCF: a regulated market within **~5 km**; poor storage → **distress sale**.
[56:2:4] - Farmer's share in the consumer rupee (RBI, Oct 2024): tomato ~**33%**, pulses higher (gram ~**75%**).
[56:2:5] TABLE head: Model Act | Key feature
  [56:2:5.0] Model APMC Act, 2003 | Direct sale to contract-farming sponsors; private markets; farmer-consumer markets
  [56:2:5.1] Model APLM Act, 2017 | Whole State one market area; single-point fee, unified licence
  [56:2:5.2] Model Contract Farming Act, 2018 | Outside APMC; sponsor buys the entire pre-agreed quantity; farmer = weaker party; registration by RARC
[56:2:6] # Farm laws 2020
[56:2:7] TABLE head: Farm law (Sept 2020) | Core provision
  [56:2:7.0] Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce Act | Trade in a "trade area" outside APMC yards, no State market fee; mentions APMCs and essential commodities but not MSP
  [56:2:7.1] Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act | Contract farming
  [56:2:7.2] Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act | Removed stock limits except in extraordinary situations
[56:2:8] - Passed under **Concurrent List Entry 33**; **repealed November 2021**.
[56:2:9] - **Post-1991 reforms (match):** GM crops → debates on food security and farmer rights; **WTO Agreement on Agriculture → market access beyond borders**; trade liberalisation → private participation/contract farming; price reforms → less government price control.
[56:2:10] - AP Markets (Amendment) Act **2005** added contract farming.
[56:2:11] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 04 p.164-168; app notes 3:56 sub 0, 1, 3, 4
## SUB 3 | Contract Farming, e-Choupal and Small Farmer Large Field
[56:3:0] - **Contract farming** = arrangement between farmer producers and agri-business firms to sell produce at a **pre-fixed Price or Quantity or Time or All Three**; buyer often supplies inputs and advice; **no land transfer**. Pioneer: **Punjab (PepsiCo, late 1980s)**.
[56:3:1] - **e-Choupal** = **ITC**'s internet-kiosk rural marketing network (2000).
[56:3:2] - **Small Farmer Large Field (UPSC 2023):** many marginal farmers in an area **organise into groups and synchronise/harmonise selected operations** – they work as one large field (no land surrender).
[56:3:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 02 p.31; app notes 3:56 sub 3; general knowledge (e-Choupal, SFLF key), not checked
## SUB 4 | Cooperative Marketing, NAFED and FPOs
[56:4:0] - **NAFED** (2 October 1958) = **apex cooperative marketing body at national level** – agricultural marketing (not FCI); PM-AASHA PSS: **pulses, oilseeds, copra**.
[56:4:1] - **TRIFED** (1987) = tribal produce marketing. **AP MARKFED** = apex of Cooperative Marketing Societies in AP; **Rs 3,000 crore Price Stabilisation Fund**.
[56:4:2] - **10,000 FPO scheme (2020):** Central Sector, **Rs 6,865 crore**; agencies **SFAC, NABARD, NCDC, NAFED**; one FPO per **block**; CBBO handholding **5 years**; management support Rs 18 lakh over 3 years; equity grant **Rs 2,000 per member** (max Rs 15 lakh); credit guarantee up to **Rs 2 crore**. Aim: bargaining power, scale, lower costs (not land transfer).
[56:4:3] - **NCDC** promotes cooperative-sector FPOs through PACS.
[56:4:4] - **Producer companies:** introduced by the **Companies (Amendment) Act, 2002** (Part IXA).
[56:4:5] - **SFAC "Millets Giveaway"** (IYM 2023): buy directly from FPOs, try ONDC's MyStore, adopt Shree Anna – **not FDI**.
[56:4:6] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.62, p.65; app notes 3:56 sub 7; general knowledge (Producer companies 2002), not checked
[56:4:7] - **10,000 FPO scheme period:** launched 2020; support continues till **2027-28**.
## SUB 5 | Operation Greens, Export Schemes and Agri Infrastructure
[56:5:0] - **Operation Greens:** **Union Budget 2018-19**, for **TOP (tomato, onion, potato)** price volatility, "**on the lines of Operation Flood**"; promotes FPOs, agri-logistics, processing; Ministry of **Food Processing Industries**.
[56:5:1] - **TOP to TOTAL:** Budget **2021-22**, **22** perishables; long-term grant 50% (**70% for FPOs**).
[56:5:2] - **Vishesh Krishi (and Gram) Upaj Yojana:** promotes **exports of agricultural produce** by offsetting freight costs.
[56:5:3] - **AIF (2020):** **Rs 1 lakh crore**; **3%** subvention on loans up to **Rs 2 crore**; guarantee via **CGTMSE**.
[56:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 02 p.11; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 07 p.11 (Budget 2018-19); app notes 3:56 sub 9
[56:5:5] - **Operation Greens timeline:** TOP announced in **Budget 2018-19**; the **2020 Atmanirbhar Bharat package** extended it temporarily to **all fruits and vegetables**; **Budget 2021-22** extended it to **22 perishables**.

## SUB 7 | Warehousing
[56:7:0] TABLE head: Act / body | Year

  [56:7:0.1] Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act | 2007

=== NOTES 3:58 | Public Distribution, Procurement and Buffer-stocking; Food Subsidy and Fci Reform
## SUB 0 | Price Terms, Economic Cost and Food Subsidy
[58:0:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [58:0:0.0] MSP | Floor price announced before sowing (CACP → CCEA)
  [58:0:0.1] Procurement price | Price at which the government buys grain for PDS and buffer stocks (announced separately at harvest from 1966-67; since 1968-69 MSP itself is the effective procurement price)
  [58:0:0.2] Central Issue Price (CIP) | Price at which the Centre supplies grain to States for distribution through fair price / ration shops
  [58:0:0.3] FPS retail price | Fixed by State Governments (States' role in PDS is operational)
  [58:0:0.4] Ceiling price | Maximum price that may be charged – protects consumers
  [58:0:0.5] Economic cost | MSP + bonus + procurement incidentals + distribution cost (UPSC 2019)
  [58:0:0.6] Food subsidy | Economic cost minus CIP
  [58:0:0.7] Hidden subsidy | FCI carrying cost financed by borrowing (NSSF loans) instead of budget releases
[58:0:1] - Pooled grain cost (MSP + bonus) ≈ **two-thirds** of economic cost. Subsidy components: **FCI subsidy + subsidy to DCP States**; **NSSF** borrowing ended and subsidy brought on budget in **Budget 2021-22**.
[58:0:2] - In the UPSC 2004 statements only **(c)** is right: wheat and rice are issued at **uniform CIPs**; procurement is **open-ended** (not target-based) and MSP is announced for pulses and oilseeds too, **not only cereals**.
[58:0:3] - **PDS issue prices were raised** to **lessen the subsidy burden**.
[58:0:4] TABLE head: Year | Food subsidy (₹ crore)
  [58:0:4.0] 1991-92 | 2,850
  [58:0:4.1] 1998-99 | 8,700 (CAG 2000: from ~2,800 in 1992-93 = more than three times)
  [58:0:4.2] 2000-01 | 12,010 total = buffer carrying cost 4,233 + consumer (PDS) subsidy ≈ 7,777 (BE 8,210)
  [58:0:4.3] 2024-25 | 1,99,500 (FCI 1,29,089 + DCP States 70,411)
  [58:0:4.4] Union Budget 2026-27 | ₹2,27,629 crore
[58:0:5] - **Flaws of the food security system:** subsidy burden, **inefficient FCI operations**, limited benefit to the poor – all of them.

## SUB 1 | Food Management and the FCI
[58:1:0] - **Objectives of PDS:** supply a **minimum quantity of grain at affordable prices to low-income groups**, equitable distribution, **control of price fluctuations**.
[58:1:1] - Procurement objectives: assure MSP, **free grain to the weak under PMGKAY**, market intervention. **Not objectives:** **controlling the production of foodgrains** (SSC 2008), **export of foodgrains**.
[58:1:2] TABLE head: FCI | Fact
  [58:1:2.0] Set up | 14 January 1965
  [58:1:2.1] Act | Food Corporations Act, 1964
  [58:1:2.2] Recommended by | Food Grains Prices Committee (L.K. Jha, 1964)
  [58:1:2.3] HQ | New Delhi
  [58:1:2.4] Role | Nodal agency for price-support purchase of wheat and paddy, with State agencies
[58:1:3] - **FCI missions:** procurement at MSP; storage, movement and distribution; operational and buffer stocks; grain at reasonable prices to weaker sections through TPDS. **Not a mission: regulation of markets in agricultural products** – that is done under **State APMC Acts** (APPSC 2018).
[58:1:4] - **OSM = Online Storage Management**, rolled out from **1 April 2022** for storage, movement and distribution under TPDS. **Anna Darpan** modernises **FCI's** supply chain (Dept of Food and PD, not Agriculture).
[58:1:5] - **OMSS (Domestic):** FCI sells wheat and rice from the Central Pool in the **open market at predetermined prices** to moderate prices.
[58:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 20 p.9; NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 01 p.37, 04 p.45, p.48; app notes 3:58 sub 0-2
## SUB 2 | Procurement, Buffer Stocks and Storage
[58:2:0] TABLE head: System | Feature
  [58:2:0.0] Centralised | FCI (directly or via State agencies) buys for the Central Pool
  [58:2:0.1] DCP (1997, with TPDS) | Designated States procure, store and distribute grain for TPDS; Centre pays their economic cost minus CIP
  [58:2:0.2] Open-ended | Wheat and paddy – all produce meeting standards at MSP
  [58:2:0.3] Target-based | PSS pulses and oilseeds – cap 25% of production
[58:2:1] - **Buffer stocks** (wheat and rice, bought from farmers at procurement prices) are released through PDS and open-market sales to **check price rise** and meet shortages.
[58:2:2] - **Buffer norms** fixed by **CCEA** quarterly – as on **1 April, 1 July, 1 October, 1 January**; 1 April norm **210.40 LMT** (rice 135.80, wheat 74.60).
[58:2:3] - **Strategic (food security) reserve:** **30 LMT wheat** (from 1 July 2008) and **20 LMT rice** (from 1 January 2009), included in the norms.
[58:2:4] - **604.02 LMT** in the Central Pool on 1 April 2026 – nearly **three times** the norm → **higher carrying costs**.
[58:2:5] - **CAP = Cover and Plinth** (grain on raised plinths under polythene covers); **steel silos under PPP**; **Grain Storage Plan** (cooperative sector): PACS chosen by **District Cooperative Development Committees**, implemented by **NCDC**.
[58:2:6] - **IGMRI** (Indian Grain Storage Management and Research Institute): **Hapur (UP)**; trains SAARC officials; field stations Hyderabad and Ludhiana.
[58:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 03 p.8; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.160-161; ies.gov.in Arthapedia "Buffer Stock" (fetched); app notes 3:58 sub 2, 5
## SUB 3 | PDS Evolution – RPDS, TPDS, AAY, NFSA, PMGKAY
[58:3:0] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [58:3:0.0] 1940s | Rationing – Bengal famine; revived in the 1960s shortages
  [58:3:0.1] June 1992 | RPDS – backward, hilly, drought-prone areas
  [58:3:0.2] June 1997 | TPDS – BPL and APL entitlements
  [58:3:0.3] 25 December 2000 | Antyodaya Anna Yojana – 35 kg per family per month to the poorest
  [58:3:0.4] 2013 | NFSA – legal entitlement for about 800 million (75% rural, 50% urban); first promulgated as an ordinance (July 2013), Act in September 2013
  [58:3:0.5] 1 Jan 2023 | Free grain under PMGKAY to 80 crore+; extended to 31 Dec 2028
[58:3:1] - Sequence: **PDS → RPDS → TPDS → AAY**. PMGKAY motto: "**One Nation-One Price-One Ration**".
[58:3:2] - **Fortified rice** (iron, **vitamin B12, folic acid**) through PDS to Dec 2028.
[58:3:3] - Of rights-based laws, only **NFSA** began as an ordinance; RTE, MGNREGA and RTI were passed directly as Acts.
[58:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 03 p.9; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.190; app notes 3:58 sub 6
## SUB 4 | PDS Reforms – ONORC, Leakage and the Shanta Kumar Committee
[58:4:0] TABLE head: Reform | Period / content
  [58:4:0.0] End-to-End Computerisation of TPDS | Oct 2012 – Mar 2020: digitised cards, online allocation, ePoS
  [58:4:0.1] IM-PDS | From April 2018; national portability (ONORC)
  [58:4:0.2] SMART-PDS | Apr 2023 – Mar 2026; part of SARTHAK-PDS
  [58:4:0.3] SARTHAK-PDS | 2026-2031 (CCEA, 28 May 2026); end-to-end tracking from procurement to FPS, real-time stock monitoring
[58:4:1] - **ONORC:** draw ration **away from where the card was issued** via ePoS, Aadhaar/biometric authentication; family draws the balance at home. App: **Mera Ration**; rollout target **1 June 2020**; now **all 36 States/UTs**.
[58:4:2] - **DBT in food:** Chandigarh, **Puducherry**, urban Dadra and Nagar Haveli (2015). **Delhi**: first **e-ration card** service (March 2015).
[58:4:3] - Anti-leakage measures: e-PoS, ONORC, biometrics (not "ending procurement").
[58:4:4] - **Coverage vs leakage:** States with **wider coverage had lower leakage** → **the lower the coverage, the higher the leakage**.
[58:4:5] - **Shanta Kumar HLC (2014-15):** PDS leakage **46%** (NSS 2011-12); only ~6% farmers sell at MSP; expand DCP; hand procurement in surplus States (Punjab, Haryana, AP) to States so FCI focuses on **eastern States**; cut NFSA coverage **67% → 40%** (not 50%); cash transfers; private storage.
[58:4:6] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.162, p.190; app notes 3:58 sub 7-8; e-ration card Delhi: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 5 | Andhra Pradesh PDS
[58:5:0] TABLE head: Indicator (APSES 2024-25) | Figure
  [58:5:0.0] Fair Price Shops | 29,796 (≈ 29,000)
  [58:5:0.1] Beneficiaries | 1.48 crore
  [58:5:0.2] Rice cards | 1.44 crore, 100% Aadhaar-seeded
[58:5:1] - APSES 2016-17: each FPS served about **450 ration cards**; AP had **one FPS per 1,376 persons** against the GoI norm of one per 2,000.
[58:5:2] - PDS in AP (2017): **ePoS**, **GPS-tracked transport vehicles**, **FPS portability**; doorstep delivery was **not** a feature then (MDU vehicles came in 2021 and were ended from **1 June 2025**; door delivery now only for those **above 65 and the disabled**).
[58:5:3] - **Mee Mart** (2026): AP Civil Supplies + NCCF turn FPS into mini-marts; first at **Lalupuram near Guntur**.

=== NOTES 3:59 | Malnutrition and Food Security – Indicators, Poshan Abhiyaan, Fortification, Pm Poshan
## SUB 0 | Malnutrition – Terms, Indicators and Burden
[59:0:0] TABLE head: Indicator | Measure | Type
  [59:0:0.0] Stunting | Low height-for-age | Chronic
  [59:0:0.1] Wasting | Low weight-for-height | Acute
  [59:0:0.2] Underweight | Low weight-for-age | Composite
[59:0:1] - **Undernutrition** = **protein-energy malnutrition + micronutrient deficiency + stunting + wasting** (i, ii, iii, v); overweight and **obesity** are **overnutrition**. Both together in one population = **double burden of malnutrition**.
[59:0:2] - Malnutrition results from **all** of: inadequate diet, disease/infection, poverty and food insecurity. Biggest factor: **poor dietary habits and food insecurity**; **open defecation and unsafe water** add through **disease-linked loss of nutrients** – it is multi-causal, not diet alone.
[59:0:3] - **Both rich and poor are malnourished** – the rich eat a wrong diet, the poor a poor diet (A and R true, R explains A).
[59:0:4] - **FAO estimate (c. 2012): about 245 million undernourished Indians** (SOFI 2022 revised series: 247.8 million in 2004-06 → **224.3 million in 2019-21**; SOFI 2025: 12.0% of the population).
[59:0:5] TABLE head: Indicator (under 5) | NFHS-5 | NFHS-6 (2026)
  [59:0:5.0] Stunting | 35.5% | 29.3%
  [59:0:5.1] Severe wasting | 7.7% | 5.2%
  [59:0:5.2] Underweight | 32.1% | 31.8% (barely moved)
  [59:0:5.3] Breastfed within 1 hour | 41.8% | 50.1%
  [59:0:5.4] Complementary feeding (6-8 months) | 45.9% | 59.5%
[59:0:6] - **Anaemia (NFHS-5):** children under 5 about **67%**, women about **57%**. **AP (NFHS-5):** stunting **31.2%**, wasting 16.1%, underweight 29.6%.
[59:0:7] TABLE head: Burden | State
  [59:0:7.0] Highest share of malnourished children (MoSPI 2011, ~60%) | Madhya Pradesh – "Ethiopia of India"
  [59:0:7.1] Stunting (Poshan Tracker, July 2025) | Uttar Pradesh (48.8%)
  [59:0:7.2] Wasting | Bihar (9.3%)
  [59:0:7.3] Underweight | Madhya Pradesh
[59:0:8] - **Anaemia** (mainly **iron** deficiency) is a leading cause of **maternal mortality**, rising in AP. FSSAI: no HFSS food sale within **50 m of schools**.
[59:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 03 p.8 (hunger types); theweek.in 7 Jul 2022 (SOFI 2022, fetched); app notes 3:59 sub 0-3; c.2012 FAO 245 million: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 1 | ICDS and National Nutrition Programmes
[59:1:0] TABLE head: Programme | Launch | Ministry
  [59:1:0.0] National Nutritional Anaemia Prophylaxis Programme | 1970 | Health
  [59:1:0.1] ICDS | 2 October 1975 | Women and Child Development
  [59:1:0.2] NIDDCP (renamed National Goitre Control Programme, 1962) | 1992 | Health and FW
  [59:1:0.3] NP-NSPE / Mid-Day Meal | 15 Aug 1995 (idea first in Tamil Nadu) | Education
  [59:1:0.4] National Programme for Prevention and Control of Fluorosis | 2008-09 | Health and FW
  [59:1:0.5] MAA (Mothers' Absolute Affection) – breastfeeding | 2016 | Health and FW
  [59:1:0.6] Anaemia Mukt Bharat | 2018 | Health and FW
  [59:1:0.7] PM POSHAN (renamed MDM) | 2021 | Education
[59:1:1] - APPSC pairs: "NIDDCP – 1999" and "Fluorosis – 2000" are **wrong**; **MAA – 2016** and **NNAPP – 1970** are **correct** (both 2 and 4).
[59:1:2] - **ICDS services:** supplementary nutrition, **pre-school non-formal education**, primary healthcare, **immunisation**, health check-up, referral, **nutrition and health education**. **Not:** **family planning**, free books, school dress.
[59:1:3] - National Nutrition Programmes include NIDDCP, National Iron Plus Initiative, Prevention and Control of Fluorosis – **not the National Oral Health Programme**.
[59:1:4] - **1000 Days approach** = conception to age two – **the nutritional foundation of the child**.
[59:1:5] - **National Nutrition Strategy (NITI Aayog, 2017)** envisages **Kuposhan Mukt Bharat**.
[59:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 03 p.9 (ICDS 1975); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.165; app notes 3:59 sub 4
## SUB 2 | PM POSHAN (Mid-Day Meal)
[59:2:0] - **NP-NSPE** (National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary Education) launched **15 August 1995** as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme in 2,408 blocks (started in UP the same year); renamed **PM POSHAN in 2021**.
[59:2:1] - Covers **Bal Vatika and classes I-VIII** in government and aided schools; financed and managed by the **Ministry of HRD (now Education)**; Centre-State **60:40** (non-NER States/UTs).
[59:2:2] - Cooking cost for Bal Vatika and primary raised to **₹6.78** per child per day.
[59:2:3] - Organised by **school management, PRIs and SHGs**; a **contractor** does not initiate or organise it. Partner NGO: **Akshay Patra Foundation** (2000, Bengaluru) – mid-day meals for school students.
[59:2:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:59 sub 7; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.165 (MDMS)
## SUB 3 | POSHAN Abhiyaan and Anaemia Mukt Bharat
[59:3:0] - **POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018):** goal **Suposhit Bharat**; pillars **convergence, technology, Jan Andolan** (people's movement); targets stunting, underweight, anaemia and low birth weight – **not adult obesity**.
[59:3:1] - **Rashtriya Poshan Maah = September**; **Poshan Pakhwada** (April, two weeks; 2025 edition) – to **improve nutrition**, especially of women and children.
[59:3:2] - **Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0** (2021-22 to 2025-26): **2 lakh** Saksham AWCs; **POSHAN Tracker** = real-time monitoring of Anganwadi services.
[59:3:3] - **Anaemia Mukt Bharat:** **IFA tablets, deworming**, outreach for **6 target groups**; **WIFS** for adolescents **10-19**; **delayed cord clamping** campaign; **periodic deworming**; addresses **non-nutritional causes** (malaria, haemoglobinopathies, fluorosis). It does **not** give prophylactic **calcium** → **only three** of the four UPSC 2023 statements are correct.
[59:3:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:59 sub 5-6; UPSC 2023 statements: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 4 | Food Fortification, GHI and SOFI
[59:4:0] TABLE head: Fortified rice phase | Year | Coverage
  [59:4:0.0] I | 2021-22 | ICDS and PM POSHAN
  [59:4:0.1] II | 2022-23 | 291 Aspirational and high-burden districts under TPDS
  [59:4:0.2] III | 2023-24 | All TPDS districts
[59:4:1] - FSSAI logo **"+F"**; **double-fortified salt = iodine + iron**.
[59:4:2] - **GHI 2025:** India **102nd of 123**, score 25.8 – "**serious**"; indicators: undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting, child mortality (not adult obesity). Government objection: **child-only indicators cannot measure hunger of the whole population**.
[59:4:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:59 sub 8-9

[59:5:0] - **Bala Sanjeevani** (plain areas; earlier **YSR Sampoorna Poshana**): take-home ration for pregnant and lactating women.

  [59:5:1.0] 36-72 months | Hot meal + egg + 100 ml milk | Meal + egg + 200 ml milk
  [59:5:1.1] 6-36 months | 2.5 kg Balamrutham + 25 eggs + 2.5 l milk | 2.5 kg + 30 eggs + 6 l milk
[59:5:2] - **Anna Amrutha Hastham:** one full meal a day at the AWC for **pregnant and lactating women**.
[59:5:3] - **Jagananna Gorumudda** renamed **Dokka Seethamma Madhyahana Badi Bojanam** (July 2024).
[59:5:4] - **AP ICDS (2024-25):** **55,607 AWCs, 257 projects**; adolescent-girl programme in **ASR, Parvathipuram Manyam and YSR Kadapa**.
