=== NOTES 3:60 | Allied Sectors – Horticulture, Animal Husbandry, Dairy, Fisheries (pmmsy), Agro-processing
## SUB 0 | Animal Husbandry Practice – Breeding, Health, Poultry and Meat
[60:0:0] - **Artificial insemination (AI):** semen of **superior bulls can reach every village**, it **avoids contagious (venereal) diseases** and it is **economical** – so "all of the above".
[60:0:1]   - **First scientific AI: Lazzaro Spallanzani** (Italy, in a dog, 1780); Ivanoff (Russia) developed it for farm animals.
[60:0:2]   - **First AI in India: Palace Dairy Farm, Mysore (1939)**, by Sampath Kumaran; Izzatnagar (UP) is the seat of IVRI.
[60:0:3] TABLE head: Delivery / reproduction term | Meaning
  [60:0:3.0] Calving / Lambing / Kidding / Whelping | Cow / sheep (ewe) / goat / dog gives birth
  [60:0:3.1] Prolapse | Falling out of part of the womb (uterus or vagina) before or after calving
  [60:0:3.2] Pyometra | Pus in the uterus (endometritis = inflammation of its lining)
  [60:0:3.3] Oestrus in buffalo | Lasts about 24-36 hours (longer than in cows)
  [60:0:3.4] Service period (cross-bred cow) | About 3 months (60-90 days) after calving → calving interval about 12-13 months
[60:0:4] - **Small ruminants = sheep and goats**; cattle and buffalo are large ruminants; horses, donkeys, pigs and rabbits are not ruminants.
[60:0:5] - **Epidural anaesthesia in cows: lignocaine (2%)** – thiopentone and propofol are general anaesthetics, morphine an opioid.
[60:0:6] - **Ranikhet (Newcastle) disease** of poultry shows **respiratory, nervous and gastrointestinal signs** – "all of these".
[60:0:7] - **Small dog breed: pug** (toy); boxer and Dalmatian are large, bulldog medium.
[60:0:8] TABLE head: Poultry practice | Norm
  [60:0:8.0] Storing hatching eggs | Best set within 1 week of laying (cool store)
  [60:0:8.1] Egg turning in the setter | At least 6-8 times a day
  [60:0:8.2] Setter → hatcher transfer | 18th day (chicken eggs hatch in 21 days)
  [60:0:8.3] Floor space, layer on deep litter | About 2 sq ft per hen
[60:0:9] TABLE head: Meat and slaughter-house norm | Value
  [60:0:9.0] Thawing meat for feeding zoo animals | 4-6 °C (in a refrigerator, not at room temperature)
  [60:0:9.1] Shelf life of canned meat | About 2 years
  [60:0:9.2] Floor gradient in a slaughter house | About 2 cm per metre (1 in 48 to 1 in 60 towards the drains)
[60:0:10] - **Rotational grazing:** livestock moved through a **sequence of paddocks (six or more)** several times a season so each paddock rests and regrows; leader-follower and creep grazing are its variants.
[60:0:11] ~~ Sources: general veterinary and animal-science knowledge, not checked against a library file (no local veterinary text); NextGen AP Economy has none of these technicalities
## SUB 1 | Horticulture – Fruits, Mango, Spices and GI
[60:1:0] - **Fruit ranks:** India is the **2nd largest producer of fruits and vegetables (China 1st)** – so "India ranks first in fruit production" is false; India is the largest producer of **mango, banana, guava, papaya**, spices, coconut and cashew.
[60:1:1] - **Top fruit by output in India: banana** (ahead of mango); **national fruit: mango**.
[60:1:2] - **Mango exports:** **Alphonso** (Maharashtra, Konkan) is the most exported and the preferred export variety; Kesar, Banganapalli and Totapuri follow.
[60:1:3] TABLE head: Mango GI | Year / State
  [60:1:3.0] Banganapalle (AP) | GI in May 2017
  [60:1:3.1] Marathwada Kesar | GI 30 Nov 2016 (Maharashtra)
  [60:1:3.2] Laxman Bhog, Himsagar | GI 2008 (West Bengal)
[60:1:4] - All four of these mangoes are now GI-registered; before May 2017 **Banganapalle** was the one not yet registered.
[60:1:5] - **GI tag** improves the **marketability** (premium price, protection from imitation) – it is not ornamental.
[60:1:6] - **'Kanchan'** is an improved variety of **aonla / amla (Indian gooseberry)**.
[60:1:7] - **Turmeric:** India is the **largest producer, consumer and exporter** (over 70% of world output); **30+ varieties**; major States **Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu** (and AP) – all three UPSC 2025 statements correct. **National Turmeric Board – Nizamabad**.
[60:1:8] - **Flowers:** the 2004 key said **Karnataka** (old floriculture leader around Bengaluru); now **Tamil Nadu** leads (about 21%), then Karnataka (16%), Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal.
[60:1:9] - **ICAR-IIHR** (Indian Institute of Horticultural Research) is at **Hesaraghatta, Bengaluru (Karnataka)**; it held the National Horticultural Fair 2023.
[60:1:10] - **FPO (Food Products Order) mark**: mandatory on processed fruit products (jams, squashes, pickles); ISI is for industrial goods, BEE for energy labels, Hallmark for gold.
[60:1:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 06 p.45 (India 2nd in fruit and vegetables; largest in mango, banana); PMF Lens July 2026 (2) p.73 (turmeric); CARE APPSC July 2026 p.21-22 (Alphonso, Banganapalli exports); IP India / web (Marathwada Kesar GI 2016); IBEF floriculture case study (Tamil Nadu 21%)
## SUB 2 | Food Processing – SAMPADA, Mega Food Parks, Operation Greens
[60:2:0] - **PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (2017)**: umbrella scheme of the **Ministry of Food Processing Industries (MoFPI)**; aim – **supplement agriculture, modernise processing and decrease agri-waste**. Its 'Unit' scheme: **32 projects sanctioned (2020)**.
[60:2:1] - **Mega Food Parks:** to **improve infrastructure for food processing**; cluster approach linking farmers, processors and retailers; aims (UPSC 2011): **good infrastructure, more processing of perishables / less wastage, and emerging eco-friendly technologies** – all three.
[60:2:2]   - Capital grant **50%** of project cost (75% in difficult / ITDP areas), ceiling ₹50 crore.
[60:2:3]   - **Italy's first Mega Food Park in India (June 2021): Fanidhar, Mehsana (Gujarat)**.
[60:2:4] - **Operation Greens (2018)**: on the lines of Operation Flood, for **Tomato-Onion-Potato (TOP)** price stabilisation; under **MoFPI**; promotes FPOs, agri-logistics and processing.
[60:2:5] - **PMFME**: micro food units under **One District One Product (ODOP)**.
[60:2:6] - **APEDA (1985, Ministry of Commerce)** promotes agri exports – e.g. an awareness camp for **potato** exports in **Agra** (Jan 2020).
[60:2:7] - **Processed food exports** = about **23%** of agri-food exports (23.4% in 2023-24, up from 13.7% in 2014-15; APPSC 2025 key "around 23").
[60:2:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 21 p.2 (Operation Greens); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.192-193 (Mega Food Parks); PMF Lens June 2026 (15) p.8 (processed food share); Rocket CA Jan 2026 p.87 (APEDA under Commerce); app notes 3:60 sub 7
## SUB 3 | Livestock – Population, Census and Schemes
[60:3:0] - **India has the largest livestock population in the world** (not China, Brazil or USA).
[60:3:1] - **20th Livestock Census (2019)**: **535.78 million** (+4.6%); cattle 192.49 million; buffalo 109.85 million.
[60:3:2] - **21st Livestock Census**: Oct 2024 – Feb 2025; **16 species**, **219** indigenous breeds.
[60:3:3] - **Output ranks:** eggs – India **2nd** (149.11 billion, 106 per head; **AP** top with 18.37%, then **Tamil Nadu**); meat – India **4th** (10.50 MT; **West Bengal** leads, 12.46%).
[60:3:4] TABLE head: Scheme | Year | Aim
  [60:3:4.0] Rashtriya Gokul Mission | 2014 | Conserve and develop indigenous bovine breeds (not high-yield exotic breeds, not slaughter ban)
  [60:3:4.1] National Livestock Mission | 2014-15; revised 2021-22 | Breed development (poultry, sheep, goat, piggery), feed and fodder, innovation and extension
  [60:3:4.2] AHIDF | 2020 | Animal husbandry infrastructure
  [60:3:4.3] LHDCP | – | Prophylactic vaccination, disease control
  [60:3:4.4] Credit Guarantee Scheme for Livestock | – (under AHIDF) | Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying – collateral-free loans (dairy, poultry); not NABARD, RBI or Finance Ministry
[60:3:5] - **National Kamdhenu Breeding Centres** (Rashtriya Gokul Mission): **Chintaladevi, Nellore (AP)** and **Itarsi (MP)**.
[60:3:6] - **Nandini Krishak Samriddhi Yojana (Uttar Pradesh, Nand Baba Mission):** units of 25 indigenous cows of **Sahiwal, Gir, Tharparkar and Gangatiri only**; beneficiary needs **at least 3 years** (not 1 year) of cattle-rearing experience.
[60:3:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 06 p.36 (largest livestock population); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 04 p.158; web (Nandini Krishak Samriddhi Yojana eligibility); app notes 3:60 sub 3-4
## SUB 4 | Dairy – Operation Flood, Cooperatives and Milk Science
[60:4:0] - **White Revolution = increase in milk production**; **Operation Flood** (NDDB) is the programme behind it – related to **milk production**, not floods or irrigation.
[60:4:1] - **Operation Flood (1970-1996)**: three phases; world's biggest dairy development programme; built on the **Anand pattern cooperatives (Amul)** – the engine of its success; India passed the USA as the largest milk producer in 1998.
[60:4:2] - **NDDB**: set up **1965 at Anand, Gujarat**.
[60:4:3] - **Co-operative dairying is most successful in Gujarat** (Anand, Amul, GCMMF) – the pioneer of India's cooperative dairy movement.
[60:4:4] - **Milk:** India 1st (about 25% of world), 471 g/day per capita; top States UP, Rajasthan, MP, Gujarat, Maharashtra. Yield **per cow is low in India**; **Denmark** has among the world's highest yields (ahead of the Netherlands and Great Britain).
[60:4:5] - **Milk science:** milk is a **colloid (emulsion)**; **skimmed milk has a higher specific gravity than whole milk** (fat, the lightest part, is removed: about 1.035 vs 1.032).
[60:4:6] - **HTST pasteurisation: 72 °C for 15 seconds** (batch/LTLT: 63 °C for 30 minutes).
[60:4:7] - India also leads world output of **butter and ghee**.
[60:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 21 p.1-2 (Operation Flood, Anand pattern; its "launched in 1966" is a slip for 1970); PMF Human & Economic Geography 06 p.31 (Gujarat pioneer of cooperative dairy); app notes 3:60 sub 4-5; general knowledge (milk density, HTST, Denmark yield)
## SUB 5 | Fisheries – Blue Revolution, Production and PMMSY
[60:5:0] - **Blue Revolution = fish production** (pisciculture); **NFDB** (autonomous, 2006, **HQ Hyderabad**) promotes it and handles **training and capacity building under PMMSY** (not MPEDA).
[60:5:1] - **China is the largest fish producer** (capture and aquaculture); (**36%** of world output in 2022, SOFIA 2024); **India 2nd** (about 8-9% of world); India **leads the world in inland capture** (2.2 MT, SOFIA 2026).
[60:5:2] - Output: 95.79 lakh t (2013-14) → **197.75 lakh t (2024-25)**; fisheries = about 7.43% of agri GVA.
[60:5:3] - **Inland fisheries** = raising and capturing fish in **fresh water**; inland = **about 77%** of output (15.16 MT of 19.78 MT, 2024-25), and most of it is **inland aquaculture (culture fisheries)** – capture is only about 2.2 MT. So the most important fish industry today is **culture inland**, not natural inland or deep-sea.
[60:5:4] - **PMMSY**: 2020, **₹20,050 crore**, FY 2020-21 to 2024-25, extended to 2025-26; Central Sector 100% (training, quarantine, harbour modernisation, data systems); Centrally Sponsored 60:40, 90:10 NE/Himalayan, 100% UTs.
[60:5:5] - **PM-MKSSY**: **Central Sector** sub-scheme under PMMSY (formalisation, micro-enterprises).
[60:5:6] - **FIDF**: fishing harbours and landing centres; credit guarantee up to ₹12.5 crore; KCC limit for fisheries raised to ₹5 lakh.
[60:5:7] - **MPEDA**: Act of Parliament **1972**; **HQ Kochi** (not Kolkata); **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**; seafood exports ₹62,408 crore (2024-25).
[60:5:8] - Fish growth rate 2024-25 (APPSC AO 2025 options 5.3 / 10.2 / 15.6 / 20.1): no official figure matching these options was found; production grew about 7.5% in 2024-25.
[60:5:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Lens July 2026 (2) p.70-71 (India 2nd, 8%, 197.75 lakh t, MPEDA, FIDF); PMF Human & Economic Geography 05 p.98-99 (China largest; inland and aquaculture 70-80%); weareaquaculture.com (Handbook 2025: inland 77%, 15.16 MT); downtoearth.org.in (SOFIA 2026: inland catch 2.2 MT); app notes 3:60 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Sericulture and Apiculture
[60:6:0] - **China is the largest silk producer; India 2nd** (with China, the bulk of world silk); India is the **only country producing all five commercial silks** – mulberry, tropical tasar, oak tasar, eri, muga.
[60:6:1] - **Mulberry silk** = the bulk of world raw silk (about **90-95%**).
[60:6:2] TABLE head: Silk | Leading State
  [60:6:2.0] Mulberry | Karnataka (about 50%); then AP, TN, WB
  [60:6:2.1] Tasar | Jharkhand
  [60:6:2.2] Muga, eri | Assam
[60:6:3] - **'Kausheya'** – ancient Sanskrit term for **silk** (from kosha, the cocoon).
[60:6:4] - **Honey bees:** the most common (domesticated) Indian species is **Apis indica (Apis cerana indica)**; Apis dorsata = rock bee, A. florea = little bee, A. mellifera = European (Italian) bee.
[60:6:5] - **National Beekeeping and Honey Mission (2020)**: **Sweet Revolution** via the **National Bee Board**.
[60:6:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC 10 p.10 (five silks, India 2nd after China, Karnataka 50% of mulberry); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.89 (mulberry States); general knowledge (Kausheya, Apis species, mulberry share)
## SUB 7 | Horticulture Missions – NHM and MIDH
[60:7:0] - **National Horticulture Mission (NHM)**: launched **May 2005** (2005-06); covered all States **except the North-Eastern and Himalayan States** (J&K, HP, Arunachal had the separate HMNEH) – so **Uttar Pradesh** is an NHM State.
[60:7:1]   - Objectives: **higher growth in horticulture**, **post-harvest management**, **human resource development**; mere "providing financial assistance" is the means, not an objective.
[60:7:2] - **MIDH** (Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture): Centrally Sponsored, **since 2014-15**; sub-schemes **NHM**, **HMNEH** (11 NE and Himalayan States), NHB, CDB, CIH (Nagaland); 60:40, 90:10 NE/Himalayan, 100% for national agencies.
[60:7:3] - Indo-Israel Centre of Excellence for Vegetables and Flowers, **Kuppam** (MIDH + MASHAV).
[60:7:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Lens July 2026 (2) p.72-73 (MIDH 2014-15, sub-schemes, NHM excludes NE/Himalayan); app notes 3:60 sub 2
## SUB 8 | Allied Sectors – Growth and Share
[60:8:0] - Farm growth now comes from allied sectors: **livestock (7.1%)** and **fishing and aquaculture (8.8%)** (ES 2025-26) – fisheries faster; ES also says allied sectors grow at a stable 5-6%.
[60:8:1] - **Livestock GVA** (2023-24): **₹15.06 lakh crore** = **30.87%** of agri GVA; **12.77%** nominal CAGR (FY15-FY24).
[60:8:2] - **Fisheries**: fastest-growing allied sub-sector – **9.08% a year since 2014-15**.
[60:8:3] - **Horticulture**: about **one-third (33%)** of agri GVA on under 14% of area; output **367.72 MT (2024-25)** > foodgrains **357.73 MT**.
[60:8:4] - Agri exports (2024-25): record **$51.9 billion** = 11.86% of merchandise exports; **processed food ≈ 23%** of agri exports.

=== NOTES 3:61 | Indian Industry – Structure, Growth, Iip and Public Sector
## SUB 0 | CPSE Profiles, Ownership and Performance
[61:0:0] # What is (and is not) a public enterprise
[61:0:1] - **CPSE** = a company in which the Central Government or other CPSEs hold **51%+** equity; the **Public Enterprises Survey** (DPE, on the **Estimates Committee's** advice) covers CPSEs with **over 50% GoI equity** and leaves out departmental undertakings, banks and insurers.
[61:0:2] - **Number of CPSEs:** **5** at the start of the First Plan (1951) → **244 by 1990** (end of the VII Plan) → **291 operating in 2024-25** (**226 profit-making, 63 loss-making**).
[61:0:3] - **Central PSUs (UPSC 2008):** **Balmer Lawrie and Co.**, **Dredging Corporation of India** and **EdCIL (Educational Consultants of India Ltd)** – all three.
[61:0:4] - **NOT public enterprises:** **TISCO / Tata Steel** (private, Jamshedpur 1907), **Essar Oil** (now Nayara Energy, private), **Indian Aluminium Co.** (private), Bharti Airtel, Renuka Sugars.
[61:0:5] - **BSNL** = **100% Government-owned**; NTPC, BHEL and SBI have public shareholders.
[61:0:6] TABLE head: CPSE | Field / fact
  [61:0:6.0] ONGC | Oil and Natural Gas Commission set up 14 Aug 1956 (statutory 1959); traditionally the top profit-maker
  [61:0:6.1] Oil India Ltd (OIL) | Oil exploration and production (crude, gas), not refining or marketing

  [61:1:0.3] Miniratna-II | 1997 | Profit 3 years running; positive net worth | ₹300 cr or 50% of net worth

## SUB 3 | Early Industry, Textiles and Major Industry Facts
[61:3:0] # Industrial firsts
[61:3:1] TABLE head: Year | Milestone
  [61:3:1.0] 1818 | First cotton mill, Fort Gloster (Ghusuri) near Kolkata – failed
  [61:3:1.1] 1854 | First successful mill, Bombay – Cowasjee Nanabhoy Davar (Bombay Spinning and Weaving Co.)
  [61:3:1.2] 1855 | First jute mill, Rishra (Bengal)
  [61:3:1.3] June 1906 | Munagala Raja's textile unit, Vijayawada – first in Madras Presidency
  [61:3:1.4] 1907 | TISCO, Jamshedpur (private)
  [61:3:1.5] 1932 | Tariff protection sets off the sugar industry
  [61:3:1.6] 3 April 1970 | Managing agency system abolished (Companies (Amendment) Act 1969)
[61:3:2] - Early **cotton mills** were mostly **Indian-owned**; **jute mills** mostly **foreign (British)-owned**.
[61:3:3] - **Textile firms by founding year:** **Bombay Dyeing (1879) → Lakshmi Mills, Coimbatore (1910) → Raymond (1925) → Grasim (1947-48)** = B, A, D, C.
[61:3:4] # Textiles
[61:3:5] - **Cotton textiles = oldest large-scale industry**; **largest textile centre = Mumbai** (also Ahmedabad).
[61:3:6] - **Textiles = largest agro-based industry**; sugar is next.
[61:3:7] - **Largest employer after agriculture** (and the industry with most workers): **textiles** – about **4.5 crore direct**.
[61:3:8] - **Largest cottage industry = handloom**; **powerlooms** make most cloth (mill, powerloom, handloom segments).
[61:3:9] - **National Handloom Development Programme:** concessional credit, marketing assistance, block-level clusters; benefits include loan waivers, concessional loans, fairs, loom upgradation, training – **both statements true**.
[61:3:10] # Sugar, cement, steel and others
[61:3:11] - **Sugar:** largest agro-based after textiles; about 5 lakh direct workers – **most employment among iron & steel, cement, sugar and petroleum**; **dual pricing** (levy + free-sale sugar); **cooperatives most successful** (Maharashtra, Gujarat).
[61:3:12] - **Sugar decontrol committee (2012):** **C. Rangarajan**.
[61:3:13] - **Cement:** about **87%** in a few States (Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh …), **near limestone** (not ports); India is **2nd**, not 1st, in world output.
[61:3:14] - **Steel:** **China > one-third** (about half) of world crude steel; India **2nd – 149.4 MT (2024)**; main imported input = **coking coal**.
[61:3:15] - **Nepanagar (MP):** **newsprint** (NEPA Ltd).
[61:3:16] - **HINDALCO, Renukoot:** sited for **abundant power** (Rihand hydel).
[61:3:17] - **Engineering industry** = largest segment of industry, about **3% of GDP** (Economic Survey 2011-12).
[61:3:18] TABLE head: Body | Ministry
  [61:3:18.0] National Automotive Board | Heavy Industries
  [61:3:18.1] Coir Board (Coir Industry Act 1953) | MSME
  [61:3:18.2] National Centre for Trade Information | Commerce and Industry
[61:3:19] - UPSC 2025: all three pairs as printed (NAB–Commerce, Coir–Heavy Industries, NCTI–MSME) are wrong → **None**.

## SUB 4 | Index of Industrial Production and Core Industries
[61:4:0] # IIP
[61:4:1] - Measures **short-term changes in the volume** of industrial production against a base period; **monthly**, by **NSO (MoSPI)** (earlier CSO).
[61:4:2] - Sectors: **mining, manufacturing, electricity**. **NOT included: construction**, agriculture, services.
[61:4:3] - **Base 2011-12 → 2022-23** (effective **1 June 2026**); basket **1,042 products** (old 809 items / 407 groups).
[61:4:4] - New weights (GVA share 2022-23): manufacturing **76.1%**, mining **11.1%**, electricity and gas **10.9%**; new: gas, water supply, sewerage, waste management.
[61:4:5] - Use-based (2011-12): **primary goods highest (~34%)**, **capital goods lowest (8.22%)**.
[61:4:6] - **Highest growth** in the early 2000s: **manufacturing** (2002-03); in **2000-01** among cement, coal, electricity, steel: **steel**.
[61:4:7] - FY 2023: capital goods and infrastructure goods grew fastest; FY 2024-25 IIP **4.0%**; **Jun 2026 IIP 7.3%** (23-month high).
[61:4:8] - **Index of Services Production:** base 2024-25; first release **14 July 2026**.
[61:4:9] # Core industries (ICI)
[61:4:10] - **Core sector** in planning = **selected basic industries**; ICI compiled monthly by the **Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT**.
[61:4:11] - **Eight:** coal, crude oil, natural gas, **refinery products**, **fertilisers**, steel, **cement**, **electricity**. NOT core: **transport, chemicals, textiles**.
[61:4:12] TABLE head: Feature | 2004-05 base | 2011-12 base | 2022-23 base (July 2026)
  [61:4:12.0] Number | 8 | 8 | 9 – iron ore added
  [61:4:12.1] Weight in IIP | 37.90% | 40.27% | 32.88%
  [61:4:12.2] Highest | Electricity | Refinery products 28.04% (electricity 19.85% 2nd) | Electricity 30.93%
  [61:4:12.3] Lowest | Fertilisers | Fertilisers 2.63% | Fertilisers 2.73%
[61:4:13] - Under the 2011-12 "new IIP", **refinery products** displaced electricity and steel as the dominant core industry.
[61:4:14] - New order: Electricity 30.93 > Refinery 22.57 > Steel 17.58 > Crude oil 7.43 > Coal 5.59 > **Iron ore 4.90** > Cement 4.41 > Natural gas 3.84 > Fertilisers 2.73; counts **only raw coal**, uses **gross steel output**.
[61:4:15] > Among coal, electricity, fertiliser and steel, **electricity** has the highest weight in every series.
[61:4:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 01 p.23-24; Rocket Indian Economy p.17; PMF Lens 2026-07-01 p.78 (revised ICI); app notes 3:61 sub 4, 5; general knowledge, not checked (2000-01 and 2002-03 growth)
## SUB 5 | Growth Phases, Structure and Problems
[61:5:0] TABLE head: Phase | Character | Growth (approx.)
  [61:5:0.0] 1951-65 | Public-sector-led heavy industrialisation | 7-8%
  [61:5:0.1] 1965-80 | Industrial deceleration: wars, droughts, infrastructure bottlenecks, licensing | about 4%
  [61:5:0.2] 1980s | Recovery with partial liberalisation | 7-8%
  [61:5:0.3] 1991 onward | Liberalisation; services outgrow industry | –
[61:5:1] - **Second Plan (1956-61):** priority to **basic and heavy industries** (Nehru-Mahalanobis model).
[61:5:2] - **IPR 1956** reserved **17** industries for the public sector; **1991** cut this to **8**.
[61:5:3] - **Commanding heights:** public sector took **capital-heavy, long-gestation** industries; early base – Hindustan Aircraft, **Sindri Fertilizers, Chittaranjan Locomotives, Integral Coach Factory, HMT**, ITI, Hindustan Cables.
[61:5:4] - **Premature deindustrialisation (Dani Rodrik):** manufacturing share peaks at a lower income level.
[61:5:5] # Since 1991
[61:5:6] - **Services, not industry,** gained the largest GDP share; **many PSEs disinvested/privatised**; **IT-software became a major growth contributor** → **only II and III** (APPSC).
[61:5:7] - Industry about **25.3% of GVA**; manufacturing real share **17-18%** (nominal fell only on relative prices); public sector about **13-14% of GDP**; medium/high-tech manufacturing **46.3%** (ES 2025-26).
[61:5:8] # Problems
[61:5:9] - **Capacity under-utilisation:** main cause = **deficient basic infrastructure** (power, transport, raw materials).
[61:5:10] - **Regional concentration:** Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka.
[61:5:11] - **Capital intensity** (reliance on machinery over labour): highest in manufacturing in **2017-18 = Madhya Pradesh**.
[61:5:12] - **Jobless growth:** directly employed workers 61% → 47% (2011-2023); contract workers about **42%**.
[61:5:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.3-5; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 14 p.4, p.10; app notes 3:61 sub 1-3
## SUB 6 | Public Sector Administration and Reform – DPE, MoU, PSE Policy 2021
[61:6:0] - **Department of Public Enterprises (DPE):** places CPSEs in **four schedules**, monitors **MoUs**, grants **Ratna status**, brings out the **Public Enterprises Survey**.
[61:6:1] - **Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises** consisted of the **Department of Heavy Industry + Department of Public Enterprises** (CDS 2020); **since July 2021 DPE is under the Ministry of Finance** and the parent is now the **Ministry of Heavy Industries**.
[61:6:2] - **PESB** (Public Enterprises Selection Board) selects **board-level executives** of CPSEs.
[61:6:3] TABLE head: Committee / body | Role
  [61:6:3.0] Arjun Sengupta (1984) | Autonomy → MoU system
  [61:6:3.1] Rangarajan (1993) | Disinvestment
  [61:6:3.2] BRPSE (2004) | Revival of sick CPSEs
[61:6:4] - **MoU:** annual targets for **all CPSEs, including subsidiaries**, through a High Power Committee.
[61:6:5] - **New PSE Policy 2021:** four **strategic** sector groups (atomic energy, space, defence; transport, telecom; power, petroleum, coal, minerals; banking, insurance, finance) keep **1 to 4** PSEs; **non-strategic** PSEs privatised or closed.
[61:6:6] - **MSMED (Amendment) Bill 2026:** every CPSE to settle MSME invoices on **TReDS**.
[61:6:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 02 p.41 (DPE under the Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises ministry); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 14 p.10 (MoU, disinvestment); app notes 3:61 sub 9; general knowledge, not checked (DPE move to Finance, July 2021)
## SUB 7 | Andhra Pradesh Industrial Profile
[61:7:0] - Industry share of AP GSVA: **21.16% (2024-25)**, **21.57% (2025-26)**; manufacturing about **11% of GSDP**.
[61:7:1] - **General Index of Industrial Production, AP, 2005-06: 188.7**.
[61:7:2] - **Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29):** ₹30 lakh crore; exports **$20 bn → $40 bn**; Ultra-Mega = above **₹5,001 cr**.
[61:7:3] - Clusters: **Visakhapatnam** (RINL steel, port), **Krishnapatnam port region – heavy industries**.
[61:7:4] - **State PSUs:** AP has many, e.g. **APIIC**, APSRTC, APGENCO (so "no state-level public enterprises" is false).

=== NOTES 3:62 | MSMEs – Definition, Contribution, Problems, Credit and Support Schemes
## SUB 0 | Support Institutions and Credit Schemes
[62:0:0] TABLE head: Institution | Year / Act | HQ / note | Role
  [62:0:0.0] SIDBI – Small Industries Development Bank of India | 2 April 1990, SIDBI Act 1989 | Lucknow | Apex bank that operates mainly for small industries / MSMEs (not IDBI, ICICI, NABARD)
  [62:0:0.1] NSIC – National Small Industries Corporation | 1955 | New Delhi; Miniratna, Ministry of MSME | Works with State SSIDCs; marketing of small industry products, raw materials, credit
  [62:0:0.2] KVIC | KVIC Act 1956; April 1957 | Mumbai | Khadi, village and coir industries; runs PMEGP
  [62:0:0.3] All India Khadi and Village Industries Board | 1953 – First Plan | – | KVIC's predecessor
  [62:0:0.4] SFCs | SFC Act, 1951 | State level | Term loans to small industry
  [62:0:0.5] Ministry of MSME | 2007 | – | SSI + Agro and Rural Industries ministries merged
[62:0:1] - **SIDBI:** **July 2022 tie-up with SVC Co-operative Bank** for MSME lending; implements **PM SVANidhi**; runs **Udyam Abhilasha** (2021).
[62:0:2] - **KVIC** opened its **first silk processing plant at Surendranagar, Gujarat** (2018).
[62:0:3] - **Udyami Helpline** = call centre of the **Ministry of MSME** (opened by Dr Manmohan Singh).
[62:0:4] - **National Level Awareness Programme (17-28 Feb 2020)** = **Ministry of MSME**.
[62:0:5] TABLE head: Tool | Key fact
  [62:0:5.0] CGTMSE – Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises | Began as the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Industries (CGFSI/CGTSI), launched 30 Aug 2000 by the Government of India and SIDBI; corpus GoI : SIDBI = 4:1; collateral-free guarantees
  [62:0:5.1] MUDRA – Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency | 8 April 2015; wholly owned subsidiary of SIDBI; refinances micro loans by banks, NBFCs and MFIs (all of these)
  [62:0:5.2] PMMY | Loans to micro and small (non-corporate, non-farm) enterprises: Shishu, Kishor, Tarun, Tarun Plus; collateral-free up to ₹20 lakh (no "Vriddhi")
  [62:0:5.3] ECLGS | Covid-era (2020) guarantee; ECLGS 5.0 (May 2026) – 100% for units hit by the West Asia crisis
  [62:0:5.4] TReDS (2017) | RBI-regulated invoice discounting – RXIL, M1xchange, Invoicemart
[62:0:6] - **MUDRA purpose:** easy finance to **set up small businesses** for the **non-corporate small business sector** – not currency reform or farm loans.
[62:0:7] - **Priority sector:** **all bank loans to MSMEs** (Udyam-registered) qualify (UPSC 2023).
[62:0:8] - **RBI (Feb 2026):** no collateral for MSE loans up to **₹20 lakh** (banks may go to ₹25 lakh). **Budget 2026-27:** all **CPSE purchases from MSMEs on TReDS**, CGTMSE guarantees for TReDS discounting.
[62:0:9] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.3, p.44; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.11; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 08 p.1; NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 04 p.53; web: eparlib.sansad.in parliamentary answer on CGFSI (30 Aug 2000, GoI and SIDBI); app notes 3:62 sub 6, 7; general knowledge, not checked (SVC tie-up, KVIC silk plant, NLAP)
## SUB 1 | MSME Definition – Evolution and Current Limits
[62:1:0] TABLE head: Year | Small-scale / MSME limit
  [62:1:0.0] 1950 | Small unit = gross fixed capital (investment) up to ₹5 lakh
  [62:1:0.1] 1966 → 1975 → 1980 | Plant and machinery ₹7.5 lakh → ₹10 lakh → ₹20 lakh
  [62:1:0.2] 1991 | Industrial Policy: small unit ₹35 lakh → ₹60 lakh; ancillary ₹45 lakh → ₹75 lakh
  [62:1:0.3] 1995-96 | Foreign / other-industry equity in SSI up to 24%
  [62:1:0.4] 1997 → 1999 | ₹3 crore → ₹1 crore (₹100 lakh) – the limit in 2004
  [62:1:0.5] 2 Oct 2006 | MSMED Act – separate manufacturing / services limits
  [62:1:0.6] 1 June 2020 | Composite investment + turnover criterion notified (effective 1 July 2020) – latest classification at the 2021 exam
  [62:1:0.7] 1 April 2025 | Limits raised (Budget 2025-26)
[62:1:1] - **Original MSMED Act limits (investment only):**
[62:1:2] TABLE head: MSMED Act 2006 | Manufacturing (plant and machinery) | Services (equipment)
  [62:1:2.0] Micro | up to ₹25 lakh | up to ₹10 lakh
  [62:1:2.1] Small | above ₹25 lakh – ₹5 crore | up to ₹2 crore
  [62:1:2.2] Medium | above ₹5 crore – ₹10 crore | up to ₹5 crore
[62:1:3] - **2020 composite criterion (Atmanirbhar package):**
[62:1:4] TABLE head: Category | 2020 (investment / turnover) | From 1 April 2025
  [62:1:4.0] Micro | ₹1 cr / ₹5 cr | ₹2.5 cr / ₹10 cr
  [62:1:4.1] Small | ₹10 cr / ₹50 cr | ₹25 cr / ₹100 cr
  [62:1:4.2] Medium | ₹50 cr / ₹250 cr (not ₹15-25 cr) | ₹125 cr / ₹500 cr
[62:1:5] - Basis now: **investment in plant and machinery/equipment AND annual turnover**; manufacturing/services distinction removed. Example: ₹8 cr investment, ₹40 cr turnover = **small** (2020).
[62:1:6] - Under the MSMED Act the categories are **micro, small and medium** – "small-scale industry" is the old (pre-2006) label.
[62:1:7] - **Nature and size of an industry** (UPSC 2001 key): **capital investment, labour force, power consumption** (turnover also relevant).
[62:1:8] - The micro **turnover ceiling was never ₹15 crore** (2020: ₹5 crore; 2025: ₹10 crore).
[62:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.2 (24% equity); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 14 p.11; app notes 3:62 sub 0, 1; web: business-standard.com 2018 / taxmann.com MSME classification FAQs (2020 and 2025 limits)
## SUB 2 | Role, Contribution and Problems
[62:2:0] # Why small and cottage industries
[62:2:1] - **Labour-intensive, low capital** → **generate large employment** (the primary reason to encourage them); disperse industry; reduce **concentration of economic power**; ancillaries to large industry; priority since the **First Plan**.
[62:2:2] - Small-scale sector = about **40% of manufacturing gross turnover** (since 1992).
[62:2:3] - **Industrial clusters** help MSMEs (inclusiveness, technology, efficiency), exist in handloom, handicrafts and modern SMEs, are run by several ministries – they **do not promote monopoly**.
[62:2:4] TABLE head: Indicator (Rajya Sabha, Aug 2026) | Figure
  [62:2:4.0] Share in GDP | 31%
  [62:2:4.1] Share in manufacturing output | 36%
  [62:2:4.2] Share in exports | 41%
  [62:2:4.3] Outstanding MSME credit | ₹38.35 lakh crore
[62:2:5] - Udyam: **6.63 crore** registered (1 July 2020 – 31 July 2025); **micro = 95.88%**.
[62:2:6] # Problems
[62:2:7] TABLE head: Problem | Detail
  [62:2:7.0] Finance / capital | Shortage of working capital = main SSI problem
  [62:2:7.1] Marketing | Weak marketing and exports
  [62:2:7.2] Raw materials | Scarce, costly
  [62:2:7.3] Delayed payments | MSME Samadhaan (2017)
  [62:2:7.4] Others | No latest technology, power, poor managerial skills, sickness
[62:2:8] - **IPR 1948** listed handicaps: **raw materials, finance, marketing, technology** → "all of the above".
[62:2:9] - **Strikes and lockouts** = problem of **large** industries, NOT SSIs; excess cheap credit is not a problem.
[62:2:10] - **Globalisation and WTO** hit **small-scale industrialists and businessmen** hardest (cheap imports, dereservation).
[62:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.12-14; app notes 3:62 sub 4, 5; general knowledge, not checked (clusters, globalisation)
## SUB 3 | MSMED Act, Procurement and Payments
[62:3:0] - **Chapter V (delayed payments):** pay an MSE within **45 days**; else **compound interest at 3 times the RBI bank rate**; disputes → **MSE Facilitation Council**.
[62:3:1] - **MSMED (Amendment) Bill 2026:** every **CPSE to settle MSME invoices on TReDS**.
[62:3:2] - **Public Procurement Policy for MSEs Order, 2012:** **25%** of annual procurement from MSEs (from **20% in 2018**); **4% SC/ST**, **3% women**; achieved FY26 (to 1 Dec 2025) **44.76%**.
[62:3:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:62 sub 2
## SUB 4 | SSI Reservation and Committees
[62:4:0] - Reservation began **1967 with 47 items** → peak about **873 (1984)** → **125 dereserved on 13 March 2007, leaving 114** (the number "until 2007") → **79 more in Feb 2008, leaving 35** → last **20 dereserved in 2015**.
[62:4:1] TABLE head: Year | Committee | Subject
  [62:4:1.0] 1955 | Karve (Planning Commission) | Village and small industries; avoid technological unemployment; decentralised development
  [62:4:1.1] 1992 | P.R. Nayak (RBI) | Working-capital credit to SSIs
  [62:4:1.2] 1997 | Abid Hussain | Small and medium industries – abolish reservation, deregulation; small units defined by capital investment
  [62:4:1.3] 2001 | S.P. Gupta | Credit access for SSI
  [62:4:1.4] 2019 | U.K. Sinha (RBI) | MSME finance
[62:4:2] - Karve = **1955** (NextGen prints "1995" – a typo). Abid Hussain also chaired the 1984 trade-policy committee.
[62:4:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.95; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.13; app notes 3:62 sub 3
## SUB 5 | Entrepreneurship Schemes
[62:5:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Key fact
  [62:5:0.0] PMEGP (2008) | = PMRY + REGP; margin-money subsidy; run by KVIC; women up to 35%
  [62:5:0.1] Stand-Up India (April 2016) | Bank loans ₹10 lakh – ₹1 crore for greenfield units of SC/ST and women; non-individual units need 51% with them
  [62:5:0.2] Udyam Abhilasha (2021) | SIDBI awareness campaign, aspirational districts
  [62:5:0.3] Udyam Registration (2020) | Free, paperless, self-declaration; linked to GeM, income tax, GST, TReDS
  [62:5:0.4] Startup India | Recognition up to 10 years; turnover ₹200 crore; deep-tech 20 years
  [62:5:0.5] PM Vishwakarma | 18 trades; ₹500/day training stipend; credit up to ₹3 lakh at 5%
[62:5:1] - **RAMP:** **World Bank**-supported; **Self-Reliant India Fund (2021):** equity through daughter funds; **MSE-CDP:** grants for **common facility centres**; **Budget 2026-27:** ₹10,000 crore **SME Growth Fund**.
[62:5:2] - **State schemes:** **Udyam Kranti Yojana** (Madhya Pradesh) = **collateral-free credit for youth self-employment**; **SEMFEX** (ex-servicemen) loans in Rajasthan through the **Rajasthan Financial Corporation (RFC)**.

## SUB 6 | Andhra Pradesh MSME
[62:6:0] - **APSFC (1956)**, **APSSIDC** and **APIIC** promote **small-scale industries** (finance, raw materials/marketing, industrial estates).
[62:6:1] - **RESTART package (2020)** = relief for **MSME units** (dues, power charges, working capital).
[62:6:2] - **YSR Navodayam (2019):** one-time **restructuring of stressed MSME loans**.
[62:6:3] - **MSME and Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29)**; MSME Policy 2026 – incentives for **women-led** MSMEs; MSE-CDP through **APIIC**.

=== NOTES 3:63 | Industrial Policy – 1948, 1956, 1977, 1980 and New Industrial Policy 1991
## SUB 0 | New Industrial Policy 1991 – Delicensing and Liberalisation
[63:0:0] # The Policy
[63:0:1] - **Date:** **24 July 1991** – PM **P.V. Narasimha Rao**, FM **Manmohan Singh**; announced amid the **balance-of-payments crisis** (forex for about two weeks of imports, June 1991).
[63:0:2] - **Liberal industrial policy = 1991:** start of **LPG**; ended the **'Licence-Permit-Quota Raj'** (term coined by C. Rajagopalachari, Swatantra Party) – licensing, expansion limits, price controls and import-export curbs removed.
[63:0:3] - **Liberalisation started with** **substantial changes in industrial licensing policy** (UPSC 2000) – not rupee convertibility or tax cuts.
[63:0:4] - **Result (APPSC AEE 2011):** **liberalisation of industrial licensing and foreign-trade regulations** – not privatisation of core PSEs, not an immediate abolition of FERA.
[63:0:5] - **Repealed Act:** **FERA 1973** was replaced by **FEMA 1999** (in force 1 June 2000) – the Act repealed as part of liberalisation; FEMA is the successor, not the repealed Act.
[63:0:6] - **Liberalisation tools:** **delicensing, import deregulation, lower import duty on capital goods** → cheaper technology and capital equipment, more competitive home manufacturing.
[63:0:7] - Government role moved from **regulator → facilitator**; NIP 1991 was the primary anchor of **liberalisation**.
[63:0:8] # Delicensing – the numbers

  [63:0:9.1] 1993 | Automobiles, white goods, leather delicensed

## SUB 1 | Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 – the 'Economic Constitution'
[63:1:0] # Background
[63:1:1] - Announced **30 April 1956** (placed before Parliament by **Jawaharlal Nehru**); reviewed IPR 1948 after the First Plan (1951-56).
[63:1:2] - Goal: **"Socialistic pattern of society"** – Lok Sabha resolution Dec 1954, Congress **Avadi session, 1955**.
[63:1:3] - Labels: **"Economic Constitution of India"**, **"Bible of State Capitalism"**; **basis of the Second Five-Year Plan** (Mahalanobis model – heavy and basic industries).
[63:1:4] - Significance: established the **public-sector-led, licence-based** model that lasted, with minor changes, until **1991**.
[63:1:5] # Three Schedules
[63:1:6] TABLE head: Schedule | Industries | Role of the State
  [63:1:6.0] A | 17 basic and strategic (defence, heavy industry, minerals, transport and communication, power); arms and ammunition, atomic energy, railways, air transport = State monopolies | Exclusive responsibility of the State
  [63:1:6.1] B | 12 (other minerals, road and sea transport, machine tools, ferro-alloys, basic chemicals, drugs, fertilisers, synthetic rubber, aluminium and non-ferrous metals) | Progressively State-owned; private sector may supplement
  [63:1:6.2] C | All remaining | Left to private initiative, subject to licensing
[63:1:7] # Major Provisions
[63:1:8] - **Provision of licensing, expansion of the public sector, emphasis on small and cottage industries** (APPSC G2 Mains 2025: all three correct); also **balanced regional development**, labour welfare, khadi and village industries.
[63:1:9] - **Licence raj:** compulsory licensing for Schedule B and many Schedule C industries was cemented in IPR 1956 – the start of the 'Licence-Quota-Permit raj'.
[63:1:10] - Licensing itself drew its legal strength from the **Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951** (not from IPR 1948 or 1956, and not from the MRTP Act).
[63:1:11] - **Basic industries:** iron and steel, cement, fertilisers, coal, power – **paper is not a basic industry** (it is a consumer-goods industry).
[63:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 21 p.7-9; NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.25, 35; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 05 p.9.4-9.5; Rocket Indian Economy p.2, 5, 54
## SUB 2 | Industrial Policy Resolution 1948 – First Policy and Mixed Economy
[63:2:0] - **First industrial (economic) policy of independent India:** **6 April 1948** (some books print 8 April), by Industry Minister **Dr Shyama Prasad Mukherjee**.
[63:2:1] - It provided for a **mixed economy** – it **defined the roles and spheres of both public and private sectors**; it neither nationalised all key industries nor left everything to private enterprise.
[63:2:2] - Preceded by the **Statement of Industrial Policy, 1945** (pre-independence); followed by the **IDR Act, 1951**.
[63:2:3] TABLE head: Category | Industries | Arrangement
  [63:2:3.0] Exclusive Central monopoly | Arms and ammunition, atomic energy, railways | State only
  [63:2:3.1] Mixed sector (6) | Coal, mineral oils, iron and steel, aircraft, shipbuilding, telephone/telegraph apparatus | New units by the State; existing private units allowed 10 years, then review
  [63:2:3.2] Centrally regulated (18) | Salt, automobiles, heavy chemicals, fertilisers, power, textiles, cement, sugar, paper etc. | Private, under Central regulation
  [63:2:3.3] Residual | All others | Private and co-operative
[63:2:4] - Also: importance to **cottage and small-scale industries**; foreign capital welcomed with control in **Indian hands**.
[63:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 21 p.5-7; NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.25, 35; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 05 p.9.3
## SUB 3 | Licensing Committees, Joint Sector and MRTP
[63:3:0] TABLE head: Person / committee | Contribution
  [63:3:0.0] Swaminathan (1964), Mahalanobis (1964) | Early reviews of licensing
  [63:3:0.1] R.K. Hazari report (1967) | Industrial licensing – big business houses had cornered the licences
  [63:3:0.2] Subimal Dutt – Industrial Licensing Policy Inquiry Committee (1967, report 1969) | Led to the MRTP Act 1969; recommended the joint sector
[63:3:1] - **Outcome of the licence regime:** it did **not** prevent concentration of economic power – a powerful industrial house could always procure fresh licences, so the result was the **expansion of big industrial houses**.
[63:3:2] - **MRTP Act 1969** (in force 1970): prevent concentration of economic power and monopolistic practices; replaced by the **Competition Act, 2002**.
[63:3:3] - **Joint sector** (State + private partnership): recommended by the **Dutt Committee (1969)**, developed in the **Industrial Policy Statement 1973**; many keys (UPPCS 2004, Rocket) link it to **IPR 1956**.
[63:3:4] - Licence raj criticised for **rent-seeking**, entry barriers, delays and red tape.
[63:3:5] > Trap: Hazari = report 1967; Dutt = Inquiry Committee 1969 → MRTP and joint sector.
[63:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 22 p.5; NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.29; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 05 p.9.5-9.6; Rocket Indian Economy p.2
## SUB 4 | Policy Statements 1973, 1977 and 1980
[63:4:0] # 1973 Statement
[63:4:1] - First identified a list of **'core sector'** industries (iron and steel, cement, coal, crude oil, refining, electricity); developed the joint sector; **FERA 1973**.
[63:4:2] - **Reservation of items for SSI** began in **1967** and continued after 1991; fully removed in **2015**.
[63:4:3] # Industrial Policy Statement 1977 (Janata Government)
[63:4:4] - Drafted largely by **George Fernandes**.
[63:4:5] - Main thrust: **small-scale, tiny and cottage industries**, khadi, handlooms – because they generate **large employment** (APPSC G1 1990-91 and G2 2017 – not heavy industry, FDI or mining).
[63:4:6] - **District Industries Centres (DICs):** one-roof support to small and cottage industries in every district.
[63:4:7] - Curbed large houses through **MRTP and FERA** → **IBM and Coca-Cola** left India; Coca-Cola left (1977) rather than dilute equity and **reveal its secret formula** to the Government.
[63:4:8] # Industrial Policy Statement 1980 (Congress)
[63:4:9] - Built on **IPR 1956**; removed the 'artificial barrier' between large and small units.
[63:4:10] - Focus: **technological upgradation**, modernisation and **export orientation** (first strong export emphasis).
[63:4:11] - **Economic federalism:** tax holidays and cheap credit for **backward districts**.
[63:4:12] - Regularised excess capacity; MRTP firms could expand capacity **25%** without approval; SSI investment limits raised.
[63:4:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 21 p.9-10; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 05 p.9.6-9.7; app notes 3:63 sub 4
## SUB 5 | NIP 1991 – Foreign Investment, MRTP and Finance
[63:5:0] - **FDI:** **automatic approval up to 51% foreign equity** in a list of **high-priority, high-investment, high-technology** industries (capital goods, entertainment electronics, food processing) – **not all industries**; NRIs were encouraged, not barred.
[63:5:1] - Automatic approval for **foreign technology agreements** in priority industries; foreign brand names allowed; 100% in EOUs, power, software parks; foreign equity up to **24%** in SSI units.
[63:5:2] - Policy towards foreign **multinationals: encouraging them** (Enron, Coke).
[63:5:3] - **FIPB** set up to speed approvals; **abolished June 2017** (Cabinet decision 24 May 2017) → approvals by ministries through the **Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal** run by **DIPP (now DPIIT)** → **National Single Window System** (Aug 2022).
[63:5:4] - **MRTP:** asset threshold (₹100 crore) **scrapped** → no prior approval for expansion, mergers, takeovers → M&A rose.
[63:5:5] - **Mandatory convertibility clause** (FIs converting term loans into equity) **no longer applicable** – abolished for new projects, ending the indirect threat of nationalisation.
[63:5:6] - Now: **100% automatic route** in most sectors.
[63:5:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 22 p.2; NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 13 p.5-7; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 05 p.9.10-9.12
## SUB 6 | NIP 1991 – Public Sector Reservation and PSU Reform
[63:6:0] TABLE head: Stage | Reserved for the public sector
  [63:6:0.0] IPR 1956 | 17 (Schedule A)
  [63:6:0.1] NIP 1991 | 8 – arms and ammunition, atomic energy, coal and lignite, mineral oils, specified minerals, atomic minerals, rail transport
  [63:6:0.2] Later | 3 – arms and ammunition, atomic energy, rail transport
  [63:6:0.3] Now (DPIIT Annual Report 2024-25) | 2 – atomic energy and railway operations
[63:6:1] - **Arms and ammunition** opened to the private sector on **9 May 2001**.
[63:6:2] - Public-sector-only list never included **pharmaceuticals**.
[63:6:3] - **1991 PSU measures:** autonomy via **Memoranda of Understanding**; up to **20% disinvestment** in selected PSUs (began **1991-92**); chronically sick PSUs referred to **BIFR**; National Renewal Fund (**1992**).
[63:6:4] - **2016:** SICA repealed, BIFR dissolved → cases to the **IBC**.
[63:6:5] > Today's two are NOT "atomic energy and defence". Reserved 17 → 8 → 3 → 2.
[63:6:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 22 p.1-2; NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.35; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 05 p.9.10; DPIIT Annual Report 2024-25 para 2.8.1 (dpiit.gov.in)
## SUB 7 | Impact and Criticism of the 1991 Policy
[63:7:0] - **Criticisms of NIP 1991:** ambiguous policy for weak industries, **threat from foreign competition**, **misplaced faith in foreign investment**, **erratic industrial growth**, regional concentration (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka), small units closed by cheap imports.
[63:7:1] - **"Neglect of agriculture"** is a criticism of the reform package as a whole (NCERT), **not** of the industrial policy (Jharkhand PSC 2013).
[63:7:2] - **NOT criticisms (achievements):** higher growth, FDI and forex surge, **increase in consumer choice**, global Indian MNCs.
[63:7:3] - MSMEs hurt by **import competition** after protection was removed.
[63:7:4] - Forex reserves record **USD 702.28 bn (Nov 2025)**.
[63:7:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 03 p.42; NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 14 p.8; app notes 3:63 sub 8
## SUB 8 | DIPP to DPIIT
[63:8:0] TABLE head: Year | Change
  [63:8:0.0] 1995 | DIPP (Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion) created as a separate department
  [63:8:0.1] 2000 | Department of Industrial Development merged into DIPP
  [63:8:0.2] 2019 | Renamed DPIIT – Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
  [63:8:0.3] Nov 2021 | Logistics mandate allotted
[63:8:1] - Mandate: **FDI policy**, industrial licensing, Startups, IPR, industrial corridors, Make in India, PLI, EoDB.
[63:8:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 22 p.16; app notes 3:63 sub 9
## SUB 9 | Andhra Pradesh Industrial Policies
[63:9:0] - **AP Industrial Policy 2005-10:** proposed changes in the State **Cooperative Act** (State subjects – the IDR and MRTP Acts are Central laws).
[63:9:1] - **AP Industrial Investment Promotion Policy 2015-20**.
[63:9:2] - **AP Industrial Development Policy 2020-23:** objectives – **employment for the youth**, match the national average of industrial GVA per capita, **balanced growth across regions and communities**, **environmentally sustainable growth** ("enhance gainful employment" is a stated goal of the national industrial policy, not this one).
[63:9:3] - **AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29):** **G.O.Ms.No.68, 26 Oct 2024**; valid **5 years or till a new policy**.
[63:9:4] - Targets: **₹30 lakh crore** investment, **USD 10 bn FDI** (not 100 bn), **5 lakh** jobs, exports **$20 → $40 bn**, **175+ industrial parks**.
[63:9:5] - Approvals: **SIPB = Chief Minister**; **SIPC = Chief Secretary**.
[63:9:6] TABLE head: Sector type / policy | Content
  [63:9:6.0] Sustenance sectors | Automobiles, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, textiles
  [63:9:6.1] Propelling sectors | Semiconductors and electronics, EVs, aerospace-defence, blue economy, green energy
  [63:9:6.2] MSME and Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29) | "One Family One Entrepreneur"; 175 MSME parks; capital subsidy 25% (45% special categories)
  [63:9:6.3] Aerospace and Defence, Space 4.0 | 2025-30
  [63:9:6.4] Maritime Policy 2024-29 | Nodal AP Maritime Board; one port in the world's top 20 by 2047; 20% of India's port cargo
[63:9:7] ~~ Sources: india-briefing.com (AP Industrial Policy 2020-23); app notes 3:63 sub 10

=== NOTES 3:65 | Industrial Licensing, Mrtp to Competition Act; Disinvestment and Pse Policy
## SUB 0 | Disinvestment – Meaning, Methods and Strategic Sales
[65:0:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [65:0:0.0] Disinvestment | Sale of government equity in PSEs – reduces equity; control may stay
  [65:0:0.1] Privatisation | Ownership + management control to the private sector
  [65:0:0.2] Strategic sale | A block of shares (usually 50% or more) with transfer of management control to a strategic partner
  [65:0:0.3] Minority disinvestment | Govt keeps >51% and control
  [65:0:0.4] Liberalisation | Removing licences, quotas, controls (no sale)
  [65:0:0.5] Complete privatisation | 100% sold – most comprehensive mode
[65:0:1] - **Methods:** cross-holding, **warehousing**, minority sale, **OFS**, IPO/FPO, **CPSE ETF**, Bharat 22, buyback, **strategic sale** – methods of **disinvestment** (SLR, CRR, repo are NOT).
[65:0:2] - **Policy recast (1999-2000):** shift from token minority sales to **strategic sale** – **majority holding (51%+) sold to a strategic private partner with change in management**.
[65:0:3] - **Rationale:** poor PSU returns, **fiscal deficit**, efficiency, listing; disinvestment is an **integral part of liberalisation**; it reduces – never raises – government equity.
[65:0:4] - **Why disinvest (UPSC 2011):** proceeds are **not** mainly for repaying external debt, and government does **not** give up control in every CPSE – so neither statement holds.
[65:0:5] - **A-R (UPPCS 2000):** disinvestment is true; "PSUs have not generated enough employment" is **false** as a reason.
[65:0:6] - **Criticism:** **"selling the family silver"** – proceeds bridge the **fiscal deficit** instead of building assets; **undervaluation**; lost dividends.
[65:0:7] TABLE head: Company | Buyer
  [65:0:7.0] Modern Food Industries (2000, first strategic sale) | Hindustan Lever
  [65:0:7.1] BALCO (2001) | Sterlite (Vedanta)
  [65:0:7.2] CMC (2001) | Tata Sons
  [65:0:7.3] VSNL (2002) | Tata group
  [65:0:7.4] HPCL (2017-18) | ONGC
  [65:0:7.5] REC (2018-19) | PFC
  [65:0:7.6] Air India (Oct 2021) | Tata Group
  [65:0:7.7] NINL (2022) | Tata Steel – no proceeds to exchequer
  [65:0:7.8] LIC IPO (17 May 2022) | Biggest IPO then
  [65:0:7.9] BPCL (52.98%) | Called off, mid-2022
[65:0:8] - **Air India + Indian Airlines** merged (2007) → **Air India**; founded by **J.R.D. Tata** as Tata Airlines (1932).
[65:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 01 p.25; NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 13 p.10-11; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 05 p.9.14-9.15; app notes 3:65 sub 4, 7
## SUB 1 | Competition Act, 2002 and the CCI
[65:1:0] - **Competition Act, 2002:** recommended by the **S.V.S. Raghavan Committee (2000)**; replaced the MRTP Act; **commenced 31 March 2003**.
[65:1:1] - **CCI** established **14 October 2003**; Chairperson + **2-6 members**; **Ministry of Corporate Affairs**.
[65:1:2] - Fully operational: anti-competitive provisions from **20 May 2009**; merger (combination) control from **June 2011**.
[65:1:3] TABLE head: Chairperson | Term
  [65:1:3.0] Dhanendra Kumar (first) | 2009 – June 2011
  [65:1:3.1] Ashok Chawla | Oct 2011 – Jan 2016
  [65:1:3.2] Ravneet Kaur | from May 2023
[65:1:4] - **Key sections of the Act:**
[65:1:5] TABLE head: Section | Covers
  [65:1:5.0] 3 | Anti-competitive agreements – cartels, bid-rigging, price-fixing
  [65:1:5.1] 4 | Abuse of dominance
  [65:1:5.2] 5-6 | Combinations – M&A above thresholds; deemed approved if CCI misses the deadline
[65:1:6] - **NCLAT** hears appeals against CCI orders (since 26 May 2017).
[65:1:7] - Cases: **Jet Airways, IndiGo, SpiceJet** fined (Nov 2015) for cartelisation in the cargo **fuel surcharge**; **Google ₹1,337 crore (2022)**; **Meta/WhatsApp ₹213.14 crore (2024)**.
[65:1:8] - **2024:** CCI engaged **Management Development Institute Society** for a market study on **AI and competition**.
[65:1:9] - **M&A (UPPCS 2004 A-R):** the M&A wave after 1991 was **explained by dilution of MRTP provisions**.
[65:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 01 p.60; NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.29; business-standard.com (Ashok Chawla is new CCI chairman, 20 Oct 2011); app notes 3:65 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Disinvestment – Committees and Bodies
[65:2:0] TABLE head: Body | Year | Key point
  [65:2:0.0] Arjun Sengupta | 1984 | PSU autonomy and MoU – NOT disinvestment
  [65:2:0.1] V. Krishnamurthy | 1991 | Early approach to disinvestment
  [65:2:0.2] C. Rangarajan Committee | 1993 (set up 1992, report April 1993) | Disinvestment up to 49% in PSUs reserved for the public sector, 74% in others
  [65:2:0.3] Disinvestment Commission | 1996 | First chair G.V. Ramakrishna; 13 reports; strategic sales
  [65:2:0.4] Reconstituted Commission | July 2002 | Chair Dr R.H. Patil
  [65:2:0.5] Department of Disinvestment | 10 Dec 1999 | Ministry of Disinvestment 2001-04; → DIPAM (14 April 2016), Ministry of Finance
  [65:2:0.6] National Investment Fund | 3 Nov 2005 | Disinvestment proceeds; see "Proceeds"
[65:2:1] - The term **disinvestment** entered policy in the **Interim Budget, July 1991**.
[65:2:2] > Trap: **Arjun Sengupta = MoU**; Rangarajan = disinvestment (Rangarajan also chaired committees on BoP, poverty, sugar).

## SUB 3 | Market Structures – the Economics behind Competition Law
[65:3:0] TABLE head: Structure | Feature
  [65:3:0.0] Perfect competition | Many sellers, homogeneous product
  [65:3:0.1] Monopolistic competition | Many sellers, differentiated but close-substitute products
  [65:3:0.2] Oligopoly | A few large firms
  [65:3:0.3] Duopoly | Two sellers
  [65:3:0.4] Monopoly | One seller – the firm's demand curve is the market demand curve
  [65:3:0.5] Bilateral monopoly | One seller and one buyer
[65:3:1] - **Prisoner's dilemma:** each player is **better off confessing** whatever the other does (dominant strategy) – the logic of cartels breaking down.
[65:3:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 01 p.53; general knowledge, not checked

## SUB 5 | Regulatory Acts – Licensing and MRTP
[65:5:0] TABLE head: Act | Year | Replaced by
  [65:5:0.0] Minimum Wages Act | 1948 | –
  [65:5:0.1] IDRA | 1951 (amended 1953) | Licensing; Development Councils
  [65:5:0.2] MRTP | 1969 (in force 1970) | Competition Act, 2002
  [65:5:0.3] FERA | 1973 | FEMA, 1999
  [65:5:0.4] SICA (BIFR) | 1985 | IBC, 2016
[65:5:1] - Order: **Minimum Wages 1948 → IDRA 1951 → MRTP 1969 → FERA 1973** (codes 4, 2, 1, 3); then SICA 1985 → FEMA 1999 → Competition Act 2002 → IBC 2016.
[65:5:2] - **Hazari Report (1967)** and **Dutt Committee (1969)** showed licences favoured **large business houses**; Dutt recommended the **MRTP Act**.
[65:5:3] - **MRTP purpose:** control **private monopolies** and **concentration of economic power**.
[65:5:4] TABLE head: Year | MRTP threshold
  [65:5:4.0] Original | Assets ₹20 crore+ or 33% market share
  [65:5:4.1] 1984-85 | Share 25%; assets ₹100 crore
  [65:5:4.2] NIP 1991 | Asset limit scrapped
[65:5:5] - Compulsory licensing **18 (1991) → 4 now**; leather delicensed **1993**. After 1991, **APIIC** turned **facilitator**.
[65:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 22 p.2, 4-5; NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.29, 35; app notes 3:65 sub 0-2
## SUB 6 | New PSE Policy 2021, Monetisation and Restructuring
[65:6:0] - **New PSE Policy for Atmanirbhar Bharat (2021):** **minimise the Government's presence** in PSEs; **4 strategic sectors** (incl. banking, insurance, financial services) with **1-4 CPSEs** each; non-strategic → privatise, merge or close.
[65:6:1] - ES 2025-26: stake in listed CPSEs may fall to **26%**.
[65:6:2] - **Asset monetisation:** **leases** brownfield assets for a fixed period, ownership stays (disinvestment **sells** equity); objective – **unlock value of existing assets through new financial structures**.
[65:6:3] - **NMP 1.0:** Aug 2021, **₹6 lakh crore** (FY22-25); **NMP 2.0:** **23 Feb 2026**, **₹16.72 lakh crore** (FY26-30).
[65:6:4] - **NLMC** (2022, under **DPE**): monetises **surplus land of CPSEs**, incl. loss-making units.
[65:6:5] - AP PPP ports: **Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram**.
[65:6:6] - **NRF (1992):** VRS and a safety net for workers.
[65:6:7] - **IBC** enacted **28 May 2016** (T.K. Viswanathan BLRC); BIFR dissolved **1 Dec 2016**; **NCLT** under **s.408** Companies Act 2013.

=== NOTES 3:66 | Make in India, Pli, National Manufacturing Policy and Ease of Doing Business
## SUB 0 | Make in India – Launch, Pillars and Sectors
[66:0:0] # Launch
[66:0:1] - **Launched:** **25 September 2014** by PM Modi (MPPSC 2020; CDS 2019 – not 2018, not 2012/2016); nodal **Ministry of Commerce and Industry (DPIIT)**, not Heavy Industries or S&T (SSC 2019).
[66:0:2] - **Aim:** encourage multinational and domestic companies to manufacture in India; make India a **global manufacturing hub** and **foster innovation**; focus on job creation and skills in **25 key sectors**.
[66:0:3] - **Logo:** a **lion** made of cogwheels (UPPSC RO 2014). Links: "Vocal for Local", "Make in India for the World".
[66:0:4] - **Central approach:** **attracting FDI and global firms** to manufacture in India; **streamlining regulatory processes** to attract foreign investment and foster innovation – not higher tariffs, subsidies to old sectors or centralised planning (APPSC ASO).
[66:0:5] - **Targets (via NMP 2011):** manufacturing **25% of GDP** and **100 million additional jobs** – by 2022, later restated **by 2025** (APPSC JA: target for 2025 = **25%**).
[66:0:6] # Four Pillars
[66:0:7] TABLE head: Pillar | Covers
  [66:0:7.0] New Processes | Ease of doing business, single window, e-Biz, faster IPR registration
  [66:0:7.1] New Infrastructure | Industrial corridors and smart cities, world-class infrastructure
  [66:0:7.2] New Sectors | FDI opened in defence, insurance, medical devices, construction, railway infrastructure
  [66:0:7.3] New Mindset | Government as facilitator, not regulator
[66:0:8] - The initiative "built on four pillars – New Processes, New Infrastructure, New Sectors, New Mindset" and integrating India into global supply chains = **Make in India** (not Start-up, Digital or Skill India).
[66:0:9] - **Strategic components:** skill development, world-class infrastructure, manufacturing hub for domestic and foreign firms – **liberal finance to rural women for new enterprises is NOT one** (APPSC JA).
[66:0:10] - **Not part of Make in India (Degree Lecturers 2017 key):** "facilitating easy exit for investors" – EoDB, 100% FDI in new sectors such as defence, and corridors/smart cities are parts. (Faster exit norms belong to the Start-up India action plan.)
[66:0:11] # Sectors
[66:0:12] TABLE head: Phase | Sectors
  [66:0:12.0] Original (2014) | 25 sectors (APPSC AEE 2016)
  [66:0:12.1] Make in India 2.0 – Economic Survey 2017-18 | 10 champion sectors for renewed focus (APPSC AMVI flashcard: 10)
  [66:0:12.2] Champion services sectors (Cabinet, Feb 2018) | 12
  [66:0:12.3] Make in India 2.0 (now) | 27 = 15 manufacturing (DPIIT) + 12 services (Dept of Commerce)
[66:0:13] - Champion sectors include capital goods, auto, defence and aerospace, pharma, ESDM, leather, textiles, food processing, renewable energy, shipping, railways.
[66:0:14] - **Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order:** preference to local suppliers in government purchase.
[66:0:15] > Most-asked: launch date (Sept 2014), 25 sectors, four pillars, lion logo, nodal ministry. Trap: "10" champion sectors (ES 2017-18) vs 12 champion services vs 27 sectors now.
[66:0:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.11 (four pillars, 25 sectors); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 05 p.24-25 (launch Sept 2014, 25 sectors, NMP targets by 2022, champion sectors); web: business-standard.com (PTI, 29 Jan 2018, "Make in India 2.0 to focus on 10 champion sectors – Eco Survey"); app notes 3:66 sub 2
## SUB 1 | National Manufacturing Policy 2011 and NIMZs
[66:1:0] # NMP 2011
[66:1:1] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [66:1:1.0] Released | 4 November 2011 (approved by Cabinet 25 Oct 2011) – "introduced in 2011"
  [66:1:1.1] Share of manufacturing in GDP | 16% → 25% within a decade, i.e. by 2022
  [66:1:1.2] Growth target | 12-14% per annum over the medium term
  [66:1:1.3] Jobs | 100 million additional jobs (by 2022)
  [66:1:1.4] Competitiveness | enhance global competitiveness, domestic value addition and technological depth
  [66:1:1.5] Infrastructure | on PPP basis; skilling of rural youth; sector-, location- and technology-neutral
[66:1:2] - **Objectives (RAS 2013):** 12-14% growth, 100 million jobs, global competitiveness = **1, 2 and 3**; "manufacturing exports to rise 25% a year" is NOT an objective – 25% is the GDP-share target.
[66:1:3] - **Present share:** manufacturing still about **16.3-17.5%** of GVA → **25% target missed**.
[66:1:4] - **National Manufacturing Mission (Budget 2025-26):** 25% share and **143 million jobs by 2035**.
[66:1:5] # NIMZ – National Investment and Manufacturing Zones
[66:1:6] - **NIMZ** = large **integrated industrial township** – zoned land use, clean and energy-efficient technology, social infrastructure, skill facilities; the main instrument of NMP 2011.
[66:1:7] - NIMZs differ from SEZs in **size, infrastructure planning, governance, exit policy and fiscal incentives**.
[66:1:8] - **India's first NIMZ was proposed in Andhra Pradesh** (UPSC 2016). In-principle approval for **Chittoor and Prakasam** (14 Aug 2013); **Prakasam** got final approval (2016).
[66:1:9] # National Capital Goods Policy 2016
[66:1:10] - Aims to **raise domestic capital goods production**, deepen technology across sub-sectors, a **technology development fund** – **increasing imports of capital goods is NOT a feature** (OPSC 2018).
[66:1:11] > NMP year asked 4 times (2011; 4 Nov 2011); target year 2022; NIMZ = AP (Chittoor and Prakasam).
[66:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.8 (NIMZ); NextGen Rocket Indian Economy p.98-99 (NIMZ = instrument of NMP 2011); Ramesh Singh part 05 p.25 (25% of GDP, 100 million jobs by 2022); app notes 3:66 sub 0-1
## SUB 2 | Ease of Doing Business – State Rankings (BRAP, ACI) and AP
[66:2:0] - **BRAP = Business Reform Action Plan**; State EoDB ranking released by **DPIIT** (Ministry of Commerce and Industry); first **2015** by DIPP with the **World Bank Group**.
[66:2:1] TABLE head: Edition | Result
  [66:2:1.0] BRAP 2015 | Gujarat 1st; AP 2nd
  [66:2:1.1] BRAP 2016 (Oct 2016) | AP and Telangana jointly 1st; Gujarat 3rd (MPPSC 2018)
  [66:2:1.2] BRAP 2017 | AP 1st, Telangana 2nd, Haryana 3rd
  [66:2:1.3] BRAP 2019 (5 Sept 2020) | AP 1st, UP 2nd, Telangana 3rd
  [66:2:1.4] BRAP 2020 (30 June 2022) | no numeric ranks – Top Achievers (7: AP, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Telangana), Achievers (MP, HP, Maharashtra, Odisha, Uttarakhand, UP), Aspirers, Emerging Business Ecosystems
  [66:2:1.5] BRAP 2024 (7th) | 435 reform points – Simplification, Elimination, Digitisation, Decriminalisation
[66:2:2] - **AP's rank in State EoDB:** **1st** (2017, 2019; Top Achiever 2020 – the APPSC 2023 keys give "1").
[66:2:3] - **DBRAP:** reforms at district level, Tier-II and Tier-III cities.
[66:2:4] - **Asian Competitiveness Institute (ACI), Singapore:** ranks States on 3 "ABC" pillars – Attractiveness to investors, Business friendliness, Competitiveness policies. **ACI EDB Index 2018: AP 1st** (up from **5th in 2016**), **Maharashtra 2nd, Delhi 3rd**.
[66:2:5] - **NITI Aayog Investment Friendliness Index (Jul 2026):** 8 pillars; AP among **Frontrunners**.
[66:2:6] - **AP Single Desk Portal (April 2015):** 99.20% approvals within SLA (2024-25). Rayalaseema hub: JSW Steel Kadapa, Kia, Royal Enfield Tirupati.
[66:2:7] - **Other State business-facilitation news:** **Kerala**'s Industries Department launched a **WhatsApp** grievance facility for entrepreneurs (January 2023); **Karunendra S. Jasti** (Coromandel Paints) elected **FAPCCI** President (2022).
[66:2:8] > APPSC loves AP's rank (1st) and the ACI order AP > Maharashtra > Delhi. Trap: BRAP 2020 had categories, not ranks; MP = "Achiever".
[66:2:9] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:66 sub 10; web: inkl.com / bizzbuzz.news (Karunendra Jasti elected FAPCCI President)
## SUB 3 | Ease of Doing Business – World Bank Report and Reforms
[66:3:0] - **Doing Business report:** **World Bank Group** (conceptualised with **IFC**); mainly **guides foreign investors**; **10 parameters** – starting a business, construction permits, getting electricity, registering property, getting credit, protecting minority investors, paying taxes, trading across borders, enforcing contracts, resolving insolvency.
[66:3:1] TABLE head: Edition | India's rank
  [66:3:1.0] DB 2015 | 142
  [66:3:1.1] DB 2018 | 100 – jump of 30
  [66:3:1.2] DB 2020 | 63 (last edition)
[66:3:2] - **Discontinued 2021** (data irregularities). Successor **B-READY** – 3 pillars: regulatory framework, public services, operational efficiency.
[66:3:3] - Weakest indicators: **enforcing contracts, registering property**.
[66:3:4] TABLE head: Reform | EoDB area
  [66:3:4.0] GST (2017), faceless assessment, e-filing | Paying taxes, unified market
  [66:3:4.1] SPICe+ (2020), MCA21 V3 | Starting a business
  [66:3:4.2] IBC 2016 | Resolving insolvency
  [66:3:4.3] Online building-plan approvals; land records (DILRMP) | Construction permits; registering property
[66:3:5] - **GST** is the reform credited with improving EoDB (APPSC G2) – "removal of all foreign ownership restrictions", nationalisation of banks and PSU expansion are NOT EoDB reforms.
[66:3:6] - **Platforms:** **e-Biz** (Mission Mode Project under NeGP); **National Single Window System** (FIF portal merged Aug 2022); **Invest India** (2009, not-for-profit JV of DIPP, FICCI, CII, NASSCOM and States).
[66:3:7] - **Jan Vishwas 2.0 Bill:** 16 Acts, 355 provisions, **288 decriminalised**. Four **labour codes** → formalisation and consolidation, yet **80%+** workers informal. IMD Competitiveness rank **41** (2025).
[66:3:8] - **Industrial-development initiatives:** Make in India, Ease of Doing Business, Start-up India – **Digital India is NOT one** (digital infrastructure and services).
[66:3:9] > Statement PYQ (APPSC ASO): Make in India = manufacturing hub ✓; Skill India = employability ✓; "success depends solely on the Centre" ✗ → 1 and 3.
[66:3:10] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:66 sub 3, 8, 9; Ramesh Singh part 05 p.24 (EoDB reforms, GST, IBC)
## SUB 4 | Flagship Missions – Chronology
[66:4:0] TABLE head: Mission | Launch | Objective
  [66:4:0.0] National Manufacturing Policy | 4 Nov 2011 | 25% GDP share
  [66:4:0.1] Make in India | 25 Sept 2014 | Manufacturing hub
  [66:4:0.2] Digital India | 1 July 2015 | Digital infrastructure (NOT industrial)
  [66:4:0.3] Skill India | 15 July 2015 | Skilling youth for jobs (not digital payments)
  [66:4:0.4] Start-up India | 16 Jan 2016 | Start-ups – 2.47 lakh recognised (Aug 2026)
  [66:4:0.5] National Policy on Electronics | 2019 | ESDM
  [66:4:0.6] PLI schemes | 2020 | 14 sectors
  [66:4:0.7] PM GatiShakti | Oct 2021 | Multimodal infrastructure
  [66:4:0.8] India Semiconductor Mission | Dec 2021 | ₹76,000 crore
  [66:4:0.9] National Logistics Policy | Sept 2022 | Logistics cost
  [66:4:0.10] ISM 2.0 / Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme | 15 Jul 2026 | ₹1,27,500 crore / ₹62,500 crore
[66:4:1] - **Atmanirbhar Bharat (May 2020):** about **₹20 lakh crore** package; **five pillars** – Economy, Infrastructure, System, Vibrant Demography, Demand (**not privatisation**).
[66:4:2] - **"China+1":** India as an added manufacturing base in diversifying global supply chains.
[66:4:3] - **Logistics cost:** historically **13-14% of GDP** – GatiShakti and NLP aim to cut it.

## SUB 5 | PLI and Sectoral Schemes
[66:5:0] - **PLI (2020):** **14 sectors**, **₹1.97 lakh crore**; incentive on **incremental sales** of goods made in India; sectors include white goods, solar PV modules, specialty steel, textiles, drones – **NOT coal mining equipment**.
[66:5:1] - Results (to Sept 2025): investment >₹2.0 lakh crore; **12.60 lakh jobs**.
[66:5:2] - **PLI-Auto:** **₹25,938 crore**; **≥50% domestic value addition**.
[66:5:3] - **PM E-DRIVE:** **Ministry of Heavy Industries**, 29 Sept 2024, **₹10,900 crore**; replaced **FAME-II**.
[66:5:4] - **Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (FY27-FY31):** **₹62,500 crore**; replaces **PLI for Large Scale Electronics Manufacturing**; up to **1.5%** extra for domestic sourcing.
[66:5:5] - **ECMS:** outlay raised to **₹40,000 crore** (Budget 2026-27).
[66:5:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:66 sub 4
## SUB 6 | Electronics and Semiconductors
[66:6:0] - **India = 2nd-largest mobile phone producer** in the world, **after China** (Indian Cellular Association data for 2017; still 2nd in 2023 and 2025-26).
[66:6:1] - Mobile output **₹5.45 lakh crore (2024-25)**; **99.2%** of phones used are made in India; **smartphones = largest export category (2025)**.
[66:6:2] - **India Semiconductor Mission:** under **Digital India Corporation (MeitY)**; **₹76,000 crore** (2021); **up to 50%** capital assistance; ISM 1.0 = **12 projects**, most in **Gujarat**.
[66:6:3] TABLE head: Unit | Location
  [66:6:3.0] Tata Electronics – PSMC (Taiwan) wafer fab; first semiconductor-fab SEZ | Dholera, Gujarat
  [66:6:3.1] Tata OSAT | Jagiroad, Morigaon, Assam
  [66:6:3.2] Micron ATMP; CG Power; Kaynes OSAT | Sanand, Gujarat
  [66:6:3.3] First advanced 3D packaging unit | Odisha
[66:6:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:66 sub 5
## SUB 7 | SEZ Basics for this Row
[66:7:0] - **SEZ Act, 2005** with SEZ Rules in force **10 February 2006**; set up by **Central Govt, State Govt or any person**.
[66:7:1] - **Sec 10AA:** **100%** tax exemption on export income for 5 years, **50%** next 5, 50% of ploughed-back profit for 5 more; **sunset** – units operational by **30 June 2020**.
[66:7:2] - **DESH** = Development of Enterprise and Service Hubs (proposed successor framework).
[66:7:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Indian Economy p.26; app notes 3:66 sub 6

=== NOTES 3:67 | Start-up India, Stand-up India, Innovation and Entrepreneurship Ecosystem
## SUB 0 | Start-up India – Launch, Bodies and Programmes
[67:0:0] # Launch
[67:0:1] - Launched **16 January 2016** (SSC CGL 2019) – to support entrepreneurs, build a start-up ecosystem and make India a country of **job creators instead of job seekers**; **16 January = National Startup Day**.
[67:0:2] - Nodal: **DPIIT**, Ministry of Commerce and Industry – also the **nodal agency for start-up recognition**. (Udyam portal = MSME registration.)
[67:0:3] - **Start-up and Stand-up India** (slogan of Jan 2016) aim to promote innovation and entrepreneurship among **enterprising youth** – Stand-Up targets SC/ST and women.
[67:0:4] - **Action plan (ES 2015-16):** self-certification, **Startup India Hub**, mobile app and portal, relaxed public procurement, fast-track patents, **faster exit norms**, ₹10,000 crore fund of funds, credit guarantee, 3-year tax exemption.
[67:0:5] # Bodies and platforms
[67:0:6] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [67:0:6.0] Startup India Hub | single online platform / point of contact for all stakeholders; operationalised 2016
  [67:0:6.1] National Startup Advisory Council | set up (notified) by Ministry of Commerce and Industry on 22 January 2020
  [67:0:6.2] Startup India Yatra | search for entrepreneurial talent in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities – not villages
  [67:0:6.3] MAARG | national mentorship platform (all sectors, not only AI) – Mentorship, Advisory, Assistance, Resilience and Growth
  [67:0:6.4] SETU | Self-Employment and Talent Utilisation – techno-financial, incubation and facilitation programme under Atal Innovation Mission (Budget 2015-16)
[67:0:7] - **States' Startup Ranking (DPIIT):** promotes **competitive federalism**; categories Best Performers … Emerging; **AP = Best Performer (2022)**.
[67:0:8] > Most-asked: launch 16 Jan 2016, Yatra = Tier-2/3 cities (asked twice), SETU expansion, NSAC Jan 2020.
[67:0:9] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 05 p.25-26 (Start-up India Jan 2016, SETU, Startup India Hub, action plan); app notes 3:67 sub 1
## SUB 1 | Stand-Up India Scheme (2016)
[67:1:0] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [67:1:0.0] Launch | 5 April 2016
  [67:1:0.1] Ministry | Ministry of Finance; portal Standupmitra
  [67:1:0.2] Target groups | SC/ST and women entrepreneurs aged 18+
  [67:1:0.3] Loan | ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore (composite: term loan + working capital)
  [67:1:0.4] Enterprise | Greenfield (first-time) only – manufacturing, services, trading, agri-allied; NOT brownfield
  [67:1:0.5] Branch norm | at least one SC/ST and one woman borrower per bank branch
  [67:1:0.6] Refinance | SIDBI ₹10,000 crore
[67:1:1] - **Non-individual enterprises** eligible if at least **51% shareholding and controlling stake** is with an SC/ST or woman entrepreneur.
[67:1:2] - Loan up to **85%** of project cost; repayment up to **7 years**, moratorium up to **18 months**.
[67:1:3] - **Working capital up to ₹10 lakh** = **overdraft** (RuPay debit card); above ₹10 lakh = cash credit limit.
[67:1:4] - **Security:** primary security plus collateral or guarantee of the **Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Stand-Up India Loans (CGFSIL)**, as decided by banks.
[67:1:5] - **PM MUDRA:** micro loans up to **₹20 lakh** (Tarun Plus).
[67:1:6] > APPSC G1 2024 statements: brownfield ✗; non-individual ✓; working capital ≤₹10 lakh as cash credit ✗ (it is overdraft); CGFSIL ✓ → **II and IV**.
[67:1:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:67 sub 2; Ramesh Singh part 05 p.25 (Start-up India and Stand-up India campaign)
## SUB 2 | Funds and Financing Sources for Start-ups
[67:2:0] TABLE head: Fund | Key facts
  [67:2:0.0] Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS) | ₹945 crore (2021); up to ₹20 lakh grant for proof of concept, prototypes, trials + ₹50 lakh investment; given through incubators, not banks
  [67:2:0.1] Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS) | ₹10,000 crore, managed by SIDBI; contributes to SEBI-registered AIFs (VC funds), not directly
  [67:2:0.2] FFS 2.0 | another ₹10,000 crore for deep tech, space, AI
  [67:2:0.3] Credit Guarantee Scheme for Start-ups | Oct 2022; via NCGTC; up to ₹20 crore per borrower; replaced the Credit Guarantee Fund for Startups
[67:2:1] TABLE head: Source | Feature
  [67:2:1.0] Bootstrapping | founder's own savings and revenue
  [67:2:1.1] Angel investors | individuals investing own money at idea/seed stage
  [67:2:1.2] Venture capital | early-stage equity with active guidance for high-growth firms
  [67:2:1.3] Crowdfunding | small sums from many people, usually online
  [67:2:1.4] Incubators, bank loans, government schemes | MUDRA, Stand-Up India, CGSS
[67:2:2] - Start-ups' needs can be met through angel investors, venture capital and crowdfunding – **all the above** (UPPSC 2017).
[67:2:3] - **Big deal:** **Walmart** bought a majority stake in **Flipkart** (2018). **Microsoft** launched the **100X100X100** programme for B2B SaaS start-ups.
[67:2:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:67 sub 3-4; Ramesh Singh part 05 p.26 (FFS ₹10,000 crore, SIDBI)
## SUB 3 | Start-up Definition and Benefits
[67:3:0] TABLE head: Criterion | Start-up | Deep-tech
  [67:3:0.0] Age | up to 10 years | up to 20 years
  [67:3:0.1] Turnover | ≤ ₹200 crore | ≤ ₹300 crore
[67:3:1] - Eligible forms: private limited company, **registered partnership firm**, LLP; split or reconstructed businesses are NOT start-ups.
[67:3:2] - Tax holiday **3 consecutive years out of 10** (Sec **80-IAC**); **self-certification** under labour and environment laws; fast-track patents; **angel tax abolished** (Budget **2024-25**).
[67:3:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:67 sub 0
## SUB 4 | Entrepreneurship Programmes and Theory

=== NOTES 3:68 | SEZs - Policy, Performance and Criticism; Industrial Corridors (dmic, Cbic, Akic) and Nicdc
## SUB 0 | EPZs and Free Trade Zones – Kandla to Surat
[68:0:0] - **SEZ = Special Economic Zone** (not Special Export / Exemption / Environment Zone) – asked 3 times.
[68:0:1] - **Kandla** (Gulf of Kutch, Gujarat), **1965**: **India's and Asia's first Export Processing Zone**; also India's first Free Trade Zone; later Kandla SEZ.
[68:0:2] - **Surat**, **1997**: **first private-sector EPZ**; converted into an SEZ on **1 November 2000**.
[68:0:3] - **Free trade zone:** area where goods are landed, stored, processed and re-exported **without customs duty**; set up for **promotion of export industries** (not backward areas, SSI or IT).
[68:0:4] TABLE head: EPZ | Place
  [68:0:4.0] Kandla | Gujarat (1965)
  [68:0:4.1] SEEPZ | Santacruz, Mumbai
  [68:0:4.2] MEPZ | Chennai
  [68:0:4.3] Falta | West Bengal
  [68:0:4.4] Others | Noida, Cochin, Visakhapatnam
[68:0:5] - **Thiruvananthapuram had no FTZ** (Kerala's zone was at Cochin) – UPPSC 1999.
[68:0:6] - **"City without an SEZ" (UPPSC 2001 key): Kandla** – listed as an EPZ, not an SEZ, then; Chennai, Kochi, Surat had SEZs. From 2006 EPZs and EOUs could convert into SEZs.
[68:0:7] - **Area-based incentive:** in 2001 PM Vajpayee announced a **5-year excise duty holiday** for industries in **earthquake-ravaged Kutch** (UPSC 2002).
[68:0:8] > Kandla is asked 7 times (Asia's first EPZ, 1965, Gulf of Kutch). Trap: Santacruz = SEEPZ, not first; Surat = first private EPZ.
