## SUB 1 | SEZ Policy and SEZ Act – Dates
[68:1:0] TABLE head: Date | Milestone
  [68:1:0.0] 1 April 2000 | SEZ policy announced in the EXIM Policy 2000-01
  [68:1:0.1] May 2005 | SEZ Act passed by Parliament
  [68:1:0.2] 23 June 2005 | President's assent
  [68:1:0.3] 10 February 2006 | SEZ Act and SEZ Rules in force
  [68:1:0.4] 2025 | semiconductor/electronic-component SEZ land cut to 10 ha
[68:1:1] - "SEZ Act came into force / became effective" = **2006** (WBCS 2017; UPPSC 2010) – not 2005.
[68:1:2] - "SEZ policy announced in" – APPSC G1 key: **both 2000 and 2006** (policy 2000; Act-based regime from 2006). Strictly the policy was announced in 2000.
[68:1:3] - **SEZ India mobile app:** January 2017 (15 Jan), **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**.

## SUB 2 | SEZ Act 2005 – Objectives and Features
[68:2:0] # Objectives
[68:2:1] - 1. Generation of **additional economic activity**.
[68:2:2] - 2. Promotion of **exports of goods and services**.
[68:2:3] - 3. Promotion of **investment from domestic and foreign sources**.
[68:2:4] - 4. Creation of **employment** opportunities.
[68:2:5] - 5. Development of **infrastructure** facilities.
[68:2:6] - So "all the above" (economic activity, employment, exports); infrastructure + foreign investment = **1 and 2 only** – "exports of **services only**" is NOT an objective (UPSC 2010); "**discouraging** foreign investment" is NOT an objective.
[68:2:7] # Features
[68:2:8] - A **duty-free enclave** for exports and FDI; developer: **Central Government, State Government or any person** (public, private, joint sector).
[68:2:9] - Purpose: manufacturing, **services** or Free Trade Warehousing Zone; proposal via **State Government → Board of Approval**; **single-window clearance**.
[68:2:10] - **100% FDI** under the automatic route for most manufacturing in SEZs.
[68:2:11] - Min. area (Rules 2006): multi-product **1,000 ha**; sector-specific reduced to **50 ha** (2019).
[68:2:12] - **Not true:** "SEZ is set up **primarily** to generate employment" – SEZs are **export-oriented** (APPSC G2 2017).
[68:2:13] - **A-R (Constable 2016 key):** SEZs attract foreign companies and give more local employment – both true, (R) taken as the explanation.
[68:2:14] - **s.18:** one IFSC per SEZ. **s.10AA:** **100%** exemption 5 years, 50% next 5, 50% of reinvested profit 5 more; holidays **phased out 2017-2020** (sunset clause).
[68:2:15] - **Japan** came forward to develop SEZs / Japanese industrial townships in India (with DMIC).
[68:2:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Indian Economy p.26 (objectives: exports, investment, employment, infrastructure, economic activity); app notes 3:68 sub 2
## SUB 3 | SEZ Performance and Criticism
[68:3:0] - Total investment in SEZs by **31 Dec 2011**: **₹2,49,630 crore** (Economic Survey 2011-12).
[68:3:1] - **Highest export growth over the previous year (2004-05 to 2007-08): 2007-08** (₹66,638 crore, about +92%).
[68:3:2] - FY 2024-25 SEZ exports **₹14.64 lakh crore**, about **21%** of India's exports; SEZs got **less than 3% of FDI**.
[68:3:3] TABLE head: State with most SEZs | Fact
  [68:3:3.0] Andhra Pradesh (combined) | most approved and operational SEZs (June 2012)
  [68:3:3.1] Tamil Nadu | most operational SEZs now
  [68:3:3.2] Telangana | most approved SEZs now
[68:3:4] - **Nandigram** (Purba Medinipur, West Bengal), **2007**: **Salim Group** chemical-hub SEZ; violent protests against **land acquisition**.
[68:3:5] - Criticism: revenue loss, idle land, **WTO-inconsistent export subsidies**; employment gains not guaranteed.
[68:3:6] - **Baba Kalyani Committee (2018):** rename SEZs as **Employment and Economic Enclaves** (3Es).
[68:3:7] - **DESH Bill** (Development of Enterprise and Services Hubs, **Budget 2022-23**): removes positive NFE condition; still pending.
[68:3:8] - **BHAVYA – Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana (2026):** ₹33,660 crore; **100** plug-and-play parks (not 50).
[68:3:9] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:68 sub 3-4; general knowledge, not checked (₹2,49,630 crore; 2007-08 exports)

=== NOTES 3:69 | Infrastructure - National Infrastructure Pipeline, Pm Gati Shakti, National Monetisation Pipeline, Logistics Policy
## SUB 0 | PM GatiShakti National Master Plan
[69:0:0] - Launched **13 October 2021** (APPSC GS: **2021**); **whole-of-government, GIS-based** planning platform for **multimodal connectivity** infrastructure to economic zones.
[69:0:1] - Brings **16 ministries** (incl. Railways, Roads, Ports) on one digital platform – so both PYQ statements (multimodal connectivity; 16 ministries) are correct.
[69:0:2] - Portal by **BISAG-N, Gandhinagar**; **Empowered Group of Secretaries** headed by the **Cabinet Secretary** → Network Planning Group.
[69:0:3] - **Seven engines:** Railways, Roads, Ports, Waterways, Airports, Mass Transport, Logistics Infrastructure – **7** (APPSC 2024); **power transmission is NOT an engine**.
[69:0:4] - **National Logistics Policy (Sept 2022)** complements it – came after GatiShakti.
[69:0:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:69 sub 0
## SUB 1 | National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP) and Infrastructure Types
[69:1:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [69:1:0.0] Period | FY2019-20 to FY2024-25
  [69:1:0.1] Investment | about ₹111 lakh crore
  [69:1:0.2] Coverage | both economic and social infrastructure; greenfield and brownfield projects
  [69:1:0.3] Funding | Centre 39%, States 40%, private 21%
  [69:1:0.4] Sector shares | Energy ~24% (largest), roads ~18%, urban ~17%, railways ~12%
[69:1:1] - **India Investment Grid (IIG)** – the **Invest India** platform that showcases NIP projects to investors (it has not "ceased").
[69:1:2] - APPSC G1 2024 statements: only economic ✗; greenfield only ✗; offers investment opportunities and attracts investment ✓; IIG ceased ✗ → **only III**.
[69:1:3] - **Economic infrastructure:** energy, roads, railways, communication; **social infrastructure:** schools, health, sanitation. UPPSC 2004 key: "not an example of economic infrastructure" = **coal mines** (a production activity).
[69:1:4] - Infrastructure multiplier **2.5-3.5**; Centre's capex **₹12.2 lakh crore** (Budget 2026-27).
[69:1:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:69 sub 1
## SUB 2 | National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP)
[69:2:0] - Announced in **Union Budget 2021-22**; monetises **brownfield core infrastructure assets**; **ownership retained by Government**.
[69:2:1] - **Strategic objective:** lets public asset owners **use new financial structures with private-sector capital** – unlocking value of public (not private) assets; leases are for a fixed period.
[69:2:2] - Instruments: PPP concessions, InvITs, TOT, securitisation.
[69:2:3] TABLE head: Item | NMP 1.0 | NMP 2.0
  [69:2:3.0] Period | FY22-FY25 | FY26-FY30
  [69:2:3.1] Value | ₹6 lakh crore | ₹16.72 lakh crore (prepared by NITI Aayog)
  [69:2:3.2] Largest sector | Roads (APPSC 2021) | Highways, MMLPs, ropeways 26%
  [69:2:3.3] Result | ₹5.3 lakh crore; coal gave most proceeds | launched 23 Feb 2026
[69:2:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:69 sub 2
## SUB 3 | Bharatmala, Sagarmala, Railways and Logistics
[69:3:0] TABLE head: Feature | Bharatmala Pariyojana | Sagarmala
  [69:3:0.0] Sector | Roads | Port-led development (ports)
  [69:3:0.1] Launch | 2017 | National Perspective Plan 2016; Sagarmala 2.0 (2025)
  [69:3:0.2] Scale | Phase-I 34,800 km, 580+ districts | 800+ projects
[69:3:1] - **Sagarmala pillars:** port modernisation, port connectivity, port-led industrialisation, coastal community development, coastal shipping and IWT – not naval stationing, not agricultural insurance.
[69:3:2] - **Railway electrification:** **50.91%** of routes by **March 2019**; **99.1%** by Oct 2025. Targets: **100% electrification by 2023** and **net-zero carbon by 2030** – both statements correct.
[69:3:3] - **National Rail Plan 2030:** freight share 28% → **45%**. **Eastern DFC** (1,337 km) – **World Bank**; **Western DFC** – **JICA**.
[69:3:4] - **Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train:** JICA loan of about ₹88,000 crore at **0.1%** a year, 50 years, 15-year moratorium.
[69:3:5] - **National Logistics Policy:** logistics cost to single digits by **2030**; **7.97%** of GDP (FY24); **ULIP** = Unified Logistics Interface Platform; **LEADS** (DPIIT, 2018) modelled on the World Bank's **Logistics Performance Index**; AP = **Achiever** (LEADS 2023); Exemplars 2025 include **Tamil Nadu**.
[69:3:6] - **Z-Morh tunnel** (6.5 km, J&K): concession agreement Jan 2020, about **₹2,379 crore**.
[69:3:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:69 sub 3-4, 6; general knowledge, not checked (JICA 0.1%, Z-Morh cost)
## SUB 4 | Infrastructure Financing and PPP
[69:4:0] - **PPP = Public Private Partnership**.
[69:4:1] - **IIFCL** (2006; NBFC-IFC since 2013) → SEBI **InvIT** regulations (2014) → **NIIF** (2015; Category II AIFs) → **NaBFID Act 2021** (paid-up ₹20,000 crore).
[69:4:2] - **Deepak Parekh Committee:** infrastructure financing (May 2007). **Vijay Kelkar Committee (2015):** revisiting and revitalising PPP; proposed an **Infrastructure PPP Adjudication Tribunal**.
[69:4:3] - **UK-India Infrastructure Financing Bridge:** launched at the **12th India-UK Economic and Financial Dialogue** (11 Sept 2023).
[69:4:4] - **Cochin airport (CIAL):** first PPP airport; world's first fully solar-powered airport (2015). **Vizhinjam (Kerala):** first deep-water transhipment port. Navi Mumbai airport: operations **25 Dec 2025**.
[69:4:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:69 sub 5, 7; general knowledge, not checked (Infrastructure Financing Bridge)
## SUB 5 | Andhra Pradesh Infrastructure
[69:5:0] - AP coastline **~1,053 km** (1,053.07 km) – **3rd** longest; **AP Maritime Board** handles ports.
[69:5:1] - Ports: **Ramayapatnam** (Nellore), **Mulapeta** (Srikakulam), **Machilipatnam** (Krishna; **MEIL**); **Krishnapatnam** (BOST, 2004; **largest private port**); Gangavaram (BOOT).
[69:5:2] - **Bhogapuram airport:** GMR, **PPP-DBFOT**, **3,800 m** runway. International airports: Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Tirupati (not Kadapa). **Orvakal** = first State-built airport in South India (2021).
[69:5:3] - Targets: Blue Economy **US$20 bn by 2035**; **4 greenfield ports + 11 fishing harbours** by 2030.
[69:5:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:69 sub 8

=== NOTES 3:70 | Energy and Power Policy - Installed Capacity Mix, Distribution Reform (uday), Renewable Targets, Energy Security
## SUB 0 | Distribution Reform – UDAY, Electricity Act 2003 and Power Tariffs
[70:0:0] # UDAY (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana)
[70:0:1] - **Launched:** Cabinet approval **5 Nov 2015** (Ministry of Power) for the **financial and operational turnaround of DISCOMs** – not household electrification (Saubhagya) or LED bulbs (UJALA).
[70:0:2] - **Debt:** States take over **75% of DISCOM debt** (50% in 2015-16, 25% in 2016-17), cutting interest from 14-15% to 8-9% – the scheme 'to reduce interest payment in the electricity sector'.
[70:0:3] - **Four initiatives:** **improving operational efficiency; reduction of cost of power; reduction in interest cost; enforcing financial discipline** – regularising DISCOM employees was NOT one.
[70:0:4] - Targets: AT&C loss ~22% → **15%**, ACS-ARR gap to zero by 2018-19; optional for States.
[70:0:5] - Replaced **Indian Electricity Act 1910, Electricity (Supply) Act 1948, ERC Act 1998**.
[70:0:6] - **Section 63** = tariffs through **competitive bidding**.
[70:0:7] TABLE head: Scheme | Year | Objective
  [70:0:7.0] DDUGJY | 2014 | Rural feeder separation
  [70:0:7.1] UDAY (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana) | Cabinet 5 Nov 2015 | DISCOM financial turnaround; States take over 75% of DISCOM debt
  [70:0:7.2] Saubhagya | 2017 | Household electrification
  [70:0:7.3] RDSS | 2021 | Cut AT&C losses; smart metering
[70:0:8] - AT&C losses **22.62% (FY14) → 15.04% (FY25)**; demand-supply gap **4.2% → zero** (Nov 2025).
[70:0:9] - **UDAY demand-side measure:** promoting **energy-efficient LED bulbs**; its other measures were operational-efficiency steps for DISCOMs.
[70:0:10] # Tariffs, consumption and policy
[70:0:11] - **Cross-subsidisation:** low domestic/farm tariffs are paid for by high industrial and commercial tariffs – why Indian household power is cheap and industrial power dear.
[70:0:12] - **Largest consumer of electricity:** **industry** (~40%), ahead of domestic and agriculture.
[70:0:13] - **Highest per capita consumption (larger States, exam answer):** **Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat**.
[70:0:14] - **National Electricity Policy:** power for all households, demand fully met by 2012, protection of consumers' interests; **'reducing the per unit price' was NOT an objective**.
[70:0:15] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 05 p.28-30; app notes 3:70 sub 7; general knowledge (tariffs, consumption), not checked
## SUB 1 | Installed Capacity, Plan Targets and Energy Types
[70:1:0] - India (31 July 2026): about **552 GW**; **non-fossil 300.5 GW = over 54%**.
[70:1:1] - Non-fossil mix: **solar 164.59 GW**, wind 58.14 GW, hydro 57.24 GW, bio-power 11.75 GW, nuclear 8.78 GW.
[70:1:2] - **Nuclear (2017):** about **6,780 MW** installed (now 8.78 GW); reactors run by **NPCIL**.
[70:1:3] - FY 2025-26: 55.29 GW non-fossil added (44.6 GW solar).
[70:1:4] - AP (31 July 2025): **27,586.93 MW**; thermal 13,907.67 MW; RE **13,488.39 MW** (solar 5,523.28, wind 4,397.78, large hydro 2,810 MW). AP added 3,865.63 MW RE in 2025-26.
[70:1:5] - Battery storage: about **500 MWh** (Sep 2025) vs **336 GWh** needed by 2029-30.
[70:1:6] # Plan targets
[70:1:7] - **11th Plan (2007-12) capacity-addition target: 78,700 MW**; cut at mid-term to **62,374 MW**; actual addition ~55,000 MW.
[70:1:8] # Energy types
[70:1:9] TABLE head: Type | Examples
  [70:1:9.0] Primary | Raw natural resources before conversion – coal, crude, sunlight, wind, tides, uranium
  [70:1:9.1] Secondary | Converted forms – electricity, incl. tidal power (so 'Primary energy – Tidal power' is the wrong pair)
  [70:1:9.2] Commercial | Coal, oil, gas, electricity
  [70:1:9.3] Non-commercial | Firewood, animal dung, crop residue
  [70:1:9.4] Non-conventional / renewable | Solar, wind, tidal, geothermal (thermal and nuclear plants are not renewable)

## SUB 5 | Coal Sector
[70:5:0] - **Nationalisation**: coking coal mines 1971-72; non-coking under **Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973**.
[70:5:1] - **Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act 2015**: after the Supreme Court cancelled coal block allocations; allocation by **auction**, run by the **Nominated Authority**.
[70:5:2] - **Coal Controller's Organisation** (Ministry of Coal; HQ **Kolkata**): checks **coal quality and grading**, settles quality complaints, collects coal statistics.
[70:5:3] - **Energy Statistics India** - published by **NSO, MoSPI** (2026 edition, 30 March 2026); coal supplies about 79% of domestic energy.
[70:5:4] - **Washed coal:** cuts ash and raises plant efficiency, but little used – washing cost raises variable cost and hurts **merit-order** dispatch ranking.
[70:5:5] - **Why India imports coal:** domestic supply of **high-quality, low-ash coking coal** (for steel) is limited; power plants **designed on imported coal** and high-grade coal for **blending** cannot use domestic coal. Coal imports are under **Open General Licence (OGL)** (PIB, Dec 2021).
[70:5:6] - **Nationalisation sequence:** **life insurance 1956 (LIC) → banks 1969 → coal 1971-73 → private oil companies 1974-76** (all under Indira Gandhi except LIC).
[70:5:7] > UPSC 2019: coal nationalised under Indira Gandhi ✓; blocks by lottery ✗ (auction); India self-sufficient, no imports ✗ → 'Only I'.
[70:5:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:70 sub 5; general knowledge (nationalisation years), not checked
## SUB 6 | Biofuels
[70:6:0] - **National Policy on Biofuels 2018** (amended 2022) / EBP: **20% ethanol blending by 2025** - to cut oil imports and help sugarcane farmers. **E20 achieved in 2025**.
[70:6:1] - Ethanol feedstocks: sugarcane juice, sugar beet, sweet sorghum, **damaged food grains**, rotten potatoes, maize, cassava.
[70:6:2] - **National Biofuel Coordination Committee (NBCC)**: headed by **Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas**; approves use of **surplus food grains** for ethanol.
[70:6:3] > A-R (APPSC G2): NBCC approval is needed for surplus food grains because in surplus years farmers risk not getting remunerative prices - **A and R true, R explains A**.
[70:6:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:70 sub 3

## SUB 8 | Energy Security – Imports, Reserves and Pricing
[70:8:0] - Imports: about **85% of petroleum** (over 80%), about **50% of gas**.
[70:8:1] - **Strategic Petroleum Reserves**: **Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur** - about **9.5 days** cover vs IEA norm **90 days**.
[70:8:2] - Price decontrol: **petrol 26 June 2010**; **diesel 19 October 2014**.
[70:8:3] - **Power imports:** India imports hydropower from **Bhutan** (Chukha, Tala, Kurichhu, Mangdechhu); also trades power with Nepal and Bangladesh.
[70:8:4] - **HELP (2016):** replaced NELP; **revenue-sharing** contracts (not production sharing); a **single licence** for all hydrocarbons.
[70:8:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:70 sub 8

=== NOTES 3:71 | Economic Reforms of 1991 - Background, Stabilisation and Structural Adjustment Measures
## SUB 0 | Persons, Dates and Committees
[71:0:0] TABLE head: Person | Role
  [71:0:0.0] P.V. Narasimha Rao | PM (took office 21 June 1991); "father of Indian economic reforms"; first phase of liberalisation under him
  [71:0:0.1] Dr. Manmohan Singh | Finance Minister; architect / "pioneer of liberalisation"; "Manmohan-Rao era" - state-controlled → market-oriented
  [71:0:0.2] C. Rajagopalachari | Coined "Licence-Permit-Quota Raj"
  [71:0:0.3] Rajiv Gandhi | 1980s partial liberalisation
  [71:0:0.4] Chandra Shekhar | His govt fell before 1991
  [71:0:0.5] Committee | Area
  [71:0:0.6] Narasimham (1991) | Banking / financial sector - interest deregulation, private banks (HDFC, ICICI)
  [71:0:0.7] Raja J. Chelliah (1991) | Tax reforms - lower rates, wider base
  [71:0:0.8] C. Rangarajan (1993) | PSU disinvestment
  [71:0:0.9] Malhotra (1993) | Insurance
  [71:0:0.10] Tarapore (1997) | Capital account convertibility - report 30 May 1997; 3-phase roadmap; shelved after East Asian crisis
[71:0:1] - **Year of reforms:** **1991** (not 1990, 1993, 1995); PM **P.V. Narasimha Rao**, FM **Manmohan Singh** – who later became PM (2004-14).
[71:0:2] - **Devaluation of ~18-20%** (1 and 3 July 1991) – under FM **Manmohan Singh**.
[71:0:3] - **Navratnas (July 1997): 9 PSEs**; **Mini-Ratnas (9 October 1997): 97** profit-making PSEs.
[71:0:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.55 (committees); NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 13 p.1-3, p.6-11; web: indiabudget.gov.in Budget 1997-98 (97 Mini-Ratnas, search result); app notes 3:71 sub 3
## SUB 1 | Globalisation – Meaning and Impact
[71:1:0] # Meaning
[71:1:1] - **Dismantling barriers** in international trade; interdependence through trade, technology, investment, people and information; **minimum possible restrictions** across borders.
[71:1:2] - **Includes**: lower import duties (incl. on capital goods), abolition of import licensing, free FDI flow, MNC entry.
[71:1:3] - **Excludes**: **disinvestment of public-sector equity** (privatisation), greater state control, reduced foreign trade.
[71:1:4] - **Free trade** = reduction or removal of trade barriers (tariffs, quotas).
[71:1:5] - Key element of India's market strategy since 1991 = **integration with the global economy**. A stable macroeconomy helps by withstanding shocks.
[71:1:6] TABLE head: Liberalisation | Globalisation
  [71:1:6.0] Removes domestic controls | Integrates with the world economy
  [71:1:6.1] De-licensing, deregulation, import liberalisation | Trade, foreign investment, MNC participation
  [71:1:6.2] Greater market orientation | Greater global integration; technology flows
[71:1:7] # Impact
[71:1:8] - Exports and imports both grew fast - but **imports grew faster than exports** (persistent trade deficit) (APPSC 2025).
[71:1:9] - India's world trade share 1.78% (1950) → 0.6% (1995); later rose.
[71:1:10] - **Largest FDI sources 1991-95: USA and Japan**. Export growth 1994-95: about **18%**.
[71:1:11] - **Services** (IT, outsourcing) benefited most; IT exports cushioned the CAD; 1,800+ GCCs earned $38.25 bn of services exports in July 2026.
[71:1:12] - Indian MNCs: Tata, Reliance, Infosys, Sun Pharma.
[71:1:13] - Net FDI: $44.0 bn (2020-21) → under $1 bn (2024-25) → $7.6 bn (2025-26); gross $94.6 bn.
[71:1:14] - **ISO 9001/9002** for many industries (BIS) and licensing liberalised on 24 July 1991 - both true, but R does not explain A.
[71:1:15] - **Major impact (APPSC 2010):** poverty fell but **economic disparities rose**.
[71:1:16] - **Trade/GDP:** merchandise trade 14.2% of GDP (1990-91) → ~43% (2011-12) – about **three times**.
[71:1:17] - **FII inflows began only after 1992** (FIIs allowed Sept 1992) – not in the 1980s.
[71:1:18] > A-R (UPSC 1996): lower import duty on capital goods is a liberalisation tool and helps firms upgrade technology – R explains A.
[71:1:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 14 p.3-7; app notes 3:71 sub 9; general knowledge (trade/GDP), not checked
## SUB 2 | LPG – Meaning, Measures and What Was Not Part
[71:2:0] TABLE head: Pillar | Meaning - action it promotes | Key measures
  [71:2:0.0] Liberalisation | Removes domestic controls - de-licensing, deregulation, import liberalisation, private-sector expansion | Licensing abolished; MRTP limits scrapped; interest rates deregulated, private banks allowed; tax rates cut, base widened; SEBI statutory (1992); RBI from regulator to facilitator
  [71:2:0.1] Privatisation | Bigger private role - disinvestment, sale of PSUs, opening sectors | Dereservation; PSU equity sale; private buyers above 51% take ownership and management; MoUs; Navratna/Maharatna autonomy
  [71:2:0.2] Globalisation | Integration with the world economy - MNC entry, import duty cuts, free flow of capital/technology | Import substitution → export promotion; QRs and EXIM scrips abolished; market rate 1993; FERA → FEMA 1999
[71:2:1] - **Import liberalisation** = cutting tariffs and QRs.
[71:2:2] - Liberalisation + privatisation = strategies; **globalisation = their outcome**; **outsourcing** is its major feature.
[71:2:3] - LPG reforms opened the door to **multinational corporations**.
[71:2:4] - **Navratnas (1997): 9 PSUs** vs **Miniratnas: 97**. **New PSE Policy (2021)**: strategic disinvestment for Atmanirbhar Bharat.
[71:2:5] # Part of NEP 1991 vs NOT Part (full list)
[71:2:6] TABLE head: Part of 1991 NEP | NOT part of 1991 NEP
  [71:2:6.0] Delicensing | Nationalisation (APPSC 2018 - odd one out)
  [71:2:6.1] Disinvestment of PSU equity | Full capital account convertibility
  [71:2:6.2] FDI liberalisation - automatic route | Demonetisation
  [71:2:6.3] Devaluation, tariff cuts, removal of import quotas | FDI in retail and defence - opened much later
  [71:2:6.4] Opening to foreign and private investment (APPSC 2018) | Strengthening Licence Raj or MRTP; import substitution; reserving more items for SSI
[71:2:7] - 100% FDI in insurance now in place (May 2026).
[71:2:8] - **First step of liberalisation:** substantial changes in **industrial licensing** (UPSC 2000).
[71:2:9] - **Private sector = engine of growth** under LPG (key role); **disinvestment** = reducing Government's share in PSUs.
[71:2:10] - **Primary goals:** boost growth, improve governance, widen people's participation; **not** employment for the poorest, more tariffs or nationalisation.
[71:2:11] - **Golden Handshake (VRS)** belongs to the first reform phase (1991-2001); Antyodaya, Food for Work, IRDP are 1970s schemes.
[71:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 13 p.1-3, p.6-11; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 06 p.119 (Golden Handshake); app notes 3:71 sub 7
## SUB 3 | Crisis Response 1991 – Devaluation, Gold and the IMF
[71:3:0] TABLE head: Measure | Status
  [71:3:0.0] Devaluation - two steps, ~20%, on 1 and 3 July 1991 | Taken - to make exports cheaper and correct BoP (APPSC 2024)
  [71:3:0.1] Gold pledge - about 67 tonnes in all | Taken - 46.91 t pledged by RBI with the Bank of England and Bank of Japan (July 1991, ~$405 mn, airlifted); 20 t sold with repurchase option via SBI to UBS (May 1991)
  [71:3:0.2] IMF loan with IMF/World Bank conditionalities | Taken; earlier IMF borrowings July 1990 and Jan 1991
  [71:3:0.3] Market-determined exchange rate | Later - 1993
  [71:3:0.4] Current account convertibility | Later - August 1994 (IMF Article VIII)
  [71:3:0.5] Demonetisation | NOT part of 1991 (India's demonetisations: 1978 and 2016)
  [71:3:0.6] Full capital account convertibility | NOT adopted - capital account still only partly convertible
[71:3:1] # Reform Sequence
[71:3:2] - 1. Devaluation (July 1991)
[71:3:3] - 2. Industrial delicensing
[71:3:4] - 3. MRTP asset limits abolished
[71:3:5] - 4. Removal of EXIM scrips and import quotas
[71:3:6] - 5. Market-determined exchange rate (1993)
[71:3:7] - **IMF Stand-By Arrangement:** **SDR 1,656 million** for **20 months**, approved by the IMF Board on **31 October 1991**; it supported the 1991-92 and 1992-93 programme.
[71:3:8] > 'Emergency IMF loan by pledging gold' is the usual key for how the crisis was tided over; strictly the gold went to the BoE/BoJ, not the IMF.
[71:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 13 p.1-3, p.6-11; web: RBI Annual Report 1991-92 as quoted in search results (46.91 t, BoE/BoJ); app notes 3:71 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Post-1991 Structural Changes and Sectors
[71:4:0] TABLE head: Variable | Direction
  [71:4:0.0] Share of agriculture in GDP | Fell (~30% in 1991 → about one-fifth, ES 2025-26); did NOT rise
  [71:4:0.1] FDI inflows | Rose
  [71:4:0.2] Forex reserves | Rose - $975 mn → $701.4 bn (~11 months of imports)
  [71:4:0.3] India's share of world exports | Rose
  [71:4:0.4] Services | Became the largest sector
[71:4:1] - GDP growth: below 1% (1991-92) → ~5% (1992-94) → **6.3% (1994-95)**; industry -0.8% → 8.6% (1994-95) → 10.6% (1996-97).
[71:4:2] - Post-reform economy: **greater global integration, larger private sector** (APPSC 2025).
[71:4:3] TABLE head: Reshaped | Largely untouched / slow
  [71:4:3.0] Telecommunications - private and foreign entry | Railways - largely a state monopoly
  [71:4:3.1] Banking - private banks, interest deregulation | Power distribution - privatisation still debated
  [71:4:3.2] Civil aviation - private airlines | Agriculture - little direct reform
  [71:4:3.3] Automobiles, consumer electronics | Ports - corporatisation only now
[71:4:4] - UPSC 2017: export share ✓, FDI ✓, forex ✓, agriculture share 'increased enormously' ✗ → **2, 3 and 4 only**.
[71:4:5] - A-R (UPPSC 1997): public-sector employment growth was sluggish **because** the State's role was reassessed – R explains A.
[71:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 14 p.3-7; NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 13 p.8, p.10 (railways reserved); app notes 3:71 sub 10
## SUB 5 | Causes and Indicators of the 1991 Crisis
[71:5:0] # 1980s Groundwork (Indira and Rajiv Gandhi, 1984-89)
[71:5:1] - **Broad-banding of licences**; easier **capital-goods imports**; higher MRTP limit; **FERA relaxed**.
[71:5:2] - Growth broke the **Hindu rate**, touched **5.5%** - but it was **debt-fuelled**.
[71:5:3] - Some liberalisation began under **Rajiv Gandhi**, but the 1991 reforms were **far more comprehensive**.
[71:5:4] # Long-term Causes
[71:5:5] TABLE head: Cause | Effect / data
  [71:5:5.0] Fiscal profligacy | Gross fiscal deficit 5.4% (1981-82) → 8.0% (1989-90); average 6.3% (Sixth Plan) → 8.2% (Seventh)
  [71:5:5.1] Licence-Permit-Quota Raj | Heavy controls; MRTP Act 1970
  [71:5:5.2] PSU losses | Low returns on public investment
  [71:5:5.3] Weak exports | World export share 2.2% (1948) → 0.5% (1983)
  [71:5:5.4] Structural | CADs financed by foreign borrowing since the 1980s, incl. short-term ECBs
[71:5:6] - The **long-term** cause = constant **fiscal profligacy** and rising fiscal deficit; the others below were **immediate triggers**.
[71:5:7] # Immediate Triggers
[71:5:8] TABLE head: Trigger | Effect
  [71:5:8.0] Gulf War (Aug 1990) | Oil prices doubled; Gulf remittances dried up (did NOT rise)
  [71:5:8.1] Political instability | Two changes of government Dec 1989 - June 1991; fall of Chandra Shekhar govt
  [71:5:8.2] Capital flight | NRIs withdrew deposits; foreign banks stopped lending
[71:5:9] - Road to crisis: 1980s fiscal profligacy → CAD on foreign borrowing → Gulf War shock → BoP crisis 1991.
[71:5:10] TABLE head: Indicator (1990-91 / 1991) | Value
  [71:5:10.0] Forex reserves (June 1991) | ~$975 million - about two weeks of imports
  [71:5:10.1] Fiscal deficit | 9.4% of GDP (Centre + States); Centre's GFD 8.4% (6.1% in 1980-81)
  [71:5:10.2] Current account deficit | 3.1-3.2% of GDP
  [71:5:10.3] Trade deficit | ₹10,644 crore (3.2% of GDP)
  [71:5:10.4] Internal debt of govt | 35% (1980-81) → 53% of GDP (1990-91)
  [71:5:10.5] GDP growth | 1.1% (1990-91); below 1% in 1991-92
[71:5:11] - Crisis = **high inflation, very low forex reserves, large fiscal deficit** (APPSC 2025).
[71:5:12] - NEP 1991 was a **response to a severe BoP crisis**.
[71:5:13] - **Immediate cause of forex loss:** **sharp rise in the oil and petroleum import bill** after the Gulf War (APPSC G1).
[71:5:14] - The crisis = a **Balance of Payments crisis**; response = **Structural Adjustment Programme** with IMF-World Bank loans (~$7 bn).
[71:5:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 13 p.1-3, p.6-11; app notes 3:71 sub 0-1
## SUB 6 | Trade and Exchange Reforms
[71:6:0] TABLE head: Year | Reform
  [71:6:0.0] July 1991 | Devaluation (~20%)
  [71:6:0.1] March 1992 | LERMS - dual rate: 60% of export earnings at market rate, 40% at official rate; rupee partly convertible on current account
  [71:6:0.2] 1992 | SEBI statutory
  [71:6:0.3] March 1993 | Unified market-determined rate
  [71:6:0.4] August 1994 | Current account convertibility
  [71:6:0.5] 1995 | WTO founding member (WTO replaced GATT, 1948, 23 countries); signed TRIPS, TRIMS, AoA
  [71:6:0.6] 1999 | FERA → FEMA
  [71:6:0.7] April 2001 | Remaining QRs removed
[71:6:1] - **Tariff cuts**: average import tariff **~125% (late 1980s) → ~30%** (early 2000s); general customs duty later **10%**.
[71:6:2] - **Export-led growth** came with the LPG reforms of 1991 (import substitution → export promotion). **Mahalanobis model** (Second Plan) = heavy industry and import substitution.
[71:6:3] - **Peak import duty:** **over 300% → 150%** in the **1991-92 Budget** (first step; later 50%).
[71:6:4] - **LERMS** announced in the **Union Budget 1992-93**, effective March 1992.
[71:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.22 (LERMS); web: indiabefore91.in '1991: Economic Reforms' (search result); app notes 3:71 sub 8
## SUB 7 | Stabilisation vs Structural Adjustment
[71:7:0] TABLE head: Basis | Stabilisation | Structural adjustment
  [71:7:0.0] Term | Short-term | Long-term (medium/long-term efficiency and growth)
  [71:7:0.1] Nature | Demand-side (demand management) | Supply-side
  [71:7:0.2] Targets | Inflation, fiscal deficit, BoP | Industrial, trade, financial, investment structures
  [71:7:0.3] Fiscal tools | Cut fiscal deficit: less wasteful spending, subsidy cuts, better tax collection | Tax-sector reform
  [71:7:0.4] Monetary tools | Tight monetary policy by RBI to control inflation | Financial-sector reform
  [71:7:0.5] Trade / exchange | Rupee devaluation to correct BoP | Tariff cuts, QR removal, export promotion
  [71:7:0.6] Industrial | - | Delicensing, MRTP relaxation, FDI opening, disinvestment
  [71:7:0.7] Lead institution | IMF | World Bank (IBRD)
[71:7:1] - Sequencing: stabilisation first, structural adjustment alongside and after.
[71:7:2] - **Structural measures**: delicensing, tariff reduction, public-sector disinvestment.
[71:7:3] # IMF-World Bank SAPs
[71:7:4] - **Structural Adjustment Programmes** = IMF and World Bank loan packages to **reduce fiscal imbalances and adjust the economy for long-term growth** (APPSC 2018).
[71:7:5] - Conditions: austerity, privatisation, deregulation, **currency devaluation**, better tax collection.
[71:7:6] - **Eighth Plan (1992-97)** began just after stabilisation and structural adjustment.
[71:7:7] - **Washington Consensus** (ten rules): fiscal discipline, tax reform, trade and FDI liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, property rights - NOT expansion of import quotas. Now seen as obsolete; blamed for the 1997 and 2008 crises (14 Mar 2026).
[71:7:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 02 p.42 (SAPs); app notes 3:71 sub 4
## SUB 8 | New Industrial Policy 1991, PSU Reform and National Renewal Fund
[71:8:0] # Industrial Policy (24 July 1991)
[71:8:1] - **Industrial licensing abolished** for all but a few industries (hazardous and strategic, e.g. hazardous chemicals, aerospace); now only **5-6** industries need a licence; reserved for public sector now only **atomic energy and railways** (+ specified minerals).
[71:8:2] - Delicensed firms: **pricing freedom**, no expansion curbs.
[71:8:3] - **Public-sector reserved industries cut from 17 (1956 policy) to 8**; later pruned further.
[71:8:4] - **MRTP**: **asset limits, pre-entry restrictions and merger/expansion controls abolished**. (SEBI's status was a separate reform.)
[71:8:5] - **FDI**: automatic approval up to **51%** in high-priority industries (now 100% in most sectors); NRIs/OCBs up to 100%; FIIs allowed into stock markets.
[71:8:6] - **BIFR**: set up to revive **sick industrial units**.
[71:8:7] # National Renewal Fund (February 1992)
[71:8:8] - A **safety net** for workers hit by industrial restructuring under the new policy.
[71:8:9] - Objectives: **retraining and redeployment** of employees affected by modernisation and restructuring; **compensation** of affected employees; counselling.
[71:8:10] - In practice mostly paid for **Voluntary Retirement Schemes (VRS)** in central PSUs; later limited to public sector units only.
[71:8:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 13 p.1-3, p.6-11; NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 01 p.23 (safety net); app notes 3:71 sub 6
## SUB 9 | 1991 Fiscal Policy Measures
[71:9:0] TABLE head: Included | NOT included
  [71:9:0.0] Control of public expenditure | Contraction of the tax net - the net was widened (APPSC 2019)
  [71:9:0.1] Subsidy cuts | 
  [71:9:0.2] Better tax collection | 
  [71:9:0.3] Lower peak income/corporate tax rates (Chelliah) | 
[71:9:1] - **PSU disinvestment** first used to **bridge the fiscal deficit**, later for efficiency.
[71:9:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:71 sub 5
## SUB 10 | Criticism and Current Relevance
[71:10:0] TABLE head: Criticism | Meaning
  [71:10:0.0] Jobless growth | Output rose faster than employment; capital-intensive growth
  [71:10:0.1] Agrarian neglect | Public investment in agriculture lagged
  [71:10:0.2] Crony capitalism | Gains held by large, politically connected firms
[71:10:1] - SAP outcomes: raised poverty and inequality in the Global South (May 2026).
[71:10:2] - Reforms 1.0 = LPG (1991); Reforms 2.0 = DPI, UPI, Jan Dhan, DBT (2014 on); "Reforms 3.0" debate (Jul 2026).
[71:10:3] - CAD 0.8% of GDP (H1 FY26), peak 4.8% (FY13); ES 2025-26: persistent CAD = structural cause of **high cost of capital**.
[71:10:4] - May 2026: PM urged citizens to cut fuel, gold and foreign-travel spending to save forex; ₹57,381 crore **Economic Stabilisation Fund** after the $100/barrel oil shock (14 Mar 2026).
[71:10:5] - **Poverty vs inequality:** post-1991 growth **cut poverty** ratios but **widened** income and regional **inequality** (rising consumption Gini).
[71:10:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:71 sub 11

=== NOTES 3:72 | Second-generation Reforms and the Reform Record Since 2014; Labour Codes, Ibc, Gst As Reforms
## SUB 0 | Four Labour Codes and Labour Laws
[72:0:0] - **29** central laws → **4 Codes**; sections 1,232 → 480. Labour = **Concurrent List**.
[72:0:1] - In force **21 November 2025**; draft rules **Dec 2025**; Central Rules May 2026.
[72:0:2] TABLE head: Code | Laws | Key laws / provisions
  [72:0:2.0] Wages, 2019 | 4 | Minimum Wages 1948, Payment of Wages 1936, Payment of Bonus 1965, Equal Remuneration 1976; universal minimum wage; Centre's national floor wage; no gender discrimination; 8-hour day
  [72:0:2.1] Industrial Relations, 2020 | 3 | Trade Unions 1926, Standing Orders 1946, Industrial Disputes 1947; lay-off permission 100 → 300
  [72:0:2.2] Social Security, 2020 | 9 | EPF, ESI, Employees' Compensation; 26-week maternity; gig workers
  [72:0:2.3] OSH, 2020 | 13 | Factories Act, Contract Labour Act 1970
[72:0:3] - Contract Labour Act → **OSH Code**, NOT Wages Code (4 laws, not 29).
[72:0:4] - **National floor wage:** **Anoop Satpathy Committee (2019)** recommended a national minimum wage of **₹375/day**
[72:0:5] - **Occupier (Factories Act 1948, Sec 2(n)):** person with **ultimate control** over a factory; in a company a **director** must be named
[72:0:6] - **2018 Standing Orders Rules**: **fixed-term employment, all sectors**; no termination notice for temporary workmen.
[72:0:7] - Gains (ES 2025-26): formalisation 60.4% → 75.5%; unions: anti-worker.
[72:0:8] TABLE head: Law | Year
  [72:0:8.0] Industrial Disputes Act | 1947
  [72:0:8.1] Minimum Wages Act | 1948
  [72:0:8.2] Factories Act | 1948
[72:0:9] - **Wages (Code on Wages, Sec. 2(y))** include **basic pay, dearness allowance, retaining allowance**; **exclude overtime allowance**, HRA, bonus.
[72:0:10] - UPPSC 2021: Code on Wages merged **Minimum Wages, Payment of Bonus, Equal Remuneration** (+ Payment of Wages) – **not Contract Labour** → 'I, II and IV'.
[72:0:11] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 07 p.25 (labour codes); app notes 3:72 sub 1; general knowledge (Sec. 2(y)), not checked
## SUB 1 | Reform Generations and the Reform Agenda
[72:1:0] TABLE head: First (1991-2000) | Second (2000-01 on) | Third (Tenth Plan)
  [72:1:0.0] Private-sector promotion (de-licensing, de-reservation, MRTP limits abolished), tariff cuts and QR removal, public-sector reform, external sector, financial sector, tax reforms | Factor-market reforms (APM dismantling – petroleum, sugar, fertiliser, drugs), public-sector reforms, reforms in government and public institutions, legal-sector reforms, critical areas (infrastructure, agriculture, health, education) | Fully functional PRIs
[72:1:1] - **'Legal system reforms' ARE a second-generation head** (Ramesh Singh); 'oil sector reforms' is not a separate head (UPPSC 2009 key said legal – disputed).
[72:1:2] - **'Greater rigour in labour laws'** is NOT an economic reform (reforms = SEZs, less SSI reservation, removal of entry barriers).
[72:1:3] - **CII 10-point agenda** for economic revival (June 2012; again 2013).
[72:1:4] - Factor markets: **land** - DILRMP, ULPIN, NGDRS; **labour** - four Codes; **capital** - IBC, capital-market reform. Next-generation pillars start with land, labour.
[72:1:5] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 04 p.107-110; web: Business Standard 2012/2013 CII agenda (search results); app notes 3:72 sub 0
## SUB 2 | GST as Structural Reform
[72:2:0] - **101st Amendment Act, 2016** (122nd Bill); in force **1 July 2017**; **Kelkar** Committee; **Canadian dual model**; **Assam** ratified first.
[72:2:1] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [72:2:1.0] 246A | Power to levy GST
  [72:2:1.1] 269A | IGST on inter-State supply
  [72:2:1.2] 279A | GST Council
  [72:2:1.3] 366(12A) | Definition
  [72:2:1.4] 286 | No State tax on supplies outside State / import-export
[72:2:2] - Destination-based; input tax credit ends cascading; subsumed **State VAT**, Central excise, service tax, CST.
[72:2:3] - **GST 2.0** (Aug 2025): rate rationalisation, **40% slab**: sin/luxury goods.
[72:2:4] - **EoDB gain:** one tax replaced many Central and State indirect taxes; ended cascading and **checkpost delays** → better **Ease of Doing Business**.
[72:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 09 p.4; NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.27; app notes 3:72 sub 2
## SUB 3 | Insurance Reform
[72:3:0] - **R.N. Malhotra Committee (1993; report Jan 1994)** recommended **private entry** → **IRDA Act 1999**.
[72:3:1] - **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act 2025**: FDI **74% → 100%**.
[72:3:2] - Not Narasimham (banking), Chelliah (tax), Rangarajan (disinvestment), Omkar Goswami (industrial sickness).
[72:3:3] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy part 05 p.119; NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 04 p.55
## SUB 4 | Reforms Since 2014 and the National Monetisation Pipeline
[72:4:0] TABLE head: Reform | Objective
  [72:4:0.0] NITI Aayog (2015) | Replaced Planning Commission; cooperative, competitive federalism
  [72:4:0.1] Corporate tax cut (Sept 2019) | 22% existing, 15% new manufacturing
  [72:4:0.2] PLI (14 sectors, ₹1.97 lakh crore) | Manufacturing and exports
  [72:4:0.3] Farm Acts | Sept 2020; repealed Nov 2021
  [72:4:0.4] New PSE Policy 2021 | Strategic disinvestment
  [72:4:0.5] Jan Vishwas Act 2023 | Decriminalise minor offences; Bill 2025: 355 provisions
  [72:4:0.6] DBT | 1 Jan 2013; JAM
[72:4:1] - Budget 2026-27: **350+ reforms**. Market Distortions Index: 82nd (2010) → 57th (2023), due to GST, IBC, trade facilitation (not import quotas).
[72:4:2] # Ease of Doing Business
[72:4:3] - World Bank rank **142 (2014) → 63 (2019)**.
[72:4:4] - **AP No. 1 since BRAP 2016**; Single Desk Portal tied to VCIC EoDB loan. BRAP 2020 Achievers: MP, HP, Maharashtra, Odisha, Uttarakhand, UP.
[72:4:5] # Power and PSB Reforms
[72:4:6] - **UDAY** (2015): States absorb **75% of DISCOM debt**; **RDSS** (2021-26, ₹3,03,758 crore): AT&C losses **12-15%**, **ACS-ARR gap zero** by 2024-25; smart meters.
[72:4:7] - **PSB recapitalisation**: **Indradhanush** (Aug 2015) ₹70,000 crore; **₹2.11 lakh crore** (Oct 2017), ₹1.35 lakh crore via **recap bonds**.
[72:4:8] - **EASE** (Jan 2018): PSB agenda: CLEAN, SMART banking; EASE 9.0: FY2026-27.
[72:4:9] # National Monetisation Pipeline
[72:4:10] - Aug 2021; **₹6 lakh crore**, FY2022-25; **brownfield** assets leased (OMT, InvITs); ownership stays, assets return, no land sale.
[72:4:11] - Shares: **roads 27%**, railways 25%, power 15%.
[72:4:12] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:72 sub 5-6
## SUB 5 | IBC 2016
[72:5:0] - CIRP **180 days** + one **90-day** extension; outer limit **330 days** (2019 amendment). **NCLT** adjudicates; **IBBI** regulates.
[72:5:1] - **Objectives:** consolidate insolvency laws for **companies, partnership firms and individuals**; resolution in a **time-bound manner** for **maximisation of value of assets**; promote **entrepreneurship and availability of credit**; balance the interests of all stakeholders; set up the **IBBI**.
[72:5:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:72 sub 3

  1 only | 2 only | *Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2
  x: The NCLT is the adjudicating authority and the IBBI is the regulator; both statements are correct.
[ga147c13ac5ed] sub5
  Which of the following is NOT an objective of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016?
  Time-bound insolvency resolution | Maximisation of the value of assets | Promotion of entrepreneurship and availability of credit | *Nationalisation of sick companies
  x: The Code seeks time-bound resolution, maximising asset value, and promoting entrepreneurship and credit; nationalisation is not an aim.

## SUB 2 | Composition of Imports
[73:2:0] - **POL (petroleum, oil and lubricants) = largest import item** for most of the post-reform period – highest import bill and most forex spent (2024-25: **US$ 185.8 bn, 25.8%** of imports).
[73:2:1] - Petroleum crude, **gold** and petroleum products = about **one-third of imports** (FY25); gold imports rose with prices.
[73:2:2] - **Two largest import groups:** **petroleum products and capital goods** (capital goods 12.3% in 2024-25).
[73:2:3] - **Edible oil** = main **agricultural** import (over 50% of agri imports); food & allied = 4.4% of imports.
[73:2:4] - **Qatar** = biggest **LNG** supplier to India (15.3 bcm of 37.9 bcm in 2024).
[73:2:5] - Most important item "in recent years" among chemicals, fertilisers, iron & steel: **petroleum (and edible oil)**.
[73:2:6] # Import order by question period
[73:2:7] TABLE head: Period | Fact
  [73:2:7.0] 1994-95 | Petroleum > capital goods > pearls & precious stones > chemicals > iron & steel (now 2, 1, 4, 3, 5)
  [73:2:7.1] 2000-01 | Highest by rupee value among edible oils, fertilisers, chemicals: pearls, precious and semi-precious stones
  [73:2:7.2] 2001-02 | Crude and products ≈ 27% of imports; exports fell (−1.6%), not +10%
  [73:2:7.3] 2004-05 | Fuel > capital goods > gold & silver > chemicals
  [73:2:7.4] General hierarchy | Fuel > POL > capital goods > chemicals > gold/silver
  [73:2:7.5] Bulk vs non-bulk | Bulk: crude, cereals, pulses, edible oils, sugar, fertiliser, ores; non-bulk: capital goods, precious products, chemicals
[73:2:8] - **Pulses** are a small import – not the largest item.

## SUB 3 | Trade Terms and Trade Theory
[73:3:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [73:3:0.0] Balance of trade | Exports minus imports of goods only (visible trade)
  [73:3:0.1] Intra-industry trade | A country imports and exports the same product (e.g. cars)
  [73:3:0.2] Inter-industry trade | Exchange of different products
  [73:3:0.3] Entrepot trade | Imported goods re-exported, with or without processing or packaging ("goods imported for export")
  [73:3:0.4] Free trade | Absence of tariffs and quantitative restrictions
  [73:3:0.5] Dumping | Exporting at a price below the home-market price or cost
  [73:3:0.6] Anti-dumping duty | Protects against goods exported below normal value
  [73:3:0.7] Countervailing duty | Levied on imported products to offset foreign subsidies; raises their domestic price
  [73:3:0.8] Tariff | Tax on imports
  [73:3:0.9] Import quota | Quantitative restriction on imports
  [73:3:0.10] Import licensing | Administrative restriction on imports
  [73:3:0.11] Rules of origin | Decide a product's national source and which goods get FTA concessions
  [73:3:0.12] SPS measures | Sanitary and phytosanitary rules (human, animal, plant health) – a non-tariff barrier
[73:3:1] - **India** used the **most anti-dumping measures in 1995-2005** (WTO data); in 2024 the USA had the most measures in force.
[73:3:2] - **Singer-Prebisch thesis:** primary-exporting LDCs suffer a **secular decline in their terms of trade** and so a **welfare loss**.
[73:3:3] - **Adam Smith = absolute advantage; David Ricardo = comparative advantage.** India's services surplus vs merchandise deficit = comparative advantage in services.
[73:3:4] - **Export promotion = outward-looking; import substitution = inward-looking.** **Direction** of trade = country/region-wise pattern; composition = items; volume = value.
[73:3:5] # Terms of trade and exchange rate
[73:3:6] TABLE head: Measure | Formula
  [73:3:6.0] Net (NTT) | Export price index / import price index × 100
  [73:3:6.1] Gross (GTT) | Import quantity / export quantity
  [73:3:6.2] Income (ITT) | NTT × export quantity index
[73:3:7] - **Devaluation/depreciation:** exports **cheaper abroad**, imports **dearer** → exports rise, imports fall.
[73:3:8] - **J-curve:** trade balance **first worsens**, then improves as volumes adjust. **Marshall-Lerner:** devaluation helps only if export + import demand elasticities **sum > 1**.
[73:3:9] - **1991 New Trade Policy:** QRs and import substitution → **price-based regime**.
[73:3:10] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.78, p.80; NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 02 p.36; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 05 p.168; app notes 3:73 sub 0-2
## SUB 4 | Trade Deficit and Balance
[73:4:0] - **Trade deficit = imports − exports** (negative balance of trade); India's story is "**oil and gold**".
[73:4:1] - **Trade surplus only twice since independence: 1972-73 and 1976-77.**
[73:4:2] - Deficit peaked in **2012-13 (US$ 195.66 bn)** and fell continuously to **2016-17 (US$ 112.44 bn)** as **both POL and non-POL deficits fell** (UPPSC 2017 A-R: both true, R explains A).
[73:4:3] - **2020-21 vs 2019-20:** deficit **declined** ($157.5 bn → $102.2 bn) – imports fell more than exports (COVID).
[73:4:4] - **UPSC 2020 (present):** merchandise exports < imports; **services exports > services imports**; India runs an overall trade/current account deficit → **1, 3 and 4** (imports of iron & steel, fertilisers, machinery did NOT fall).
[73:4:5] - **Causes since 1991:** oil and gold imports, **South-East Asian crisis 1997-98**, competition from **China**, **non-tariff barriers** of partners, import liberalisation (capital goods, APIs, electronics). **NOT** "lacklustre services" – services were in surplus.
[73:4:6] TABLE head: Item | Value
  [73:4:6.0] Merchandise exports FY25 | US$ 437.7 bn
  [73:4:6.1] Merchandise imports FY25 | US$ 721.2 bn
  [73:4:6.2] Total exports / imports FY25 | $825.3 bn / $919.9 bn
  [73:4:6.3] Merchandise deficit FY25 | $283.5 bn (+17.6%); overall deficit $94.7 bn
  [73:4:6.4] Merchandise deficit FY26 (RBI BoP) | $337.3 bn
[73:4:7] - **Twin deficit hypothesis:** a rising **fiscal deficit** goes with a rising **trade deficit**.
[73:4:8] - **Services surplus** (IT/ITeS) and **remittances** cushion the merchandise deficit.
[73:4:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 01 p.10; Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary (Vision IAS) part 1 p.38-39; app notes 3:73 sub 6

  [73:5:0.0] Share in world merchandise exports | 1.85% (1950) → 0.5-0.7% in the 1990s (0.6%) → 1.7% (2013) → 1.7% (2018) → 1.6% (2020) → 1.8% (2024)
  [73:5:0.1] Merchandise exporter rank 2024 | 18th; importer 9th (2.8%)
  [73:5:0.2] Commercial services exporter | 8th in 2014; 2024: 8th, share 2% (2005) → 4.3%
  [73:5:0.3] Services importer 2024 | 9th (3.4%)
[73:5:1] - Countries ahead of India in services exports include **Ireland** (3rd-4th) – not Russia or Indonesia.
[73:5:2] - Services exports FY25 a record **$387.5 bn** (+13.6%); **record surplus $188.8 bn** financing about 2/3 of the merchandise deficit; services ≈ **49%** of total exports (May 2026).
[73:5:3] - India **3rd in the Global South** for trade-partner diversity (UNCTAD TDR 2025), after China and UAE.

  x: SPS measures are health rules for humans, animals and plants under the WTO SPS Agreement; they act as a non-tariff barrier.
[na2c2528ad38] sub3
  According to the Marshall-Lerner condition, when does devaluation improve the trade balance?
  Only export demand is perfectly inelastic | *The sum of export and import demand price elasticities is greater than one | The sum of export and import demand price elasticities is equal to zero | The sum of export and import demand price elasticities is less than one
  x: The Marshall–Lerner condition is satisfied when the sum of the absolute values of export and import demand price elasticities exceeds one.
[n94f8202a13f] sub3
  How is Net Terms of Trade (NTT) calculated?
  Import price index / Export price index × 100 | *Export price index / Import price index × 100 | Export quantity / Import quantity × 100 | Import quantity / Export quantity × 100
  x: NTT = export price index / import price index × 100; gross terms of trade is import quantity over export quantity.
[n7f7c4e52afe] sub3
  According to the J-curve effect, what generally happens to the trade balance after a currency depreciation?
  Worsens only when exports become cheaper abroad | Remains unchanged because prices do not change | Improves immediately and then worsens permanently | *First worsens and improves only after export and import volumes adjust
  x: Under the J-curve effect, import bills rise immediately after depreciation, so the trade balance initially worsens; it improves later as quantities adjust.
[n3fa1bb49183] sub3
  What is the immediate effect of devaluation or depreciation of a currency?
  Exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home | *Exports become cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home | Both exports and imports become cheaper | Export and import prices are unaffected
  x: Devaluation or depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers and imports dearer at home.

[f1381002fb665] sub3
  How is Gross Terms of Trade (GTT) measured?

  x: GTT = import quantity / export quantity; the first option is NTT and the third is ITT.
[gb787514adda5] sub3
  How is the Income Terms of Trade (ITT) measured?
  Export price index / import price index × 100 | Import quantity / export quantity | Import price index × export quantity index | *Net terms of trade × export quantity index
  x: Income terms of trade = NTT multiplied by the export quantity index.

  x: The services surplus, especially from IT and IT-enabled services, together with remittances, offsets a substantial part of the merchandise deficit.

=== NOTES 3:74 | Foreign Trade Policy - Objectives, Incentives, Eous; Trade Facilitation and Logistics Costs
## SUB 0 | Trade Promotion and Export Credit Bodies
[74:0:0] TABLE head: Body | Year / role
  [74:0:0.0] ECGC (Export Credit Guarantee Corporation, now ECGC Ltd) | 1957, wholly government-owned; export credit-risk insurance – the body that insures exporters
  [74:0:0.1] EXIM Bank | Act 1981, set up 1982, Mumbai; finance for foreign trade – lines of credit, buyer's/seller's credit, project exports; not an insurer
  [74:0:0.2] MMTC | 1963; minerals, metals, precious metals; largest international trading organisation / trading government company; was the largest non-oil importer
  [74:0:0.3] STC (State Trading Corporation) | 1956; canalising agency for bulk goods; foreign trade, not insurance
  [74:0:0.4] IBEF (India Brand Equity Fund/Foundation) | 1996, trust of the Department of Commerce; promotes the "Made in India" brand abroad
  [74:0:0.5] PEC (Project and Equipment Corporation) | Under the Ministry of Commerce, not Industry
  [74:0:0.6] DGFT | Attached office of the Department of Commerce, Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi; issues FTP authorisations
[74:0:1] - **Insurance of export risk = ECGC only** (not EXIM Bank, GIC, STC or RBI); "export financing and insurance" = ECGC.
[74:0:2] - **Pre-shipment inspection / quality control** = **Export Inspection Council**, NOT an ECGC objective (UPSC 2002: only statement 1 – MMTC – correct).
[74:0:3] - **NIRVIK** (Niryat Rin Vikas Yojana, **Budget 2020-21**): ECGC scheme – higher insurance cover, lower premium for **exporters**.
[74:0:4] - Channelising (canalising) exports and imports – UPPSC 1999 key: **MMTC, EXIM Bank, STC and FCI (all four)**. Promote foreign trade: **ECGC, MMTC, STC (all)**.
[74:0:5] - **Neelachal Ispat Nigam Ltd (NINL)** was set up by **MMTC jointly with the Government of Odisha** (Odisha PSUs); sold to Tata Steel in 2022.
[74:0:6] - Agri goods exporters: **NAFED, STC, MMTC**; **IFFCO** (fertilisers) is NOT one.
[74:0:7] - Status holders: earlier **Export House → Trading House → Star Trading House → Super Star Trading House** (high, sustained export performance = Star Trading Houses); now **One-Star to Five-Star Export Houses**.
[74:0:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.79; NextGen Indian Economy P1 - APPSC 04 p.52; PEC, NINL, Export Inspection Council: general knowledge, not checked; app notes 3:74 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Export Incentive Schemes and Towns of Export Excellence
[74:1:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Fact
  [74:1:0.0] EPCG | Export Promotion Capital Goods: zero-duty import of capital goods against an export obligation
  [74:1:0.1] Duty drawback | Refund of import (customs) and excise duties on inputs used in exports – not income tax, not export duty
  [74:1:0.2] Advance Authorisation | Duty-free import of inputs for export production
  [74:1:0.3] MEIS (FTP 2015-20) | Goods exports reward; replaced five schemes – Focus Product, Focus Market, Market Linked Focus Product, VKGUY, Agri Infrastructure Incentive Scrip
  [74:1:0.4] SEIS | Services exports reward (FTP 2015-20)
  [74:1:0.5] RoDTEP | Replaced the WTO-challenged MEIS; refunds unrebated central, state and local taxes; run online by CBIC
  [74:1:0.6] RoSCTL | Replaced RoSL; apparel and made-ups
  [74:1:0.7] Vishesh Krishi (and Gram) Upaj Yojana (2004) | Promoted exports of fruits, vegetables, flowers, minor forest produce and their value-added products
  [74:1:0.8] Gold Card Scheme (RBI, EXIM Policy 2003-04) | Quicker, cheaper credit for creditworthy exporters
  [74:1:0.9] Niryat Bandhu | DGFT training/outreach – mentoring new and first-generation entrepreneurs in export-import
[74:1:1] - **Towns of Export Excellence (TEE):** **Tirupur** (hosiery), **Ludhiana** (woollen knitwear), **Panipat** (woollen blankets) – 2003; **Madurai** (handlooms) is also a TEE – so "Madurai was not a TEE" is wrong; Visakhapatnam and Bhimavaram (seafood) are AP's TEEs.
[74:1:2] - **Export Promotion Mission:** ₹25,060 crore, FY 2025-26 to 2030-31, run by **DGFT**; merges **Interest Equalisation + Market Access Initiative**; for **MSMEs and first-time exporters**.
[74:1:3] - **RELIEF Scheme 2026:** ₹497 crore via **ECGC** for **war-risk and logistics costs in West Asia**.
[74:1:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.79; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 05 p.178, p.181-182; web – howtoexportimport.com "List of Towns of Export Excellence" (fetched); MEIS predecessor schemes and VKGUY: general knowledge, not checked; app notes 3:74 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Foreign Trade Policy – History and Targets
[74:2:0] TABLE head: Policy | Fact
  [74:2:0.0] First EXIM Policy | 1985-88
  [74:2:0.1] EXIM Policy 1992 | Five years (1992-97)
  [74:2:0.2] EXIM Policy 2000 | Announced 31 March 2000 (1997-2002 framework); SEZ policy 1 April 2000
  [74:2:0.3] FTP 2004-09 (Aug 2004) | First "Foreign Trade Policy"; double India's share of world merchandise trade to 1.5% by 2009; stressed growth and employment
  [74:2:0.4] FTP 2015-20 (1 April 2015) | Raise share of world exports from 2% to 3.5%; MEIS/SEIS; extended to 31 March 2023
  [74:2:0.5] FTP 2023 | From 1 April 2023, no end date; $2 trillion exports by 2030
[74:2:1] - FTP 2023: incentives → **remission and entitlement**; **Districts as Export Hubs**; rupee trade and **merchanting trade**; one-time **amnesty** for EPCG and Advance Authorisation defaults.
[74:2:2] - FTP services target: **4.2%** share of world services exports by 2022.
[74:2:3] - Administered by the **Department of Commerce, Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, through **DGFT**.
[74:2:4] - 1992 partial convertibility: **60% market rate : 40% official rate**.
[74:2:5] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 05 p.168, p.181; Rocket Indian Economy p.79; app notes 3:74 sub 1-2
## SUB 3 | Export-Import Procedure, Documents and Rules of Origin
[74:3:0] TABLE head: Document | Purpose
  [74:3:0.0] Indent | Importer's order to buy goods – the import process begins with the indent
  [74:3:0.1] Letter of credit | Produced by the importer (through its issuing bank), promising payment to the exporter (beneficiary)
  [74:3:0.2] Shipping bill | Customs document for clearing export goods
  [74:3:0.3] Mate's receipt | Ship's mate acknowledges goods loaded on board
  [74:3:0.4] Bill of lading | Shipping company's receipt and document of title
[74:3:1] - **Rules of origin:** fix a product's **national source**; tell customs which **duties, regulations and fees** apply; used for **trade statistics**; matter because duties and restrictions depend on the **source of imports** – **all four statements correct**.
[74:3:2] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.80; app notes 3:74 sub 8
## SUB 4 | Trade Policy Instruments and Economic Integration
[74:4:0] - **Import substitution industrialisation (ISI):** inward-looking; produce substitutes at home to **reduce import dependence** (India's policy for about four decades) – not open trade, FDI or liberalisation.
[74:4:1] - **Import quota** = quantitative restriction; tariffs, countervailing and anti-dumping duties = price-based.
[74:4:2] TABLE head: Stage | Feature
  [74:4:2.0] FTA | Free internal trade; members keep own external tariffs
  [74:4:2.1] Customs union | Free internal trade + common external tariff
  [74:4:2.2] Common market | Customs union + free movement of factors
  [74:4:2.3] Economic union | Common market + coordinated economic policies
[74:4:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.80; app notes 3:74 sub 0
## SUB 5 | Agri-Export Promotion and Trade Facilitation
[74:5:0] - India's first **Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre**: **Pune, May 2021** (APEDA with MCCIA).
[74:5:1] - First **Deendayal Hastkala Sankul** (trade facilitation centre for handicrafts): **Varanasi**.
[74:5:2] - **APEDA**: APEDA Act **December 1985**, in force 1986; under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**; nodal agency for **Agri Export Zones**. **MPEDA** = marine products.
[74:5:3] - **Agriculture Export Policy 2018:** **double** agri exports to about **$60 bn by 2022**.
[74:5:4] TABLE head: Platform | Meaning
  [74:5:4.0] ICEGATE | CBIC customs e-filing portal
  [74:5:4.1] SWIFT | Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade – single-window import clearance
  [74:5:4.2] PM Gati Shakti | 2021; cut logistics costs
  [74:5:4.3] National Logistics Policy | 2022; cut logistics costs
[74:5:5] - **LEADS 2025** (DPIIT): **Andhra Pradesh = Accelerator** among coastal states; **Tamil Nadu = Exemplar**.
[74:5:6] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (10th ed.) part 05 p.178; Pune AEFC and Varanasi Hastkala Sankul: general knowledge, not checked; app notes 3:74 sub 5, 9
## SUB 6 | EOUs, EHTPs, STPs and SEZs
[74:6:0] TABLE head: Unit | Covers / nature
  [74:6:0.0] SEZ | Duty-free enclave treated as foreign territory; policy 1 April 2000, Act 2005, Act + Rules in force 10 Feb 2006; concept from EXIM Policy 1997-2002; 100% FDI automatic for most manufacturing
  [74:6:0.1] EOU | Goods generally
  [74:6:0.2] EHTP | Electronics hardware
  [74:6:0.3] STP | Software
[74:6:1] - EOU/EHTP/STP: **export all output**, can be **located anywhere** (need not be in an SEZ), duty-free inputs.
[74:6:2] - SEZ aims: exports, investment, employment, infrastructure; internationally competitive, hassle-free, **simplified business-friendly** environment.
[74:6:3] - First EPZ: **Kandla, 1965** (Asia's first).
[74:6:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.26, p.79; app notes 3:74 sub 6
## SUB 7 | Districts as Export Hubs
[74:7:0] - Each district plan prioritises **2-3 high-potential products/services**; products identified in **734 districts**, action plans for 590 (2025).
[74:7:1] - 90-day DEH campaign from **1 June 2026**: AP priority districts **Ananthapur, Chittoor, East Godavari, Guntur, Krishna, Visakhapatnam** (not Srikakulam).
