=== NOTES 3:75 | Balance of Payments - Structure, Current and Capital Account, Convertibility, Forex Reserves
## SUB 0 | Meaning of BoP – BoP vs Balance of Trade
[75:0:0] # Definition
[75:0:1] - **Balance of Payments (BoP):** a **systematic and complete record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world** during a period, **normally one year**.
[75:0:2] - BoP has **two main accounts – the current account and the capital account** (NextGen); it is not "only capital" or "only current" or "only exports and imports".
[75:0:3] - **IMF BPM6** uses **three accounts – current, capital and financial**; the **RBI generally combines capital and financial** under "Capital Account".
[75:0:4] - BoP includes **visible trade, invisible trade and borrowings** – "all of the above"; the term is used in relation to **exports and imports** (foreign trade), not factory sales or tax collection.
[75:0:5] - UPSC 2013 wording: BoP = systematic record of "**all import and export transactions** of a country during a given period, normally a year" – the official key, the closest fit (goods exports only, government-to-government deals or capital movements alone are parts).
[75:0:6] # Balance of Trade vs Balance of Payments
[75:0:7] TABLE head: Basis | Balance of Trade (BoT) | Balance of Payments (BoP)
  [75:0:7.0] Coverage | Goods only (visible) | All transactions: goods, services, transfers, income, capital
  [75:0:7.1] Formula | Goods exports − goods imports | Whole external account, double-entry
  [75:0:7.2] Place | Part of the current account | Current + capital/financial account
  [75:0:7.3] Picture | Not the complete record | Better, complete picture
[75:0:8] - **A-R (UPSC 2006):** BoP gives a better picture than BoT **because** it covers both **visible and invisible** items – A and R both true, R explains A.
[75:0:9] - **BoT surplus**: goods exports > goods imports; **BoT deficit**: goods imports > goods exports. "Exports minus imports" is the BoT, **not** the BoP.
[75:0:10] - **Favourable BoP** – achieved by **stepping up exports and reducing imports** (both).
[75:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.15-17 (BoP definition, two accounts, BoT); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.49 (UPSC 2013 wording); Rocket Indian Economy p.36 (BoT vs BoP table); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.21 (IMF three parts); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.19 (BPM6)
## SUB 1 | Structure – Current Account vs Capital Account
[75:1:0] TABLE head: Current account | Capital (and financial) account
  [75:1:0.0] Merchandise exports and imports (visible trade; trade balance) | Foreign loans, FDI, portfolio investment (FPI/FII), ADRs/GDRs
  [75:1:0.1] Invisibles – services: software, travel, transport, banking, insurance | ECB, external assistance
  [75:1:0.2] Invisibles – primary income: interest, dividends, profits, wages | NRI deposits (FCNR(B)), banking capital
  [75:1:0.3] Secondary income: private remittances, gifts, grants | Short-term trade credit; change in forex reserves
[75:1:1] - **Current account** = goods + services + income + transfers; it **includes the Balance of Trade**. **Capital receipts and payments are NOT** part of it (CDS 2014).
[75:1:2] - **Invisibles** = services + income + transfers; **invisible export = export of services**. Services = **non-factor** (shipping, banking, tourism, software) + factor income.
[75:1:3]   - "Invisible items" in the classic sense = **service transactions**; goods are the visible items.
[75:1:4] - **Capital account** (UPSC 2013): **foreign loans, FDI and portfolio investment** – **private remittances are current account** (so codes with remittances are wrong). **FDI is NOT current account.**
[75:1:5] - **Current-account balance** = exports − imports of goods and services + net primary income + net secondary income.
[75:1:6] # Credit and debit
[75:1:7] - Every **inflow of foreign exchange = credit side**; every outflow = debit (double-entry book-keeping).
[75:1:8] - **Gift to foreigners = debit** in the current account; gift from foreigners = credit; exports of goods/services = credit.
[75:1:9] - Residents **buying foreign assets = capital-account debit**; **sale of Indian assets to foreigners = credit**.
[75:1:10] TABLE head: Item | BoP placement
  [75:1:10.0] Software services exports | Current account (services)
  [75:1:10.1] Foreign loans, FDI, FPI | Capital account
  [75:1:10.2] Private remittances | Current account – secondary income (transfers)
  [75:1:10.3] Crude oil imports | Merchandise trade
[75:1:11] # The identity
[75:1:12] - **Current + Capital + Financial account + Net Errors & Omissions = 0** – BoP **always balances** in accounting terms; a surplus in one account = deficit in another. **BoT need not balance.**
[75:1:13] - **Autonomous** transactions ("above the line") happen for their own sake; **accommodating** ones ("below the line") fill the gap – **official reserve changes, official borrowing**.
[75:1:14] - Overall BoP **positive → adds to reserves; negative → draws them down**; monetary authority = ultimate financier.
[75:1:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.16-18 (current account, invisibles, capital-account debit/credit, autonomous vs accommodating); Rocket Indian Economy p.36 (item-account table); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.58 (invisible trade = services); app notes 3:75 sub 1-2
## SUB 2 | Convertibility, FERA/FEMA and Rupee Milestones
[75:2:0] TABLE head: Type | Freedom to convert for
  [75:2:0.0] Current account convertibility | Trade, income and transfers (current international transactions)
  [75:2:0.1] Capital account convertibility | Investment and financial assets (FDI, portfolio, borrowing) without capital controls
[75:2:1] - The rupee is **fully convertible only on the current account** – **not** on the capital account (still partial) and **not into gold** (UPSC 2000).
[75:2:2] - **IMF Article VIII** makes **current account convertibility** obligatory; India accepted it in **August 1994** (operationalised 19 Aug 1994).
[75:2:3] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [75:2:3.0] 1948 | Rupee linked to sterling till 1948
  [75:2:3.1] 1973 | FERA (prevent outflow of foreign exchange)
  [75:2:3.2] Sep 1975 | Rupee delinked from pound sterling, pegged to a basket of currencies
  [75:2:3.3] July 1991 | Rupee devalued in two steps (1 and 3 July) – about 22% – to meet the BoP crisis
  [75:2:3.4] 1992-93 Budget | LERMS: dual rate – 40% official, 60% market; partial convertibility
  [75:2:3.5] 1 Mar 1993 | Unified, market-determined exchange rate (trade account convertibility)
  [75:2:3.6] Aug 1994 | Full current account convertibility – Article VIII accepted
  [75:2:3.7] 1999 / 1 June 2000 | FEMA enacted / in force, replacing FERA
[75:2:4] - **FEMA preamble:** "to **facilitate external trade and payments**" and promote orderly development of the forex market – not import control.
[75:2:5] TABLE head: Feature | FERA 1973 | FEMA 1999
  [75:2:5.0] Nature | Criminal | Civil
  [75:2:5.1] Approach | Control of outflow | Management and regulation
  [75:2:5.2] Character | Strict, restrictive | Liberal
[75:2:6] # Committees
[75:2:7] TABLE head: Committee | Chair | Key point
  [75:2:7.0] High Level Committee on BoP (1991-93) | C. Rangarajan | Sustainable CAD about 1.6% of GDP; market-determined exchange rate
  [75:2:7.1] Committee on Capital Account Convertibility (1997) | S.S. Tarapore | Roadmap to fuller capital account convertibility; preconditions: fiscal consolidation, inflation, strong banks
  [75:2:7.2] Committee on Fuller CAC (2006) | S.S. Tarapore | Revisited the roadmap
[75:2:8] - **UPSC 2001 A-R:** current-account forex ceilings were changed in 2000 under FEMA, but **foreign currency assets did not fall** (rose from $38.0 bn, March 1999 to $42.3 bn, March 2001) – R false.
[75:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.22 (LERMS, 1 Mar 1993, Aug 1994 Article VIII); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.32-33 (1975 delink, FERA 1973, FEMA, Tarapore 2006); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.54 (fully convertible on current account); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 05 p.170-171 (19 Aug 1994, Article VIII, Tarapore 1997); Rocket Indian Economy p.37, p.69-70, p.95 (convertibility, two devaluations 1991, Tarapore I/II)
## SUB 3 | Forex Reserves
[75:3:0] TABLE head: Component (RBI) | Note
  [75:3:0.0] Foreign Currency Assets (FCA) | Largest (most of the total)
  [75:3:0.1] Gold | Second
  [75:3:0.2] SDRs | IMF allocation; third
  [75:3:0.3] Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) in the IMF | Smallest; unconditional drawing right
[75:3:1] - Order of share (March 2025): **FCA > Gold > SDRs > RTP**. Loans from foreign countries or the World Bank, NRI deposits, "fiscal deficit deposits" are **NOT** reserves.
[75:3:2] - **1991 low:** reserves fell to about **$1.2 bn (Jan 1991)**; FCA **below $1 bn**, about two weeks of imports.
[75:3:3] - **Milestones:** crossed **US$ 100 bn in Dec 2003** ($110.48 bn on 19 Dec 2003); **$608.99 bn on 25 June 2021 – 5th largest** (after China, Japan, Switzerland, Russia; Ministry of Finance); **$640.3 bn (27 Dec 2024)**.
[75:3:4] - **2026:** $701.4 bn (Jan 2026) ≈ **94% of external debt**; **$682.3 bn (29 May 2026) ≈ 11 months of import cover**; all-time high **$785.71 bn (15 Sep 2026)**, India **4th** after China, Japan, Switzerland; $721.0 bn (16 Oct 2026); FCA $597.6 bn (9 Oct 2026).
[75:3:5] - **July 2026:** overall BoP surplus **$20.8 bn**, capital account $27.7 bn, driven by RBI's **special FCNR(B) deposit scheme** – possibly one-time comfort.
[75:3:6] - **Import cover** = months of imports the reserves can pay for.
[75:3:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.63 (four components); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 05 p.165 (forex = FCA + gold + SDRs + reserve tranche); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.32 (FCA under $1 bn in 1991; the $1.2 bn Jan 1991 figure is general knowledge, not checked), p.48 (import cover), p.50 (UPSC 2013); PIB Ministry of Finance release 1736885, 19 Jul 2021 (5th largest, $608.99 bn); app notes 3:75 sub 5 (2024-26 levels)
## SUB 4 | CAD, Invisibles and Remittances – Trends
[75:4:0] - **CAD**: payments exceed receipts from **goods, services, transfers and net income** (excess of total imports over total exports). A CAD is **not** caused by exporting more.
[75:4:1] - India runs a **persistent trade deficit** in goods; services and remittances only partly offset it.
[75:4:2] TABLE head: Period | CAD / current account
  [75:4:2.0] 1990-91 | 3.1-3.2% of GDP (crisis); IMF drawn in 1991
  [75:4:2.1] 2001-02 to 2003-04 | Surplus three years running (first in 24 years in 2001-02) – the only such run
  [75:4:2.2] FY13 | Peak 4.8% of GDP (taper tantrum) – higher than 1990-91
  [75:4:2.3] 2013-14 | Trade deficit, net invisibles positive, capital account in surplus (financed the CAD)
  [75:4:2.4] Q4 2023-24 | Surplus $5.7 bn (0.6%) – net services receipts $42.7 bn (software, travel, business services)
  [75:4:2.5] FY 2025-26 | $25.2 bn (~0.6% of GDP); merchandise deficit $337.3 bn; Q3 FY26 $13.2 bn (1.3%)
  [75:4:2.6] Q1 2026-27 | $4.2 bn, 0.5% of GDP
[75:4:3] - **FY24 external recovery:** **moderation in merchandise export growth + sharp decline in import growth**; **services exports cushioned the trade deficit** (up 4.85% to **USD 341.06 bn**).
[75:4:4] - **Causes of CAD:** structural – oil and gold imports, low export competitiveness, savings-investment gap; **cyclical – temporary global slowdown**, commodity shocks.
[75:4:5] # Invisibles and remittances
[75:4:6] - **Largest source of net invisibles among the classic items: private transfers = foreign remittances** (APPSC 2008); since the 2010s **net software services** are larger still – **record services surplus $188.8 bn (FY25)**, about **two-thirds** of the merchandise deficit; **software = largest part**.
[75:4:7] - **India = world's largest remittance recipient** (also in **2015**): **$135.4 bn (3.5% of GDP) in FY25**; World Bank 2024: India $129 bn > **Mexico** $68 bn > China > Philippines > Pakistan.
[75:4:8] - **Sources (RBI survey 2023-24): USA 27.7% > UAE 19.2% > UK 10.8%.**
[75:4:9] - Remittances are **counter-cyclical** and create **no debt**; **net primary income is an outflow** for India.
[75:4:10] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.37 (CAD definition); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.32 (3.2% in 1990-91); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 05 p.169 (three consecutive surplus years); RBI press release prid=58147, 24 Jun 2024 (Q4 2023-24 surplus from services); Economic Survey 2025-26 p.1 (trade deficit, services and remittances); app notes 3:75 sub 3-4 (FY25-27 figures, remittance shares)
## SUB 5 | Correcting BoP Disequilibrium
[75:5:0] TABLE head: Expenditure-switching | Expenditure-reducing / financing
  [75:5:0.0] Devaluation/depreciation | Tight fiscal policy: cut government spending, raise taxes
  [75:5:0.1] Import duties (tariffs), quotas, import substitution | Tight monetary policy: higher interest rates
  [75:5:0.2] Export incentives, tourist promotion | Foreign loans, IMF assistance, foreign investment (FDI); exchange control
  [75:5:0.3] Higher gold import duty | 
[75:5:1] - **Not a correction:** **levying higher export duties** (cuts exports); **increasing** government spending on domestic projects (raises demand and imports).
[75:5:2] - **Encouraging FDI** *finances* a deficit rather than correcting it – the "NOT typically used" answer when devaluation, tariffs and cutting government spending are the other options.
[75:5:3] - **Removing a BoP surplus** (elastic demand): **appreciate/revalue** the currency; devaluation, import controls or inflation abroad would widen the surplus.
[75:5:4] - A country with a **large current-account surplus** has a **larger capacity to give aid and loans** abroad.
[75:5:5] - **1991:** rupee **devalued twice** (1 and 3 July 1991) to adjust the BoP deficit.
[75:5:6] - **May 2026:** appeal to cut gold and fuel imports + gold import-duty hike = expenditure-switching steps.
[75:5:7] - **Rekhi Committee (1992) = indirect taxes** (not export-import simplification); Rangarajan = BoP; Goiporia = bank customer service.
[75:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.15-16 (devaluation as expenditure-switching; methods incl. foreign investment); Rocket Indian Economy p.69-70 (two devaluations 1991); app notes 3:75 sub 7; general economics (surplus removal, aid capacity), not checked against a library file
## SUB 6 | IMF and SDR
[75:6:0] - **IMF main function:** help members solve **balance of payments problems**; loans meet **temporary BoP deficits** (not development projects – that is the World Bank); core function **surveillance**; **lender of last resort** when reserves cannot cover a deficit. India drew on the IMF in **1991**.
[75:6:1] TABLE head: Facility | Meaning
  [75:6:1.0] Reserve (gold) tranche | Member's unconditional drawing right from its quota – a credit system of the IMF
  [75:6:1.1] Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI) | Rapid help for any member with an urgent BoP need
  [75:6:1.2] Rapid Credit Facility (RCF) | Concessional, for low-income countries
  [75:6:1.3] Stand-By Arrangement / Extended Fund Facility | Regular lending windows
[75:6:2] - RBI swaps, SAARC swap framework and **Special Rupee Vostro Accounts** are **NOT** IMF instruments.
[75:6:3] - **SDR** = IMF reserve asset ("paper gold", 1969), exists only as **book-keeping entries**, not paper currency or metal.
[75:6:4] - Original SDR rule (reconstitution, abolished 1981): members kept on average **30%** of allocations over five years – so about **70% could be used without repayment**.
[75:6:5] TABLE head: SDR basket (from 1 Aug 2022) | Weight
  [75:6:5.0] US dollar | 43.38%
  [75:6:5.1] Euro | 29.31%
  [75:6:5.2] Chinese renminbi | 12.28%
  [75:6:5.3] Japanese yen | 7.59%
  [75:6:5.4] Pound sterling | 7.44%
[75:6:6] - **Five** currencies; next review due by end-July 2027.
[75:6:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.41-42 (IMF functions, reserve tranche, RFI, RCF); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.56 (main function); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.21 (SDR 1969, five currencies); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.51 (SDR artificial currency); app notes 3:75 sub 8 (weights); general knowledge, not checked (SDR 30% reconstitution rule)
## SUB 7 | External Vulnerability and Debt
[75:7:0] - **Immunity to a global financial crisis (UPSC 2020): not depending on short-term foreign borrowings** – only this; more foreign banks and full capital account convertibility raise exposure.
[75:7:1] - **Reduce currency-crisis risk (UPSC 2019): IT-sector forex earnings and remittances** – higher government spending does not.
[75:7:2] - Safeguards: **adequate reserves** (import cover), **low short-term debt**, less reliance on volatile **hot money** (FPI, debt flows). FCNR(B) and ECB inflows are **temporary**; **FDI** supports a self-sustaining capital surplus.
[75:7:3] - **US Fed rate hikes + strong dollar** → higher US yields → hot money leaves emerging markets → rupee weakens.
[75:7:4] - **2013 taper tantrum:** Morgan Stanley's "**Fragile Five**" included India. Morgan Stanley 1998 emerging-markets rating: India **3rd** (printed key).
[75:7:5] - **FY26:** FPIs pulled out **$16.4 bn**; net FDI only **$6.9 bn**.
[75:7:6] TABLE head: External debt, end-June 2026 | Fact
  [75:7:6.0] Total | $778.2 bn
  [75:7:6.1] Debt-to-GDP | 20.8%
  [75:7:6.2] Short-term debt | 19.7% of total
  [75:7:6.3] Largest currency | US dollar 54.8%, rupee 29.8%
[75:7:7] ~~ Sources: UPSC CSE 2019 and 2020 official keys as carried by the app; app notes 3:75 sub 6 (2026 figures); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.56 (FCNR(B) deposits)

  How does the IMF presentation of the Balance of Payments differ from that generally followed by the RBI?

=== NOTES 3:76 | Exchange Rate Systems and Rupee Movement; Currency Internationalisation
## SUB 0 | Devaluation, Depreciation, Appreciation and Revaluation
[76:0:0] - **Devaluation:** an **official reduction in the value of a currency vis-a-vis major internationally traded currencies**, made by the government / monetary authority under a **fixed** exchange-rate system (more rupees per dollar) – not a general "decline in values" or a rise in inflation.
[76:0:1] TABLE head: Term | System | Meaning | Done by
  [76:0:1.0] Devaluation | Fixed | Official reduction of the currency's value | Government / monetary authority
  [76:0:1.1] Revaluation | Fixed | Official rise in the currency's value | Government / monetary authority
  [76:0:1.2] Appreciation | Flexible | Market-driven rise in value – fewer rupees per $ | Demand and supply
  [76:0:1.3] Depreciation | Flexible | Market-driven fall in value – more rupees per $ | Demand and supply
[76:0:2] # Reading a rate change
[76:0:3] - **$1 = ₹60 → ₹58:** the **rupee appreciated** and the **dollar depreciated**.
[76:0:4] - **$1 = ₹60 → ₹65 (or ₹70) by market forces:** the **rupee depreciated** (not "devalued" – that word is for an official change). ₹96 → ₹94 per $ = rupee appreciated.
[76:0:5] - **"Rate of exchange falls"** (foreign currency per rupee falls = rupee cheaper), ceteris paribus: **exports rise and imports fall**.
[76:0:6] > Exam angle: official change → devaluation / revaluation; market change → depreciation / appreciation. Wrong-pair MCQs swap these.
[76:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.19-20; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.69-70
## SUB 1 | Effects of Devaluation
[76:1:0] - Devaluation makes **exports cheaper abroad** (their foreign-currency price falls) and **imports dearer at home** → it **promotes exports**; it is an **expenditure-switching** policy (spending switches to home-produced goods) used to **correct the balance of trade / BoP**.
[76:1:1] - **A-R pattern:** "Devaluation may promote exports" (A) is explained by "the price of the country's products in the international market falls" (R) – **A true, R true, R explains A**. A reason saying devaluation **raises** export prices is **false**.
[76:1:2] - Devaluation does **not necessarily** improve the trade balance or raise the currency's foreign value: it **necessarily** only improves export competitiveness (UPSC 2021: "1 only"). Limits: **imported inflation** (it **raises domestic prices**), inelastic oil imports, costlier ECB repayment.
[76:1:3] - It **raises the cost of imports** and does **not curb inflation** – so "to fix the balance of trade" is the purpose, not "reduce import costs" or "curb inflation".
[76:1:4] - **When does it work?** When exports actually **become cheaper to importers** abroad, i.e. export prices fall in proportion to the devaluation and domestic prices do not rise to cancel it (CDS 2017; APPSC 2011 key: "exports change proportionately").
[76:1:5] - **1991:** the rupee was devalued to **make exports cheaper**; export growth rose after 1991 and the devaluation is credited for it (UPSC 2000 key: A and R true, R explains A).
[76:1:6] - **Trade imbalance and controls:** import duties, exchange controls and devaluation are used to **wipe out** the trade imbalance and keep the rate stable (APPSC 2011 key).
[76:1:7] - BoP correction methods (NextGen): monetary policy, **exchange depreciation, devaluation, exchange control**, import duties and quotas, export promotion, foreign loans and investment.
[76:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.15-16; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.69-70; testbook.com CDS 2017 question page
## SUB 2 | Rupee Devaluation Episodes – 1949, 1966, 1991
[76:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Extent / steps
  [76:2:0.0] Sept 1949 | First devaluation, with sterling; about 30.5% (₹3.30 → ₹4.76 per US$)
  [76:2:0.1] June 1966 | ₹4.76 → ₹7.50 per US$ = rupee down 36.5% (dollar's rupee price up 57.5%); wars, drought, 36% inflation; "short-lived liberalisation"
  [76:2:0.2] July 1991 | Two steps, 1 and 3 July; about 18% (17.38% against sterling, 18.7% against the US$; Ramesh Singh says 22%); BoP crisis; last formal devaluation
[76:2:1] - **Count:** 1949 (1st), 1966 (2nd), July 1991 two steps (3rd and **4th**) – so the fourth devaluation fell in **1991**.
[76:2:2] > Trap: the 1991 steps were on **1 and 3 July**, not 1 and 2 July. 1966's "57.5%" is the rise in the dollar's price; the rupee itself lost 36.5%.
[76:2:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.69-70; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 13 p.1; Spectrum A Brief History of Modern India p.690; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. (05) p.169
## SUB 3 | Exchange Rate and Forex Market Terms
[76:3:0] - **Exchange rate:** the price / value of one currency in terms of another (₹50 for $1 = ₹50 per dollar). **Forex market** participants: commercial banks, brokers, authorised dealers, monetary authorities.
[76:3:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [76:3:1.0] Direct quote | Units of domestic currency per one unit of foreign currency (₹95 = $1)
  [76:3:1.1] Indirect quote | Units of foreign currency per one unit of domestic currency
  [76:3:1.2] Spot rate | Immediate delivery – settled within two days
  [76:3:1.3] Forward rate | Agreed now for future delivery; an importer's forward contract covers exchange-rate risk
  [76:3:1.4] Hedging / speculation | Covering exchange risk (forwards) / taking an open position on expected moves
  [76:3:1.5] Arbitrage | Buying a currency where it is cheaper and simultaneously selling it where it is dearer
  [76:3:1.6] Hot currency (money) | Foreign currency that migrates quickly between markets for the highest short-term return
  [76:3:1.7] Tobin tax | Tax on foreign exchange transactions (James Tobin)
  [76:3:1.8] Currency war | Countries competitively devaluing their currencies to gain export advantage
  [76:3:1.9] Hawala | Illegal transactions of foreign exchange (informal transfer outside banking channels)
[76:3:2] - **Money laundering** turns the **proceeds of crime** (drugs, smuggling, corruption) into apparently legal money – hence "drugs and crime"; hawala is a common channel.
[76:3:3] - **Import cover:** the **number of months of imports that could be paid for by the country's reserves** – about **11 months** with $701.4 bn (16 Jan 2026, Economic Survey 2025-26).
[76:3:4] - **Most valuable currency (in ₹): Kuwaiti dinar**; of pound, euro and US dollar the costliest is the **pound sterling** (₹125.18 vs euro ₹109.05, $ ₹93.00 on 17 Apr 2026).
[76:3:5] - **International liquidity problem** = shortage of **dollars and other hard currencies** (internationally accepted reserve assets).
[76:3:6] - **RBI** (through authorised dealers, under FEMA) sanctions foreign exchange for imports.
[76:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.19; app notes 3:76 sub 0 (Carpediem CA, 17 Apr 2026 rates; ES 2025-26 import cover); general knowledge for hawala / money laundering
## SUB 4 | Exchange Rate Regimes and Determinants
[76:4:0] TABLE head: Regime | Meaning
  [76:4:0.0] Fixed / pegged | Government fixes the rate (to gold, a currency or a basket); the central bank buys / sells forex to hold it, so private demand and supply need not come into balance
  [76:4:0.1] Exchange control | Rate fixed and held by rationing out the available foreign exchange
  [76:4:0.2] Flexible / floating | Set by demand and supply of foreign currency in the market – not by the central bank
  [76:4:0.3] Managed float (dirty float) | Market-set, with central-bank intervention to curb volatility – India's market-determined system
[76:4:1] - **Post-Bretton Woods classes:** **fixed** – currency unions, dollarised regimes, **currency boards (Argentina 1991 – Jan 2002)**, pegs; **intermediate** – bands, crawling pegs; **flexible** – managed and independent floats.
[76:4:2] - **Floating rates:** traders face the risk of an **exchange-rate loss**; price differences between markets give scope for **arbitrage** (APPSC 2019 key).
[76:4:3] - **Determinants:** demand for the country's **goods and services**, **stability of its government**, economic potential – the **World Bank does not decide a currency's price** (UPSC 2012 key: II and III).
[76:4:4] - **Raghuram Rajan:** **high inflation, high fiscal deficit and high crude oil prices** all weaken the rupee's exchange value.
[76:4:5] - **PPP theory:** equality of purchasing power (the **inflation differential**) decides the long-run **rate of exchange**. Long-run anchors (ES 2025-26): PPP, savings-investment balance, current account.
[76:4:6] - **Capital flows:** large inflows → **appreciation** (Dutch disease); higher imports can coexist with a stable rupee if backed by **net investment inflows**; a repo hike attracts **carry-trade** capital; deliberate undervaluation (alleged of China) = **currency manipulation**.
[76:4:7] - **Impossible trinity (Mundell-Fleming trilemma):** no country can have a **fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and an independent monetary policy** at once.
[76:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.16; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.20-21; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.70; app notes 3:76 sub 8
## SUB 5 | Bretton Woods, IMF and India's Exchange-Rate History
[76:5:0] - **Gold standard (1870-1914):** the epitome of the fixed-rate system.
[76:5:1] - **Bretton Woods Conference** = **United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference**, **1-22 July 1944**, **New Hampshire (USA)**, **44 nations**: set up the **IMF and IBRD** (not the UN or WTO) and fixed rates centred on the **dollar** (two-tier convertibility – the origin of **currency convertibility**).
[76:5:2] - **IMF:** formally created **27 December 1945**; **India a founding member (27 Dec 1945)**; **191 members** (Liechtenstein 191st, Oct 2024); India's quota **2.75%** of SDRs, votes 2.63% (March 2026). Its purposes are monetary cooperation, trade growth, exchange **stability** and multilateral payments – **not** promoting flexible exchange rates.
[76:5:3] TABLE head: Year | India's exchange-rate step
  [76:5:3.0] 1947-1971 | Par value system under the IMF (rupee linked to sterling)
  [76:5:3.1] 1971 | Smithsonian Agreement – ±2.25% band (NextGen: 2.5%), lasted 14 months
  [76:5:3.2] Sept 1975 | Rupee delinked from pound sterling, pegged to a basket of currencies – the end of the strict fixed system (Ramesh Singh: "between fixed and floating")
  [76:5:3.3] 1992-93 | LERMS (Budget 1992-93): dual rate – 40% official, 60% market; partial convertibility
  [76:5:3.4] 1 March 1993 | Rates unified; market-determined
  [76:5:3.5] August 1994 | IMF Article VIII – current account convertibility
[76:5:4] - **Official exchange rate of the rupee:** associated with a **basket of selected currencies** (NextGen; the 1975 basket peg); since 1993 it is market-determined, with the US dollar as the RBI's reference and intervention currency.
[76:5:5] - **India's current policy:** **market-determined exchange rate** (managed float).
[76:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.20-22, p.32-33; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. (05) p.168-169; imf.org India country page and IMF at a Glance
## SUB 6 | FERA to FEMA and Rupee Convertibility
[76:6:0] - **FERA 1973** (restrictive, to prevent outflow of currency) → replaced by **FEMA 1999**: proposed in the **1997-98 Budget**; **in force 1 June 2000**, with a **two-year sunset clause** for FERA cases (ended 31 May 2002 – "finally implemented 2002" in the UPPSC key). **FEMA regulates the flow of foreign exchange**; no "Foreign Exchange Control Act" ever replaced FERA.
[76:6:1] - **Convertibility:** **freely permitting the conversion of the rupee to other currencies and vice versa** – not conversion into gold, nor fixing by market forces.
[76:6:2] - **Full convertibility** may mean the rupee's **free float**, its **direct exchange anywhere** inside and outside India, and its acting **like any other international currency** (UPSC 2002: 1, 2 and 3).
[76:6:3] - India: **full current account** convertibility (Aug 1994), only **partial capital account** convertibility.
[76:6:4] TABLE head: Committee | Facts
  [76:6:4.0] Tarapore I | 1997 – roadmap to capital account convertibility
  [76:6:4.1] Tarapore II | Appointed 2006 (report 31 July 2006) – fuller capital account convertibility
[76:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.33; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.37, p.95; app notes 3:76 sub 7
## SUB 7 | SDR, Reserve Tranche and Paper Gold
[76:7:0] - **SDR (Special Drawing Rights)** – relates to the **IMF**; an **artificial currency / international reserve asset** created in **1969** (agreed 1967) to **supplement members' official reserves**; called **"paper gold"**; exists only as **book-keeping entries**. ADR / GDR are depository receipts, not currency.
[76:7:1] - **Basket (since 1 Oct 2016):** US dollar, euro, **renminbi** (the currency proposed / added in 2015-16), yen, pound sterling – **no rupee**. Largest allocation **about $650 bn, August 2021**.
[76:7:2] - **Reserve (gold) tranche:** the part of a member's quota paid in reserve assets (historically gold); a **credit facility of the IMF to its members** drawable **without conditions**; the **smallest** component of India's reserves (FCA > gold > SDR > RTP).
[76:7:3] - **Reserves:** **RBI is the custodian**; reserves rose to **$785.71 bn on 15 Sep 2026 – India 4th**, overtaking Russia; rising **gold share** = diversification; **India-Japan bilateral swap** renewed from 28 Feb 2026 (two-way, local currencies against US dollars).
[76:7:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.21; app notes 3:76 sub 10 (Carpediem CA, Sep 2026)
## SUB 8 | NEER and REER
[76:8:0] - **NEER:** weighted average of the rupee's bilateral **nominal** rates against a **trade-weighted basket**; RBI indices of **40 and 6 currencies**, **base 2015-16 = 100**. **A rise in NEER = rupee appreciation.**
[76:8:1] - **REER** = NEER **adjusted for relative inflation** differentials – the better competitiveness measure. A **rise in REER = loss of competitiveness** (overvalued rupee), not an improvement.
[76:8:2] - Higher domestic inflation than abroad **widens the divergence between NEER and REER** (UPSC 2022: statements A and C correct).
[76:8:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.69; vajiramandravi.com UPSC 2022 solution page
## SUB 9 | Rupee Movement and RBI Tools
[76:9:0] - **RBI aim:** curb **excessive volatility**, not defend a fixed level. If the rupee falls fast, the RBI **sells dollars**; if US / EU rates fall and inflows surge, it **buys dollars**; to fight high inflation it **sells** (not buys) government securities (UPSC 2022: B and C).
[76:9:1] TABLE head: Tool | Example
  [76:9:1.0] Spot intervention | Selling dollars from reserves
  [76:9:1.1] Forex swap | Buy/sell swap: banks sell dollars to the RBI and buy them back later at a premium
  [76:9:1.2] NDF curbs | Restricting domestic banks in offshore Non-Deliverable Forward markets; Net Open Position limits
  [76:9:1.3] FCNR(B) support | RBI bore the full hedging cost on fresh FCNR(B) deposits till 30 Sep 2026
[76:9:2] - **NOT RBI tools:** **fiscal policy adjustments** (APPSC 2025); **import curbs and export promotion** are Government structural measures.
[76:9:3] - **To stop a slide:** curb non-essential imports, promote exports, **masala bonds**, ease **ECB** norms – but **not an expansionary monetary policy** (UPSC 2019).
[76:9:4] - **Recent:** FY 2025-26 (to Jan 2026) rupee **depreciated about 5.4%**; crossed **₹96.2/$ on 19 May 2026** (Brent near $110, FPI outflows over ₹2 lakh crore). In 2002-07 the rupee **gained against the US dollar** (₹48.4 → ₹44.3).
[76:9:5] ~~ Sources: superkalam.com UPSC 2022 solution page; app notes 3:76 sub 9 (Carpediem CA); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 06 p.2
## SUB 10 | Rupee Internationalisation, Bonds and World Currencies
[76:10:0] - **INR trade settlement:** RBI framework of **July 2022**, built into the **Foreign Trade Policy 2023** – it **encourages the use of the rupee in cross-border trade**. **Special Rupee Vostro Accounts** = foreign banks' rupee accounts with Indian banks; surplus may go into **corporate bonds and CPs** (2025). **Vostro** = foreign bank's account with a domestic bank; **Nostro** = ours abroad.
[76:10:1] - **SAARC Currency Swap Framework:** RBI, **2012**; 3-month tenor, rollable twice; 2024-27 **₹250 bn INR window**; first INR drawdown **Maldives, April 2026**.
[76:10:2] - **SWIFT:** member-owned **cooperative** founded **1973**, headquartered in **Belgium**; a **messaging** network – not a payment network and no power to impose sanctions (APPSC G1 2023: none correct).
[76:10:3] TABLE head: Bond | Facts
  [76:10:3.0] Masala bond | Rupee-denominated, issued abroad – Indian entities raise money in rupees; first by IFC (Nov 2014), first State Kerala (2019)
  [76:10:3.1] Samurai / Panda | Yen bond (Japan) / yuan bond (China)
  [76:10:3.2] Resurgent India Bonds | SBI, 5 Aug 1998, in US dollar, pound sterling and Deutsche Mark
[76:10:4] - **Rupee symbol ₹:** adopted **15 July 2010**, designed by **D. Udaya Kumar**.
[76:10:5] TABLE head: Country / union | Currency
  [76:10:5.0] European Monetary Union | Euro – used by 21 of 27 EU states (Bulgaria joined 1 Jan 2026; earlier 20)
  [76:10:5.1] Bangladesh | Taka
  [76:10:5.2] China | Yuan (renminbi)
  [76:10:5.3] Seychelles | Rupee (Bhutan ngultrum, Malaysia ringgit, Maldives rufiyaa)
[76:10:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:76 sub 11 (Carpediem CA); ecb.europa.eu press release 1 Jan 2026 (Bulgaria, 21 states)

=== OWN MCQs of 3:76 (97)
[n3f2d6fdd84b] sub0
  Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
  Revaluation – Official raising of the currency's value under a fixed regime | Depreciation – Market rise in the domestic-currency price of foreign currency | *Devaluation – Official raising of the currency's value under a fixed regime | Appreciation – Market fall in the domestic-currency price of foreign currency
  x: Devaluation is the official lowering, not raising, of a currency's value under a fixed regime; official raising is revaluation.

  Which of the following is NOT correct about exchange-rate terminology?

  x: Depreciation and appreciation are market-driven changes under a flexible regime; official changes under a fixed regime are devaluation and revaluation.

  x: An official rise is revaluation; an official cut is devaluation, a market-driven fall is depreciation and a market-set value is a floating rate.

=== NOTES 3:77 | India and the Wto - Agreements, Ministerial Conferences, Public Stockholding, Fisheries Subsidies, Appellate Body Crisis
## SUB 0 | WTO Basics – Establishment, HQ, Members, DG, Principles
[77:0:0] # Core facts
[77:0:1] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [77:0:1.0] Established | 1 January 1995 (not 1994 – 1994 is the Marrakesh Agreement)
  [77:0:1.1] Created by | Marrakesh Agreement (signed April 1994) that ended the Uruguay Round
  [77:0:1.2] Predecessor | GATT – WTO is "the new name of GATT"; the WTO replaced the GATT as an organisation
  [77:0:1.3] HQ | Geneva, Switzerland (also ILO Geneva; UN New York; FAO Rome)
  [77:0:1.4] India | Member since 1 January 1995 (founder member of both GATT and WTO)
  [77:0:1.5] Members | 166 (as of April 2026); 164 from 29 July 2016 (Afghanistan 164th); Nepal 147th (23 April 2004); Serbia = observer, not a member
  [77:0:1.6] Director-General | Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (Nigeria) – 7th DG and first woman, appointed Feb 2021, took office 1 March 2021
  [77:0:1.7] Earlier DG | Roberto Azevedo (Brazil) – 6th DG, replaced Pascal Lamy on 1 September 2013 (second term 2017)
[77:0:2] - **Nature:** an **international organisation** (GATT was only an agreement) with a **broader multilateral framework** – goods, **services, IPR and investment measures**.
[77:0:3] - **"Third pillar" of the world economy** with the **IMF and World Bank**; the "**main security guard of international trade**"; promotes **multilateral trade** (not financial support or unilateral trade).
[77:0:4] - **Aims (UPSC 1996):** free trade and resource flows, protection of IPR, managed/balanced trade and bringing former East-bloc economies into the system – answer "**1, 2, 3 and 4**".
[77:0:5] - **Has a dispute-settlement system** (Dispute Settlement Body) – "it has no way to solve trade disputes" is NOT a valid criticism. Valid criticisms: puppet of MNCs, reduces sovereignty, favours free trade over product quality.
[77:0:6] # Principles
[77:0:7] TABLE head: Principle | Meaning
  [77:0:7.0] Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) | An advantage given to one partner must go to all WTO partners – non-discrimination between nations ("most favour to all countries")
  [77:0:7.1] National treatment | Imported product, once inside, treated like the domestic product for internal tax and regulation
[77:0:8] - US unilateral tariffs (2025-26) are criticised as violating MFN and bound-rate obligations.
[77:0:9] > Most asked: HQ Geneva (×5), year 1995 (×4), earlier name GATT (×4), DGs (×4), MFN (×3). Trap: "1994" (Marrakesh signing) and "most favour to some countries".
[77:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheet Indian Economy p.15 (WTO facts table); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.33 ("main security guard"), p.57; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 05 p.194 (WTO origin, MFN and national treatment, 164 members); app notes 3:77 sub 2
## SUB 1 | GATT, Uruguay Round and the Dunkel Draft
[77:1:0] # GATT
[77:1:1] - **GATT = General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade**; signed **30 October 1947** at **Geneva** by **23** founding contracting parties (not Marrakesh); in force **1948**; GATT office set up at **Geneva, 1948**.
[77:1:2] - **India**: GATT member since **8 July 1948**.
[77:1:3] - Focus: cut **tariffs and quantitative restrictions** in goods; **8 rounds** of negotiations; GATT survives as part of the WTO agreements.
[77:1:4] TABLE head: Basis | GATT | WTO
  [77:1:4.0] Set up | 1947 (in force 1948) | 1 January 1995
  [77:1:4.1] Nature | An agreement | An international organisation
  [77:1:4.2] Coverage | Mainly goods | Goods, services, IPR, investment measures
[77:1:5] # Uruguay Round (1986-1993/94)
[77:1:6] - **8th GATT round**; launched **September 1986** at **Punta del Este**; concluded **1993** (December), Final Act signed **1994**; **123** contracting parties.
[77:1:7] - It "pertains to" **GATT** and **created the WTO** (not UNICEF, IMF, UNESCO).
[77:1:8] - Extended rules beyond goods: **GATS** (services), **TRIPS** (IPR), **TRIMS** (investment). Aims: cut farm subsidies, lift investment restrictions, open services (banking, insurance), protect IPR.
[77:1:9] # Dunkel Draft
[77:1:10] - **Arthur Dunkel**: **Director-General of GATT** (1980-1993), chair of the Trade Negotiations Committee.
[77:1:11] - **Dunkel Draft** (Draft Final Act of the Uruguay Round) tabled **20 December 1991**; concerned with **trade**; best known for **intellectual property** rules (RAS 1992).
[77:1:12] - **UPSC 1994 statements:** acceptance was **all-or-nothing** (single undertaking – "mandatory to accept all proposals") and agriculture proposal = **cut farm subsidies** → correct; it **phased out** (did not reiterate) the **Multi-Fibre Arrangement**, and Parliament never "accepted" it → answer "**1 and 2**".
[77:1:13] - **CDS 2018 chronology:** Uruguay Round concluded 1994 ✔, WTO 1995 ✔, Nasdaq 1971 ✔ – **SWIFT** began in **1973** (live 1977), **not 1985**.
[77:1:14] > Repeats: Dunkel = GATT (×3), Uruguay Round → WTO (×3), GATT office Geneva 1948. NextGen p.55 prints "20 October 1991" and "110 countries" for GATT – the Draft Final Act is dated 20 December 1991, and 23 were the founders (110 is later membership).
[77:1:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheet Indian Economy p.15-16 (GATT signed 30 Oct 1947, 23 parties, Geneva; Uruguay 1986-1993, GATS/TRIPS/TRIMS); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.18 (Uruguay Round, 123 parties, objectives); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.55 (Dunkel Draft); app notes 3:77 sub 0-1
## SUB 2 | Agreement on Agriculture – Pillars and Subsidy Boxes
[77:2:0] # Pillars
[77:2:1] - AoA negotiated in the Uruguay Round, in force **1 January 1995**. **Three pillars: market access, domestic support, export competition** – **anti-dumping and countervailing duties are NOT a pillar**.
[77:2:2] - "Agreement on Agriculture", "SPS Agreement" and "**Peace Clause**" = **WTO** terms (UPSC 2015), as are **amber, blue and green boxes** (UPSC 2016).
[77:2:3] # Subsidy boxes
[77:2:4] TABLE head: Box | Covers | Treatment
  [77:2:4.0] Green | Research, pest/disease control, infrastructure, public stockholding for food security, decoupled income support, environment, regional development | Minimal or no trade distortion; no limits
  [77:2:4.1] Blue | "Amber box with conditions" – direct payments under production-limiting programmes | Trade-distorting but exempt from reduction; no spending limit
  [77:2:4.2] Amber | Price- or quantity-linked support: MSP, power, fertiliser, seed, irrigation (measured as AMS) | Trade-distorting; to be reduced to de minimis
[77:2:5] - **Blue Box = "production-limiting subsidies that distort trade"** (APPSC Group 2).
[77:2:6] - **No Red Box** in the AoA (traffic-light "red = forbidden" belongs to the SCM Agreement); **White, Pink, Yellow** are not boxes either.
[77:2:7] - **S&D box**: special and differential support for developing countries.
[77:2:8] - **India + China proposal (July 2017):** eliminate developed countries' **Amber Box (AMS)** support beyond de minimis first.
[77:2:9] # Mechanics
[77:2:10] TABLE head: Term | Rule
  [77:2:10.0] De minimis | Amber support allowed up to 5% of production value (developed), 10% (developing)
  [77:2:10.1] Total AMS cut | 20% over 6 years (developed); 13.3% over 10 years (developing)
  [77:2:10.2] Blue Box conditions | Payments on fixed areas and yields, or on 85% or less of base production, or a fixed number of livestock
  [77:2:10.3] Tariffication | Non-tariff barriers converted into tariffs; cuts 36% over 6 years (developed), 24% over 10 years (developing)
  [77:2:10.4] Export subsidy cut | Developed: 36% by value or 21% by volume over 6 years; developing 24% / 14% over 10 years
[77:2:11] - **A-R (UPPSC 1998):** "India need not reduce subsidies under WTO" is **false** although India is a developing country (R true) – developing countries also had reduction commitments.
[77:2:12] - **Price-gap payment (MSP minus market price) paid directly to farmers:** keyed **Blue Box** by UPPSC 2016 (direct payment); strictly, such deficiency payments are Amber unless tied to production limits.
[77:2:13] > Most asked: boxes (×9) – blue box definition, no red box, MSP = amber, Amber in the India-China proposal. Trap: "Red box" and "Blue box is subject to cuts".
[77:2:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 20 p.9-10 (green, blue, amber boxes; de minimis 5%/10%); NextGen Rocket Sheet Indian Economy p.16 (boxes); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 04 p.186-188 (traffic lights, "nothing like red box", blue = amber with conditions, S&D box); app notes 3:77 sub 5
## SUB 3 | TRIPS, TRIMS, SPS and India's Compliance Laws
[77:3:0] # Agreements
[77:3:1] TABLE head: Agreement | Subject | India
  [77:3:1.0] TRIPS (1995) | Minimum IPR standards (patents, GI, designs, copyright) | Patents Act amended 2005 (product patents); GI Act 1999; Designs Act 2000 (in force 11 May 2001); PPV&FR Act 2001
  [77:3:1.1] TRIMS – Trade-Related Investment Measures | Investment measures affecting trade in goods only | Phase-out of local-content and trade-balancing rules
  [77:3:1.2] GATS | Trade in services | Liberalisation commitments
  [77:3:1.3] SPS / TBT | Food safety, plant and animal health / technical standards | Food Safety and Standards Act 2006
  [77:3:1.4] TFA (Bali 2013) | Simplify customs | Ratified April 2016
  [77:3:1.5] ITA (1996) | Zero duty on IT products | Signatory
[77:3:2] - **TRIMS (UPSC 2020):** **quantitative restrictions on imports by foreign investors are prohibited** ✔; apply to **goods, not services** ✘; **not concerned with regulating foreign investment** itself ✔ → "**1 and 3 only**". TRIPS and TRIMS = **WTO**.
[77:3:3] - **SPS:** for food-safety standards in dispute settlement the WTO uses the **Codex Alimentarius Commission** (set up by **FAO and WHO, 1963**).
[77:3:4] - **Trade Facilitation Agreement (UPSC 2017):** India ratified it ✔, part of the **Bali package (MC9, 2013)** ✔; it entered into force **22 February 2017**, not January 2016 → "**I and II only**".
[77:3:5] # India's IPR laws
[77:3:6] - **GI of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999** (in force 15 September 2003) – enacted to comply with **WTO (TRIPS)** obligations, not ILO/IMF/UNCTAD. GI = an IPR; India relies on **TRIPS**, not the Lisbon Agreement.
[77:3:7] - GI examples: **Darjeeling Tea – India's first GI (2004-05)**; **Allahabad Surkha guava (2007-08)**; **Lucknow Chikan craft (2008-09)**; **Banaras brocades and sarees (2009-10)**; Nizamabad black pottery (2015-16). So all four in the UPPSC 2011 question are protected.
[77:3:8] - **Patents Act 1970** came into force **20 April 1972**, on the **N. Rajagopala Ayyangar Committee (1957)** report; **Patents (Second Amendment) Act, 2002** (Act 38 of 2002, passed 2002); product patents from 2005.
[77:3:9] - **Industrial designs:** protection since **11 May 2001** under the **Designs Act, 2000**, enacted for **TRIPS**; it adopted the **Locarno classification** of designs.
[77:3:10] # Subsidies (SCM Agreement)
[77:3:11] - **Prohibited ("red light")**, **actionable** (countervailing duty), **non-actionable** (R&D, regional development, environmental). Amber Box is AoA, not SCM.
[77:3:12] # India's trade policy and the WTO
[77:3:13] - **A-R (UPSC 2003):** EXIM Policy 2002-07 was liberal and market-oriented ✔; GATT/WTO aided liberalisation ✔ – both true, **R not the explanation**.
[77:3:14] - **A-R (UPSC 1998):** the **USA threatened** WTO sanctions against developing countries for not observing **ILO conventions** ✔; but the USA **has not itself ratified** most of those conventions ✘.
[77:3:15] - India prohibits GM food imports without approval; six India-US disputes settled (June 2023), India imports US apples.
[77:3:16] > Most asked: GI Act ↔ WTO (×2), TRIMS statements (×2), Codex (×2), TRIMS full form, Patents Act dates (×2).
[77:3:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 14 p.1 (TRIPs, TRIMs agreements); NextGen Rocket Sheet Indian Economy p.16 (TRIMS); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 04 p.188 (SPS, international standards); web: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geographical_indications_in_India (GI registration years, from the GI Registry list); app notes 3:77 sub 8
## SUB 4 | Ministerial Conferences, Doha Round and Country Groups
[77:4:0] # Ministerial Conference
[77:4:1] - **Highest decision-making body** (trade ministers); meets **at least once every two years**.
[77:4:2] TABLE head: MC | Venue, year | Key outcome
  [77:4:2.0] MC1 | Singapore, 1996 | First MC; "Singapore issues" (investment, competition policy, transparency in government procurement, trade facilitation); ITA
  [77:4:2.1] MC2 | Geneva, 1998 | E-commerce customs-duty moratorium begun
  [77:4:2.2] MC3 | Seattle, 1999 | Collapsed amid protests
  [77:4:2.3] MC4 | Doha, 2001 | Doha Development Agenda launched; TRIPS-public health declaration
  [77:4:2.4] MC5 | Cancun, 2003 | Collapsed; G-33 formed
  [77:4:2.5] MC6 | Hong Kong, 2005 | Farm export subsidies to end; duty-free quota-free access for LDCs
  [77:4:2.6] MC7-8 | Geneva, 2009, 2011 | Stock-taking
  [77:4:2.7] MC9 | Bali, 2013 | Bali Package: Trade Facilitation Agreement + interim Peace Clause
  [77:4:2.8] MC10 | Nairobi, 2015 | Elimination of agricultural export subsidies; first MC in Africa
  [77:4:2.9] MC11 | Buenos Aires, 2017 | No declaration; fisheries work programme
  [77:4:2.10] MC12 | Geneva, June 2022 | Fisheries Subsidies Agreement (Phase 1); COVID-19 TRIPS waiver; moratorium extended
  [77:4:2.11] MC13 | Abu Dhabi, UAE, 26 Feb-2 Mar 2024 | Moratorium extended to 31 Mar 2026; no PSH solution
  [77:4:2.12] MC14 | Yaounde, Cameroon, 26-29 Mar 2026 | No declaration (only a draft "Yaounde package"); e-commerce moratorium lapsed; seen as a failure
[77:4:3] - **MC14:** **India blocked** adding the **Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD)** plurilateral to **Annex 4**, though 129 of 166 members backed it.
[77:4:4] # Doha Round and groups
[77:4:5] - **Doha Round** (MC4, 2001): "development round"; **central issue = agriculture**; also NAMA, services; **still unfinished**.
[77:4:6] TABLE head: Group | Members / focus
  [77:4:6.0] G-33 | 2003, 40+ developing countries incl. India; food security, Special Safeguard Mechanism, special products
  [77:4:6.1] NAMA-11 | Developing countries (incl. India) in Non-Agricultural Market Access talks
  [77:4:6.2] G-90 | African Group + ACP countries + LDCs
[77:4:7] - **Special Safeguard Mechanism (SSM)** = a **WTO** tool letting developing countries **raise tariffs for a short time** against import surges or price falls (UPSC 2010).
[77:4:8] > Asked: MC13 venue Abu Dhabi, Doha = agriculture, NAMA-11 = developing, SSM = WTO. Chronology: MC9 Bali 2013 → MC12 Geneva 2022 → MC13 Abu Dhabi 2024 → MC14 Yaounde 2026.
[77:4:9] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 05 p.194-195 (MCs are the highest body, meet at least every two years; list of MCs Singapore 1996 to Buenos Aires 2017; Nairobi package, SSM, PSH); app notes 3:77 sub 3-4 (MC12-MC14)
## SUB 5 | Public Stockholding and the Peace Clause
[77:5:0] - **Peace Clause (Bali MC9, 2013):** no country is legally barred from **food-security public stockholding (PSH)** even if the subsidy **breaches de minimis or AMS limits**, until a permanent solution is found.
[77:5:1] - Conditions: **existing programmes and traditional staples only**; **notification** required; no harm to others' food security. It was **not made permanent** at MC13 or MC14.
[77:5:2] - The Peace Clause concept sits in the **Agreement on Agriculture** (original "due restraint" clause, Art. 13).
[77:5:3] - **India first to invoke it** – for **rice** (2020, for marketing year 2018-19).
[77:5:4] - India's complaint: MSP procurement for the **NFSA** is counted as Amber Box on an **outdated historical reference price** (1986-88).
[77:5:5] - India with the **African Group** seeks a **permanent solution**; not achieved at **MC13** or **MC14**.
[77:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.30 (Peace Clause); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 05 p.195 (Nairobi decision on public stockholding); app notes 3:77 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Fisheries Subsidies and E-commerce
[77:6:0] # Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies (AFS)
[77:6:1] - Adopted at **MC12 (Geneva, June 2022)**; **in force September 2025**.
[77:6:2] - Bans subsidies to **IUU fishing**, fishing on the **unregulated high seas**, and **overfished stocks** (unless rebuilding).
[77:6:3] - Covers **marine wild capture**; **aquaculture and inland fishing are exempt**. A **Fish Fund** helps poorer members.
[77:6:4] - **First WTO agreement with an environmental-sustainability objective**; TFA and AFS = the **only two new multilateral agreements in 30 years**.
[77:6:5] - **India = 123rd** member to deposit its Instrument of Acceptance (**July 2026**).
[77:6:6] - **Phase 2** (overcapacity, overfishing): **deferred at MC14 to the General Council, Geneva**.
[77:6:7] - **AP angle:** Indian fisher bodies, incl. **AP's marine fisher folk**, want a "**fisher-centric**" approach.
[77:6:8] # E-commerce
[77:6:9] - **Moratorium** on customs duties on electronic transmissions (since **MC2, 1998**) **lapsed on 31 March 2026**.
[77:6:10] - **E-Commerce Agreement** (plurilateral): **66 members** signed separately. India's concern: plurilaterals (IFD, E-commerce) may **fragment the WTO** by moving away from consensus.
[77:6:11] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:77 sub 7 (AFS, moratorium, MC14)
## SUB 7 | Dispute Settlement and the Appellate Body Crisis
[77:7:0] - **Appellate Body** non-functional since **December 2019** – the **USA blocked appointments**.
[77:7:1] - **MPIA** (Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement, **EU-led, 2020**) = stop-gap; **India has not joined**.
[77:7:2] - **BRICS New Delhi Declaration (September 2026):** IMF/World Bank quota and voting reform + **restoration of the WTO Appellate Body** (two-tier dispute settlement).
[77:7:3] TABLE head: Dispute | Subject | Result
  [77:7:3.0] DS456 (US) | Solar cells – domestic content, National Solar Mission | India lost, 2016
  [77:7:3.1] DS541 (US) | Export subsidies: MEIS, SEZ, EOU | Against India 2019; appealed into the void
  [77:7:3.2] Sugar (Brazil, Australia, Guatemala) | Sugarcane prices, export subsidies | Against India 2021; appealed
  [77:7:3.3] ICT tariffs (EU, Japan, Taiwan) | Duties on phones and ICT goods | Against India 2023
[77:7:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:77 sub 9

=== NOTES 3:78 | Fdi and Fpi Policy in India - Routes, Sectoral Caps, Trends; Ftas and Cepas Signed by India
## SUB 0 | FDI, FPI and FII – Meaning and What Counts
[78:0:0] # FDI
[78:0:1] - **FDI**: investment for **lasting interest and management control**; a **largely non-debt-creating** capital flow (UPSC 2020) – not debt-servicing, not FII buying G-secs; longer-term and **stable**.
[78:0:2] - Legal line: capital instruments bought by a person resident outside India in an **unlisted** Indian company (any stake), or **10% or more** of post-issue paid-up equity of a **listed** company; 10% threshold from the **Arvind Mayaram Committee**.
[78:0:3] - Instruments: equity shares, debentures, preference shares, share warrants.
[78:0:4] - **Counts as FDI (UPSC 2012):** **subsidiaries of foreign companies**, **majority foreign equity** in Indian companies, **companies exclusively financed by foreign companies** – **portfolio investment is NOT** → "**1, 2 and 3 only**".
[78:0:5] - **Can be included in FDI (UPSC 2021):** **FCCBs**, **FII investment with certain conditions**, **GDRs** – **NRE deposits are not** → "**1, 2 and 3**".
[78:0:6] - **Not FDI:** buying **bonds or stocks** of a company overseas (portfolio). FDI = acquiring a mill abroad, a wholly owned firm abroad, building a new plant abroad.
[78:0:7] TABLE head: Type | Meaning | Example
  [78:0:7.0] Greenfield | New facility | Hyundai, Sriperumbudur
  [78:0:7.1] Brownfield | Acquisition | Vodafone-Hutchison Essar
[78:0:8] - Brings capital, **technology**, management skills, competition, jobs; finances the CAD with stable capital. **Gross FDI is not all fresh capital** (includes reinvested earnings, accounting changes).
[78:0:9] - **MNCs** locate near markets (A) because they seek **more profit** (R) – both true, R explains A.
[78:0:10] # FDI vs FPI / FII
[78:0:11] TABLE head: Basis | FDI | FPI / FII
  [78:0:11.0] Threshold | ≥10% listed, or any unlisted stake | <10% of a listed company
  [78:0:11.1] Nature | Long-term, stable, control | Liquid, short-term "hot money", more volatile
  [78:0:11.2] Brings | Capital + technology + management | Only financial capital – raises capital availability in general
  [78:0:11.3] Target | Specific sectors / enterprises | Securities (secondary market)
  [78:0:11.4] Regulator | DPIIT + RBI | SEBI (registration) + RBI
[78:0:12] - **Key difference (UPSC 2011):** "**FII helps in increasing capital availability in general, while FDI only targets specific sectors**".
[78:0:13] - **FII** = portfolio investment by foreign institutional investors. **SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019** unified **FIIs, sub-accounts and QFIs** as FPIs. FPI opened to India in **1992**.
[78:0:14] - **Most volatile flows:** **FPI and NRI deposits** (interest-rate driven) – "Both". Excess portfolio flows drove the **East Asian and Latin American crises** → **FDI** is the good inflow for a host country (UPSC 2002).
[78:0:15] - **SEBI relaxing norms for sovereign wealth funds** (CDS 2011) – to **attract more foreign investment**.
[78:0:16] > Most asked (×18): what counts as FDI, non-debt character, FII vs FDI difference, P-Notes. Trap: "FII is more stable than FDI".
[78:0:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheet Indian Economy p.27 (FDI non-debt, FDI vs FPI, what FDI includes), p.29 (FII vs FDI; SEBI FPI Regulations 2019); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.37, p.51 ("FII helps in increasing capital availability in general, while FDI only targets specific"); app notes 3:78 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Forms of Foreign Capital – ADR/GDR, P-Notes, ECB, NRI Deposits
[78:1:0] - Foreign capital includes **FDI, trade credit, NRI deposits and ECBs**.
[78:1:1] TABLE head: Form | Classification
  [78:1:1.0] FDI | Non-debt, long-term, control (≥10%)
  [78:1:1.1] FPI / FII | Non-debt, portfolio (<10%)
  [78:1:1.2] ECB, trade credit, FCCB | Debt
  [78:1:1.3] NRI deposits (FCNR(B), NRE) | Banking capital (debt)
  [78:1:1.4] ADR / GDR | Equity raised abroad = Foreign Equity Investment; counted under portfolio investment in BoP
  [78:1:1.5] Participatory Notes | Offshore derivative instruments
  [78:1:1.6] Masala bond | Rupee-denominated bond issued abroad
[78:1:2] - **P-Notes**: issued by **registered FIIs/FPIs** to overseas investors who want exposure to Indian stocks **without registering with SEBI** (UPSC 2007, 2019).
[78:1:3] - **FCNR(B)** replaced FCNR(A) on **15 May 1993** – term deposit in foreign currency.
[78:1:4] - **ECBs** are regulated by the **RBI under FEMA**.
[78:1:5] - **Old data PYQs:** largest forex inflow in **2005-06 = portfolio investment**; FII investment in **calendar 2005 ≈ US $10.7 bn**.

## SUB 2 | Routes, Sectoral Caps and Prohibited Sectors
[78:2:0] # Routes and bodies
[78:2:1] TABLE head: Route | Approval
  [78:2:1.0] Automatic | No prior approval; post-facto reporting to RBI
  [78:2:1.1] Government | Prior approval of the concerned Ministry via the Foreign Investment Facilitation (FIF) Portal
[78:2:2] - **Negative-list approach**; **over 90%** of sectors automatic – not all.
[78:2:3] TABLE head: Act / body | Role
  [78:2:3.0] FEMA 1999 | Replaced FERA 1973
  [78:2:3.1] FIPB | Abolition announced in Budget 2017-18; abolished June 2017
  [78:2:3.2] DPIIT | Nodal for FDI policy and data; under Ministry of Commerce and Industry
  [78:2:3.3] NSWS | FIF Portal part of the National Single Window System since August 2022
[78:2:4] # Sectoral caps (2026)
[78:2:5] TABLE head: Sector | Cap / route
  [78:2:5.0] Insurance | 100% (Union Budget 2025-26, if the entire premium is invested in India); IRDAI HQ Hyderabad; insurance = Entry 47, Union List
  [78:2:5.1] Defence | 74% automatic; up to 100% Government route
  [78:2:5.2] Telecom | 100% automatic
  [78:2:5.3] Single-brand retail | 100% automatic
  [78:2:5.4] Multi-brand retail | 51%, Government route (since 2012)
  [78:2:5.5] Private banks | 74% (49% automatic)
  [78:2:5.6] Public sector banks | 20%, Government route
  [78:2:5.7] Scheduled civil aviation | 100% (49% automatic; NRIs 100% automatic)
  [78:2:5.8] Pharma | Greenfield 100% automatic; brownfield 74% automatic
  [78:2:5.9] Food products made in India – trading incl. e-commerce | 100%, Government route
  [78:2:5.10] E-commerce | Marketplace 100% automatic; inventory model not allowed (July 2026: allowed where inventory is used to export domestically made goods)
[78:2:6] # History of caps (PYQ dates)
[78:2:7] TABLE head: Year | Change
  [78:2:7.0] 2001-02 | Tea: foreign firm to disinvest 26% to an Indian partner in 5 years (not 33% in 4); print media 26% FDI with the largest Indian shareholder holding more than 26%
  [78:2:7.1] 2002-03 | Private banks: 49% automatic FDI from all sources; no 49% ceiling on Indian promoters (minimum 40%)
  [78:2:7.2] Budget 2004-05 | Caps raised in telecom, insurance, civil aviation – banking is the odd one
  [78:2:7.3] 2004 | Private banks 49% → 74%
  [78:2:7.4] 2006 | Retail opened: single-brand up to 51%
  [78:2:7.5] 2012 | Multi-brand 51% (Cabinet Sept 2012; announced 2011-12); foreign airlines up to 49%; single-brand 100%; insurance 26 → 49% proposed (4 Oct 2012); FDI from Pakistan allowed (decision 13 April 2012)
  [78:2:7.6] Insurance | 26% → 49% (2015) → 74% (Budget 2021-22, from 19 May 2021) → 100% (Budget 2025-26)
[78:2:8] - **Not a post-2010 change:** 100% FDI in the **automotive** sector (allowed earlier, 2002).
[78:2:9] - **Defence production** opened **fully to private (Indian) investment** in 2001.
[78:2:10] - Post-2014: caps raised in defence, insurance, pension.
[78:2:11] # Prohibited sectors
[78:2:12] - **Lottery**; gambling, betting, casinos; **chit funds**; **Nidhi companies**; trading in **TDRs**; real estate business and farmhouses; **cigars and cigarettes** of tobacco; **atomic energy**; **railway operations** (except permitted activities).
[78:2:13] - **Railway infrastructure is NOT prohibited** (100% automatic); petroleum refining, cable networks, newspapers, defence, health care allow FDI.

## SUB 4 | FPI Limits and Flows
[78:4:0] - **G-sec limits (General Route):** **6%** of Central G-secs, **2%** of State securities; also VRR and FAR routes. Limits for 2024-25 were kept **unchanged**.
[78:4:1] - **Corporate bonds:** FPI limit raised to **15% (from 9%)** in **Union Budget 2020-21**.
[78:4:2] - **2024-25 (APPSC Group 2 Mains 2025):** rupee moved in a **narrow range** despite FPI outflows; RBI set FPI limits for debt and **Credit Default Swaps**; G-sec and corporate bond limits **unchanged**; RBI **framework (Nov 2024)** to **reclassify FPI holdings above 10% as FDI** → "**All the above**".
[78:4:3] - **JP Morgan EM bond index:** India's target weight **10%**.
[78:4:4] - Drivers: **US Fed rates and global risk appetite**. FY26 outflows about **₹2.2 lakh crore**.
[78:4:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:78 sub 8
## SUB 5 | Press Note 3 – Land-border Countries
[78:5:0] - **April 2020**: all FDI from a country sharing a **land border** with India needs the **Government route**.
[78:5:1] - Covers China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Myanmar, Bhutan, Afghanistan – **Sri Lanka not covered**.
[78:5:2] - **Amended March 2026, effective 1 May 2026:** firms with up to **10%** Chinese/Hong Kong beneficial ownership may use the **automatic route**; beneficial owner as per **PML Rules, 2005**.

  [78:6:0.6] CETA | UK | In force 15 July 2026

[78:6:2] - **RCEP**: signed **15 Nov 2020** by **15** members (ASEAN 10 + China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand); in force **1 January 2022**. **India is not a member** – opted out in 2019 over **China's market dominance** and the trade deficit (**$53.5 bn in 2018-19**).

=== NOTES 3:79 | Structure of the Indian Financial System – Banks, Nbfcs, Dfis, Cooperatives
## SUB 0 | Development Finance Institutions – IFCI to NaBFID
[79:0:0] # Timeline (asked most)
[79:0:1] TABLE head: Institution | Set up | Role / key fact
  [79:0:1.0] IFCI | 1 July 1948 (IFC Act 1948) | First DFI – first all-India term-lending institution; its setting up began the era of development financing; public limited company 1993; now an NBFC-ND-SI
  [79:0:1.1] ICICI | January 1955 | Second all-India industrial FI; World Bank initiative, joint sector (not public sector); reverse-merged into ICICI Bank → universal bank (2002)
  [79:0:1.2] IDBI | July 1964 (RBI subsidiary; to the Government 1976) | Apex institution for industrial finance – long-term finance to medium and large industry; IDBI Ltd 2004; reclassified a private sector bank after LIC took majority control (2019)
  [79:0:1.3] EXIM Bank | January 1982 (EXIM Bank Act 1981) | Finances, facilitates and promotes exports and imports; Lines of Credit abroad; wholly Government-owned; HQ Mumbai
  [79:0:1.4] NABARD | 12 July 1982 (Act 1981) | Apex agriculture and rural credit (see the NABARD page)
  [79:0:1.5] NHB | 9 July 1988 (NHB Act 1987) | Apex housing finance institution; on the advice of a high-level group under C. Rangarajan
  [79:0:1.6] SIDBI | 2 April 1990 (SIDBI Act 1989) | Apex institution for financing, promoting and developing small-scale industries / MSMEs; began as a wholly owned subsidiary of IDBI; HQ Lucknow
  [79:0:1.7] MUDRA | 2015 | Development and refinance for loans to micro units
  [79:0:1.8] NaBFID | 2021 (NaBFID Act 2021) | Newest DFI – infrastructure; capital ₹20,000 crore + ₹5,000 crore grant; HQ Mumbai
[79:0:2] - **Chronology codes:** IFCI 1948 → ICICI 1955 → IDBI 1964 → NABARD 1982 = **1, 2, 3, 4** (IAS 2002, asked twice). With UTI: **UTI February 1964 came before IDBI July 1964** → IFCI, ICICI, UTI, IDBI = **1, 2, 4, 3** (IAS 1995).
[79:0:3] - **Development banks** (NextGen list): **NABARD, SIDBI, IFCI, EXIM Bank, NHB, MUDRA** – so "SIDBI is a **development bank**", not an RRB, commercial or cooperative bank; IFCI "works as a **development bank**".
[79:0:4] - **Long-term industrial finance:** IFCI, ICICI and IDBI **all** gave medium and long-term industrial finance ("all of the above"); single answer for "long-term finance to industries" = **IDBI** (not SBI, LIC, RBI).
[79:0:5] - **For small industries:** **SIDBI** (IDBI/IFCI = medium-large industry; NABARD = agriculture).
[79:0:6] - **Why DFIs:** banks hold mostly short-term deposits, so long-term lending creates an asset-liability mismatch; DFIs fill this **long-term finance gap**.
[79:0:7] - **IDBI Bank sale:** Government + LIC selling a combined **60.72%** stake to a private buyer.
[79:0:8] - **State Financial Corporations (SFCs):** under the SFC Act 1951; the **first SFC was set up in Punjab** (Ramesh Singh dates it 1955; usually 1953); AP SFC 1956; SIDBI is the quasi-regulator of SFCs.
[79:0:9] > Most-asked: first DFI = IFCI (asked 4 times), EXIM 1982 (asked 4 times), SIDBI = MSME apex, April 1990, Lucknow; the chronology codes.
[79:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.10-11 (development banks; IFCI 1948; EXIM 1982; NHB 1988; SIDBI 2 April 1990, Lucknow, ex-IDBI subsidiary), 08 p.1 (NHB, MUDRA); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 05 p.67-70 (IFCI 1948, ICICI 1955 joint sector, IDBI 1964, SIDBI 1990; SFCs first in Punjab); RBI Report on Trend and Progress of Banking 2003-04, ch. V, Chart V.1; NextGen AP Economy Static-1 01 p.4 (APSFC 1956); app notes 3:79 sub 1
## SUB 1 | All-India Financial Institutions – Classification and RBI Control
[79:1:0] # RBI classification (Report on Trend and Progress 2003-04)
[79:1:1] TABLE head: Segment | Institutions
  [79:1:1.0] All-India development banks | IDBI (1964), SIDBI (1990), IIBI (1997), IFCI (1948), IDFC (1997)
  [79:1:1.1] Specialised financial institutions | EXIM Bank (1982), IVCF, ICICI Venture, TFCI (1989)
  [79:1:1.2] Investment institutions | UTI (1964), LIC (1956), GIC (1972)
  [79:1:1.3] Refinance institutions | NABARD, NHB, SIDBI
  [79:1:1.4] State level | SFCs (18), SIDCs (28)
[79:1:2] - **"Out of 17 AIFIs, the Reserve Bank regulates and supervises only nine"** (2003-04): IFCI, IDBI, EXIM Bank, IIBI, TFCI, IDFC (term-lending) + NABARD, NHB, SIDBI (refinance) → answer **9** (APPSC AEE).
[79:1:3]   - **Now 5 RBI-regulated AIFIs:** **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI + NaBFID** (added 2022); EXIM = term-lending institution; NABARD, NHB, SIDBI = **refinance institutions** (APPSC AEE: **NHB**, not IFCI, TFCI or EXIM).
[79:1:4] - **"All-India development finance institution"** (G2 2017): **SIDBI** – an all-India development bank; EXIM Bank is a specialised FI, UTI an investment institution, ECGC an "other" institution.
[79:1:5] - **Under the control of the RBI:** **NABARD** – RBI held **72.5%** of NABARD until it sold 71.5% in **October 2010** (residual sold 26 Feb 2019); **NHB** was **100% RBI-owned until 19 March 2019**. IDBI was an RBI subsidiary only from 1964 to **1976**.
[79:1:6] - **Set up with RBI help:** IDBI, SIDBI, NABARD, NHB, EXIM Bank (**not SEBI**); all now Government-owned.
[79:1:7] - **Quasi-regulators:** NABARD (RRBs, cooperative banks), SIDBI (SFCs), NHB (HFCs – supervision).
[79:1:8] - **Decline of DFIs:** with the capital market and banks entering term lending, "the role of DFIs as an exclusive source of development finance has **diminished**"; ICICI (2002) and IDBI (2004) became banks → the institution whose importance has **fallen most = development banks** (UPPCS 2010).
[79:1:9] - **Public sector dominance (IAS 1993):** commercial banking (nationalised banks) – the keyed answer; but in 1993 the organised term-lending FIs (IFCI, IDBI, SIDBI, IIBI) were also wholly public sector, ICICI excepted.
[79:1:10] > Traps: 9 of 17 (2003-04) vs 5 now; refinance = NABARD, NHB, SIDBI; EXIM = term-lending; NABARD (not IDBI) was RBI-owned in the 1990s.
[79:1:11] ~~ Sources: RBI Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India 2003-04, ch. V "Financial Institutions" p.1-2 and Chart V.1 (rbi.org.in/upload/Publications/PDFs/58849.pdf); millenniumpost.in "With RBI exiting, Govt now owns 100% in NHB, NABARD" (2019); Ramesh Singh part 05 p.67-68 (AIFIs, decline, four RBI-regulated AIFIs); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 08 p.1 (NHB 100% Government 2019); app notes 3:79 sub 2
## SUB 2 | NABARD and Rural Credit – RRBs, SHG-Bank Linkage
[79:2:0] # NABARD
[79:2:1] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [79:2:1.0] Full form | National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development
  [79:2:1.1] Set up | 12 July 1982 under the NABARD Act 1981 – "came into existence in 1982"
  [79:2:1.2] Recommended by | B. Sivaraman Committee (CRAFICARD) – not Narasimham, Rangarajan or PAC
  [79:2:1.3] Replaced | RBI's Agricultural Credit Department and Rural Planning and Credit Cell, and ARDC (Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation) – "ARDC was merged with NABARD"
  [79:2:1.4] Role | Apex institution for agriculture and rural credit; set up specifically to boost rural development; also cottage, small and village industries
  [79:2:1.5] Capital / HQ | initial ₹100 crore (RBI and GoI 50:50); HQ Mumbai; fully Government-owned since 2019
[79:2:2] - **Apex bank of agriculture** = **NABARD**, not RBI, cooperatives, SBI, PNB or Central Bank.
[79:2:3] - NABARD took over **RBI's agricultural-credit functions** and **ARDC's refinance** portfolio (housing refinance = NHB, so "NABARD for housing refinance" is false).
[79:2:4] - Refinances **StCBs, RRBs, land development banks** (₹3,25,497.81 crore, 2024-25); manages **RIDF**, funded by banks' **PSL shortfalls** (₹42,714 crore, 2024-25); supervises RRBs and cooperative banks.
[79:2:5] # RRBs
[79:2:6] - First RRB 2 October 1975 (Prathama Grameen Bank); **RRB Act 1976**; shares Centre 50 : State 15 : sponsor bank 35; supervised by NABARD; now **28** RRBs. **Swabhimaan** = rural banking campaign.
[79:2:7] # SHG-Bank Linkage and JLG
[79:2:8] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [79:2:8.0] SHG-BLP | NABARD, pilot 1992; through commercial banks, RRBs and cooperative banks; "world's largest microfinance movement"
  [79:2:8.1] Idea | group lending of the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh (Muhammad Yunus)
  [79:2:8.2] JLG scheme | NABARD 2006; 4-10 members (tenant farmers, oral lessees – not large landowners); mutual guarantee
[79:2:9] > Most-asked: NABARD 1982 (Act 1981), Sivaraman Committee, apex of agricultural credit, ARDC merged into it.
[79:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.8 (RRBs), p.10 (NABARD: Sivaraman Committee, 12 July 1982, Act 1981, replaced ACD, RPCC and ARDC, HQ Mumbai, SHG-BLP); app notes 3:79 sub 8
## SUB 3 | Microfinance – Grameen Model, AP Crisis and Malegam Committee
[79:3:0] # Origin
[79:3:1] - **Microfinance pioneer:** **Prof. Muhammad Yunus** (Bangladesh), founder of the **Grameen Bank** (Nobel Peace Prize 2006) – the Grameen model was developed in **Bangladesh**.
[79:3:2] # AP crisis to regulation
[79:3:3] - 1. **AP crisis 2010:** multiple lending, over-indebtedness, coercive recovery, borrower suicides; the AP MFI loan book then **collapsed** (did not expand).
[79:3:4] - 2. **AP MFI Ordinance, October 2010** (Act 2011): MFIs to register with **district authorities**; doorstep recovery curbed, interest capped.
[79:3:5] - 3. **Malegam Committee** (RBI sub-committee, **October 2010**, Y.H. Malegam) – set up **after the AP crisis**; created the **NBFC-MFI** category (framework **2 December 2011**); margin and interest caps; no more than **2 MFIs per borrower**. (Y.H. Malegam also chaired SEBI's 1995 committee on primary-market disclosure – hence "Malegam = capital market reforms" against Kelkar (tax), Naresh Chandra (corporate governance), Swaminathan.)
[79:3:6] - 4. **MFIN** (**2009**, association of NBFC-MFIs) and **Sa-Dhan**: RBI-recognised **SROs (2014)**.
[79:3:7] # Framework and issues
[79:3:8] - **NBFC-MFI:** non-deposit-taking; at least **75%** of assets in microfinance loans; minimum NOF **₹10 crore** (new registrations from 1 Oct 2022; earlier ₹5 crore, ₹2 crore in the North East).
[79:3:9] - **Microfinance loan (RBI, March 2022):** **collateral-free**; household annual income up to **₹3 lakh**; repayments ≤ **50%** of income.
[79:3:10] - **Funding:** MFIs borrow mainly from **banks and FIs** (they cannot take deposits) – **not government subsidies**.
[79:3:11] - **Impact:** unregulated lending can cause **over-indebtedness**; **technology** cuts costs; regulation (lending caps, margin and interest ceilings) **affects profitability**.
[79:3:12] - **Borrowers:** **95% women**, 80% rural; portfolio share (Mar 2025): **NBFC-MFIs 39%**, banks 32%, SFBs 16%, NBFCs 12%; banks' MFI book fell 40% (Q3 FY26); NCGTC guarantee scheme to June 2026.
[79:3:13] > Statements (APPSC ASO): over-indebtedness ✓, government subsidies the main source ✗, technology cuts costs ✓ → **1 and 3**.
[79:3:14] ~~ Sources: RBI Consultative Document on Regulation of Microfinance, 2021 (rbi.org.in PublicationsView id=20377: AP crisis 2010, Malegam Committee, NBFC-MFI framework 2 Dec 2011, NOF ₹5 crore / ₹2 crore NE, NBFC-MFIs borrow); scconline.com (6 Apr 2022: NOF ₹10 crore for NBFC-MFIs from 1 Oct 2022, glide path to March 2027); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.10 (SHGs and microfinance); app notes 3:79 sub 9

[79:4:4] # Housing finance

[79:4:7] # Regulators

  [79:4:8.0] RBI | Banks, NBFCs, HFCs (since 2019) | RBI Act 1934
  [79:4:8.1] SEBI | Securities markets, merchant bankers, venture capital, stock brokers | statutory 1992
  [79:4:8.2] IRDAI | Insurance companies | IRDA Act 1999
  [79:4:8.3] PFRDA | Pensions / NPS | PFRDA Act 2013
  [79:4:8.4] IFSCA | Unified regulator of IFSCs – GIFT City, Gandhinagar (India's first IFSC) | IFSCA Act 2019; set up 27 April 2020
  [79:4:8.5] State Government | Chit fund companies | Chit Funds Act 1982
[79:4:9] - **Finance Act 2019:** HFC regulation moved from **NHB to the RBI**; NHB keeps supervision and refinance. NHB was wholly **RBI-owned** until the Centre took it over in **2019**.
[79:4:10] - **Infrastructure finance – IL&FS:** **Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services** – an infrastructure finance and leasing firm (NBFC); its **September 2018** defaults set off a liquidity crisis; board superseded through an **NCLT** order.
[79:4:11] - **DHFL (2019):** first financial services company resolved under the **IBC (Sec 227)**; acquired by **Piramal (2021)**, not 2019.
