## SUB 5 | NBFCs – Definition, Regulators, Categories and Scale-Based Regulation
[79:5:0] # What an NBFC is
[79:5:1] - A company registered under the **Companies Act** engaged in **loans and advances, acquisition of shares, stocks, bonds, debentures and government securities**, leasing, hire-purchase – banking services **without a banking licence**.
[79:5:2] - **Principal business (50-50) test:** financial assets > 50% of total assets **and** financial income > 50% of gross income.
[79:5:3] - **100% FDI** through the automatic route; **FDI is prohibited in Nidhi companies** (and chit funds).
[79:5:4] - **Liquid debt mutual funds** = main source of short-term funds for NBFCs.
[79:5:5] # NBFC vs bank
[79:5:6] TABLE head: Basis | Bank | NBFC
  [79:5:6.0] Demand deposits | Yes | No (deposit-taking NBFCs take term deposits only)
  [79:5:6.1] Cheques drawn on itself | Yes | Cannot issue
  [79:5:6.2] Payment and settlement system | Part of it | Not part
  [79:5:6.3] Deposit insurance (DICGC) | Covered | Not covered
  [79:5:6.4] CRR / SLR | Both | No CRR; deposit-taking NBFCs keep liquid assets
  [79:5:6.5] RBI LAF (repo) access | Yes | No
[79:5:7] - **Not all NBFCs register with the RBI:** venture capital, merchant banking, stock broking → **SEBI**; insurance → **IRDAI**; HFCs → NHB (supervision; regulation now RBI); **Nidhi** → **Ministry of Corporate Affairs**; **chit funds → State Governments**.
[79:5:8] - **UPSC 2010:** "cannot acquire government securities" ✗; "cannot accept demand deposits" ✓ → **B only**. **UPSC 2026:** no demand deposits ✓, all must register with RBI ✗, part of payment system / issue cheques ✗, no DICGC cover ✓ → **1 and 4**.
[79:5:9] - **Payments banks cannot lend**; 11 Small Finance Banks (differentiated banks, Nachiket Mor Committee 2013).
[79:5:10] # Categories and capital
[79:5:11] - Categories: **AFC, Loan Company, Investment Company, IFC, NBFC-MFI, CIC, HFC, IDF, NBFC-P2P** – "Regional Rural Banking Company" is NOT one.
[79:5:12] - **NBFC-P2P (2017):** RBI-regulated online platforms for **peer-to-peer lending** – **individuals lend to individuals through online services**.
[79:5:13] TABLE head: Category | Minimum Net Owned Fund
  [79:5:13.0] NBFC-MFI | ₹10 crore (new from 1 Oct 2022; existing ₹7 crore by March 2025, ₹10 crore by March 2027)
  [79:5:13.1] NBFC-ICC | ₹10 crore (raised from ₹2 crore; glide path to March 2027)
  [79:5:13.2] HFC | ₹20 crore
[79:5:14] # Scale-Based Regulation (Oct 2021)
[79:5:15] TABLE head: Layer | Who / what applies
  [79:5:15.0] Base | Smaller non-deposit NBFCs
  [79:5:15.1] Middle | All deposit-taking NBFCs; HFCs, IFCs, CICs
  [79:5:15.2] Upper | Identified by RBI; bank-like norms for at least 5 years; listing within 3 years
  [79:5:15.3] Top | Kept empty; only for a sharp rise in systemic risk
[79:5:16] - NBFC-UL list 2026-27: **17** companies incl. **Tata Sons** (15 in April 2026); RBI rejected Tata Sons' bid to surrender its licence and asked it to list (13 Sep 2026); proposed single ₹1 lakh crore asset test for UL.
[79:5:17] - **NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018** → merged into the **RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021**.

## SUB 6 | Cooperative Credit Structure and Urban Cooperative Banks
[79:6:0] # Rural tiers
[79:6:1] TABLE head: Tier | Short-term | Long-term
  [79:6:1.0] State | State Cooperative Bank (StCB) | State Cooperative ARDB
  [79:6:1.1] District | Central Cooperative Bank (DCCB) | –
  [79:6:1.2] Village | PACS | PCARDB (Primary Cooperative ARDB)
[79:6:2] - Cooperative banks were the first Government-sponsored, -supported and -subsidised financial agency in India.
[79:6:3] - **Operates at district level** = **Central Cooperative Bank** (asked twice) – not the StCB, PACS or RBI.
[79:6:4] - **StCBs and DCCBs:** licensed by the **RBI**, inspected by **NABARD**; **PACS** under **State Registrars**.
[79:6:5] - **Consumer cooperative stores:** set up by members, registered by the Registrar of Cooperative Societies.
[79:6:6] - **World Bank (2007):** loans and credit of **$600 million** for India's **rural cooperative credit structure**.
[79:6:7] # Urban Cooperative Banks
[79:6:8] - Earlier **dual control**: State Registrar of Cooperative Societies + RBI; brought under the **BR Act 1949** in **1966**.
[79:6:9] - **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act 2020** (after the **PMC Bank** crisis): UCBs and multi-state cooperative banks under the RBI on management, capital, audit and resolution; UCBs **can issue equity and preference shares** (with RBI approval).
[79:6:10] - **UPSC 2021:** "supervised by local boards of State Governments" ✗; "can issue equity and preference shares" ✓; "brought under the BR Act by the 1966 amendment" ✓ → **2 and 3 only**.
[79:6:11] - **Number of UCBs:** **1,618** at end-March 2012 (1,645 at end-March 2011); **1,457** (6 Aug 2026); RBI to resume **on-tap licensing** after more than two decades.
[79:6:12] - **NUCFDC** = umbrella body for UCBs; RBI nod to NABARD's **Sahakar Sarathi** shared-services entity.
[79:6:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.10 (3-tier short-term, long-term LDBs); RBI speech, rbi.org.in BS_SpeechesView Id=756 ("As on March 2012 there were 1618 UCBs"); RBI Trend and Progress 2011-12 cooperative-banking chapter, search extract only (1,645 at end-March 2011); app notes 3:79 sub 7
## SUB 7 | Organised vs Unorganised Financial System
[79:7:0] TABLE head: Organised (RBI-regulated) | Unorganised
  [79:7:0.0] Commercial banks, cooperative banks, foreign banks, DFHI, provident funds, STCI, mutual funds | Indigenous bankers, moneylenders, unregulated finance/loan companies, chit funds, nidhis
  [79:7:0.1] Instruments: call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills, certificates of deposit, CPs, repo, MMMFs | Serves farmers, artisans, small traders
[79:7:1] - **Finance companies are NOT part of the organised money market** (APPSC G2 2017); commercial banks, DFHI and cooperative banks are inside it.
[79:7:2] - **Unregulated non-bank intermediaries:** indigenous bankers, moneylenders, loan companies, chit funds – **commercial and trade bills** are organised money-market **instruments**, not intermediaries.
[79:7:3] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [79:7:3.0] Indigenous banker | Accepts deposits and lends, combining banking with trade or commission business; deals in hundis (Shroffs, Seths, Mahajans, Multanis, Chettiars)
  [79:7:3.1] Moneylenders | Professional or agricultural; covered by state money-lending laws
  [79:7:3.2] Chit funds | Regulated by the State Government (Chit Funds Act 1982)
  [79:7:3.3] Shadow banking | Bank-like credit intermediation outside full bank regulation; term coined by Paul McCulley, 2007
  [79:7:3.4] Regulatory arbitrage | Using gaps in regulatory treatment to work outside the stricter banking framework
[79:7:4] - One who "**lends only in kind**" is **NOT** an indigenous banker.
[79:7:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:79 sub 0; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 08 p.3 (chit funds – State Governments)

  [79:8:3.1] AP MACS Act, 1995 | Tribunal has original jurisdiction

=== NOTES 3:80 | Reserve Bank of India – Establishment, Organisation and Functions
## SUB 0 | Establishment, Nationalisation and Headquarters
[80:0:0] # Origin
[80:0:1] - **Hilton Young Commission** = **Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance (1926)**: recommended a central bank; the RBI was set up **on its recommendation** (not Narasimham, Gorwala or Malhotra, which came later).
[80:0:2] - **B.R. Ambedkar's 1925** evidence to this Commission shaped the idea of the RBI.
[80:0:3] - Earlier, the **Royal Commission on Indian Finance and Currency (1913)** was chaired by **Austen Chamberlain** (Chamberlain Commission) – not Keynes, who was only a member.
[80:0:4] # Timeline
[80:0:5] TABLE head: Event | Date
  [80:0:5.0] Hilton Young Commission recommends a central bank | 1926
  [80:0:5.1] RBI Act passed | 1934
  [80:0:5.2] RBI established / starts functioning (shareholders' bank, Central Office Calcutta) | 1 April 1935
  [80:0:5.3] Central Office moves Calcutta → Bombay (permanent) | 1937
  [80:0:5.4] Nationalised – fully State-owned, under RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948 | 1 January 1949
  [80:0:5.5] RBI Hyderabad office becomes operational | 1956
  [80:0:5.6] RBI@90 | 1 April 2024
[80:0:6] - Act **1934** → established **1935** → nationalised **1949**. "Established in 1949" is wrong; "nationalised on 26 January 1950" is wrong (UPSC 2004); "nationalised in 1937" is wrong (1937 = move to Bombay).
[80:0:7] - **Headquarters: Mumbai** (Mint Street) since 1937; it is a **statutory body** and the **central bank** of India.
[80:0:8] - **Seal**: **tiger and palm tree** – the tiger replaced the **lion** of the East India Company double mohur.
[80:0:9] # Accounting year
[80:0:10] TABLE head: Period | RBI accounting year
  [80:0:10.0] 1935-1940 | January–December
  [80:0:10.1] 1940 to 2019-20 | July–June
  [80:0:10.2] From 2020-21 | April–March (transition year of nine months, July 2020–March 2021)
[80:0:11] - Questions set before 2020 (IAS 1998, UPPSC 2013) are keyed **July–June**; today it is **April–March**, the same as banks and Government.
[80:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 05 p.10 (1935, 1949 Act of 1948, Hilton Young 1926, Ambedkar 1925, seal, Calcutta → Bombay 1937, HQ Mumbai); Rocket Indian Economy p.3, p.10 (established 1 April 1935, nationalised 1949, HQ 1937); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.42 (set up 1935 as a private bank), p.55 (accounting year July–June, cut short to 31 March 2021); rbi.org.in Hyderabad office profile (operational since 1956); app notes 3:80 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Organisation and Governors
[80:1:0] # Governance
[80:1:1] - **Central Board of Directors**: **21** members, appointed by the Government of India under the RBI Act; directors hold office for **4 years**.
[80:1:2] - **Governor and Deputy Governors**: appointed (nominated) by the **Central Government**; tenure **not more than 5 years**. The head of the RBI is called the **Governor**; the Governor draws power from the **RBI Act**.
[80:1:3] - **Four Deputy Governors**: two from within RBI + one commercial banker + one **economist** (heads monetary policy). **Rohit Jain** appointed May 2026 for 3 years, replacing T. Rabi Sankar.
[80:1:4] - **Local Boards: four** – Mumbai (West), Kolkata (East), Chennai (South), New Delhi (North); members appointed by the Central Government for 4 years; each sends one director to the Central Board (not functioning since 2022 for lack of quorum). Hyderabad has none.
[80:1:5] - Offices at 31 locations; **AP regional office** began 22 Aug 2022 (working from Hyderabad), moved to **Vijayawada** in 2025; AP currency work stays with the **Hyderabad** office.
[80:1:6] # Governors
[80:1:7] TABLE head: Governor | Note
  [80:1:7.0] Sir Osborne Smith (1935-37) | First Governor; signed no Indian currency note
  [80:1:7.1] C.D. Deshmukh (1943-49) | First Indian Governor; later Finance Minister (1950-56)
  [80:1:7.2] Manmohan Singh | 1982-85
  [80:1:7.3] C. Rangarajan | 1992-97
  [80:1:7.4] Bimal Jalan | 1997-2003
  [80:1:7.5] Y.V. Reddy | 2003 – Sept 2008 (Governor at the 2008 exams)
  [80:1:7.6] D. Subbarao | Finance Secretary, then 22nd Governor from 5 Sept 2008 (to 2013; Governor in 2011)
  [80:1:7.7] Shaktikanta Das | 2018-2024
  [80:1:7.8] Sanjay Malhotra | Governor since 11 Dec 2024 (as of 2026); chairs MPC and Payments Regulatory Board
[80:1:8] - **Raja J. Chelliah** was **never** an RBI Governor (tax-reform economist); Usha Thorat was a Deputy Governor.
[80:1:9] # Training colleges and institutes
[80:1:10] - **Reserve Bank Staff College – Chennai**; **College of Agricultural Banking – Pune**.
[80:1:11] - Autonomous institutes run by RBI: **NIBM, IGIDR, IDRBT** (the Staff College is not one of them).
[80:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 05 p.10 (31 offices, 4 regional representations, Staff College Chennai, CAB Pune, NIBM/IGIDR/IDRBT), p.11 (Osborne Smith first Governor, Deshmukh first Indian Governor 1943-49, Governor/Deputies nominated by GoI for up to 5 years, 21-member Board, 4 years); Rocket Indian Economy p.3 (Deshmukh, Finance Minister 1950-56); Rocket CA 2026-01 p.11 (Governor Sanjay Malhotra); app notes 3:80 sub 1 (Governors table, Local Boards, AP office)
## SUB 2 | Central Banking Functions – Banker to Government and Banker's Bank
[80:2:0] # The central bank
[80:2:1] - The **RBI performs the central banking functions** in India; it is the **Central Bank** (not SBI, NABARD, SBH or Central Bank of India, which are banks/DFIs). It is the regulator of the entire banking system.
[80:2:2] TABLE head: Function | Legal basis / content
  [80:2:2.0] Bank of issue | Sec 22: sole right to issue notes except the ₹1 note
  [80:2:2.1] Banker, agent and adviser to Government | Sec 20 (Centre), Sec 21/21A (States, by agreement); payments, receipts, public debt management, borrowing programme, Ways and Means Advances, overdrafts
  [80:2:2.2] Banker's bank | Holds SCBs' deposits and reserves (CRR); lender of last resort; guides and advises banks
  [80:2:2.3] Monetary authority | Price stability with growth in mind; MPC sets the repo rate
  [80:2:2.4] Custodian of forex | Manages forex reserves under FEMA 1999; stabilises the rupee's external value
  [80:2:2.5] Controller of credit | Controls money and credit (quantitative and qualitative measures)
  [80:2:2.6] Payments | Regulates and upgrades payment systems (PSS Act 2007)
  [80:2:2.7] Regulator | Banks, NBFCs (Chapter IIIB), AIFIs, HFCs
[80:2:3] # Banker to Government
[80:2:4] - Manages **public debt of Centre and States** and handles the **Government of India's borrowing programme** (not the Department of Expenditure – UPSC 2004); maintains Government accounts; **Public Debt Office** functions under it.
[80:2:5] - Banker to **all State Governments except Sikkim** (Sikkim: limited agreement, public debt only).
[80:2:6] - **Fiscal agent and adviser** to Government in monetary and financial matters; **represents India at the IMF** (Government's agent for India's IMF membership) and World Bank.
[80:2:7] - **UPSC 2001:** banker to Centre, formulates monetary policy, agent for IMF membership, handles GoI borrowing – **all four correct**.
[80:2:8] # Banker's bank and lender of last resort
[80:2:9] - **Banker's bank** (IAS 2012): (i) other banks **keep deposits/reserves with the RBI**, (ii) the RBI **lends to banks in need**, (iii) it **advises banks on monetary matters** – **all three**.
[80:2:10] - **Lender of last resort (LoLR)** – exclusive RBI function: **emergency liquidity to banks facing a temporary crisis** (UPSC 2021: **2 only**); it is **not** lending to trade/industry or financing budget deficits.
[80:2:11] - **Bank Rate** = rate at which the **RBI lends to / rediscounts bills of commercial banks** (also called the discount rate) – not the rate banks charge borrowers or pay depositors.
[80:2:12] - **FEMA A-R (APPSC):** RBI administers FEMA 1999 "to facilitate external trade and payments and promote orderly development of the forex market"; it also upgrades **payment systems** – both true, **R does not explain A**.
[80:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 05 p.9-10 (central bank, regulator); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 06 p.1 (Sec 20, 21, 21A; public debt, IMF, advice), p.2 (banker to banks, BR Act, LoLR, custodian of forex), p.3 (FED: FEMA purpose), p.4 (LoLR = liquidity to a bank facing severe liquidity problems; credit control), p.6 (Bank Rate = lending/rediscounting); Rocket Indian Economy p.10-12 (functions table, banker's bank, banker to Government, IMF agent); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.3 (Bank Rate), p.53 (DEA, not Dept of Expenditure); app notes 3:80 sub 2
## SUB 3 | Monetary Authority, Credit Control and What RBI Does Not Do
[80:3:0] # Monetary policy and credit control
[80:3:1] - **Monetary (and credit) policy is formulated and implemented by the RBI** (MPC since 2016; six members) – the RBI **regulates and announces the repo and reverse repo rates**, not the Finance Ministry, PM, President, CAG or SBI.
[80:3:2] - **Price stability / controlling inflation** = **RBI** (flexible inflation targeting; target set by the **Finance Ministry in consultation with the RBI**) – not the FSDC, Dept of Consumer Affairs or Expenditure Management Commission.
[80:3:3] - RBI **controls "money and credit"** and **controls credit creation by commercial banks** through quantitative (Bank Rate, repo, CRR, SLR, OMO) and qualitative (selective credit control, margins, moral suasion) tools.
[80:3:4] - Other than market forces, the **RBI intervenes (buys/sells dollars) to manage the exchange rate**.
[80:3:5] - **A-R (APPSC 2024):** institutions ensure stability through monetary policy **because** central banks use repo and CRR to manage liquidity and inflation – **R explains A**.
[80:3:6] - **Regulating and controlling banks** = an activity of the **RBI** (powers under the **Banking Regulation Act 1949**).
[80:3:7] - 2016 framework (MPC + inflation-targeting law) gave **operational independence** on policy rates.
[80:3:8] # What the RBI does NOT do
[80:3:9] - **Credit creation** – done by **commercial banks**; the RBI only **controls** it.
[80:3:10] - **Regulation of foreign trade** (Commerce Ministry/DGFT) – the RBI regulates **currency, credit and forex reserves**.
[80:3:11] - **Fiscal policy** – formulated by the **Ministry of Finance** (not RBI, Finance Commission or Planning Commission).
[80:3:12] - **Granting corporate deeds**; lending to the public; minting coins; issuing the ₹1 note; income-tax collection.
[80:3:13] - **Savings bank interest rate** in nationalised banks: fixed by the **RBI until it was deregulated on 25 Oct 2011** – now each bank fixes it; never the Finance Ministry, Finance Commission or IBA (UPSC 2010: **None of the above**).
[80:3:14] - Does not regulate securities (SEBI), insurance (IRDAI) or pensions (PFRDA).
[80:3:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 06 p.4-6 (credit control, quantitative/qualitative instruments, price stability, monetary policy); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 05 p.10 (regulates money supply and credit); Rocket Indian Economy p.10, p.12 (monetary policy, controller of credit, instruments); app notes 3:80 sub 2 (what RBI does not do, savings rate deregulation 25 Oct 2011, inflation target)
## SUB 4 | Currency Management – Note Issue, Reserve System and Demonetisation
[80:4:0] # Who issues what
[80:4:1] TABLE head: Item | Issued by | Signed by | Legal tender
  [80:4:1.0] ₹1 note | Government of India (Ministry of Finance) | Finance Secretary | Unlimited
  [80:4:1.1] All other notes (₹2 upward; ₹10 and above in the new series) | RBI (Sec 22, sole right, on behalf of the Centre) | RBI Governor | Unlimited
  [80:4:1.2] Coins | Government of India (minted by GoI; RBI only distributes them as GoI's agent) | – | Limited (up to ₹1,000, Coinage Act)
[80:4:2] - So "RBI issues **all** types of currency notes" is **wrong**; the ₹100 note carries the **Governor's** signature.
[80:4:3] - RBI can issue notes up to **₹10,000** (Sec 24); first ₹10,000 note 1938, demonetised 1946, re-introduced 1954, demonetised 1978.
[80:4:4] # Reserve system for note issue
[80:4:5] TABLE head: System | Rule
  [80:4:5.0] Proportional Reserve System (till 1956) | 2/5 of assets in gold or sterling securities; gold at least ₹40 crore
  [80:4:5.1] Minimum Reserve System (1956) | ₹515 crore = ₹400 crore foreign securities + ₹115 crore gold
  [80:4:5.2] Amended 1957 (present) | ₹200 crore of gold and forex, of which at least ₹115 crore in gold
[80:4:6] - India's note issue is based on the **Minimum Reserve System**; beyond the floor the RBI can issue currency **to any extent**.
[80:4:7] - Notes are issued against **gold coin and bullion, foreign securities, rupee coin and GoI securities** (Sec 33) – "all of the above".
[80:4:8] # Demonetisation
[80:4:9] TABLE head: Year | Notes withdrawn
  [80:4:9.0] 1946 | High-denomination notes (before Independence)
  [80:4:9.1] 16 Jan 1978 | ₹1,000, ₹5,000, ₹10,000 – first after Independence (HDBN Demonetisation Act; Morarji Desai)
  [80:4:9.2] 8 Nov 2016 (from midnight) | ₹500 and ₹1,000 (Mahatma Gandhi series); SC upheld 4:1 (2023)
[80:4:10] - Power: **Sec 26(2) of the RBI Act** – the Government notifies **on the recommendation of the RBI Central Board** (the 2016 notification followed the Board's recommendation).
[80:4:11] - **Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017**: holding old ₹500/₹1,000 notes above the limit → fine of **₹10,000** or five times the face value, whichever is higher.
[80:4:12] - **₹2,000** note: issued Nov 2016, withdrawn from circulation **May 2023**, still legal tender.
[80:4:13] - Printing cost of a new ₹500 note: about **₹2.87–3.09** (2016-17) → nearest **₹3**.
[80:4:14] # Notes – features and security
[80:4:15] TABLE head: Note (new series) | Size | Colour | Motif
  [80:4:15.0] ₹10 | 123 × 63 mm | Chocolate brown | Konark Sun Temple
  [80:4:15.1] ₹50 | 135 × 66 mm | Fluorescent blue | Hampi with chariot
  [80:4:15.2] ₹100 | 142 × 66 mm | Lavender | Rani ki Vav
  [80:4:15.3] ₹2,000 | 166 × 66 mm | Magenta | Mangalyaan
[80:4:16] - **17 languages** on notes: Hindi and English on the front, a **language panel of 15** at the back.
[80:4:17] - **MANI** (Mobile Aided Note Identifier) – RBI app (2020) that helps the **visually impaired** identify notes.
[80:4:18] - **FICN = Fake Indian Currency Note** (counterfeit).
[80:4:19] - **Polymer ₹10 notes** (field trial, 1 billion pieces, 5 cities): objectives **longer life** (primary) and **combating counterfeiting** – not cheaper "minting".
[80:4:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 05 p.2 (Proportional and Minimum Reserve System, ₹200 crore/₹115 crore, Sec 22, Dewas/Nashik), p.3 (demonetisation 1946, 1978, 2016; ₹10,000; 17 languages), p.4-8 (note sizes, colours, motifs), p.11 (₹1 note by Ministry of Finance, Finance Secretary's signature; coins by GoI; minimum reserve since 1957; backing assets; 8 Nov 2016 midnight); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.41 (Minimum Reserve System ₹200 crore, ₹115 crore gold); Rocket Indian Economy p.11 (₹1 note, coins = GoI); millenniumpost.in "Pilot project: Govt to launch 1 bn plastic Rs 10 bank notes in 5 cities" (polymer objectives); app notes 3:80 sub 3 (Sec 24, 26(2), 33; SC 4:1; ₹2,000; MANI)
## SUB 5 | Note Presses and Mints
[80:5:0] TABLE head: Unit | Owner | Location
  [80:5:0.0] Currency Note Press | SPMCIL (GoI) | Nashik (Maharashtra)
  [80:5:0.1] Bank Note Press (BNP) | SPMCIL (GoI) | Dewas (Madhya Pradesh)

  [80:5:0.3] BRBNMPL presses | RBI-owned | Mysuru (Karnataka), Salboni (West Bengal)
  [80:5:0.4] Mints (4) | SPMCIL, not RBI | Mumbai, Noida, Kolkata, Hyderabad

## SUB 6 | Regulatory Role, Committees and Publications
[80:6:0] # Regulation of banks
[80:6:1] - **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** gave the **RBI** extensive powers: licensing, branches, management, amalgamation, inspection, audit.
[80:6:2] - **UPSC 2013:** the RBI regulates banks in **liquidity of assets, branch expansion, merger and winding-up** – **all four**.
[80:6:3] TABLE head: Act / Section | Provision
  [80:6:3.0] BR Act Sec 22(1) | Licensing of banks, incl. payments banks
  [80:6:3.1] BR Act Sec 26A | DEA Fund (2014): deposits unclaimed 10+ years; depositor's right survives
  [80:6:3.2] RBI Act Chapter IIIB | NBFC regulation
  [80:6:3.3] PSS Act 2007 | Payment systems
[80:6:4] - No bank or NBFC may open without an **RBI licence**; **mergers approved by the RBI**, which can seek the **winding up** of a bank.
[80:6:5] - **Branch expansion**: banks, SFBs, payments banks, LABs, RRBs may open branches without prior approval if **25%** of new branches are in **unbanked rural** areas.
[80:6:6] # Boards and committees
[80:6:7] TABLE head: Body | Year | Purpose
  [80:6:7.0] Board for Financial Supervision | 1994 | Integrated supervision of banks, FIs, NBFCs
  [80:6:7.1] Tarapore Committee | 1997; 2006 | Capital account convertibility
  [80:6:7.2] Bimal Jalan panel (High Level Advisory Committee) | 2013-14 | Scrutinised applications for new bank licences (report 25 Feb 2014)
  [80:6:7.3] Inter-disciplinary Standing Committee | – | Cyber security
  [80:6:7.4] Payments Regulatory Board | Oct 2025 | Six members, Governor chairs, 3 Government nominees; replaced the BPSS
  [80:6:7.5] RB-IOS 2026 | 1 July 2026 | "One Nation One Ombudsman"; banks, RRBs, UCBs, NBFCs, payment operators; no cap on amount
[80:6:8] - **PCA = Prompt Corrective Action** (RBI framework for weak banks).
[80:6:9] # RBI publications – frequency
[80:6:10] TABLE head: Publication | Frequency
  [80:6:10.0] Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India | Annual
  [80:6:10.1] Monetary Policy Report | Half-yearly (bi-annual)
  [80:6:10.2] RBI Bulletin | Monthly
  [80:6:10.3] Basic Statistical Return (BSR-1, outstanding credit) | Quarterly
[80:6:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 06 p.2 (BR Act 1949 powers), p.5 (licence for banks/NBFCs); Rocket Indian Economy p.10 (banking regulation); app notes 3:80 sub 5 (BR Act sections, branch rule, BFS, PRB, RB-IOS, cyber committee, Jalan licence panel); RBI publications frequency – general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 7 | RBI Autonomy, Income and Developmental Role
[80:7:0] # Key sections of the RBI Act
[80:7:1] TABLE head: Section | Provision
  [80:7:1.0] 7 | Centre may give directions in public interest after consulting the Governor (a power in the RBI Act, not the Constitution)
  [80:7:1.1] 22 | Sole right of note issue
  [80:7:1.2] 24 | Highest denomination ₹10,000
  [80:7:1.3] 26(2) | Demonetisation
  [80:7:1.4] 30 | Centre can supersede the Central Board
  [80:7:1.5] 47 | Net profit after provisions → Central Government (surplus transfer)
[80:7:2] - **UPSC 2021:** Governor appointed by the Centre ✓; directions power is in the **RBI Act**, not "provisions in the Constitution" ✗; Governor draws power from the RBI Act ✓ → **1 and 3 only**.
[80:7:3] - **Finance Commission** is formed by the President under **Article 280** (not an RBI body).
[80:7:4] # Income and surplus
[80:7:5] - Income: **interest on GoI securities and profit from buying/selling Government bonds (OMO)**, **interest and gains on foreign currency assets (buying/selling forex)**, interest on loans to Governments and banks, fees/commission.
[80:7:6] - **Not income:** printing and distributing notes (a **cost** – currency printing is an expense), pension fund management (PFRDA), lending to private companies, income tax → **UPSC 2025: 1 and 2 only** (official key).
[80:7:7] - **Bimal Jalan Committee** (Economic Capital Framework, 2018-19): separated **realised equity from revaluation balances**; **Contingent Risk Buffer 5.5–6.5%** → revised **4.5–7.5%** (2025).
[80:7:8] - Surplus **FY 2025-26: record ₹2.86 lakh crore**, 6.7% above FY25.
[80:7:9] # Developmental role
[80:7:10] - RBI helped set up **IDBI, NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank and NHB** (developmental role; ownership later moved to the Government – RBI sold its NABARD stake to GoI). But the **EXIM Bank** (Jan 1982) was **established by the Government of India** under the EXIM Bank Act, 1981 – "who established EXIM Bank?" → **GoI**, not RBI.
[80:7:11] - SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA are separate regulators, not RBI creations.
[80:7:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.42 (EXIM Bank 1982, RBI sold NABARD stake); app notes 3:80 sub 6-8 (Sections 7, 30, 47; ECF and CRB; FY26 surplus; developmental role); pw.live/upsc/exams/official-upsc-answer-key-wrong (UPSC 2025 official key: 1 and 2 only; printing = expenditure)

  x: Both are true: the RBI is the lender of last resort because it gives banks emergency liquidity when no one else will. R explains A.

  Payment systems – Management of foreign exchange reserves | Banker to Government – Oversight of payment systems | Forex management – Public debt management | *Controller of credit – Controls money and credit through monetary policy
  x: As controller of credit the RBI runs monetary policy. As banker to Government it handles transactions and public debt; it also manages forex reserves and oversees payment systems.

=== NOTES 3:81 | Money Supply – M0 to M4, High-powered Money, Money Multiplier, Velocity
## SUB 0 | Money – Functions, Kinds and Key Terms
[81:0:0] TABLE head: Class | Functions of money
  [81:0:0.0] Primary | Medium of exchange; measure of value (unit of account)
  [81:0:0.1] Secondary | Store of value; standard of deferred payments; transfer of value
  [81:0:0.2] Contingent | Basis of credit; distribution of national income; giving liquidity
[81:0:1] - **Not a function:** **production of goods** (APPSC).
[81:0:2] # Kinds of money
[81:0:3] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [81:0:3.0] Fiat money | Notes and coins with no intrinsic value; money by government order; also legal tender
  [81:0:3.1] Legal tender | Money a creditor is under compulsion to accept in settlement of claims (UPSC 2018); RBI notes unlimited, coins limited legal tender
  [81:0:3.2] Commodity money | Money with intrinsic value (gold, silver); a paper note is not commodity money
  [81:0:3.3] Near money | Liquid assets that cannot directly pay: bills of exchange, time deposits, T-bills, bonds near redemption, savings certificates
  [81:0:3.4] Plastic money | Credit cards (and debit/prepaid cards), mainly issued by banks; used in place of cash but not legal tender
  [81:0:3.5] Cheque | Bank (credit) money – an alternative to cash; can be refused, so not legal tender
  [81:0:3.6] Hard / soft money | Hard = backed by gold or credible assets; soft = paper backed by government bonds
  [81:0:3.7] Bank money / cash | Bank money = secondary money; cash = high-powered money
  [81:0:3.8] Token coin | Face value higher than metal value (rupee coin)
[81:0:4] - **Digital Rupee** = legal tender under the RBI Act, amended by the **Finance Act 2022**; not every highly liquid asset is legal tender.
[81:0:5] # Key terms
[81:0:6] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [81:0:6.0] Seigniorage | Face value minus cost of producing currency = issuer's (central bank's) profit from issuing notes; a ₹500 note costs about ₹4 – not a tax
  [81:0:6.1] Gresham's Law | Bad money drives good money out: good (full-value) coins are hoarded, melted and exported; applies to metallic coins
  [81:0:6.2] Velocity | Average number of times a unit of money changes hands in a period; ₹10 used twice = ₹20 of transactions
  [81:0:6.3] Required Reserve Ratio | Fixed percentage of deposits every bank must keep as reserves
[81:0:7] - **Money supply** = **currency + deposit money** (deposits of the public with banks).
[81:0:8] - **Small coins** are phased out when their **production cost exceeds face value**.
[81:0:9] - **Currency expansion** → value of money falls → **higher prices**.
[81:0:10] - **Money supply is NOT part of a country's wealth** (mines, dams, livestock are).
[81:0:11] > Traps: plastic money = credit card, not a coated note; seigniorage = profit, not a tax; Gresham = good money hoarded, melted AND exported.
[81:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 05 p.1-2; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.16 (seigniorage), 04 p.3; OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 p.82 (legal tender, cheques); Ramesh Singh 10th ed. Glossary (Gresham's Law, commodity money, velocity); app notes 3:81 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Demonetisation and Currency Issue
[81:1:0] TABLE head: Year | Notes withdrawn | How
  [81:1:0.0] January 1946 | ₹1,000 and ₹10,000 | By ordinance
  [81:1:0.1] 16 January 1978 | ₹1,000, ₹5,000, ₹10,000 | High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act, 1978 – PM Morarji Desai
  [81:1:0.2] 8 November 2016 | ₹500 and ₹1,000 (Mahatma Gandhi series) | Announced by the PM on the night of 8 Nov, effective midnight; new ₹500 and ₹2,000 issued
[81:1:1] - **Legal basis:** **Section 26(2), RBI Act 1934** (withdrawal of legal tender), on the recommendation of RBI's **Central Board** – not PMLA or the Banking Regulation Act.
[81:1:2] - **Aims (Economic Survey 2016-17):** curb **corruption**, **counterfeiting**, use of high-denomination notes for **terrorist activities**, and accumulation of **black money**. Digital payments was a later, added aim.
[81:1:3] - **Size:** SBNs were nearly **86%** of the value of notes in circulation on 8 Nov 2016 (RBI Annual Report 2016-17).
[81:1:4] - **Returned:** RBI AR 2016-17 – ₹15.28 of ₹15.44 lakh crore = **98.96%** (to 30 June 2017); final, RBI AR 2017-18 – ₹15.31 of ₹15.42 lakh crore = **99.3%**.
[81:1:5] - **₹2,000 notes:** **50.2%** of the value of banknotes in circulation at end-March 2017 (RBI AR 2016-17); withdrawn **May 2023**, still legal tender.
[81:1:6] - **Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017:** after the grace period a person may hold **not more than 10 notes** (any denomination), or 25 for study/research/numismatics; fine up to ₹10,000 or five times the face value.
[81:1:7] - **Paradox noticed:** the cash crunch cut spending – the **paradox of thrift** (APPSC G2 Mains 2019).
[81:1:8] - SC upheld the 2016 move **4:1** (2023). **FICN**: NCRB Crime in India 2024 → **₹54.61 crore** fake currency seized.
[81:1:9] - **Abroad – Venezuela (Dec 2016):** Maduro withdrew the **100-bolivar** note, then **backtracked** after protests and cash shortages.
[81:1:10] # Issuing authority
[81:1:11] TABLE head: Item | Issued by
  [81:1:11.0] ₹1 note and all coins | Government of India (Ministry of Finance; ₹1 note signed by the Finance Secretary)
  [81:1:11.1] Other notes | RBI (Sec 22, RBI Act)
[81:1:12] - **Minimum Reserve System** (since 1956-57): ₹200 crore of gold and forex, of which **₹115 crore gold**.
[81:1:13] > NextGen 05 p.3 lists the 1978 notes as ₹500, ₹1,000 and ₹10,000 – the Act covered ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000.
[81:1:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 05 p.2-3, p.11; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.4; RBI Annual Report 2016-17 (rbi.org.in AnnualReportPublications Id=1208); zeenews.india.com (RBI AR 2016-17: 15.28 of 15.44 lakh crore); scroll.in/latest/892345 (RBI AR 2017-18: 99.3%); Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act 2017 s.5 (thc.nic.in); theprint.in (1946, 1978 notes); app notes 3:81 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Monetary Aggregates M1 to M4 and Liquidity Aggregates
[81:2:0] TABLE head: Aggregate | Components | Type
  [81:2:0.0] M1 | Currency with public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBI (NCERT: CU + DD) | Narrow money, most liquid
  [81:2:0.1] M2 | M1 + post office savings bank deposits | Narrow
  [81:2:0.2] M3 | M1 + time deposits with banks | Broad money ("aggregate monetary resources")
  [81:2:0.3] M4 | M3 + all post office deposits (excluding NSCs) | Broad, least liquid
[81:2:1] - **Second Working Group on Money Supply (1977)** → RBI publishes M1–M4 besides Reserve Money.
[81:2:2] - **M3** = most commonly used broad money = **currency with public + demand deposits + time deposits + other deposits with RBI** (all four).
[81:2:3] - **M3 − M1 = time deposits**; time deposits are **not in M1**; M3 = M1 (not M2) + time deposits.
[81:2:4] - **Liquidity order:** M1 > M2 > M3 > M4; assets: **currency > demand deposits > savings deposits > time deposits** (4-1-3-2).
[81:2:5] - **Highly liquid asset** = converted into cash in a very short time with little loss of value.
[81:2:6] - **Banks' liabilities:** deposits are the main liability; **time deposits** = the largest component, far above demand deposits.
[81:2:7] # New aggregates (1998)
[81:2:8] - **Third Working Group** (1998), chaired by **Y. V. Reddy**: residency-based **NM0–NM3** (separate short-term and long-term deposits).
[81:2:9] - **L1, L2, L3** = **liquidity aggregates**: add post-office deposits, term money and CDs of FIs, NBFC public deposits.
[81:2:10] > APPSC repeats: L1-L3 = liquidity aggregates; M1 = narrow money; M3 components; liquidity order.
[81:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 04 p.11-12; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.20, 04 p.3-4, p.40; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #38 p.56-57; OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 p.82-83; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. ch.12 p.12.30-12.31; app notes 3:81 sub 5
[81:2:12] - **Demand deposits** can be withdrawn instantly; **time deposits** are locked for a fixed period and are the least liquid.
## SUB 3 | Money Multiplier and Credit Creation
[81:3:0] - **Money multiplier = money supply ÷ reserve money (M3 ÷ M0)**; m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr).
[81:3:1] - 10% reserves, no leakages: m = 1/0.10 = **10**; ₹100 supports about **₹1,000** of deposits.
[81:3:2] - **Credit creation:** banks lend beyond their cash; **loans exceeding deposits = credit creation**; capacity depends on **cash reserves** (strictly, a bank lends out its **excess reserves**).
[81:3:3] - **Interbank transfer** to a bank brings it **reserves**, raising its lending potential.
[81:3:4] TABLE head: Money creator | Creates
  [81:3:4.0] RBI | Reserve money (notes)
  [81:3:4.1] Government | Coins and ₹1 note
  [81:3:4.2] Commercial banks | Deposit money by lending beyond CRR/SLR
[81:3:5] # What moves the multiplier and money supply
[81:3:6] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [81:3:6.0] Higher CRR, SLR or cash preference (cdr) | Lower multiplier, less credit creation
  [81:3:6.1] Stronger banking habit | Higher multiplier (UPSC 2019, 2021)
  [81:3:6.2] RBI buys G-secs from the public; Government borrows from RBI | Money supply rises (UPSC 2012: 1 and 3)
  [81:3:6.3] RBI sells G-secs; public deposits currency in banks | Falls / no rise
  [81:3:6.4] Cash withdrawal ₹1 lakh from a demand deposit | Unchanged (DD −₹1 lakh, currency +₹1 lakh) (UPSC 2020)
[81:3:7] - **Raising SLR** locks more funds in liquid assets (kept by the bank itself; CRR is kept with RBI) → fewer loanable funds; an SLR cut frees funds.
[81:3:8] - **CRR increase** → banks have less to lend.
[81:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 04 p.10-11; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.47; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #38 p.56, #41 p.61; OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 p.82-86; app notes 3:81 sub 6
## SUB 4 | Indian Currency History
[81:4:0] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [81:4:0.0] Late 18th century | Paper money introduced by private and state-sponsored banks: Bank of Hindostan (1770), General Bank of Bengal and Bihar (1773); then Presidency Banks
  [81:4:0.1] 1861 | Paper Currency Act: Government of (British) India gets the monopoly of note issue – "paper currency introduced by the British Government"
  [81:4:0.2] 1899 | Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act (Curzon): India on the gold standard
  [81:4:0.3] 1935 | Note issue transferred to RBI (1 April 1935)
  [81:4:0.4] 1 April 1957 | Decimal coinage (Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955); ₹1 = 100 naye paise
  [81:4:0.5] 1 June 1964 | "Naya" dropped – naya paisa became paisa
[81:4:1] - **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** issued **token copper/brass coins**, not paper currency.
[81:4:2] ~~ Sources: RBI Paper Money – Early Issues (rbi.org.in/Scripts/pm_earlyissues.aspx); RBI British India issues (rbi.org.in/Scripts/pm_britishindia.aspx); RBI Republic India Coinage (rbi.org.in); app notes 3:81 sub 2
## SUB 5 | Demand for Money, Interest and Monetary Theories
[81:5:0] TABLE head: Theory | Economist
  [81:5:0.0] Quantity theory MV = PT | Irving Fisher
  [81:5:0.1] Cash-balance M = kPY (k = 1/V) | Marshall, Pigou (Cambridge)
  [81:5:0.2] Liquidity preference (transactions, precautionary, speculative motives) | J. M. Keynes
  [81:5:0.3] Inventory model (square-root rule) | Baumol (1952), Tobin (1956)
  [81:5:0.4] Modern quantity theory, monetarism | Milton Friedman
  [81:5:0.5] IS-LM model | J. R. Hicks
  [81:5:0.6] Pure Monetary Theory of Trade Cycle | R. G. Hawtrey
  [81:5:0.7] Austrian cycle theory; free-market economics | Friedrich Hayek
  [81:5:0.8] Effective demand; paradox of thrift popularised | Keynes
[81:5:1] - Demand for money is **positively** related to **income** (more transactions); at **higher interest rates** money demand falls; speculative demand varies **inversely** with interest.
[81:5:2] - **Money supply fixed + money demand rises → interest rate rises** (UPSC 2013); demand falls → rate falls.
[81:5:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.53, p.96-97; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.1; OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 (demand for money); app notes 3:81 sub 7
## SUB 6 | High-powered Money (Reserve Money, M0)
[81:6:0] - Names: **reserve money, monetary base, base money, central bank money** = **M0** – the "most important indicator"; **basis of credit creation**.
[81:6:1] - **H = currency held by the public + cash reserves of banks (with themselves and with RBI) + other deposits with RBI**; no time deposits, no post-office deposits, no forex held by persons.
[81:6:2] TABLE head: Side | Components
  [81:6:2.0] Uses side | Currency with public + banks' cash in hand + bankers' deposits with RBI (legal reserves) + other deposits with RBI
  [81:6:2.1] Sources side | Net RBI credit to Government + RBI credit to banks and commercial sector + net forex assets of RBI + Government's currency liabilities − net non-monetary liabilities of RBI
[81:6:3] - **Currency in circulation** = notes + rupee coins + small coins (held by public + banks' cash in hand).
[81:6:4] - **"Other" deposits with RBI**: quasi-government and financial institutions, foreign central banks and governments, international agencies such as the **IMF**.
[81:6:5] > High-powered money = M0, not M2 (an old APPSC key gave M2).
[81:6:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 04 p.7-8, p.12; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.19-20, 04 p.1, p.40; Ramesh Singh 10th ed. ch.12 p.12.31; app notes 3:81 sub 4
## SUB 7 | e-Rupee (CBDC) and Current Data
[81:7:0] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [81:7:0.0] Pilots | Wholesale Nov 2022; retail 1 Dec 2022
  [81:7:0.1] Nature | Sovereign currency issued by RBI in alignment with monetary policy; liability on RBI's balance sheet (UPI money = bank liability); legal tender
  [81:7:0.2] Convertibility | Freely convertible against commercial bank money and cash, 1:1
  [81:7:0.3] Interest | Non-interest bearing, like cash; not inflation-proof
  [81:7:0.4] Form | Same denominations as paper currency and coins; distributed through banks; P2P and P2M
  [81:7:0.5] Uses | Offline payments, programmable for DBT, UAE cross-border pilot; not a mandatory replacement of bank deposits
  [81:7:0.6] 2026 | Digital Food Currency pilot in Puducherry
[81:7:1] - **31 Dec 2025**: money multiplier **6.21**; M3 grew 12.1%, M0 2.9% (Economic Survey 2025-26).
[81:7:2] - **CRR cut 100 bps to 3.0%** of NDTL → about **₹2.5 lakh crore** released (Dec 2025).
[81:7:3] - Notes in circulation (May 2026): **174 billion** notes worth over ₹42.12 lakh crore.

=== NOTES 3:82 | Monetary Policy – Objectives, Instruments (crr, Slr, Repo, Reverse Repo, Msf, Omo, Laf), Transmission
## SUB 0 | CRR and SLR – Reserve Ratios
[82:0:0] # Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)
[82:0:1] - **CRR = Cash Reserve Ratio:** the share of a bank's **Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)** that it must keep as **cash balances with the RBI** (CDS 2020; APPSC AEE 2008).
[82:0:2] - **"Required reserve ratio"** = the **certain percentage of deposits every bank must keep as reserves** = **CRR** (APPSC Degree Lecturers 2023).
[82:0:3] - CRR is **fixed by the RBI (the central bank)**, not the Finance Ministry or the market (APPSC G2 2011); governed by **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934**; **no floor or ceiling** since 2006.
[82:0:4] - Banks get **no interest** on CRR balances; CRR is in **cash only**.
[82:0:5] - **Raising CRR:** commercial banks have **less money to lend** (not the RBI or the Union Government) → **liquidity falls**, **credit creation falls** → helps control inflation (UPSC 2010 ×4; UPPSC 2004, 2010; CGPSC 2017).
[82:0:6]   - APPSC G1: a CRR hike causes **fall in money circulation** and **low demand for goods and services** (I and II); it does **NOT** raise purchasing power or the banks' lending capacity.
[82:0:7] - **Lowering CRR:** **credit creation increases** (APPSC G2 2017); banks get **higher leverage to liquidity** and the economy **may see increased investment** (NextGen: lower CRR "helps banks provide loans … for investment purposes" and "boosts the growth rate").
[82:0:8] - **Temporary I-CRR (Aug 2023):** **10%** on the increase in NDTL (19 May–28 Jul 2023), announced **10 Aug 2023**, effective fortnight from 12 Aug; **impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore**; released in phases (9 Sep, 23 Sep, 7 Oct 2023) (APPSC G2 Mains 2025: both statements correct).
[82:0:9] - CRR applies to the **whole NDTL**; the I-CRR applied only to the **incremental deposit base** (not to "new borrowers") (APPSC G1 2024).
[82:0:10] # Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
[82:0:11] - **SLR:** minimum share of NDTL a bank keeps **with itself** in liquid assets **before lending** – **cash, gold and unencumbered approved/Government securities (G-secs, T-bills, SDLs)**; **not priority-sector loans** (APPSC G1 2023: I, II and III).
[82:0:12] - **SLR = mechanism by which commercial banks provide credit to the Government** (they buy G-secs to meet it) (UPSC 2010 ×3).
[82:0:13] - Older wording "ratio between cash in hand and total assets" = **SLR** (UPSC 1998; UPPSC 2007) – strictly SLR is liquid assets to NDTL.
[82:0:14] - Governed by **Section 24, Banking Regulation Act, 1949**; range **0%–40% of NDTL**; the **25% floor** was removed by the **BR (Amendment) Act, 2007**; **MSS securities count** towards SLR.
[82:0:15] - **Shortfall penalty:** **bank rate + 3%**, then **bank rate + 5%** if it continues.
[82:0:16] - **SLR cut of 50 bps** → more lendable funds → **scheduled commercial banks may cut lending rates** (UPSC 2015 ×2) – not "GDP up drastically" or "liquidity down".
[82:0:17] - **Raise SLR to fight inflation; cut SLR for growth.**
[82:0:18] # Trend
[82:0:19] TABLE head: Date | SLR | CRR
  [82:0:19.0] 1991-92 | 38.5% | 15%
  [82:0:19.1] Since reforms | Both reduced (Narasimham Committee) | Both reduced
  [82:0:19.2] 5 Jan 2019 | 19.25% (Dec 2018 review: −25 bps every quarter) | 4%
  [82:0:19.3] 11 Apr 2020 | 18% | 3% (Mar 2020)
  [82:0:19.4] 2026 (now) | 18% | 3% (cut 4% → 3% in 2025, ~₹2.5 lakh crore released)
[82:0:20] # CRR vs SLR
[82:0:21] TABLE head: Basis | CRR | SLR
  [82:0:21.0] Kept | With RBI | By the bank itself
  [82:0:21.1] Form | Cash only | Cash, gold, approved securities
  [82:0:21.2] Return | No interest | Earns interest on G-secs
  [82:0:21.3] Law | Sec 42, RBI Act 1934 | Sec 24, BR Act 1949
[82:0:22] > Trap: SLR "19.25%" (APPSC G2, 2019 review) is now 18%; "required reserve ratio" = CRR, not SLR.
[82:0:23] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 06 p.11-12 (CRR, effect of raising/lowering); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.1-2 (SLR assets, 0-40%, 38.5%, Narasimham, credit to Govt, penalty); Rocket Indian Economy p.12, p.61 (CRR vs SLR, SLR before lending); RBI notification 5 Dec 2018 on SLR (rbi.org.in NotificationUser Id=11427); RBI Annual Report 2023-24 ch. III para III.18 (I-CRR ₹1.1 lakh crore); app notes 3:82 sub 4, 6
## SUB 1 | Policy Rates – Repo, Reverse Repo, Bank Rate, MSF and LAF
[82:1:0] # Definitions
[82:1:1] TABLE head: Rate | Who lends to whom | Key point
  [82:1:1.0] Repo | RBI lends to banks short term (overnight) against G-secs (repurchase agreement) | Principal policy rate; injects liquidity, regulates money supply
  [82:1:1.1] Reverse repo | Banks lend to / park funds with RBI | Absorbs surplus liquidity; always below repo
  [82:1:1.2] Bank Rate | RBI's official / discount rate for long-term loans; rediscounts bills of exchange | Penal rates linked to it; signal rate
  [82:1:1.3] MSF | Banks borrow overnight from RBI in emergency, dipping into SLR | Contains volatility in the overnight inter-bank rate; ceiling of corridor
  [82:1:1.4] SDF | Banks park surplus with RBI without collateral | Floor of corridor (since April 2022)
[82:1:2] - **Repo** = "Repurchase Option": bank sells G-secs to RBI and buys them back later; the difference is the interest – it is **not the cost of collateral** (CDS 2020) and has **nothing to do with the rupee's exchange value** (UPPSC 1998: "None of the above").
[82:1:3] - **Rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks / at which banks borrow from RBI = Repo rate** (UPPSC 2005, 2008, 2013; SI 2019; APPSC G2; AP recruitment); comes under **monetary policy**; used **to regulate liquidity** (APPSC G2 2017).
[82:1:4] - **Rate at which banks lend to / park funds with RBI = Reverse repo** (UPPSC 2008 ×2).
[82:1:5] - **Bank Rate** = rate at which **RBI discounts / rediscounts bills of exchange** (UPSC 1995; Degree Lecturers 2017); = **official rate of interest charged by the central bank** (State PSC).
[82:1:6] - **BPSC 2015 trap:** "Bank Rate = short-term" and "Repo = long-term" are **both wrong** (swapped): Bank Rate is long-term, repo short-term.
[82:1:7] - **LAF (June 2000):** the window through which banks **borrow via repos** and **lend via reverse repos** – "borrowing through repurchase agreements" = **LAF** (APPSC G2).
[82:1:8] - **MSF (May 2011):** began at repo + **100 bps**, up to **1% of NDTL**; now repo + **25 bps**, up to **2%** of NDTL; aligned with Bank Rate in **Feb 2012**; minimum ₹1 crore.
[82:1:9] - **MSF rate and NDTL** are terms of **banking operations** (UPSC 2014 ×2).
[82:1:10] - **LAF access:** scheduled commercial banks and **standalone Primary Dealers** (registered as NBFCs); other NBFCs (HFCs, MFIs, asset-finance cos) cannot use it.
[82:1:11] - **Repo − reverse repo gap:** **1.00 percentage point** in June 2010 – June 2011 (from Sep 2010); from **May 2011** only repo is fixed and reverse repo set **100 bps below** it.
[82:1:12] # The corridor
[82:1:13] TABLE head: Date | SDF (floor) | Repo | MSF = Bank Rate (ceiling) | Stance
  [82:1:13.0] 5 Aug 2026 | 5.00% | 5.25% (unanimous hold) | 5.50% | Neutral
  [82:1:13.1] 7 Oct 2026 | 5.25% | 5.50% (+25 bps, unanimous) | 5.75% | Calibrated tightening
[82:1:14] - Corridor width **50 bps**: SDF = repo − 25 bps; MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 25 bps. **Fixed-rate reverse repo 3.35%** (May 2026), used at RBI's discretion since SDF.
[82:1:15] - **SDF** (proposed 2015, enabled by **Budget 2018-19**, began **April 2022**): absorbs surplus liquidity **without collateral** – the only collateral-free absorption tool (APPSC G2).
[82:1:16] # Stances
[82:1:17] TABLE head: Stance | Meaning
  [82:1:17.0] Accommodative | Supports growth; cuts likely
  [82:1:17.1] Neutral | Either way, data-dependent
  [82:1:17.2] Calibrated tightening | No cuts; hikes measured, not at every meeting
  [82:1:17.3] Hawkish / Dovish | Worried about inflation, tightens / worried about growth, easing bias
[82:1:18] - Path: neutral → accommodative (Apr 2025) → **neutral (June 2025)**, kept through Aug 2026 → **calibrated tightening (Oct 2026)**.
[82:1:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 06 p.6-10 (bank rate, LAF, MSF, repo, reverse repo); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.26-28 (bank rate long term; repo short term; repo = reverse repo + 1%); Rocket Indian Economy p.12, p.60, p.62; RBI MPC minutes 5-7 Oct 2026 (rbi.org.in press release prid=63839); app notes 3:82 sub 3; houseofupsc.com UPSC 2024 PYQ page (PD access)
## SUB 2 | OMO, Sterilisation and Liquidity Management
[82:2:0] # Open Market Operations
[82:2:1] - **OMO** = **purchase and sale of Government securities (and T-bills) by the RBI** (UPSC 2013; UPPSC 2010 ×2; NDA 2012) – "trading in securities", not forex auctions or gold.
[82:2:2] - OMO relates to **both sale and purchase** of G-secs (APPSC G2 2011); RBI deals **through banks, not directly with the public**.
[82:2:3] - **Sell G-secs → absorbs liquidity** (fights inflation); **buy G-secs → injects liquidity**, money supply up, **interest rates fall** (OPSC 2018: "to lower interest rates, purchase securities").
[82:2:4] - OMO is a **quantitative** tool and "**a part of credit policy**"; main tool for **durable** liquidity.
[82:2:5] - **Money supply rises** with **central-bank purchase of G-secs from the public** and **Government borrowing from the central bank** (UPSC 2012: I and III); depositing currency in banks only shifts money; sale of G-secs reduces it.
[82:2:6] # Sterilisation
[82:2:7] - **Sterilisation** = offsetting the rupee liquidity created by forex inflows (RBI buying dollars) by **selling G-secs through OMO / MSS** or VRRR – part of sterilisation = **conducting OMOs** (UPSC 2023 ×2).
[82:2:8] - **MSS (April 2004):** T-bills/dated securities issued to withdraw excess liquidity; proceeds in a **separate account the Government cannot spend**.
[82:2:9] # Other liquidity tools
[82:2:10] TABLE head: Tool | Feature
  [82:2:10.0] VRR / VRRR | Auction-based repo / reverse repo; VRRR absorbs for longer than overnight SDF
  [82:2:10.1] Fine-tuning operations | Short VRR/VRRR auctions to keep liquidity in line with the monetary policy stance – 49 in FY24 (APPSC G2 Mains 2025)
  [82:2:10.2] LTRO (2020) | 1–3 year funds at repo against G-secs
  [82:2:10.3] USD/INR buy-sell swap | Injects rupees without changing RBI's balance-sheet size ($5 bn, 3-year, Dec 2025)
[82:2:11] - **Surplus liquidity** pulls money-market rates **below repo** and speeds transmission; 4 Sep 2026: RBI absorbed **₹6.02 lakh crore** through two 3-day VRRRs.
[82:2:12] - **G-sec yields** are influenced by **US Fed actions, RBI actions and domestic inflation and short-term rates** – all three (UPSC 2021).
[82:2:13] > UPSC 2024 (official key: all three): NBFCs via Primary Dealers can use LAF; **FIIs/FPIs can hold G-secs**; **stock exchanges can run separate debt platforms**.
[82:2:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 06 p.10-11 (OMO, through banks, part of credit policy); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.41 (MSS April 2004); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 06 p.9 (LTRO); RBI Annual Report 2023-24 ch. III (fine-tuning VRR operations; the FY24 count of 49 from the APPSC G2 2025 paper); app notes 3:82 sub 6, 8
## SUB 3 | Quantitative vs Qualitative Instruments
[82:3:0] TABLE head: Basis | Quantitative (general) | Qualitative (selective)
  [82:3:0.0] Aim | Volume and cost of total credit / money supply | Direction of credit among borrowers and sectors
  [82:3:0.1] Other name | Traditional methods | Selective credit control
  [82:3:0.2] Tools | Bank rate, repo, reverse repo, OMO, CRR, SLR (variable reserve ratios) | Margin requirements, moral suasion, rationing of credit, consumer-credit regulation, direct action, differential interest rates, guidelines
[82:3:1] - **Not selective / not qualitative:** **variable (cash) reserve ratios** (UPSC 1995 ×2; NDA 2014) and **Bank Rate policy** (APPSC G1).
[82:3:2] - **Not quantitative:** **rationing of credit** (UPPSC 2017). **OMO** = quantitative (UPPSC 2017).
[82:3:3] - **Selective controls of RBI:** **margin requirements and moral suasion** – not CRR/SLR (CDS 2017).
[82:3:4] - **Margin** = value of security − loan; a **higher margin = smaller loan** against the same security.
[82:3:5] - **Moral suasion:** persuasion – closed-door meetings, appeals, warnings – not force.
[82:3:6] - **Not a credit-control method:** **devaluation of the rupee** (exchange-rate step).
[82:3:7] - **Components of monetary policy:** **Bank rate and OMO** – **public debt and public revenue are fiscal** (UPSC 2015; CDS 2017).
[82:3:8] - **Variable reserve ratios and OMO** are means of **monetary policy** (UPSC 1993).
[82:3:9] TABLE head: Policy | Instrument (APPSC G2 Mains 2025 match)
  [82:3:9.0] Monetary policy | Bank rate
  [82:3:9.1] Trade policy | Imports and exports
  [82:3:9.2] Credit policy | Margin
  [82:3:9.3] Fiscal policy | Tax rate
[82:3:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 06 p.4, p.6 (quantitative vs qualitative table); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.2-3 (margin, consumer credit, rationing, moral suasion, direct action); Rocket Indian Economy p.60, p.76; app notes 3:82 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Tool → Effect: Dear vs Cheap Money
[82:4:0] TABLE head: Tool | Control inflation (dear, tight, contractionary) | Boost growth (cheap, easy, expansionary)
  [82:4:0.0] CRR, SLR | Raise | Cut
  [82:4:0.1] Repo, reverse repo, Bank Rate, MSF | Raise | Cut
  [82:4:0.2] OMO | Sell G-secs | Buy G-secs
[82:4:1] - **'Dear money'** = **high rate of interest**, money hard to borrow (APPSC AEE 2011); cheap money = low rates.
[82:4:2] - **Inflation rising steadily** → central bank **increases the repo rate** (SSC 2020).
[82:4:3] - **Anti-inflation set:** **raise Bank Rate, CRR and SLR** – **buying** G-secs is expansionary (UPPSC RO 2016: 1, 2 and 3).
[82:4:4] - **Lowering Bank Rate** → **more liquidity** (UPSC 2011); it is **not a remedy for inflation** (APSLPRB 2012) – so CPI inflation **rises if Bank Rate is decreased** (RAS 2016 key).
[82:4:5] - **Increase in Bank Rate** = **tight (dear) money policy** (UPSC 2013).
[82:4:6] - **Expansionist policy would NOT increase the MSF rate**; it would cut SLR, Bank Rate and repo (UPSC 2020: only II).
[82:4:7] - **Interest-rate cut** → **higher investment expenditure** (UPSC 2014 ×2) – not lower consumption, more tax or more savings.
[82:4:8] - CRR/SLR cut → more lendable funds and a higher **money multiplier**; policy rates regulate the **capacity for credit creation**.
[82:4:9] - Monetary tools act on **demand**; supply-driven food inflation needs **buffer stocks, duty cuts, farm reform**.
[82:4:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 06 p.6-7 (dear vs cheap money, bank rate and inflation); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.26-27 (dear money policy); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 06 p.146 ('dear money' = higher interest rates); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.2 (instrument table); Rocket Indian Economy p.76
## SUB 5 | Objectives, Authority and Post-1991 Shifts
[82:5:0] - **Monetary policy** = macro policy on **money supply**, **framed by the RBI** (APPSC Welfare Organiser; UPPSC 2006) under the **RBI Act, 1934**; the **MPC** fixes the repo rate since 2016.
[82:5:1] - **Primary objective:** **price stability while keeping in mind growth** (MPPSC 2025; APPSC flashcard); also financial stability, exchange-rate stability.
[82:5:2] - **Not an objective:** **equitable distribution of income and assets** – a fiscal goal (UPPSC 2011).
[82:5:3] - **Fiscal vs monetary:** fiscal = Government, **taxes, spending, public debt**, direct but slow (legislative lags); monetary = RBI/MPC, indirect, quick (meets every two months). Fiscal deficit is fiscal policy.
[82:5:4] - **Post-1991 policy change:** **deregulation of interest rates** (AP recruitment).
[82:5:5] - **Post-1991 challenge:** **volatility in exchange rates** from open capital flows (not high reserves, low inflation or revenue surplus); ad hoc T-bills ended 1997 → **Ways and Means Advances**.
[82:5:6] TABLE head: Phase | Framework
  [82:5:6.0] 1985–1998 | Monetary targeting with feedback (M3; Chakravarty 1985)
  [82:5:6.1] 1998–2014/16 | Multiple indicator approach (LAF 2000, MSS 2004, MSF 2011) – dropped as opaque
  [82:5:6.2] 2016 onwards | Flexible inflation targeting (Urjit Patel Committee 2014)
[82:5:7] - Transmission obstacles: administered **small-savings rates** (Rakesh Mohan Committee 2004: align with G-sec yields), NPAs, informal credit outside RBI's reach, heavy Government borrowing (**fiscal dominance**).
[82:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 06 p.4-5 (credit control, monetary policy, inflation and growth in mind); Rocket Indian Economy p.10 (RBI conducts monetary policy); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 04 p.132 (Chakravarty Committee 1985); app notes 3:82 sub 0, 1, 9
## SUB 6 | Lending-rate Benchmarks and Transmission
[82:6:0] TABLE head: Fixed by RBI / MPC | Set by each bank | Market-determined
  [82:6:0.0] Repo, SDF, MSF, Bank Rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR | PLR/BPLR (old), Base Rate, MCLR, spread over EBLR | Call money rate (WACR), TREPS, T-bill and G-sec yields
[82:6:1] - **RBI does NOT fix the PLR** (APPSC G2 2011; UPPSC 2008).
[82:6:2] TABLE head: Benchmark | From | Key point
  [82:6:2.0] PLR | 1994 | Rate for best borrowers, set by each bank
  [82:6:2.1] Base Rate | 1 July 2010 (replaced BPLR) | Minimum (floor) rate below which banks may not lend; average cost of funds
  [82:6:2.2] MCLR | 1 April 2016 | Marginal cost of funds + CRR/SLR cost + operating cost + tenor premium; internal benchmark
  [82:6:2.3] EBLR | 1 Oct 2019 | New floating personal/retail and MSME loans linked to repo, 3/6-month T-bill or FBIL rate; fastest
[82:6:3] - **Base rate of interest** = the **minimum rate for all loans** (few exceptions such as DRI and staff loans); the **actual lending rate = base rate + borrower-specific charges**.
[82:6:4] - **MCLR purposes (UPSC 2016):** **transparency** in banks' lending-rate method **and** credit at rates **fair to borrowers and banks** – both; also faster transmission.
[82:6:5] - **APPSC G1 2024 statements:** CRR hike **reduces** credit creation (I ✗); I-CRR targeted **incremental deposits**, not borrowers (II ✗); **tenor premium is an MCLR component** (III ✓); MSF is an **overnight** rate **equal to** Bank Rate, not long-term or lower (IV ✗) → **only III**.
[82:6:6] - Janak Raj Internal Study Group (2017) → external benchmark; draft RBI (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026 apply from 1 April 2027.
[82:6:7] - Transmission: repo up → money-market rates up → costlier credit → lower demand → inflation cools; channels: interest rate, credit, **exchange rate (weaker rupee helps exports)**, asset price, expectations.
[82:6:8] - Repo cut **125 bps** (Feb 2025–Feb 2026, 6.50% → 5.25%); fresh-loan WALR fell about **93 bps**; MCLR loans reset periodically, EBLR loans quickly.
[82:6:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 07 p.4-5 (MCLR components incl. tenor premium, transparency, EBLR 1 Oct 2019); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 05 p.80 (Base Rate = rate below which SCBs lend no loans, floor, from 1 July 2010); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.42 (Base Rate = minimum lending rate); app notes 3:82 sub 7, 8
