## SUB 2 | Market Players and Terms – Bull, Bear, Stag, Blue Chip, Beta
[90:2:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [90:2:0.0] Bull (Tejadia) | Expects prices to rise; bull market = rising
  [90:2:0.1] Bear (Mandadia) | Expects prices of a security to fall; sells now to buy back lower
  [90:2:0.2] Stag | Buys IPO shares to sell soon after listing
  [90:2:0.3] Lame duck | A share-market term (with Bull, Bear, Stag)
  [90:2:0.4] Blue chip | Shares of large, well-established, financially sound companies giving consistent high returns
  [90:2:0.5] Beta | Measures a stock's fluctuations (systematic risk) relative to the overall market (beta 1 = moves with the market)
  [90:2:0.6] Short selling | Selling borrowed shares to buy back lower
  [90:2:0.7] Circuit breaker | Trading halt when an index or stock moves past limits
  [90:2:0.8] Sweat equity | Shares issued to employees or directors for know-how or services, often at a discount
  [90:2:0.9] Insider trading | Trading on non-public, material information – a share-market offence
[90:2:1] - **Bull and Bear** are **share-market** terms, not foreign trade, banking or manufacturing.
[90:2:2] - **Speculators:** Bull, Bear, Stag. A **broker** is a registered member who buys and sells on clients' behalf for a commission – **not a speculator** (nor a "bookie").
[90:2:3] - **Settlement:** **T+1** (one trading day after the trade); optional **T+0**.
[90:2:4] > NOT-angle: "not a speculator" / "not a bookie" → **Broker** (UP RO/ARO 2017, twice).
[90:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #55 p.81, #56 p.82, p.83 (blue chip, beta); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.33 (insider trading); Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.133 (broker), 06 p.141 (short selling); app notes 3:90 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Primary vs Secondary Market and the IPO Process
[90:3:0] TABLE head: Basis | Primary (new issue) market | Secondary market
  [90:3:0.0] Deals in | New securities (issued for the first time) | Existing securities
  [90:3:0.1] Transactions | Issuing company → investors | Investor ↔ investor
  [90:3:0.2] Examples | IPOs, FPOs, rights issues, private placement | Stock-exchange trading; trading in the gilt-edged (G-Sec) market
  [90:3:0.3] Price | Fixed by the firm | Demand and supply
  [90:3:0.4] Money goes to | The issuer | The selling investor
[90:3:1] - Transactions in the **stock exchange and the gilt-edged market** = **secondary market**; SEBI regulates both markets.
[90:3:2] - **Gilt-edged market** = market for government and semi-government securities ("of the best quality", no default risk), backed by the RBI.
[90:3:3] - **Offer for sale (OFS):** proceeds go to **selling shareholders**; only a **fresh issue** brings money to the company.
[90:3:4] TABLE head: IPO term | Meaning
  [90:3:4.0] Book building | Bids within a price band; final price set from the bids
  [90:3:4.1] Anchor investors | QIBs bidding before the issue opens, with a lock-in
  [90:3:4.2] SME IPOs | Separate platforms BSE SME and NSE Emerge (2012)
  [90:3:4.3] Listing | Within T+3 days of issue closing
  [90:3:4.4] Large-company float | Very large firms may offer only 2.75% (earlier 5%) (SEBI, Sep 2025)
  [90:3:4.5] ASBA | Application Supported by Blocked Amount (SEBI, 2008): money stays blocked in the investor's account until allotment
  [90:3:4.6] Greenshoe option | Over-allotment of usually up to 15% extra shares
[90:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 10 p.23, 11 p.2 (primary, secondary, gilt-edged); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.32; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #10 p.13; Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.132 (SME platforms), p.137, p.139 (greenshoe); app notes 3:90 sub 0, 1
## SUB 4 | Instruments – Shares, Debentures, Mutual Funds and ETFs
[90:4:0] TABLE head: Holder / instrument | Claim
  [90:4:0.0] Shareholders | Owners; dividends; residual claim on earnings and assets
  [90:4:0.1] Debenture holders | Creditors – debentures are long-term debt at a fixed rate of interest; paid before shareholders in liquidation
  [90:4:0.2] Mutual funds | Pooled money priced at NAV (computed at the end of each trading session); arbitrage funds keep at least 65% in equity
  [90:4:0.3] ETF | Fund traded on exchanges like a share, price changes through the day; NAV still computed daily; high liquidity and low costs
[90:4:1] - Debenture holders are **not** shareholders, debtors or directors of the company.
[90:4:2] - **ETF NOT-statement (CDS 2018):** "ETFs have **lower** liquidity and **higher** fees than mutual funds" is **wrong** – ETFs are known for low costs.
[90:4:3] - **Equity crowdfunding** is not permitted: SEBI called online platforms offering it unauthorised (2016).
[90:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 10 p.23, 11 p.1 (shares, debentures, mutual funds, NAV); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.25 (ETF); Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.65 (ETFs), p.140 (debenture holders' primacy); app notes 3:90 sub 5
## SUB 5 | Derivatives and Transaction Taxes (STT, CTT)
[90:5:0] TABLE head: Type | Meaning
  [90:5:0.0] Futures | Obligation to buy/sell at a fixed future price
  [90:5:0.1] Options | Right, not obligation: call = right to buy, put = right to sell
  [90:5:0.2] Swaps | Exchange of cash flows (fixed vs floating interest)
  [90:5:0.3] Commodity derivatives | Regulated by SEBI since the FMC merger (2015); NCDEX RAINMUMBAI = India's first weather derivative
[90:5:1] - Derivatives derive their value from an **underlying** (equity, index, interest rate, commodity); they are securities under the **SCRA, 1956**.
[90:5:2] - F&O market designed by the **L.C. Gupta (1998)** and **J.R. Varma (2002)** Committees.
[90:5:3] - Indian exchanges handled about **84%** of equity options traded worldwide (Q1 2024); SEBI: **9 in 10** option traders lost money.
[90:5:4] - **STT** (Securities Transaction Tax, 2004) on exchange trades; **Budget 2026-27**: futures **0.02% → 0.05%**, options **0.10% → 0.15%** – aim: **curb speculation**.
[90:5:5] - **Commodity Transaction Tax (CTT):** introduced in the **Union Budget 2013-14**, **0.01%** on non-agricultural commodity futures.
[90:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 10 p.23 (derivatives), 09 p.3 (STT 2004); Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.140-141 (derivatives, SCRA), p.208 (CTT 2013-14, 0.01%); Union Budget 2026-27 Speech (STT); app notes 3:90 sub 6

=== NOTES 3:91 | Sebi – Establishment, Powers and Functions; Investor Protection and Market Regulation
## SUB 0 | SEBI – Establishment, Statutory Status and Board
[91:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [91:0:0.0] Full form | Securities and Exchange Board of India
  [91:0:0.1] Set up (non-statutory) | 12 April 1988, by a government resolution
  [91:0:0.2] Statutory powers | 30 January 1992 (ordinance) under the SEBI Act, 1992 (Act passed April 1992); SEBI dates its statutory establishment to 12 April 1992
  [91:0:0.3] Recommended by | Narasimham Committee (1991) – statutory status for SEBI, abolition of the Controller of Capital Issues
  [91:0:0.4] Took over from | Controller of Capital Issues
  [91:0:0.5] Headquarters | Mumbai (regional offices New Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Ahmedabad)
  [91:0:0.6] Ministry | Ministry of Finance
  [91:0:0.7] Chairperson | Tuhin Kanta Pandey (from March 2025; in office 2026)
  [91:0:0.8] Role | Main regulator of the capital and securities (stock) market
[91:0:1] - **"SEBI was established in …"**: most books say **1988** (non-statutory); the statutory body, as SEBI itself puts it, was established in **1992** – read the options and the exam key (APPRB 2011 key: 1992).
[91:0:2] - **Parent law:** the **SEBI Act, 1992**, not the SCRA, 1956.
[91:0:3] - **SEBI Act Preamble:** **investor protection**, **development** and **regulation** of the securities market; bank lending rates are the RBI's job.
[91:0:4] - **Why statutory powers:** to **prevent (recurrence of) scams** in the capital market (Harshad Mehta, 1992) – the Government gave regulatory powers to **SEBI**, not RBI, SBI or ICICI.
[91:0:5] - **Board (SEBI Act, Sec. 4):** **Chairman** + **2** members from the **Finance and Law** ministries + **1** from the **RBI** + **5** other members, of whom **at least 3 are whole-time**.
[91:0:6] - **Functions:** registering intermediaries, levying fees, **investor education**, inspection and audit of exchanges and intermediaries.
[91:0:7] TABLE head: Chronology | Year
  [91:0:7.0] SEBI non-statutory | 1988
  [91:0:7.1] SEBI statutory (SEBI Act) | 1992
  [91:0:7.2] NSE set up / recognised | Nov 1992 / April 1993
  [91:0:7.3] SAT set up | 1995
  [91:0:7.4] FMC merged into SEBI | 2015
[91:0:8] - ⚠ The Chakravarty Committee (monetary system), Chelliah Committee (tax reform) and Tendulkar Committee (poverty) had nothing to do with SEBI.
[91:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 11 p.3 (12 Apr 1988; statutory 30 Jan 1992; autonomous 12 Apr 1992; HQ, regional offices); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #10 p.13, #55 p.81; Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.134 (board, functions); testbook.com WBCS 2017 solution (Narasimham Committee); app notes 3:91 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Regulator Map, SEBI's Regulated Entities and Mutual Funds
[91:1:0] TABLE head: Body | Sector
  [91:1:0.0] SEBI | Capital and securities market – stock exchanges, brokers, depositories, mutual funds, credit rating agencies
  [91:1:0.1] RBI | Money and banking system; government securities; money-market, G-Sec and forex CCPs
  [91:1:0.2] NABARD | Agricultural credit
  [91:1:0.3] IRDAI | Insurance
  [91:1:0.4] PFRDA | Pensions
  [91:1:0.5] IFSCA | Exchanges in GIFT City IFSC
[91:1:1] - **Entities SEBI regulates:**
[91:1:2] TABLE head: Regulated by SEBI | Notes
  [91:1:2.0] Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs) – stock exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories | NSE, BSE; NSDL, CDSL
  [91:1:2.1] Brokers, merchant bankers, registrars, investment advisers | SEBI Stock Brokers Regulations 2026 replaced the 1992 rules
  [91:1:2.2] Mutual funds, AIFs, FPIs | FPIs through the SWAFAT-FI single window (2025)
  [91:1:2.3] REITs, InvITs | 5 listed REITs (2026)
  [91:1:2.4] Credit rating agencies | SEBI, not RBI: CRISIL (1987, first) → ICRA (1991) → CARE (1993)
  [91:1:2.5] Commodity derivatives | Since the FMC merger (2015)
[91:1:3] - FEMA (foreign exchange) and the MRTP Act do not control the share market; **SEBI** does.
[91:1:4] - **Self Regulatory Organisations (SROs):** bodies such as stock exchanges that regulate their own members under SEBI's oversight.
[91:1:5] TABLE head: Year | Mutual fund milestone
  [91:1:5.0] 1964 | UTI – India's first mutual fund (1 Feb 1964, under the UTI Act, 1963)
  [91:1:5.1] 1987 | Non-UTI public-sector mutual funds (SBI, GIC, Indian Bank …)
  [91:1:5.2] 1993 | Private-sector mutual funds permitted; first SEBI Mutual Funds Regulations
  [91:1:5.3] 1996 | Revised SEBI Mutual Funds Regulations
[91:1:6] - **Largest mutual fund (1995):** **Unit Trust of India**; today (by AUM) SBI Mutual Fund.

## SUB 2 | Commodity Regulation – Forward Markets Commission
[91:2:0] - **Forward Markets Commission (FMC):** statutory regulator of **commodity futures** trading, set up **1953** under the **Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952**; HQ Mumbai; moved from the Consumer Affairs Ministry to the **Ministry of Finance (2014)**.
[91:2:1] - In 2010 (UPSC) the FMC regulated **commodities futures trading** – not currency, equity or financial futures (those were SEBI's).
[91:2:2] - **Merged with SEBI on 28 September 2015**; SEBI now regulates commodity derivatives (now the answer to "who regulates commodity futures" = **SEBI**).
[91:2:3] - After the merger: brokers, NSE/BSE and FPIs allowed into commodity derivatives; **Category III AIFs** allowed.
[91:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.51; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #11 p.14; Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.135-136 (FMC, merger Sep 2015); app notes 3:91 sub 3
## SUB 3 | SEBI Powers, SAT and Investor Protection
[91:3:0] TABLE head: Power | What it covers
  [91:3:0.0] Quasi-legislative | Framing regulations
  [91:3:0.1] Quasi-judicial | Orders, penalties, disgorgement
  [91:3:0.2] Investigative | Inspection, search and seizure
[91:3:1] - **Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT):** set up **1995** under the SEBI Act (**Section 15K**); headed by a **Presiding Officer**; hears appeals against **SEBI and stock exchanges**; further appeal **SAT → Supreme Court**.
[91:3:2] - **NSE co-location and dark-fibre cases:** the Supreme Court disposed of SEBI's appeals after a **₹1,492 crore** settlement.
[91:3:3] TABLE head: Tool | Meaning
  [91:3:3.0] Insider trading (PIT Regulations) | Trading on non-public, material (price-sensitive) information; 2025 amendment widened UPSI
  [91:3:3.1] PFUTP Regulations | Ban fraudulent and unfair trade practices
  [91:3:3.2] SCORES | SEBI's online investor complaints redress system
  [91:3:3.3] IEPF Authority | Under the Companies Act 2013, Ministry of Corporate Affairs – not SEBI
  [91:3:3.4] Mission Jagrook | Launched on SEBI's 38th Foundation Day
[91:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.33 (insider trading = share market); Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.130 (insider trading not allowed); app notes 3:91 sub 4, 5
## SUB 4 | Scams and Committees That Shaped Regulation
[91:4:0] TABLE head: Scam | Reform triggered
  [91:4:0.0] Harshad Mehta (1992) | Statutory powers for SEBI; screen-based trading on NSE
  [91:4:0.1] Ketan Parekh (2001) | Badla ended; rolling settlement
  [91:4:0.2] Satyam (2009) – "India's Enron" | Audit and board reforms in the Companies Act 2013; NFRA
  [91:4:0.3] Sahara OFCDs | Private placement capped at 50 investors
[91:4:1] - **SEBI-appointed and related committees:**
[91:4:2] TABLE head: Committee | Subject
  [91:4:2.0] K.M. Birla (1999) | Corporate governance; Clause 49 of the listing agreement
  [91:4:2.1] Sodhi (2013) | Principle-based insider-trading regulations
  [91:4:2.2] Uday Kotak (2017) | Corporate governance; separate Chairman and MD/CEO
  [91:4:2.3] T.K. Viswanathan (2017, SEBI) | Fair market conduct
  [91:4:2.4] T.K. Viswanathan (2015) | Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee → IBC 2016 (not SEBI's)
[91:4:3] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.140 (Sahara, 50 investors); app notes 3:91 sub 6, 7
## SUB 5 | Recent SEBI Reforms – T+0, BRSR, Finfluencers, Securities Markets Code
[91:5:0] - **T+0 (same-day) settlement:** **optional**, alongside **T+1**. Goals (APPSC G2 2025): **enhance liquidity, reduce settlement risk, minimise counterparty risk, market efficiency, less impact of volatility** – **not** higher operational costs → **I, II and III**.
[91:5:1] - **BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report):** prescribed by **SEBI (not RBI)** for the **top 1,000 listed companies** (not all); disclosures are **largely non-financial** (ESG); **replaced the BRR**; **BRSR Core** needs **reasonable assurance**.
[91:5:2] - **Finfluencers:** stock tips or return claims need **SEBI registration**; verified "tick mark" for broker apps with **Google**.
[91:5:3] - **SME IPOs** surged **87%** (FY23-25); **AP:** AP MSME Development Corporation + NSE SME IPO awareness programme in **Vijayawada**.
[91:5:4] - **Securities Markets Code Bill, 2025** (Lok Sabha, Dec 2025): merges the **SEBI Act 1992, SCRA 1956, Depositories Act 1996**; SEBI board up to **15**; **MIIs** get statutory status.
[91:5:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:91 sub 8 (T+0, BRSR, finfluencers, SMC Bill)
## SUB 6 | Debt Market and Infrastructure Financing
[91:6:0] - **REIT and InvIT Regulations** (SEBI, **2014**); **municipal bonds** – SEBI frames the issue and listing regulations.
[91:6:1] - **Large corporate framework (2018):** large listed companies must raise **25%** of fresh borrowing through **debt securities** (bonds).
[91:6:2] - SEBI **lowered** (did not raise) the **bond ticket (face value) size** to draw retail investors.
[91:6:3] - **RBI Retail Direct Scheme:** retail investors buy **G-Secs** directly from the **RBI** – an RBI scheme, not a SEBI-RBI one.
[91:6:4] > APPSC G1 2024: only the 25%-debt framework statement is valid → **Only II** (statement I's "exempted" is wrong – SEBI eased the InvIT/municipal bond rules; III and IV false).
[91:6:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:91 sub 9; general knowledge, not checked (2018 large-corporate framework, 25%)

=== NOTES 3:92 | Financial Instabilities – Crises, Systemic Risk, Shadow Banking, Macroprudential Regulation
## SUB 0 | Global Financial Crisis 2007-09 – Sub-prime, Lehman, Teaser Loans
[92:0:0] - **Origin:** the **US sub-prime mortgage** market (surfaced July 2007) – loans to borrowers with poor credit records, caused by the **US housing (real-estate) bust**, **not by oil prices**.
[92:0:1] - **Chain:** 1. loans to **weak borrowers** → 2. sold on and **securitised** into **mortgage-backed securities** sold worldwide → 3. rates rise, **home-loan defaults** → 4. **failure of US banks** → 5. FPI outflows and a **crash in the Indian stock market**.
[92:0:2] - UPPSC 2010 statements: caused by oil prices ✗; home-loan defaults ✓; failure of US banks ✓; crash in Indian market ✓ → **2, 3 and 4 only**.
[92:0:3] - **Lehman Brothers** (US investment bank) filed for **Chapter 11 bankruptcy on 15 Sep 2008**; sub-prime lending was a main cause of the crisis → A and R both true, **R explains A**.
[92:0:4] - **Teaser loans:** **low fixed rate in the first years, higher later** (e.g. SBI home loans, 2008-09) – an aspect of **sub-prime lending**; banks risk **future defaults**. They were home loans, **not** loans to inexperienced entrepreneurs for factories or exports → **A only** (UPSC 2011).
[92:0:5] - **Credit Default Swap:** insurance-like derivative on bonds; seller pays on default; **counterparty risk**.
[92:0:6] - **Response in India:** FSDC set up **Dec 2010** (G-20 initiative after the crisis); shadow banking came under scrutiny worldwide.
[92:0:7] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 06 p.220 (sub-prime steps, teaser loans), 06 p.141 (CDS, shadow banking after 2007-08), 05 p.158 (FSDC after the sub-prime crisis); app notes 3:92 sub 0, 1
## SUB 1 | East Asian Crisis 1997 and the Taper Tantrum 2013
[92:1:0] - **East Asian crisis (1997):** hit **Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, South Korea**; began with the **fall of the Thai baht** (devalued 2 July 1997). Cause (UPSC 1999 key): the **prolonged over-valuation of local currencies vis-à-vis the US dollar** (pegs), with heavy short-term foreign debt and weak banks – not a Western recession.
[92:1:1] - **India** suffered only limited harm – **capital controls and low short-term debt**.
[92:1:2] - **Taper tantrum (2013):** in **May 2013** the **US Fed** signalled it would **taper** its asset purchases; money left emerging markets and the **rupee fell about 17%** against the dollar by 3 Sep 2013.
[92:1:3] ~~ Sources: Federal Reserve History, "Asian Financial Crisis" (federalreservehistory.org); UPSC 1999 printed key (overvaluation); app notes 3:92 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Indian Bank Failures and Scams
[92:2:0] TABLE head: Episode | Cause | Outcome
  [92:2:0.0] Harshad Mehta scam (1992) | Bank money moved into stocks via ready-forward G-Sec deals and fake bank receipts | SEBI statutory; NSE screen trading
  [92:2:0.1] Bank of Karad (1992) | Issued bank receipts for the Harshad Mehta group | Closed – taken into liquidation (Bombay HC, 1992)
  [92:2:0.2] ICICI Bank – Videocon (2018) | "Sweetheart" loans to the Videocon group (CEO Chanda Kochhar) | Governance crisis at ICICI
  [92:2:0.3] PMC Bank (2019) | Hidden exposure to one realty group (HDIL); dual control (RBI + State Registrars) | Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020
  [92:2:0.4] Yes Bank (2020) | Bad loans, governance failure | RBI moratorium; SBI-led reconstruction; CEO Prashant Kumar replaced by Vinay Tonse (Apr 2026)
[92:2:1] - Metropolitan (cooperative) Bank was also used in the scam; National Housing Bank lost money but was not closed; Grindlays was not closed.
[92:2:2] ~~ Sources: web search listing (Janakiraman Committee report on 'Bank of Karad Ltd. (in liquidation)'; Rajya Sabha PQ 166, 23 Mar 1993 – pages not opened); Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.138 (badla, rolling settlement); app notes 3:92 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Shadow Banking, NBFCs and the 2018 Shadow-Lender Crisis
[92:3:0] - **Shadow banking** = credit creation by **financial institutions outside the regular banking regulatory framework** (hedge funds, NBFCs; also unregulated activities of regulated entities) – they escape CRR/SLR and capital rules.
[92:3:1] - **Shadow-lender crisis (2018-19):** began with **IL&FS** defaults; it hit **NBFCs** (not SFCs, IFC or LIC).
[92:3:2] - **Asset-liability mismatch:** NBFCs **borrow short** (CPs, liquid mutual funds) and **lend long** (infrastructure, housing).
[92:3:3] - **NBFCs:** registered under the **Companies Act**; **cannot take demand deposits, issue cheques or join the payment system**; deposits **not DICGC-covered**.
[92:3:4] - **Scale-Based Regulation (Oct 2022):** **Base, Middle, Upper, Top** layers.
[92:3:5] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 06 p.141 (shadow banking); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 08 p.1-2 (NBFCs, demand deposits, liquid funds); app notes 3:92 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Systemic Risk – Systemically Important Institutions
[92:4:0] TABLE head: Category | Named by | Entities
  [92:4:0.0] D-SIBs | RBI | SBI, ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank – extra CET1 surcharge (Axis Bank is not a D-SIB)
  [92:4:0.1] D-SIIs | IRDAI | LIC, GIC Re, New India Assurance
  [92:4:0.2] G-SIBs | Financial Stability Board | No Indian bank
[92:4:1] - **"Too big to fail":** failure would disrupt the whole financial system → closer supervision and higher governance norms.
[92:4:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:92 sub 3
## SUB 5 | FSDC and Financial Stability Bodies
[92:5:0] TABLE head: Body | Chair / publisher | Note
  [92:5:0.0] FSDC (Dec 2010) | Union Finance Minister | Apex forum; monitors macroprudential supervision, inter-regulatory coordination, financial-sector development, financial literacy and inclusion; not a NITI Aayog organ
  [92:5:0.1] FSDC sub-committee | RBI Governor | –
  [92:5:0.2] CFSA | RBI Deputy Governor + Finance Secretary (co-chairs) | –
  [92:5:0.3] Financial Stability Report | RBI, half-yearly (June, December) | Dec 2025: banks and NBFCs resilient in stress tests; June 2026: flags fintech unsecured lending
[92:5:1] - **UPSC 2016:** organ of NITI Aayog ✗; headed by the Finance Minister ✓; monitors macroprudential supervision ✓ → **2 and 3 only**.
[92:5:2] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 05 p.158 (FSDC objectives, chair, macro-prudential supervision); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #58 p.87 (FSDC); app notes 3:92 sub 4
## SUB 6 | Macroprudential Tools and Bank Health
[92:6:0] TABLE head: Tool | Purpose
  [92:6:0.0] Countercyclical capital buffer | Build capital in good times, release in downturns; RBI kept it inactive (May 2026)
  [92:6:0.1] Leverage ratio | Non-risk-based cap on borrowing against capital
  [92:6:0.2] LTV cap | Limit on a loan against property value (housing)
  [92:6:0.3] Risk weights | Higher weights to cool hot sectors
[92:6:1] - **BR (Amendment) Act, 2020:** **urban and multi-state cooperative banks** under **RBI supervision**.
[92:6:2] - **DICGC cover:** **₹5 lakh** per depositor per bank.
[92:6:3] - **Prompt Corrective Action (PCA):** weak banks watched on **capital, asset quality (NPAs), leverage** – not the credit-deposit ratio.
[92:6:4] - **Bank health:** **GNPA 2.2%, NNPA 0.5%** (Sep 2025); **CRAR 17.3%** (Mar 2025).
[92:6:5] - **AP credit-deposit ratio 157.40%** → banks in AP **lent far more than the deposits** they raised there.
[92:6:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:92 sub 5, 6

=== NOTES 3:93 | Inflation – Types, Causes, Measurement (cpi, Wpi, Core), Effects and Control
## SUB 0 | Measuring Inflation – CPI, WPI and the Headline Index
[93:0:0] # Who compiles what
[93:0:1] TABLE head: Index | Compiled by | Base year (as of 2026) | Main use
  [93:0:1.0] CPI (Rural / Urban / Combined) | NSO, MoSPI (earlier CSO) | 2024 (replaced 2012; first release 12 Feb 2026 for Jan 2026) | Headline inflation; RBI's inflation target
  [93:0:1.1] CPI-IW (Industrial Workers) | Labour Bureau, Ministry of Labour and Employment | 2016 (from Sep 2020) | Dearness allowance of industrial workers and Central Government employees
  [93:0:1.2] CPI-AL / CPI-RL (Agricultural / Rural Labourers) | Labour Bureau | 2019 (from June 2025; earlier 1986-87) | Farm and rural labourers' wages
  [93:0:1.3] CPI-UNME (Urban Non-Manual Employees) | CSO (not the Labour Bureau) | 1984-85 | Discontinued from January 2011 after CPI-Urban began
  [93:0:1.4] WPI | Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry | 2022-23 (revised 2026; earlier 2011-12, 2004-05) | Wholesale prices; contract escalation
  [93:0:1.5] CFPI (Consumer Food Price Index) | NSO | Same as CPI | Food inflation
  [93:0:1.6] GDP deflator | NSO | National-accounts base | Widest measure – all goods and services produced
[93:0:2] - **CPI-IW base**: **1982 → 2001 → 2016** (w.e.f. September 2020).
[93:0:3] - **Labour Bureau**: set up **1920**, at **Chandigarh**, under the **Ministry of Labour and Employment**.
[93:0:4] - **Odd one out** among CPI-IW, CPI-AL, CPI-RL, CPI-UNME: **CPI-UNME** – the only one compiled by the **CSO** (UPSC 2010).
[93:0:5] - **Dearness allowance (DA)** is fixed on the **Consumer Price Index – CPI-IW** (not national income or per capita income); linking pay to a price index is **indexation** ("fixing of wage compensation").
[93:0:6] - **IIP** measures **industrial output, not prices** (NSO).
[93:0:7] # Headline measure – from WPI to CPI
[93:0:8] - WPI was India's **headline / "primary" / most common** inflation measure **till April 2014**.
[93:0:9] - **April 2014**: RBI adopted **CPI (Combined)** as its key measure (Urjit Patel Committee); **headline inflation is now based on CPI-C**.
[93:0:10] - India still publishes inflation on CPI, WPI and the labour CPIs, but the **policy (headline) measure is CPI-Combined**.
[93:0:11] - Inflation rate = **year-on-year % change in CPI** (current month's CPI over the CPI of the same month last year).
[93:0:12] # WPI
[93:0:13] - Prices of goods traded in bulk (first point); **no services** – CPI covers goods **and services**.
[93:0:14] - **2011-12 series**: **697 items**; **manufactured products = largest weight, 64.23%** (primary articles 22.62%, fuel and power 13.15%; 2004-05 series: manufactured 64.97%).
[93:0:15] - **New WPI (base 2022-23, 2026)**: **957 items**; weights on **Gross Value of Output**; runs with a new **Producer Price Index (PPI)** for **5 years**, then WPI is phased out.
[93:0:16] - **PPI** measures the **average change in prices received by producers** (output PPI: goods leaving production; input PPI: inputs entering it).
[93:0:17] - WPI was released **weekly** (primary articles, fuel) until 2012, so "WPI only monthly" was wrong in 2010; WPI gives **less weight to food** than CPI-IW.
[93:0:18] - WPI series on base **2004-05** was introduced on **14 September 2010**.
[93:0:19] # CPI structure
[93:0:20] - New CPI (base 2024): **12 divisions** (COICOP 2018), **358 items**; **food and beverages 36.75%** (about 46% in the 2012 series); 12 online platforms and rural house rent added.
[93:0:21] - **Food has a bigger weight in CPI than in WPI** (UPSC 2020).
[93:0:22] # Committees on price indices
[93:0:23] TABLE head: Committee | Subject
  [93:0:23.0] Abhijit Sen (2007; report May 2008) | WPI revision – base 2004-05
  [93:0:23.1] Saumitra Chaudhuri (2012) | WPI revision – base 2011-12
  [93:0:23.2] Ramesh Chand (NITI Aayog, 2025) | WPI base 2022-23
  [93:0:23.3] Urjit Patel (2014) | CPI as nominal anchor; flexible inflation targeting
[93:0:24] # GDP deflator
[93:0:25] - **GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100**; the **broadest** measure (all goods and services produced).
[93:0:26] - A **rise in the GDP/GNP deflator** = rising prices → **fall in the purchasing power of money**.
[93:0:27] > Exam angle: "headline / most common measure" now = **CPI-Combined**; older keys (pre-2014) = WPI. DA = CPI-IW (Labour Bureau). WPI = Commerce Ministry, manufactured goods ~64%.
[93:0:28] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.13-14; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.5-6; Rocket Indian Economy p.75-76; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 4 p.126 (WPI weights, CPI-IW, CPI-UNME); PMF Lens 2026-06-07 (new WPI, PPI); Praveen CA360 June 2026 (WPI 2022-23, 957 items); PMF Lens 2026-02-08 (CPI 2024 food 36.75%); old app notes 3:93 sub 5-7; WPI weekly release history general knowledge, not checked
[93:0:29] - **National income and GDP estimates**: **NSO** under MoSPI (earlier CSO).
## SUB 1 | Causes and Types of Inflation by Cause
[93:1:0] # By cause
[93:1:1] TABLE head: Type | Cause
  [93:1:1.0] Demand-pull | Aggregate demand > aggregate supply: expansionary fiscal and monetary policy, fiscal stimulus, higher purchasing power, rising money supply – "too much money chasing too few goods"
  [93:1:1.1] Cost-push | Rise in prices of factors of production (wages, raw materials, fuel) → supply falls while demand is constant
  [93:1:1.2] Structural / bottleneck | Deficiencies in the economy – poor farm productivity, supply bottlenecks, inefficient distribution and storage; persists long and is hard for government to tackle
  [93:1:1.3] Export-led | Strong export demand drains domestic supply
[93:1:2] - **Inflationary gap**: excess of aggregate demand (spending) over aggregate supply at **full-employment** output.
[93:1:3] - Demand-pull is **not** caused by **inflation-indexing of wages** (cost side) or **rising interest rates** (they cut demand) – UPSC 2021: 1, 2 and 4 only.
[93:1:4] - A **permanent fall in input costs** reduces cost-push pressure.
[93:1:5] # Causes of price rise in India
[93:1:6] TABLE head: Side | Factors
  [93:1:6.0] Demand | Increase in money supply, rise in non-developmental public expenditure, deficit financing / deficit budget, loose monetary policy, rapid GDP growth, population growth
  [93:1:6.1] Supply | Erratic / less agricultural production, hoarding, higher MSPs, rise in crude oil and fertiliser prices (oil shocks), inefficient storage and marketing, rupee depreciation, cartelisation
[93:1:7] - General price rise may come from **more money supply**, **lower aggregate output** and **higher effective demand** (UPSC 2013: all three).
[93:1:8] - **Food inflation** (UPSC 2011): changing **consumption pattern with rising incomes** and **structural constraints in the food supply chain** – not a 30% fall in foodgrain area.
[93:1:9] - **Unstable currency** works **against** inflation management; stability, sound monetary policy and balanced supply-demand help.
[93:1:10] # Crude oil benchmarks
[93:1:11] - **Brent** (North Sea), **West Texas Intermediate (WTI)** (US) and **Dubai** – grades of **crude oil** used as price benchmarks; oil-price shocks feed cost-push inflation.
[93:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.15, p.17-18; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.6; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 4 p.117 (bottleneck, inflationary gap); Rocket Indian Economy p.76; old app notes 3:93 sub 2-3
[93:1:13] - **Better storage and distribution efficiency** eases supply shocks; **supply shocks** (erratic monsoon, El Nino, costlier crude, rupee depreciation) are the **dominant cause** of inflation in India.
[93:1:14] - **Inflation expectations** also feed inflation (wage-price spiral).
## SUB 2 | Meaning of Inflation and Its Kinds by Speed
[93:2:0] # Definition
[93:2:1] - **Inflation**: a sustained **rise in the general price level** and a **fall in the purchasing power (value) of money**; the essential attribute is **increase in prices**.
[93:2:2] - During inflation prices **increase**; when all prices rise, the purchasing power of money **decreases**.
[93:2:3] - A **rise in a commodity's price** = **fall in the value of currency and rise in the value of the commodity** (in money terms).
[93:2:4] - Effects together: prices rise **and** the value of money falls (not "exchange rate improves").
[93:2:5] - **Economic growth** is usually coupled with **(moderate) inflation** – rising income and demand push prices up.
[93:2:6] # Related terms
[93:2:7] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [93:2:7.0] Deflation | Persistent fall in the general price level (negative inflation) – not a currency fall or a fall in the inflation rate
  [93:2:7.1] Disinflation | Fall in the rate of inflation, still positive (e.g. 3% → 2%)
  [93:2:7.2] Reflation | Inflation returning after deflation – sign of recovery
  [93:2:7.3] Stagflation | High inflation + slow growth / stagnant output + high unemployment
  [93:2:7.4] Skewflation | Inflation in some items (e.g. food) while others are stable or falling
[93:2:8] - A **fall in the inflation rate** means only that **prices are rising more slowly** – not that prices fell, food supply rose or industry stagnated.
[93:2:9] # Stagflation factors
[93:2:10] - Inflationary pressure (e.g. from **higher government spending**) **plus** **declining industrial production and sluggish growth** → stagflation.
[93:2:11] - A **fall in aggregate demand** and **currency appreciation** pull prices **down** – they slow growth but do not create the inflation half of stagflation.
[93:2:12] # By speed
[93:2:13] TABLE head: Type | Rate
  [93:2:13.0] Creeping | Gradual, below about 3%
  [93:2:13.1] Walking / trotting | 3-10%
  [93:2:13.2] Galloping | Double or triple digit (20%, 100%, 200% a year)
  [93:2:13.3] Hyperinflation | Large and accelerating; prices shoot up overnight
[93:2:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.11-12, p.15-16, p.20-21; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.7; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 4 p.113; Rocket Indian Economy p.76; old app notes 3:93 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Controlling Inflation
[93:3:0] # Tools
[93:3:1] TABLE head: Type | Measures
  [93:3:1.0] Monetary (RBI) | Decrease money circulation: raise repo, reverse repo, Bank Rate, CRR, SLR; sell government securities (OMO) – reducing interest rates is not an anti-inflation step
  [93:3:1.1] Fiscal (Government) | Cut non-developmental spending, avoid deficit financing, raise direct taxes, cut indirect taxes on essentials
  [93:3:1.2] Supply / administrative | Control demand, rationing, prevent hoarding and black marketing, ban exports of scarce goods, suspend futures trading, buffer stocks
[93:3:2] - Control needs a **combination of monetary, fiscal and exchange-rate policies** – monetary policy alone cannot fix supply-side inflation; controlling inflation is **not** the Government's job only – the **RBI** has the key role.
[93:3:3] - **Dual price policy** (to control prices): **sugar** – a share of output (**levy sugar**) bought at a controlled price for the PDS, the rest sold in the open market (levy abolished 2013).
[93:3:4] - **Price Stabilisation Fund (PSF)**: Central Sector Scheme, **2014-15 (launched March 2015)**; began with **onion and potato**; pulses added later.
[93:3:5] - **Bharat Atta** (subsidised wheat flour) helped contain **wheat inflation**; **Bharat Dal** (chana dal, July 2023) was extended to **moong dal**; sold via NAFED, NCCF, Kendriya Bhandar (APPSC G1 2024: II and IV).
[93:3:6] - OMSS (Domestic): FCI sells **wheat and rice**.
[93:3:7] - **RBI's biggest concern** in its policy statements: **inflation**.
[93:3:8] - Repo rate (as of 7 Oct 2026): **5.50%** (was 5.25% in Aug 2026); repo acts on demand, **cannot directly fix supply shocks** (onion, crude oil).
[93:3:9] # Inflation-Indexed Bonds (IIBs)
[93:3:10] - **Principal and/or interest linked to an inflation index** → protect investors from **uncertainty about inflation** (real return).
[93:3:11] - Government can **reduce coupon rates** on its borrowing (no inflation-risk premium); interest and capital gains are **taxable** (UPSC 2022: A and B only).
[93:3:12] - RBI issued IIBs in **2013**.
[93:3:13] # AP measures
[93:3:14] - **State-level Price Monitoring Committee** headed by the **Chief Secretary**; **DES monitors 8 essential commodities daily** (groundnut and palm oil added Feb 2025).
[93:3:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.18-19; Rocket Indian Economy p.76; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 4 p.162 (PSF); RUNBOOK settled facts (repo 5.50%, RBI MPC 7 Oct 2026); old app notes 3:93 sub 10; dual price sugar general knowledge, not checked
[93:3:16] - **Onion exports**: ban lifted **4 May 2024** with **40% duty** and US$550 MEP; MEP removed and duty cut to **20%** on **13 Sep 2024**; NCCF and NAFED released 47,786 MT of PSF onion (to 8 Oct 2025).
[93:3:17] - **Bharat Chana Dal** sold at **₹60/kg** from July 2023.
## SUB 4 | Effects of Inflation and Deflation
[93:4:0] # Gainers and losers of inflation
[93:4:1] TABLE head: Gain | Lose
  [93:4:1.0] Debtors (borrowers) – repay money of lower real value | Creditors (lenders) – hurt most
  [93:4:1.1] Businessmen, producers, big farmers (profits rise faster than costs) | Fixed-income groups – pensioners, salary and wage earners
  [93:4:1.2] Holders of real assets, equity investors | Bond / debenture holders, savings-account holders
  [93:4:1.3] Exporters (if the rupee depreciates) | Consumers, the poor
[93:4:2] - Rule: **inflation benefits debtors**; it does **not** benefit bond-holders, consumers or fixed-income groups.
[93:4:3] - Price-hike: businessmen gain and consumers must curtail needs (most keys: both true, R not the explanation; strictly not "all" businessmen gain).
[93:4:4] - Other effects: falling saving (MPS falls), shift to gold, rising inequality, wage-price spiral, discourages exports; **food inflation is regressive** (the poor spend more of income on food); **menu costs** of re-pricing.
[93:4:5] # Deflation
[93:4:6] - Purchasing power of money **rises** → **fixed-income groups (pensioners, salary earners)** and **creditors gain**; **debtors lose** (heavier real debt).
[93:4:7] - **Deflationary spiral**: postponed purchases → lower profits → higher unemployment → heavier real debt burden.
[93:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.12, p.18-20; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 4 p.122; old app notes 3:93 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Headline, Core and Food Inflation
[93:5:0] TABLE head: Basis | Headline inflation | Core inflation
  [93:5:0.0] Covers | Total inflation, including food and energy (oil, gas) | Excludes volatile food and fuel / energy
  [93:5:0.1] Shows | Raw figure – what consumers feel | Underlying, long-run trend
  [93:5:0.2] Volatility | More volatile | More stable
  [93:5:0.3] Index | Change in CPI-Combined | CPI excluding food and fuel
[93:5:1] - **Headline** = rate of change of the CPI (basket of a typical family); **core** = CPI change after excluding volatile items such as food and fuel – both statements true (RAS 2023).
[93:5:2] - Core does **not** include food and energy; headline does **not** exclude food (RAS 2024: only "headline is more volatile" is correct).
[93:5:3] - Inflation that leaves out commodities with volatile prices = **core inflation**.
[93:5:4] - **Food inflation**: measured by the **CFPI** (10 sub-groups; cereals carry the highest weight).
[93:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.16, p.22; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.7-8; Rocket Indian Economy p.75; old app notes 3:93 sub 1
## SUB 6 | Index Numbers and the Business Cycle
[93:6:0] - A **price index** is a **statistical device** to measure changes in the general price level.
[93:6:1] - **Laspeyres** index: **base-year (initial-year) quantities** as weights; **Paasche**: current-year weights; **Fisher's ideal index** = geometric mean of the two.
[93:6:2] - **Irving Fisher** is the economist most associated with **index numbers** (ideal index, tests of index numbers).
[93:6:3] - **Business cycle** phases: **expansion / recovery** (real GDP rising) → **peak / boom** → **recession** (falling) → **trough / depression** (bottom).
[93:6:4] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 4 p.136-137 (boom, recession, recovery); index-number facts general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 7 | Recent Inflation Data and Forecasts
[93:7:0] TABLE head: Period | Fact
  [93:7:0.0] December 2016 | CPI-Combined 3.41% (3-year low, after demonetisation)
  [93:7:0.1] 2024-25 (FY2025) | RBI projection (Feb 2024 MPC): 4.5% (Q1 5.0, Q2 4.0, Q3 4.6, Q4 4.7)
  [93:7:0.2] Early 2024 | Food > Headline > Core (APPSC G1 2024); retail inflation eased in early 2024 (5.7% Dec 2023 → about 5.1% Jan 2024)
  [93:7:0.3] 2025 (year) | CPI 2.2% (12-year low); food -0.2% → Core > Headline > Food; Oct 2025 0.3%
  [93:7:0.4] May 2026 | Headline 3.93%, food 4.85%, core 3.73% → Food > Headline > Core; AP 4.9% vs India 3.9%
  [93:7:0.5] June – Aug 2026 | 4.38% (June, first breach of 4% in the new series) → 4.8% (Aug, 20-month high); WPI (2022-23 base) 9.87% June – West Asia fuel costs
[93:7:1] ~~ Sources: RBI press release 8 Feb 2024 (rbi.org.in prid=57277); domain-b.com 13 Jan 2017 (Dec 2016 CPI 3.41%); old app notes 3:93 sub 9
## SUB 8 | Inflation Targeting and the Phillips Curve
[93:8:0] TABLE head: Step | Year | Provision
  [93:8:0.0] Urjit Patel Committee | 2014 | CPI as nominal anchor
  [93:8:0.1] Monetary Policy Framework Agreement | Feb 2015 | Led to RBI Act amendment
  [93:8:0.2] RBI Act 1934 amended | 2016 | Statutory flexible inflation targeting; Sec 45ZA target set by Centre with RBI every 5 years; Sec 45ZB six-member MPC; Sec 45ZN report after 3 consecutive quarters of breach (first invoked 2022)
[93:8:1] - **Target (1 Apr 2026 – 31 Mar 2031)**: **4% CPI-Combined ± 2% (2-6%)**; 6% is only the upper limit.
[93:8:2] - Average CPI fell from 6.8% (2012-16) to about 4.9% under the framework.
[93:8:3] - **Phillips curve** (A.W. Phillips, 1958): **inverse relation between unemployment and (wage) inflation**; Friedman: long-run curve **vertical**; India's curve is flat (about 92% informal workers).
[93:8:4] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 4 p.120; old app notes 3:93 sub 7-8

=== NOTES 3:94 | Indian Tax System – Direct and Indirect Taxes, Tax Buoyancy, Tax-gdp Ratio, Progressivity
## SUB 0 | Direct and Indirect Taxes – Classification and Taxable Events
[94:0:0] # Direct vs indirect
[94:0:1] TABLE head: Basis | Direct tax | Indirect tax
  [94:0:1.0] Burden | Cannot be shifted – impact and incidence on the same person | Shifted to the consumer through prices – impact and incidence on different persons
  [94:0:1.1] Examples | Income tax, corporation tax, wealth tax, capital gains, property, gift, estate duty, expenditure tax, STT | Customs, excise, sales tax, VAT, service tax, GST, entertainment, octroi, entry tax
  [94:0:1.2] Nature | Generally progressive | Generally regressive
  [94:0:1.3] Price effect | Non-inflationary; does not directly raise the price of goods | Inflationary – raises prices
  [94:0:1.4] Administered by | CBDT – statutory body under the Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963 | CBIC (formerly CBEC)
[94:0:2] - **Not direct**: customs duty, sales tax, excise, octroi – the usual "odd one out" against income, corporation, wealth and gift taxes.
[94:0:3] - **Indirect pair**: **customs and excise** (corporation and wealth taxes are direct).
[94:0:4] - **Income, corporate and wealth taxes – all direct**; "1 and 2 only" for income + corporate tax against service tax and customs.
[94:0:5] - **Income tax** does not directly increase the price of a commodity – trade/business tax, import and excise (manufacturing) duties do.
[94:0:6] - **GST** – a comprehensive **indirect** tax on supply, **destination-based**; it is not related to income.
[94:0:7] - **Service tax** – an **indirect tax levied by the Central Government**, introduced **1994-95** (subsumed in GST 2017).
[94:0:8] - **STT** – a **direct tax** on **transactions through the stock market** (from **1 October 2004**), though collected by the exchange.
[94:0:9] - **"Paper taxes"**: wealth, gift and estate duty – never yielded much revenue; **wealth tax** gives the **least** revenue of the major taxes.
[94:0:10] - **Impact** = on whom the tax is first imposed; **incidence** = who finally bears it; moving the burden forward (consumers) or backward (suppliers) = **tax shifting**. Property tax cannot be shifted through prices.
[94:0:11] - **Incidence and elasticity**: if demand is **perfectly inelastic (elasticity zero)** the price rises by the full tax and the **consumer bears it all**; with infinite elasticity the price cannot rise.
[94:0:12] - **Cut in direct taxes** → higher **disposable income** and consumption demand.
[94:0:13] # Base / taxable event of each tax
[94:0:14] TABLE head: Tax | Taxable event / base
  [94:0:14.0] Central excise | Manufacture / production of goods (paid by the manufacturer) – "manufacture only"
  [94:0:14.1] Customs | Import and export (Customs Act, 1962)
  [94:0:14.2] Sales tax / VAT | Sale of goods
  [94:0:14.3] Service tax | Provision of service
  [94:0:14.4] GST | Supply of goods or services (from 1 July 2017)
  [94:0:14.5] Corporation tax | Income / net profit of companies – not production, sales or stock
  [94:0:14.6] Income tax | Income of individuals, HUFs, firms (Income Tax Act, 1961)
  [94:0:14.7] Capital gains tax | Gain on sale of a capital asset
  [94:0:14.8] Wealth tax | Net wealth – 1957 to 2015 (abolished)
[94:0:15] - **Toll** – a levy (tax) for using a road or bridge; tolls are a **State List** subject.
[94:0:16] > Exam angle: "which is not a direct tax / which is indirect" is the single most repeated tax question (APPSC, UPPSC, MPPSC, Police).
[94:0:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.2-3; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.3-5; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.52-53; Rocket Indian Economy p.64-65; old app notes 3:94 sub 2-3
## SUB 1 | Union and State Taxes – Who Levies, Who Shares
[94:1:0] # Constitutional division
[94:1:1] TABLE head: Article / entry | Provision
  [94:1:1.0] Article 265 | No tax levied or collected except by authority of law
  [94:1:1.1] Taxing entries | Union List 15, State List 20, Concurrent List 3
  [94:1:1.2] Residuary taxing power | Parliament (gift, wealth, expenditure taxes)
  [94:1:1.3] Article 276 | Profession tax – a State levy; ceiling ₹2,500 per person per year
  [94:1:1.4] State List Entry 46 | Agricultural income tax – States only; exempt under Income-tax Act Sec 10(1)
  [94:1:1.5] Article 271 | Surcharges – retained by the Union, not shared
  [94:1:1.6] 80th Amendment, 2000 | Net proceeds of all Union taxes (minus cess, surcharge, collection cost) shareable on Finance Commission advice; effective 1 April 1996
[94:1:2] # Union taxes
[94:1:3] - **Union alone (Union List)**: **customs duties, corporation tax**; not levied by States.
[94:1:4] - **Corporation tax** is **imposed by the Central Government**; before 2000 its proceeds were **not shared** with States (Art. 270 then covered only income tax; Union excise under Art. 272) – the basis of old keys "not shared" / "accrues wholly to the Centre". **Since the 80th Amendment it is in the divisible pool.**
[94:1:5] - **Tax on income other than agricultural income** – the classic tax **levied and collected by the Union but distributed** between Union and States.
[94:1:6] - Pre-GST pairs that are **not Union taxes**: **tolls and tax on mineral rights**, **taxes on intoxicants (State excise) and entertainment** – State List; customs, estate duty and terminal taxes on goods/passengers by rail, air or sea are Union.
[94:1:7] - **Income tax on salary (TDS)** is collected and paid into the account of the **Central Government**.
[94:1:8] - **Agricultural income tax** – **not shared** by the Centre (it is a State tax). Income from **poultry, dairy, wool rearing** is **not** agricultural income (taxable); **nursery saplings** are agricultural income; **rural agricultural land is not a capital asset** under the Income-tax Act, 1961.
[94:1:9] # State taxes
[94:1:10] - **Levied by States / local bodies**: **sales tax** (pre-GST), **entertainment tax** (State List, List II), **road / motor vehicle tax**, profession tax, property tax, land revenue, **State excise on liquor**, stamp duty and registration, electricity duty, agricultural income tax.
[94:1:11] - **Sales tax on toothpaste** (pre-GST) – **imposed and collected by the State Government**.
[94:1:12] - **Not a State / AP own-revenue source**: **customs duty**, corporation tax ("taxes on companies").
[94:1:13] - **Most important source of State revenue**: **sales tax** (pre-2017) – now **SGST**.
[94:1:14] - **States' revenue receipts**: **own tax revenue** is the largest component (~50%, FY25); share in Central taxes second (~32%); CAG average 2014-24: own tax 47%, tax share 28%, grants 17%.
[94:1:15] - **AP (2024-25 RE)**: **SGST** largest own-tax source – ₹36,296 crore (**38%**) of ₹94,967 crore; **State Excise** ₹21,300 crore (**22%**).
[94:1:16] - Union Budget 2017-18: farmers who gave land for **Amaravati** (AP capital) under land pooling – exempted from **capital gains tax**.
[94:1:17] > Exam angle: "levied by the Union but shared" questions were set on the pre-2000 scheme; after the 80th Amendment every Union tax (except cess and surcharge) is shareable.
[94:1:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.52-53, p.55; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.2; old app notes 3:94 sub 1, 6
## SUB 2 | VAT, MODVAT, CENVAT, Sales Tax and Service Tax
[94:2:0] # Value Added Tax
[94:2:1] - **VAT** = tax on the **value added at each stage** between production and final sale – a **multi-point**, **destination-based**, **non-cascading** tax on final consumption, borne by the consumer; invoice-credit trail makes it **self-enforcing**; a **harmonised** commodity tax that **improves revenue buoyancy** ("will diminish revenue buoyancy" is **not** VAT's idea).
[94:2:2] - State VAT was a **State subject** (State List Entry 54) – not "basically a subject of the Central Government".
[94:2:3] - VAT applies to **commodity taxes – excise duties** (MODVAT/CENVAT) and sales tax; not to income tax, estate duty or agricultural income tax.
[94:2:4] - Concept first proposed by **Wilhelm von Siemens** (Germany); first implemented by **France (1954)**.
[94:2:5] - **L.K. Jha Indirect Taxation Enquiry Committee (1976)** – suggested VAT at the manufacturing stage.
[94:2:6] - **VAT rate for medicines/drugs**: the **4%** slab (pre-GST State VAT).
[94:2:7] - Some goods (petroleum, alcohol) are still outside GST – **State VAT** continues on them.
[94:2:8] # Chronology
[94:2:9] TABLE head: Event | Date
  [94:2:9.0] MODVAT – on Union excise duties, to end cascading (first indirect tax reform) | 1 March 1986 (Budget 1986-87)
  [94:2:9.1] Service tax (Chelliah Committee advice; 3 services) | 1994-95
  [94:2:9.2] Uniform floor rates of sales tax (Standing Committee of State Finance Ministers) | 1 January 2000
  [94:2:9.3] CENVAT – replaced MODVAT; Union excise (an indirect tax) | 1 April 2000
  [94:2:9.4] First State VAT – Haryana | 1 April 2003
  [94:2:9.5] State VAT nationwide (20 States/UTs) | 1 April 2005
  [94:2:9.6] Last States to join (TN 2007, UP 2008) | by 2008-09
  [94:2:9.7] GST | 1 July 2017
[94:2:10] - **Uniform sales tax**: in **January 2000** the Standing Committee of State Finance Ministers recommended **uniform floor rates of sales tax**, implemented from **1 January 2000**.
[94:2:11] - About **7 States** had not implemented VAT by December 2005 (Rajasthan, Gujarat, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand – 2006; TN 2007; UP 2008).
[94:2:12] - **Karnataka** – early e-payment of VAT/commercial taxes; **Maharashtra** – the State the **IMF** had advised earlier not to adopt VAT (APPSC key).
[94:2:13] - **Sales tax** was **not levied in Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep** (question period); GST now covers all India.
[94:2:14] - **Central Sales Tax (CST)** – levied on **inter-State trade** and in **Union Territories**; **SEZs exempt**; subsumed in GST.
[94:2:15] # Service tax
[94:2:16] - **Indirect**, **Central** tax; introduced **1994-95** (Manmohan Singh as FM) on **Raja Chelliah Committee** advice.
[94:2:17] - Rates: **10% → 12% (Budget 2006-07)**; **12% → 14% (Budget 2015-16)**; from 2012-13, 12% on all services except the **negative list**.
[94:2:18] - **T.R. Rastogi (Rustagi) Panel** (2006) – Finance Ministry panel to review **service tax** issues and circulars.
[94:2:19] - **Swachh Bharat Cess** – **0.5%** on **all taxable services** (from 15 Nov 2015).
[94:2:20] - **Multiple tax rates** – chief drawback: **misclassification** of goods and services (disputes, evasion).
[94:2:21] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.26-27, p.33, p.52-53; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.4-5, p.35; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.204-206; Tribune 1 Apr 2003 (Haryana VAT); old app notes 3:94 sub 9
## SUB 3 | Composition of Central Tax Revenue – Then and Now
[94:3:0] # Largest tax by period (Receipts Budget figures, ₹ crore)
[94:3:1] TABLE head: Year | Largest | Order of the big four
  [94:3:1.0] 1994-95 | Union excise (37,347) | excise > customs (26,789) > corporation 13,822 > income 12,025
  [94:3:1.1] 2002-03 | Union excise (91,433) | excise > corporation 48,616 > customs 45,193 > income 42,524
  [94:3:1.2] 2004-05 BE | Union excise (1,09,199) | excise > corporation 88,436
  [94:3:1.3] 2005-06 BE/RE | Union excise (1,21,533 / 1,12,000) | excise > corporation (1,10,573 / 1,03,573)
  [94:3:1.4] 2007-08 RE | Corporation tax (1,86,125) | corporation > excise 1,27,947 > income 1,18,320 > customs
  [94:3:1.5] 2008-09 BE | Corporation tax (2,26,361) | corporation > income (1,38,314) > excise (1,37,874) > customs (1,18,930)
  [94:3:1.6] 2013-14 | Corporation tax | corporation > income
  [94:3:1.7] 2025-26 / 2026-27 | Income tax | income > corporation > GST
[94:3:2] - **Union excise** was the largest Central tax until **2005-06**; **corporation tax** led from **2006-07** to about 2019-20; **income tax** since then.
[94:3:3] - **Two largest Central taxes in the 1990s**: **Union excise and customs**.
[94:3:4] - **First four decades of planning**: main Central revenue from **indirect taxes**; developing countries still get more from indirect taxes.
[94:3:5] - **Excise share** of gross tax revenue fell sharply in 2005-10 (ES 2009-10).
[94:3:6] - **Growth in gross tax revenue** highest in **2016-17** among 2013-14 to 2016-17 (about 18%).
[94:3:7] - Direct taxes were about **4-5% of GDP/GNP** in the early 2000s; 2026-27 BE: direct **6.9%** of GDP, indirect **4.3%**.
[94:3:8] - **Direct share** of gross tax revenue: **61.2% (2026-27 BE)**; more than half since 2007-08 (about 56% in 2013-14).
[94:3:9] - **Subsidy** is expenditure, **not public revenue** (income tax, borrowing and VAT are).
[94:3:10] # Centre's rupee – Budget 2026-27

  [94:3:11.0] Borrowings and other liabilities | 24% (largest receipt)
  [94:3:11.1] Income tax | 21% (largest tax)
  [94:3:11.2] Corporation tax | 18%
  [94:3:11.3] GST and other taxes | 15%
  [94:3:11.4] Non-tax revenue | 10%
  [94:3:11.5] Union excise | 6%
  [94:3:11.6] Customs | 4%
[94:3:12] - 2026-27 BE: **income tax ₹14,66,000 cr > corporation tax ₹12,31,000 cr > GST ₹10,19,020 cr**.
[94:3:13] - Direct taxes collected by the IT department in **AP and Telangana** rose about **8.5%** in 2022-23 (APPSC 2023 key).

## SUB 4 | Progressive, Regressive and Degressive Taxes; Laffer Effect
[94:4:0] TABLE head: Type | Feature | Example
  [94:4:0.0] Progressive | Tax rate rises as income rises – average burden rises with income ("ability to pay") | Income tax
  [94:4:0.1] Regressive | Takes a higher proportion of income from low incomes than from high | Indirect taxes, GST on essentials
  [94:4:0.2] Proportional | One rate for all incomes | Flat-rate tax
  [94:4:0.3] Degressive | Rate rises at first, then becomes flat | Progressive slabs with a top flat rate
[94:4:1] - **Indirect taxes are regressive** because they are charged at the **same rate for all income groups**.
[94:4:2] - **Income tax in India**: **progressive and direct** – not collected by States, not proportional; **GST, sales tax, motor vehicles tax** are not progressive.
[94:4:3] - **India's tax system**: **progressive in nature but overall degressive** (progressive slabs up to a flat top rate; regressive indirect taxes).
[94:4:4] - **Redistribution** of income is best achieved by **progressive taxation combined with progressive expenditure**.
[94:4:5] - **Laffer effect**: **reduction in tax rates leads to a more than proportionate increase in tax yield**; Laffer curve – **inverted U**, zero revenue at 0% and 100%; **Arthur Laffer** (1974); term coined by **Jude Wanniski**.
[94:4:6] - Beyond a point, **higher tax rates may reduce revenue**.
[94:4:7] - **Widening the tax base** (lower exemption threshold, fewer exemptions) raises revenue without changing rates – the **Chelliah approach: lower rates, broader base**.
[94:4:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.64; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.2; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.33; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.204
## SUB 5 | Tax Reform Committees
[94:5:0] TABLE head: Committee | Year | Focus
  [94:5:0.0] K.N. Raj Committee | 1972 | Agricultural holding tax (agricultural wealth and income)
  [94:5:0.1] L.K. Jha (Indirect Taxation Enquiry) | 1976 | VAT at manufacturing stage → MODVAT
  [94:5:0.2] Raja J. Chelliah (Tax Reforms Committee) | 1991-93 | Direct and indirect taxes; lower rates, broader base; service tax; MODVAT → full VAT; "Father of Indian tax reforms"
  [94:5:0.3] Vijay Kelkar Task Forces | 2002 | Both direct and indirect taxes (two reports); GST idea; the latest tax committee as of 2004
  [94:5:0.4] Parthasarathi Shome | 2012 | GAAR; scrap retrospective tax
  [94:5:0.5] Tax Administration Reform Commission – Parthasarathi Shome | 2013 | Tax administration restructuring
[94:5:1] - **Kelkar final report (27 Dec 2002)** **scaled down** its original proposals after criticism – it kept a **₹50,000 rebate on housing-loan interest** instead of abolishing it.
[94:5:2] - **Global Trust Bank** was amalgamated with **Oriental Bank of Commerce** (14 August 2004), not PNB.
[94:5:3] - **Simpler tax system** → **productivity gains** by removing **deadweight costs** and resource-allocation distortions (APPSC G1 2024: A and R true, R explains A).
[94:5:4] - **Direct Tax Code** – to replace the Income Tax Act, 1961 with a single law.
[94:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.26-27, p.33, p.55; Rocket Indian Economy p.95; Tribune 28 Dec 2002 (Kelkar final report); old app notes 3:94 sub 8-9
## SUB 6 | Tax, Fee, Cess and Surcharge
[94:6:0] TABLE head: Levy | Key feature
  [94:6:0.0] Tax | Compulsory pecuniary burden imposed by legislative authority to support government; no quid pro quo
  [94:6:0.1] Fee | Paid for a specific service – quid pro quo
  [94:6:0.2] Cess | "Tax on tax" for a specific purpose; ends when the purpose is met; not shared
  [94:6:0.3] Surcharge | Additional charge on the tax payable – classically a levy to raise revenue temporarily (in practice long-running); none if no tax is due; not shared (Art. 271)
[94:6:1] - **Ad valorem tax** = **% of the value** of a commodity; **specific tax** = fixed amount per unit (weight/quantity).
[94:6:2] - **Clean Energy Cess** on coal (Finance Act 2010) → renamed **Clean Environment Cess** (Budget **2016-17**).
[94:6:3] - Budget **2016-17**: income-tax **surcharge 15%** on income **above ₹1 crore** (12% earlier).
[94:6:4] - **SAT** (Securities Appellate Tribunal) is **not a tax**; **MAT** (Minimum Alternate Tax, 1996-97), GST and VAT are.
[94:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.46 (Clean Environment Cess); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.55 (MAT); old app notes 3:94 sub 0
## SUB 7 | Tax-GDP Ratio and Tax Buoyancy
[94:7:0] # Tax-GDP ratio
[94:7:1] - **Tax-GDP ratio = total tax revenue / nominal GDP** – yardstick of fiscal capacity.
[94:7:2] - **Low ratio** → large **informal sector** or high **evasion**; **falling ratio** → revenue growing **slower than GDP** (buoyancy < 1), less fiscal space, more borrowing – it does **not** by itself show less equitable distribution.
[94:7:3] TABLE head: Measure | Value
  [94:7:3.0] Centre gross tax revenue | 9.9% of GDP in 2019-20 (ES 2021-22); ~11.5% post-pandemic (FY22-FY25, ES 2025-26)
  [94:7:3.1] Combined Centre + States | ~19.6% (States' own tax ≈ 7% of GSDP)
  [94:7:3.2] 2008-09 (general government) | 16.39%
  [94:7:3.3] India average 2001-22 | 16.36% – lowest among emerging economies; below OECD
  [94:7:3.4] World Bank tipping point | 15%
[94:7:4] # Buoyancy and elasticity
[94:7:5] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [94:7:5.0] Buoyancy | % change in revenue / % change in GDP, including discretionary changes (rates, base); above 1 = revenue grows faster than GDP
  [94:7:5.1] Elasticity | Same response excluding discretionary changes
[94:7:6] - **2026-27 BE**: gross buoyancy **0.8**; **direct 1.1**, **indirect 0.3**.
[94:7:7] - Buoyant revenues helped bring the fiscal deficit to **4.4% of GDP in FY26** (ES 2025-26).
[94:7:8] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Highlights 01 p.11-13; old app notes 3:94 sub 7-8

=== NOTES 3:95 | Direct Tax Reforms – Income Tax Slabs, Corporate Tax Cuts, Faceless Assessment, Dtc Debate
## SUB 0 | Direct Tax Committees and Task Forces
[95:0:0] TABLE head: Committee | Year | Focus
  [95:0:0.0] Nicholas Kaldor | 1956 | First suggested expenditure tax; also wealth, gift, capital gains taxes
  [95:0:0.1] Wanchoo (Direct Taxes Enquiry) | 1971 | Black money, tax evasion
  [95:0:0.2] K.N. Raj | 1972 | Taxation of agricultural wealth and income – proposed the Agricultural Holding Tax
  [95:0:0.3] Raja J. Chelliah (Tax Reforms Committee) | 1991-93 | Lower rates, broader base, minimum incentives/exemptions; basis of the 1992 wealth-tax revision; "father of Indian tax reforms"
  [95:0:0.4] Vijay Kelkar Task Forces (direct and indirect taxes) | Set up Sept 2002, report Dec 2002 | Abolish rebates under Section 88 (also 80L, Sec 10 interest); abolish wealth tax and the standard deduction; exempt dividends and capital gains on listed equity; exemption limit ₹1 lakh, ₹1.5 lakh for senior citizens and widows
  [95:0:0.5] Kelkar Task Force on FRBM | 2004 | First proposed a national GST
  [95:0:0.6] Parthasarathi Shome | 2012 | GAAR review; drop retrospective tax
  [95:0:0.7] Justice R.V. Easwar | 2015-16 | Simplifying the Income-tax Act
  [95:0:0.8] T.R. Rustagi | – | Restructuring of the CBDT
  [95:0:0.9] Task force on a new direct tax law | Nov 2017 | Convener Arbind Modi; later headed by Akhilesh Ranjan (report 2019)
[95:0:1] - Agricultural holding tax / agricultural wealth and income → **K.N. Raj** (not Chelliah, not Wanchoo = black money, not Bhoothalingam = rationalisation of wages/incomes, not Kaldor).
[95:0:2] - Kaldor = wealth (1957), expenditure (1958), gift (1958); FM **T.T. Krishnamachari** brought in the expenditure tax.
[95:0:3] > Exam angle: committee ↔ subject items – Raj = agricultural taxation (5 PYQs), Kelkar = Section 88 rebates, Kaldor = expenditure tax, Chelliah = lower rates/fewer incentives.
[95:0:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.26-27, p.33, p.55; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.95, p.97; tribuneindia.com 28 Dec 2002 (Kelkar highlights, web); app notes 3:95
## SUB 1 | Income Tax – History, Budgets, Slabs and Deductions
[95:1:0] - **Income tax** first introduced **1860** by **James Wilson**, the first **Finance Member** (Act assent **24 July 1860**); a **progressive direct tax**; the **Income-tax Act, 1961** took effect **1 April 1962**.
[95:1:1] - Budget **1997-98** (FM **P. Chidambaram**, "dream budget"): cut almost **every tax**; income-tax rates **10, 20, 30%** (from 15, 30, 40%); corporate tax 40% → 35%.
[95:1:2] - **One-by-six scheme**: return filing compulsory for anyone showing any one of six lifestyle signs; the **telephone connection** criterion was dropped in Budget **2002-03**.
[95:1:3] TABLE head: Budget | Exemption / slab fact
  [95:1:3.0] 2005-06 | Senior citizens exempt up to ₹1.5 lakh
  [95:1:3.1] 2012-13 | ₹2 lakh general; ₹2.5 lakh senior citizens (60-80); ₹5 lakh very senior (80+)
  [95:1:3.2] 2020-21 (first new optional regime) | 0-2.5 lakh nil; 2.5-5 lakh 5%; 5-7.5 lakh 10%; 7.5-10 lakh 15%; 10-12.5 lakh 20%; 12.5-15 lakh 25%; above 15 lakh 30%
  [95:1:3.3] 2023-24 | Up to 3 lakh nil; 3-6 lakh 5%; 6-9 lakh 10%; 9-12 lakh 15%; 12-15 lakh 20%; above 15 lakh 30%; top surcharge (above ₹2 crore) cut 37% → 25%
  [95:1:3.4] 2025-26 (unchanged in 2026-27) | 0-4 lakh nil; 4-8 lakh 5%; 8-12 lakh 10%; 12-16 lakh 15%; 16-20 lakh 20%; 20-24 lakh 25%; above 24 lakh 30%
[95:1:4] - **New regime (Section 115BAC)**: **default, exemption-free**; old regime with deductions stays optional. **Section 87A rebate**: income up to **₹12 lakh** tax-free; **₹12.75 lakh** for salaried after the **standard deduction of ₹75,000**.
[95:1:5] - Old regime: senior citizens ₹3 lakh, very senior ₹5 lakh exemption limit.
[95:1:6] - **Deductions**: interest on a **housing loan** (Sec 24(b)) is deductible; interest on an **education loan** is also deductible (**Sec 80E**); **Section 80C** covers NSC (and its accrued interest), PPF, EPF, life insurance, tuition fees of **two** children, home-loan **principal**.
[95:1:7] > Exam angle: budget-specific slab questions – key the slab of the budget asked about; the 12-15 lakh slab was 20% (2023-24) but 12-16 lakh is 15% now.
[95:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.26; Union Budget 2026-27 Speech; app notes 3:95 (budget slabs); general knowledge for Sec 80E / 24(b)
## SUB 2 | Minimum Alternate Tax and Corporate Tax Cuts
[95:2:0] - **MAT** taxes **"zero-tax companies"** – companies showing **book profits** but paying little or no regular tax because of exemptions and deductions.
[95:2:1] TABLE head: Milestone | Fact
  [95:2:1.0] First introduced | Budget 1987-88 (announced 1986-87; Finance Act 1987, Sec 115J; effective AY 1988-89); rate 15.75%
  [95:2:1.1] Withdrawn / reintroduced | Withdrawn 1990; reintroduced in Budget 1996-97 (Sec 115JA, from AY 1997-98) – the year most books and keys give as "introduced"
  [95:2:1.2] Before 2026 | 15% of book profits
  [95:2:1.3] Budget 2026-27 | 14%, a final tax; no new MAT credit after 1 April 2026; old credit set off up to 1/4 of liability (new regime only)
[95:2:2] - **Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019** (Sept 2019 ordinance): domestic companies **30% → 22%** (Sec **115BAA**, effective ~**25.17%**); new manufacturing companies after 1 Oct 2019 **15%** (Sec **115BAB**, ~**17.01%**); **no MAT** for those opting in.
[95:2:3] - Taxes on the **corporate sector**: corporation tax on company profit, MAT, Fringe Benefit Tax (2005-09). **Capital gains tax** is the usual "not corporate" answer (a levy on an investor's gain), though companies too pay it.
[95:2:4] > Exam angle: MAT = zero-tax companies (2 PYQs); "introduced in" → **1996-97** in the options (strictly 1987-88).
[95:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.22; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.39, p.55; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.3; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.210; Union Budget 2026-27 Highlights p.15
## SUB 3 | Special Direct Taxes – Introduced and Status
[95:3:0] TABLE head: Tax | Introduced | Status
  [95:3:0.0] Estate duty | 1953 | Abolished 1985
  [95:3:0.1] Wealth tax | 1957 (Wealth Tax Act; Kaldor) | Abolished 2015
  [95:3:0.2] Expenditure tax | 1958 – FM T.T. Krishnamachari, on Kaldor's advice | Abolished (1962; revived briefly 1964-66)
  [95:3:0.3] Gift tax | April 1958 | Abolished October 1998
  [95:3:0.4] STT | 1 October 2004 | In force
  [95:3:0.5] DDT | – | Abolished from 1 April 2020; dividends taxed in shareholders' hands
  [95:3:0.6] Angel tax | Budget 2012 – on share premium of unlisted start-ups above fair value (Sec 56(2)(viib)) | Abolished in Budget 2024-25
[95:3:1] - **Capital gains**: arise on **transfer** of a capital asset; tax on sale of **inherited property** = **capital gains tax** (no inheritance tax in India).
[95:3:2] - Short-term asset: held **up to 24 months** (general rule); **LTCG 12.5%** (as of Aug 2026); **indexation** uses the **Cost Inflation Index** (CBDT, base **2001-02**).
[95:3:3] - **Rural agricultural land** is **not a capital asset**; agricultural income is tax-free (State subject).
[95:3:4] - **Poll tax** (Community Charge, 1989-90) – the unpopular tax linked to **Margaret Thatcher's** downfall (1990).
[95:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.26; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.21; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.209; app notes 3:95; general knowledge (poll tax)
## SUB 4 | Black Money and Disclosure Schemes
[95:4:0] - Main worry from black money: **loss of revenue** to the Exchequer through **tax evasion** (UPSC 2021).
[95:4:1] TABLE head: Scheme | Key fact
  [95:4:1.0] VDIS 1997 | Voluntary disclosure of black income
  [95:4:1.1] IDS 2016 | 1 June – 30 Sept 2016; 45% levy
  [95:4:1.2] PMGKY 2016 (Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana) | After demonetisation; 50% levy; declarations 17 Dec 2016 – 31 March 2017
  [95:4:1.3] Taxation Laws (Second Amendment) Act, 2016 | Tax on undisclosed income/unexplained deposits (Sec 115BBE) raised to 60% (+25% surcharge, cess, penalty)
  [95:4:1.4] Operation Clean Money (Jan 2017) | Income Tax Department; e-verification of post-demonetisation deposits – about 18 lakh persons/accounts with suspicious cash deposits flagged
  [95:4:1.5] Vivad se Vishwas | Direct Tax Vivad se Vishwas Act, 2020; second scheme 2024 – settle pending disputes
  [95:4:1.6] FAST-DS 2026 | Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers – Disclosure Scheme (Budget 2026-27): 30% tax + equal amount = 60%; limit ₹1 crore, or ₹5 crore for previously taxed but unreported assets (₹1 lakh fee); file till 31 Dec 2026; immunity under the Black Money Act, 2015
[95:4:2] ~~ Sources: Union Budget 2026-27 Speech; app notes 3:95; general knowledge (PMGKY dates, Operation Clean Money, not checked)
## SUB 5 | Cross-border and Digital Taxation
[95:5:0] - **BEPS** (OECD/G20): **15 actions** to curb **tax avoidance by multinational companies** shifting profits to low-tax places (UPSC 2016).
[95:5:1] - **OECD Pillar Two**: **15% global minimum** corporate tax for **large MNEs** (not all companies).
[95:5:2] - **Equalisation levy**: **6%** on online advertisement services by non-residents (Finance Act **2016**, a **separate levy, not part of the Income Tax Act**, so **no DTAA credit**; abolished from 1 April 2025); **2%** on e-commerce (2020, dropped 2024).
[95:5:3] - **Vodafone** (SC, 2012) → **Finance Act 2012** taxed **indirect transfers retrospectively**; **Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021** withdrew such demands (Vodafone, Cairn).
[95:5:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:95; general knowledge (equalisation levy, not checked)
## SUB 6 | Tax Administration and PAN
[95:6:0] - **CBDT**: statutory under the **Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963**; in the **Department of Revenue** (not Expenditure).
[95:6:1] - **Faceless assessment + Taxpayers' Charter**: **13 August 2020**; **faceless appeals** September 2020; **Project Insight** (2017, working 2019) – AI and data analytics; **AIS** shows all reported transactions; **e-Sahyog** – online check of mismatches.
[95:6:2] - **PAN** (e.g. AFZPK7190K): 10 characters – 5 letters, 4 numbers, a letter; **4th character** = holder type (**P = individual/person**, C = company, H = HUF, F = firm); shows name, father's name, DOB – **not proof of address**.
[95:6:3] - **TCS on LRS** for education and medical cut **5% → 2%** (2026-27).
[95:6:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:95; Union Budget 2026-27 Speech
## SUB 7 | Direct Taxes Code and Income-tax Act, 2025
[95:7:0] - **Direct Taxes Code** idea: one law to replace the Income-tax Act 1961 (and Wealth Tax Act) – it relates to **income tax** and other direct taxes; DTC Bills 2009/2010 lapsed.
[95:7:1] - **Income-tax Act, 2025** replaced the 1961 Act **w.e.f. 1 April 2026** (not 2025); a single **Tax Year** replaces Assessment Year and Previous Year.
[95:7:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:95
