=== NOTES 3:96 | Goods and Services Tax – Structure, Slabs, Gst Council, Igst Settlement, Compensation Cess
## SUB 0 | GST – Nature and Objectives
[96:0:0] - **GST (Goods and Services Tax)**: an **indirect tax**; **single, comprehensive, multi-stage, destination-based** tax levied on **every value addition** – a **value-added consumption tax**, **not a gross value tax**.
[96:0:1] - **Taxable event: supply** of goods and services (not manufacture, not sale).
[96:0:2] - **Destination principle**: tax accrues to the State where goods/services are **consumed**, **not where produced**.
[96:0:3] - Constitutional definition: **Article 366(12A)** – a tax on supply of goods or services except **alcoholic liquor for human consumption**.
[96:0:4] - In force **1 July 2017**; **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016**; biggest indirect-tax reform since Independence – a unified framework for many indirect taxes.
[96:0:5] - Objectives: **"one nation, one tax"**; **end cascading ("tax on tax")** through input tax credit; **one national market** (replaces multiple taxes of multiple authorities); transparency in **indirect** taxes; designed to be **non-inflationary** (A-R: avoids tax-on-tax → correct explanation).
[96:0:6] - Not an advantage: GST does not "drastically cut the current account deficit" or make India "overtake China" (UPSC 2017: only I).
[96:0:7] - GST involves **both Centre and States** (dual GST) – "only at the central level" is false.
[96:0:8] > Exam angle: statements on nature – destination-based (4 PYQs), replaces indirect taxes, not direct taxes, not gross value.
[96:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.4; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.19-20; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.204-206
## SUB 1 | Origin, Timeline and Ratification
[96:1:0] TABLE head: Step | Fact
  [96:1:0.0] L.K. Jha Committee (1976) → MODVAT (1986) → CENVAT (2000) | Path to VAT on manufacture
  [96:1:0.1] State VAT | Haryana first (April 2003); 20 States/UTs in April 2005; rest by 2008-09; Maharashtra had earlier taken IMF advice on VAT design
  [96:1:0.2] First proposed | Under the Vajpayee government; Empowered Committee of State FMs (2000, first chair Asim Dasgupta)
  [96:1:0.3] First recommended national GST | Vijay Kelkar Task Force (FRBM implementation, 2004)
  [96:1:0.4] EC roadmap / First Discussion Paper | "A Model and Roadmap for GST" 2008; First Discussion Paper Nov 2009
  [96:1:0.5] Target dates announced | 1 April 2010 (FM, July 2009) → April 2011 (FM's speech, Feb 2010) → 1 April 2017 (target in 2016) → actual 1 July 2017
  [96:1:0.6] 115th Amendment Bill | March 2011 (lapsed)
  [96:1:0.7] 122nd Amendment Bill | Tabled Dec 2014; passed by Rajya Sabha Aug 2016
  [96:1:0.8] 101st Amendment Act | Presidential assent 8 September 2016
  [96:1:0.9] First State to ratify | Assam (12 Aug 2016), then Bihar
  [96:1:0.10] GST Council formed | By the President, September 2016
  [96:1:0.11] Rollout | Midnight 30 June / 1 July 2017
  [96:1:0.12] Last State to adopt | Jammu and Kashmir (8 July 2017) – the only one not in on 1 July
  [96:1:0.13] GST 2.0 | In effect 22 Sep 2025
[96:1:1] - Concept first used in **France** (1954); India follows the **Canadian dual** model; brand ambassador **Amitabh Bachchan**.
[96:1:2] - **Revenue Neutral Rate**: rate that keeps GST revenue equal to pre-GST revenue – **Arvind Subramanian** Committee (Dec 2015): RNR **15-15.5%**, standard rate **17-18%**.
[96:1:3] - Threshold in the original design: **₹20 lakh** turnover (₹10 lakh in special category States); from April 2019 **₹40 lakh** for suppliers of goods (States may opt), ₹20 lakh for services.
[96:1:4] > Exam angle: "Bill 122nd vs Act 101st"; Assam first to ratify; dates of rollout (1 July 2017) and proposed dates.
[96:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.4; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.26-27; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.206-207; app notes 3:96
## SUB 2 | Constitutional Basis – 101st Amendment
[96:2:0] TABLE head: Article | Content
  [96:2:0.0] 246A | Parliament and State legislatures both make GST laws (simultaneous power); Parliament alone for inter-State supply
  [96:2:0.1] 269A | IGST on inter-State trade – levied and collected by the Union, apportioned between Centre and States on Council advice
  [96:2:0.2] 279A | GST Council, constituted by the President
  [96:2:0.3] 366(12A) | Definition of GST
  [96:2:0.4] 268A | Service tax – omitted
[96:2:1] - **Ratification** by at least **half the State legislatures** (federal provisions touched).
[96:2:2] - **VAT** before GST was a **State subject** (Entry 54, State List).
[96:2:3] > Exam angle: 122nd Bill = 101st Act; 279A Council vs 269A IGST.
[96:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.4-5; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.20; app notes 3:96
## SUB 3 | GST Council
[96:3:0] - **Constitutional body** under **Article 279A**; **never statutory** (APPSC G1 2024: "statutory, later constitutional" is false).
[96:3:1] - **Chairperson**: **Union Finance Minister** (first: Arun Jaitley). **Members**: Union **MoS Revenue/Finance** (only a member); Finance/Taxation Minister of each State and UT with legislature; **Vice-Chairperson** chosen by State members.
[96:3:2] TABLE head: Rule | Value
  [96:3:2.0] Quorum | One-half of total members
  [96:3:2.1] Centre's weight | 1/3 of votes cast
  [96:3:2.2] All States together | 2/3 of votes cast – each State has an equal vote
  [96:3:2.3] Decision | 3/4 majority of weighted votes of members present and voting
[96:3:3] - Recommends **tax rates, exempted goods, threshold limits**, model laws, special rates, date for petroleum – the **Council recommends**, the Centre and States **notify** rates (rates are not fixed by Parliament, EC or the Finance Commission).
[96:3:4] - **Disputes**: the Council itself sets up a dispute mechanism (not the PAC); proceedings are **not invalid** due to a vacancy or defect in appointment.
[96:3:5] - **Mohit Minerals (2022)**: recommendations **persuasive, not binding**; simultaneous power under 246A; "flexible federation".
[96:3:6] > Exam angle: chair = Union FM (5 PYQs); statements on status, voting and functions.
[96:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.5; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.19-21; app notes 3:96
## SUB 4 | Taxes Subsumed vs Not Subsumed
[96:4:0] TABLE head: Central taxes subsumed | State taxes subsumed
  [96:4:0.0] Central Excise Duty, Additional Excise Duties, excise on medicinal and toilet preparations | State VAT / Sales Tax, Central Sales Tax
  [96:4:0.1] Service Tax | Purchase Tax, Luxury Tax, Entry Tax (all forms), Octroi
  [96:4:0.2] CVD and SAD on imports | Entertainment Tax (except by local bodies)
  [96:4:0.3] Central cesses and surcharges on supply | Taxes on advertisements, lotteries, betting, gambling
[96:4:1] - GST replaced **indirect** taxes only – conventionally **8 Central + 9 State** taxes (subsumed **Central as well as State** taxes) – **not** income tax, corporation tax, capital gains tax or property tax.
[96:4:2] - **Not subsumed**: **Basic Customs Duty**, **stamp duty**, electricity duty, motor vehicle tax, property tax, **State excise on alcoholic liquor**.
[96:4:3] > Exam angle: "Which tax was subsumed / abolished?" → VAT, excise, service tax, octroi, purchase tax ("all of these"); not customs.
[96:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.5-6; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.207; app notes 3:96
## SUB 5 | Items Outside GST and Exemptions
[96:5:0] TABLE head: Item | Position
  [96:5:0.0] Alcoholic liquor for human consumption | Excluded by the Constitution (Art. 366(12A))
  [96:5:0.1] Five petroleum products: crude, petrol, high-speed diesel, natural gas, ATF | Within GST constitutionally; levied only from a date the Council recommends (Art. 279A(5)); also kept out in the 2011 Bill
  [96:5:0.2] Electricity | Outside
  [96:5:0.3] Ghee | Under GST
[96:5:1] - Lubricating oil, kerosene, naphtha are **not** among the five petroleum products.
[96:5:2] - APPSC G2 2025: no GST on petrol/diesel, liquor, electricity supply to consumers, services of charitable entities → **"All of the above"**.
[96:5:3] - **Exempt** (UPSC 2018): cereal grains hulled, chicken eggs cooked, newspapers with advertising; **not** processed canned fish.
[96:5:4] TABLE head: Term | Meaning | ITC
  [96:5:4.0] Nil-rated / Exempt | 0% / notified out of tax | No ITC
  [96:5:4.1] Zero-rated | Exports, SEZ supplies | Full ITC refund
[96:5:5] - **GST 2.0**: exempts **individual life and health insurance premiums**; rare-disease medicines fully exempt (Jun 2026).
[96:5:6] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.207; app notes 3:96
## SUB 6 | Dual GST Components and IGST Settlement
[96:6:0] TABLE head: Component | Levied / collected by | Supply
  [96:6:0.0] CGST | Centre | Intra-State
  [96:6:0.1] SGST | States | Intra-State (equal halves with CGST)
  [96:6:0.2] IGST | Centre (Art. 269A) | Inter-State and imports
  [96:6:0.3] UTGST | Centre, for UTs without legislature | Intra-UT
  [96:6:0.4] Compensation cess | Centre | Luxury / sin goods
[96:6:1] - **IGST revenue settles to the destination (consuming) State**; Centre administers **CGST and IGST**; States SGST.
[96:6:2] - **AP angle**: **SGST** is AP's **largest own-tax source** (₹36,296 crore, 38%, 2024-25 RE).
[96:6:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.4-5; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.21; app notes 3:96
## SUB 7 | Rates and Rate-change Procedure
[96:7:0] - 2017: **four slabs 5, 12, 18, 28%** + exempt + compensation cess; **GST 2.0** (56th Council meeting, effective **22 Sep 2025**): **5% (merit)**, **18% (standard)**, **40% (sin / ultra-luxury)**.
[96:7:1] - Rates are changed by **government notification on GST Council advice**, within **statutory ceilings** (**CGST 20%**, IGST 40%) – not by amending the Acts.
[96:7:2] - Item rates in PYQs: **sugar 5%**; **lottery** uniform **28%** (from March 2020; 40% under GST 2.0); **music books** 12% → **nil** (31st meeting, Dec 2018).
[96:7:3] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.207; app notes 3:96; general knowledge (lottery, music books, sugar rates, not checked)
## SUB 8 | GST Mechanisms – ITC, Anti-profiteering, Composition
[96:8:0] TABLE head: Mechanism | Meaning
  [96:8:0.0] Input Tax Credit (ITC) | Credit of tax paid on inputs by a registered person, set off against output tax; avoids double taxation/cascading; not available for exempt or non-taxable supplies, or under composition
  [96:8:0.1] Reverse Charge (RCM) | Liability moves from supplier to recipient
  [96:8:0.2] Anti-profiteering (Sec 171, CGST Act) | Rate-cut / ITC benefit must reach consumers (NAA)
  [96:8:0.3] Composition scheme | Goods turnover up to ₹1.5 crore (1%), services ₹50 lakh (6%); no ITC
  [96:8:0.4] Inverted duty structure | ITC refund allowed
[96:8:1] - **Anti-profiteering chain**: **NAA → CCI (Dec 2022) → GSTAT Principal Bench (from 1 Oct 2024)**.
[96:8:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 09 p.6; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.29; app notes 3:96
## SUB 9 | GSTN, Saksham, E-way Bill and E-invoicing
[96:9:0] - **GSTN**: IT backbone for GST; set up (2013) as a **not-for-profit, non-government company** (Centre 24.5%, States 24.5%, private institutions **51%**); made **fully government-owned** (decision **2018**). **GSTIN** = **15** digits.
[96:9:1] - **Project Saksham**: CBEC/CBIC IT project for the **new indirect tax (GST) network** (approved Sept 2016).
[96:9:2] - **E-way bill**: goods **above ₹50,000**; valid **1 day per 200 km**. **E-invoicing** curbs fake invoices, checks ITC.
[96:9:3] - Budget 2026-27: automated registration within **3 working days** for low-risk applicants.
[96:9:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:96; general knowledge (Saksham, not checked)
## SUB 10 | GST Compensation and Cess
[96:10:0] TABLE head: Step | Fact
  [96:10:0.0] GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 | 5 years at 14% annual growth over base year 2015-16
  [96:10:0.1] June 2022 | Compensation ended; cess continued to repay loans
  [96:10:0.2] 22 Sep 2025 | Cess scrapped for all goods except tobacco
  [96:10:0.3] 1 Feb 2026 | Higher excise on tobacco (Central Excise (Amendment) Act, 2025); Health Security se National Security Cess on pan masala units (on machine capacity; to the CFI, not shared)
  [96:10:0.4] 31 March 2026 | Compensation cess ended
[96:10:1] - **Unutilised fund** at the end: shared **equally (50:50)** – half to the Centre, half among States in proportion to their **SGST revenue** in the last year of transition.
[96:10:2] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.207; app notes 3:96

=== NOTES 3:97 | Impact of Gst on Commerce, Industry and State Finances; Unresolved Gst Issues
## SUB 0 | GST Collections and Revenue Effects
[97:0:0] TABLE head: Period | Gross GST
  [97:0:0.0] Oct 2020 | Above ₹1 lakh cr (₹1,05,155 cr) – first post-COVID month above ₹1 lakh cr
  [97:0:0.1] April 2024 | First month above ₹2 lakh cr
  [97:0:0.2] FY 2024-25 | ₹22.08 lakh cr; avg ₹1.84 lakh cr/month
  [97:0:0.3] FY 2025-26 | Highest ever ₹22.27 lakh cr, +8.3%
  [97:0:0.4] April 2026 | Record ₹2.43 lakh cr, +8.7%; net ₹2.11 lakh cr
[97:0:1] - **Economic Survey 2025-26**: GST 2.0 = **third pillar** of tax reform (after the **2019 corporate tax cut** and **2025 personal income-tax reform**); rate-cut **volume effects** may offset revenue loss.
[97:0:2] - **Revenue Neutral Rate**: **Arvind Subramanian** Committee (4 Dec 2015) – RNR **15-15.5%**, standard rate 17-18%.
[97:0:3] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary Part 1 p.15-16; app notes 3:97
## SUB 1 | Rate Structure and GST 2.0
[97:1:0] - 2017 slabs **5, 12, 18, 28%** + exempt + cess – meant as **transitional**.
[97:1:1] - **GST 2.0** (**56th meeting**, effective **22 Sep 2025**): **0, 5% (merit), 18% (standard), 40% (demerit)**; ~**99%** of old 12% items → 5%; ~90% of old 28% items → 18%.
[97:1:2] - **40% slab**: pan masala, tobacco, aerated sugary drinks, large luxury cars, yachts and **private aircraft**, online money gaming. Special: rough diamonds **0.25%**; gold, silver, jewellery **3%**.
[97:1:3] - Drawback of multiple rates: **classification disputes** and litigation.
[97:1:4] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary Part 1 p.15; app notes 3:97
## SUB 2 | Impact on Commerce and MSMEs
[97:2:0] - **Common national market** through tax harmonisation; **ITC** at every stage ends cascading.
[97:2:1] - **E-way bill** (above ₹50,000; 1 day per 200 km) → inter-State **check-posts removed** → less transit time and logistics cost.
[97:2:2] - Formalisation: taxpayers **66.5 lakh (2017) → 1.51 crore (2025)**.
[97:2:3] - **Composition scheme**: up to ₹1.5 crore (goods, **1%**), ₹50 lakh (services, **6%**); **no ITC**. Reform agenda: pre-filled returns, automated registration and refunds.
[97:2:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:97
## SUB 3 | Key Terms
[97:3:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [97:3:0.0] Inverted Duty Structure | Input tax > output tax → ITC piles up, working capital blocked
  [97:3:0.1] ITC fraud | Bogus entities issue invoices without supply
  [97:3:0.2] Destination principle | Favours consuming States
  [97:3:0.3] IGST | Levied by the Centre and apportioned; State share goes to the destination State
[97:3:1] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:97
## SUB 4 | Impact on States and Compensation
[97:4:0] - States gave up VAT, entry, luxury, entertainment tax, octroi → more **dependence on transfers**.
[97:4:1] - **Producing States** (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka) feared loss → **compensation July 2017 – June 2022** at **14%** growth over **2015-16**.
[97:4:2] - Cess continued to repay **COVID-19 loans**; scrapped 22 Sep 2025 except **tobacco**; unused balance **50% Centre, 50% States** by **SGST revenue**.
[97:4:3] - **VAT** was the main State tax subsumed.
[97:4:4] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. Part 5 p.207; app notes 3:97
## SUB 5 | Unresolved GST Issues
[97:5:0] - **Petroleum** (crude, petrol, HSD, natural gas, ATF) and **electricity** outside; petroleum date set by the Council under **Art. 279A(5)**.
[97:5:1] - **Council voting**: Centre 1/3 can block a **3/4** decision → **effective veto**.
[97:5:2] - **Mohit Minerals (2022)**: recommendations **not binding**; **simultaneous** power under Art. 246A; "**flexible federation**".
[97:5:3] - **GSTAT** (Finance Act 2024): Principal Bench **New Delhi**; launched Sep 2025, hearings Dec 2025; mid-2025 no functional benches in many States.
[97:5:4] - **Cesses outside the divisible pool** → concern over State fiscal autonomy.
[97:5:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:97
## SUB 6 | AP Angle
[97:6:0] - AP is a **consuming State** – gains via **IGST settlement**; **Net GST = SGST + IGST settlement share**.
[97:6:1] - Own tax revenue 2024-25 RE: **GST 38%** (largest); **State Excise 22%** (second).
[97:6:2] - **AP High Court (May 2026)**: in overlapping Central/State GST probes, authorities decide **inter se** who proceeds.
[97:6:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:97

=== NOTES 3:99 | Finance Commissions – Mandate and Key Recommendations of the 13TH, 14TH, 15TH and 16TH
## SUB 0 | Finance Commissions and Their Chairmen

## SUB 1 | Article 280 – Mandate, Composition and Nature
[99:1:0] - **Article 280:** the **President** constitutes a Finance Commission **every fifth year or earlier**; **Chairman + 4 members**; members are eligible for re-appointment.
[99:1:1] - **Qualifications:** fixed by **Parliament** – **Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951**: Chairman = experience in **public affairs**; members from: a High Court judge (or one qualified), finance and accounts of government, financial matters and administration, economics.
[99:1:2] TABLE head: Clause | Duty (recommendation to the President)
  [99:1:2.0] 280(3)(a) | Distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical) and among the States (horizontal)
  [99:1:2.1] 280(3)(b) | Principles of grants-in-aid to States out of the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 275)
  [99:1:2.2] 280(3)(bb), (c) | Measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund for panchayats and municipalities, on State Finance Commission advice – added 1992 (73rd/74th Amendments)
  [99:1:2.3] 280(3)(d) | Any other matter referred by the President in the interests of sound finance
[99:1:3] - **Art. 281:** the President lays the report and an **explanatory memorandum** on action taken before **each House**.
[99:1:4] - **Nature:** **quasi-judicial**; recommendations **advisory**, not binding (Rajamannar: should not be turned down without compelling reasons); **"balancing wheel of fiscal federalism"**.
[99:1:5] - **Not permanent:** it is constituted afresh each time and its **tenure is fixed by the President's order** (it reports in about two years) – not a five-year or permanent body.
[99:1:6] - **Not its job:** preparing the Budget, assessing income tax, controlling expenditure, **Art. 282 discretionary grants**, GST sharing (GST Council), devolving State taxes such as trade/sales tax.
[99:1:7] > Exam angle: "primary function = distribute revenue between Centre and States"; "constituted by the President under Art. 280".
[99:1:8] - Also not an FC job: **maintaining the income-expenditure accounts** of the Union and the States.
[99:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity full p.430-432; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Part 02 p.163; NextGen Rocket Sheets Polity p.65-66; app notes 3:99 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Thirteenth and Fourteenth Finance Commissions
[99:2:0] TABLE head: Item | 13th FC (Kelkar, 2010-15) | 14th FC (Y.V. Reddy, 2015-20)
  [99:2:0.0] States' share | 32% (from 30.5%) | 42% (+10 points, largest-ever rise)
  [99:2:0.1] Highest-weight criterion | Fiscal capacity distance 47.5% | Income distance 50%
  [99:2:0.2] Other criteria | Population 1971 25%, area 10%, fiscal discipline 17.5% | Population 1971 17.5%, population 2011 10%, area 15%, forest cover 7.5% (first time)
[99:2:1] - **14th FC approach:** **tax devolution, not grants,** as the primary route ("compositional shift"); took a State's **entire revenue expenditure** – **ended the Plan/non-Plan distinction**; **no distinction** between general and **Special Category** States; **no sector-specific grants**; States to share more of CSS costs.
[99:2:2] - **14th FC fiscal roadmap:** Centre's fiscal deficit **3% of GDP** (2016-17 to 2019-20); States anchored at **3% of GSDP**; States **excluded from NSSF** loans from **1 April 2015**.
[99:2:3] - **14th FC local bodies:** **₹2,87,436 crore** (2015-20), of which gram panchayats **₹2,00,292 crore**; distributed **90% population (2011), 10% area**.
[99:2:4] - Government accepted the 14th FC report on **24 Feb 2015**.
[99:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.8-9; NextGen Polity full p.431-432; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 03 p.1; app notes 3:99 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Fifteenth Finance Commission
[99:3:0] - Constituted **27 Nov 2017**, chairman **N.K. Singh**; two reports – **2020-21** (interim) and **2021-22 to 2025-26**.
[99:3:1] - **States' share 41%** (one point less than 42%, because **J&K became a Union Territory**).
[99:3:2] TABLE head: Criterion | Weight
  [99:3:2.0] Income distance | 45%
  [99:3:2.1] Population (2011) | 15%
  [99:3:2.2] Area | 15%
  [99:3:2.3] Forest and ecology | 10%
  [99:3:2.4] Demographic performance | 12.5%
  [99:3:2.5] Tax effort | 2.5% (reintroduced to reward fiscal performance)
[99:3:3] - Not a criterion: **income tax collected in a State**.
[99:3:4] - **Grants:** revenue-deficit, **sector-specific**, **State-specific**, local-body and disaster grants (about **₹10.1 lakh crore**); **₹4,800 crore** (₹1,200 crore a year, **2022-23 to 2025-26**) to improve **educational outcomes**; **₹45,000 crore** performance incentive for **agricultural reforms**; rural local bodies **₹2.36 lakh crore**.
[99:3:5] - **Terms of reference rows:** mandated to use **Census 2011** population → **southern States** objected; ToR also covered disaster financing and a **non-lapsable fund for defence** (and internal security).
[99:3:6] > Exam angle: UPSC 2025 – ₹4,800 crore education, ₹45,000 crore agriculture, tax effort true; "45% share" false (41%).
[99:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.9; NextGen Rocket Sheets Polity p.66; app notes 3:99 sub 3-5
## SUB 4 | Sixteenth Finance Commission (2026-31)
[99:4:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [99:4:0.0] Constituted | 31 December 2023 (not 2024)
  [99:4:0.1] Chairman | Arvind Panagariya
  [99:4:0.2] Report submitted | 17 November 2025
  [99:4:0.3] Tabled in Parliament | 1 February 2026 (with Budget 2026-27, Art. 281)
  [99:4:0.4] In force | 1 April 2026; award 2026-27 to 2030-31
  [99:4:0.5] States' share | 41% retained (States' demand for 50% rejected)
[99:4:1] - **Horizontal formula:** income distance **42.5%**, population (2011) **17.5%**, demographic performance 10%, area **10%** (cut from 15%), forest 10%, **contribution to GDP 10% (new)**; **tax effort dropped**. It is the **first FC to use contribution to GDP**.
[99:4:2] - All **five southern States'** shares rose (AP **4.217%**).
[99:4:3] - **Grants:** total about **₹9.47 lakh crore**; **local bodies ₹7.91 lakh crore** (rural 4.35, urban 3.56); disaster corpus (SDRF + SDMF) **₹2,04,401 crore**; **no revenue-deficit, sector-specific or State-specific grants**.
[99:4:4] - **Disaster cost-share:** **90:10** for North-Eastern and Himalayan States, **75:25** for others; **heatwave and lightning** to be notified disasters.
[99:4:5] - **Fiscal path:** Centre's fiscal deficit **3.5% of GDP by 2030-31**; States **3% of GSDP**; combined debt projected to fall from 77.3% to 73.1% of GDP; off-budget borrowing to stop.
[99:4:6] - Budget 2026-27 gave States **₹1.4 lakh crore** as FC grants for 2026-27.
[99:4:7] - **16th FC terms of reference** (notified **31 Dec 2023**): the Art. 280(3) items – tax sharing, principles of grants-in-aid, augmenting States' funds for local bodies – plus clause (iv): it **may review the present arrangements on financing disaster management** (DM Act 2005 funds).
[99:4:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket CA Jan 2026 p.12; PMF LENS Feb 2026 Part 1 p.11; Union Budget 2026-27 Speech p.22; Praveen CA360 Feb 2026 p.121; app notes 3:99 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Earlier Commissions (10th to 12th) and Disaster Funds
[99:5:0] - **States' shares:** 10th **29%** (Alternative Scheme of Devolution, gross Central taxes); 11th **29.5%**; 12th **30.5%**.
[99:5:1] - **Disaster funds:** 9th FC – Calamity Relief Fund; 10th FC – National Fund for Calamity Relief; **11th FC – National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF)**, ₹500 crore corpus (renamed **National Disaster Response Fund** in 2010). Papers call it a "National Disaster Reserve Fund" – the intended answer is the **11th FC**.
[99:5:2] ~~ Sources: Arthapedia (ies.gov.in) National Calamity Contingency Fund; app notes 3:100 sub 2
## SUB 6 | Andhra Pradesh and the Finance Commissions
[99:6:0] - **Sec 46(1), AP Reorganisation Act, 2014:** the **13th FC** award to undivided AP is apportioned between AP and Telangana on **population ratio and other parameters**; the **14th FC** was asked to make **separate awards**.
[99:6:1] - AP relied on the **14th FC** revenue-deficit grant (about **₹22,113 crore**, 2015-20) and **15th FC** revenue-deficit grants and disaster funds; a special package was given **in lieu of Special Category Status**.
[99:6:2] - Revenue deficit 2014-15 to 2018-19: about **₹16,000 crore**; projected **₹48,000 crore** (2025-26).
[99:6:3] - **16th FC:** AP share **4.047% → 4.217%**; loss of up to ₹38,000 crore from dropped grants.
[99:6:4] ~~ Sources: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 s.46 (Gazette p.12); PMF LENS Feb 2026 Part 1 p.11; app notes 3:99 sub 6

=== NOTES 3:101 | Fiscal Decentralisation to Local Bodies – State Finance Commissions and Local Revenue
## SUB 0 | Union Finance Commission Grants to Local Bodies
[101:0:0] TABLE head: FC | Local-body grants | Key features
  [101:0:0.0] 10th | ₹4,380 crore PRIs + ₹1,000 crore ULBs | First (ad hoc) local-body grants, before Parts IX and IX-A took effect
  [101:0:0.1] 11th | ₹8,000 crore rural + ₹2,000 crore urban | Weights: population (1991) 40%, index of decentralisation 20%, distance from highest per capita income 20%, revenue effort 10%, area 10%
  [101:0:0.2] 12th | ₹25,000 crore (80:20 rural:urban) | Population 40% (Census 2001), area 10%, income distance 20%, deprivation 10%, revenue effort 20%
  [101:0:0.3] 13th | ₹87,519 crore | Share of divisible pool; basic + performance grants
  [101:0:0.4] 14th | ₹2,87,436 crore | Gram panchayats ₹2,00,292.2 crore, municipalities ₹87,143.8 crore; 90% population, 10% area
  [101:0:0.5] 15th | ₹4,36,361 crore | Rural ₹2,36,805 crore; all three PRI tiers; 60% tied
  [101:0:0.6] 16th | ₹7,91,493 crore | Rural 4.35, urban 3.56 lakh crore; urban share 36% → 45%
[101:0:1] - **14th FC:** grants only to **gram panchayats** (not block/district tiers); **basic : performance = 90:10** for gram panchayats and **80:20** for **municipalities**; rural-urban split by population, so the **same per capita** amount (about ₹488 per head a year) for both.
[101:0:2] - **14th FC performance grant:** from **2016-17**, released in a later year against **audited annual accounts** and a rise in **own revenue**.
[101:0:3] - **14th FC on local taxes:** States should empower local bodies to levy **advertisement tax**; property-tax reform, municipal bonds, professional tax up to ₹12,000.
[101:0:4] - **15th FC conditions:** rural grants **60% tied** (drinking water, rainwater harvesting; sanitation/ODF) and **40% untied** (not for **salaries**); provisional and **audited accounts online** by at least **25%** of rural bodies (all from 2023-24); ULBs also notify **floor (baseline) property-tax rates**; SFC compliance required.
[101:0:5] TABLE head: 16th FC component | Share | Tied / untied
  [101:0:5.0] Basic | 80% | Half tied (water, sanitation), half untied
  [101:0:5.1] Performance | 20% | Fully untied
  [101:0:5.2] Special infrastructure (ULBs) | ₹56,100 crore | Wastewater, cities of 10-40 lakh
  [101:0:5.3] Urbanisation Premium | ₹10,000 crore | One-time; merging peri-urban villages, Rural-to-Urban Transition Policy
[101:0:6] - **16th FC entry conditions:** elected bodies, **audited accounts online**, timely SFCs – **municipal bonds are not** a condition.
[101:0:7] - Union FCs have **not in practice based** local-body grants on SFC reports (irregular, unsynchronised), using their own criteria instead.
[101:0:8] > Exam angle: APPSC Panchayat Secretary papers ask amounts (₹2,00,292.20 crore), ratios (80:20, 90:10) and weights (40% population).
[101:0:9] ~~ Sources: AP Fifth SFC Report 2025-30 p.22-31 (apfinance.gov.in); NextGen Polity full p.431-432; Business Standard 25 Feb 2015 (web search); app notes 3:101 sub 5
## SUB 1 | Constitutional Provisions and State Finance Commissions
[101:1:0] TABLE head: Article | Body | Provision
  [101:1:0.0] 243H | Panchayats | State Legislature may authorise taxes, tolls, fees; assign State taxes; give grants
  [101:1:0.1] 243-I | Panchayats | Governor constitutes an SFC every five years
  [101:1:0.2] 243X | Municipalities | Same enabling power
  [101:1:0.3] 243Y | Municipalities | The same SFC (243-I) reviews municipal finances – no separate SFC
  [101:1:0.4] 280(3)(bb), (c) | Both | Central FC suggests measures to augment the State fund on SFC recommendations
[101:1:1] - Clause 280(3)(bb)/(c) was added by the **73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)** – not the 80th (2000), which changed tax sharing.
[101:1:2] - **SFC functions:** review the **financial position** of panchayats and municipalities; recommend the **distribution of State revenues between the State and local bodies**, and among rural and urban bodies; grants-in-aid. It **determines its own procedure**.
[101:1:3] - **"May" = enabling** – the State is not forced to impose taxes.
[101:1:4] - **Eleventh Schedule** (Art. 243G): **29** subjects; **Twelfth Schedule** (Art. 243W): **18** subjects → **funds, functions, functionaries (3Fs)** rarely move together.
[101:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity full p.337, p.394, p.405; NextGen Rocket Sheets Polity p.66; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Part 02; app notes 3:101 sub 0
## SUB 2 | State Finance Commissions of Andhra Pradesh
[101:2:0] TABLE head: SFC | Constituted | Chairman | Key facts
  [101:2:0.0] 1st | 22 June 1994 | T. Laxmana Swamy | Report May 1997; devolution = 39.24% of State own revenue; gram panchayats graded by stage of development (ordinary, advanced, backward, tribal)
  [101:2:0.1] 2nd | 8 Dec 1998 | Prof. D.L. Narayana | Award 2000-05; 40.92% of State net revenue
  [101:2:0.2] 3rd | 2002, reconstituted 29 Dec 2004 | D.L. Narayana, then Prof. B. Satyanarayana | Award 2005-10
  [101:2:0.3] 4th | 5 Jan 2015 | Prof. M.L. Kantha Rao; wound up March 2017; reconstituted 8 Feb 2018 under Prof. G. Nancharaiah | Report 30 Oct 2019; award 2020-25
  [101:2:0.4] 5th | – | Prof. S. Rathna Kumari | Report 31 Dec 2024 for 2025-30 (e.g. meter all gram panchayat electrical installations)
[101:2:1] - AP SFC: **chairman + 4 members**, appointed by the **Governor**, at the end of every fifth year.
[101:2:2] ~~ Sources: AP Fifth SFC Report 2025-30 p.17-22 (apfinance.gov.in); app notes 3:101 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Panchayat Revenue
[101:3:0] - **Property (house) tax** = major own revenue of panchayats; they levy only **State-authorised** taxes: **local fairs**, house tax, fees, tolls.
[101:3:1] - Sources: **FC grants**, **Central Cooperative Banks**, **CSS** allocations, **SFC** allocations, **loans from the State**. **NABARD** is not a direct panchayat source; **sales tax, land revenue** are State levies.
[101:3:2] - **Grant dependence:** limited taxing power → panchayats depend substantially on **grants** (FC, SFC, CSS funds).
[101:3:3] - **Matching grant:** the panchayat raises about **10%** as its matching share.
[101:3:4] - **BRGF:** States had to pass Central funds to PRIs within **15 days**.
[101:3:5] - Gram sabhas spend only **4%** of meeting time on revenue (13% on local issues).
[101:3:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:101 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Urban Local Body Revenue
[101:4:0] TABLE head: Type | Sources
  [101:4:0.0] Tax | Property tax (most important), professional tax (ceiling ₹2,500), advertisement, entertainment, water, market taxes; octroi (traditional)
  [101:4:0.1] Non-tax | Rents, fees, fines, user charges (water supply, sewerage)
  [101:4:0.2] Other | Grants, SFC devolution, loans; municipal bonds in a few large cities
[101:4:1] - Payment for municipal water supply = **user charge** (non-tax). Property tax is a **local**, not Central, tax.
[101:4:2] - Weak municipalities = **under-assessment and under-collection** of property tax.
[101:4:3] - **ES 2016-17:** **satellite imagery** estimated the property-tax gap in **Bengaluru and Jaipur**.
[101:4:4] - **SVAMITVA** drone maps → panchayat property-tax baseline; **AMRUT 2.0** rewards property-tax reform and bonds.
[101:4:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:101 sub 1
## SUB 5 | Committees on Local Finance
[101:5:0] TABLE head: Committee | Period | Chair
  [101:5:0.0] Local Finance Enquiry Committee | 1949-51 | P.K. Wattal
  [101:5:0.1] Taxation Enquiry Commission | 1953-54 | John Matthai
  [101:5:0.2] Panchayati Raj Finances | 1963 | K. Santhanam (special powers to levy taxes on land revenue and house tax)
  [101:5:0.3] Rural-Urban Relationship Committee | 1963-66 | A.P. Jain
  [101:5:0.4] National Commission on Urbanisation | 1985-88 | Charles Correa
[101:5:1] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:101 sub 3
## SUB 6 | Challenges of Local Finance
[101:6:0] - **IIHS** (80 ULBs, 2012-17): transfers ≈ **40%** of ULB revenue.
[101:6:1] - India's intergovernmental transfers to local bodies ≈ **0.5% of GDP** vs global **2-5%**.
[101:6:2] - No **accrual accounting**, weak balance sheets → no bond market access.
[101:6:3] - SFCs **not constituted regularly**; State governments accept and release only part of SFC awards.
[101:6:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:101 sub 6; AP Fifth SFC Report p.17-22
## SUB 7 | Andhra Pradesh Local Body Finances
[101:7:0] - ULB terms ended **15 March 2026**, panchayats **4 April 2026** → run by **Special Officers**; FC grants at risk (they need elected bodies, audited accounts, SFC compliance).
[101:7:1] - 16th FC to AP: rural local bodies **₹16,627 crore**, urban local bodies **₹12,158 crore**.
[101:7:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:101 sub 7

=== NOTES 3:102 | Public Expenditure – Revenue and Capital, Developmental and Non-developmental, Trends; Subsidies
## SUB 0 | Largest Items and Trends of Union Expenditure
[102:0:0] - **Largest item of Union revenue expenditure = interest payments** – larger than defence, subsidies, pensions or grants to States; it was also the **largest non-plan item** (1991-92 onwards). BE 2026-27: **₹14,03,972 crore** = about **26% of total spending** and **40% of revenue receipts** (37% in 2013-14; 42% in 2020-21).
[102:0:1] - **Revenue expenditure** is the largest block of the Budget (bigger than plan, non-plan or capital expenditure): **88% of total (2014-15) → about 77%** (2026-27).
[102:0:2] - **Centre + States** spending ≈ **28% of GDP** (Economic Survey 2016-17).
[102:0:3] - Total Union spending BE 2026-27 **₹53,47,315 crore = 13.6% of GDP** (+7.7%); revenue expenditure ₹41.25 lakh crore (10.5% of GDP).
[102:0:4] - **Committed expenditure** (salaries, pensions, interest) = **65.3%** of revenue receipts.
[102:0:5] - **Why spending grows:** urbanisation, interest payments, subsidies and defence – all of them.
[102:0:6] TABLE head: Rupee goes to | 2023-24 BE | 2026-27 BE
  [102:0:6.0] States' share of taxes | 18% | 22%
  [102:0:6.1] Interest | 20% | 20%
  [102:0:6.2] Central Sector Schemes | 17% | 17%
  [102:0:6.3] Defence | 8% | 11%
  [102:0:6.4] Major subsidies | 7% (not 9%) | 6%
[102:0:7] - Then CSS 8%, FC transfers 7%, pensions 2% (2026-27).
[102:0:8] > Exam angle: "largest item of (revenue / non-plan / total) expenditure" = **interest payments** – asked by UPPCS, CGPSC and APPSC almost every year.
[102:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.10, p.58; Union Budget 2026-27 at a Glance; app notes 3:102 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Revenue vs Capital Expenditure
[102:1:0] TABLE head: Revenue (no asset) | Capital (asset / liability change)
  [102:1:0.0] Salaries, pensions, interest | Roads, airports, irrigation, buildings
  [102:1:0.1] Subsidies (food, fertiliser) | Defence equipment (capital outlay)
  [102:1:0.2] Grants to States (even if assets are made) | Loans and advances to States, PSUs
  [102:1:0.3] Maintenance of existing assets | Repayment of loans
[102:1:1] - **Test:** changes the government's **assets or liabilities** = capital; the rest = revenue. Capital expenditure buys, creates, upgrades or **extends the life** of assets.
[102:1:2] - **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
[102:1:3] - **Golden Rule:** borrow only for **asset creation** (capital expenditure).
[102:1:4] - Firms too: **acquiring new technology = capital expenditure**; debt vs equity is a way of **financing**, not a type of expenditure.
[102:1:5] - **Plan expenditure** had **both revenue and capital** parts.
[102:1:6] - **Budget terms:** the **per capita method** of estimation fixes a minimum amount per head; **budget control** keeps spending within the sanctioned budget and the laid-down rules.
[102:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.10; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.8; app notes 3:102 sub 2
## SUB 2 | Plan vs Non-Plan Expenditure
[102:2:0] - Plan/non-plan split **ended with Budget 2017-18** (end of 12th Plan), announced in the Budget Speech 2016-17; replaced by **revenue vs capital**. **Andhra Pradesh** also dropped it from its **2017-18** Budget.
[102:2:1] - **C. Rangarajan High Level Expert Committee on Efficient Management of Public Expenditure (Planning Commission, 2011):** the split was **"dysfunctional"**, an obstacle to **outcome-based budgeting** → remove it.
[102:2:2] - **Non-plan items:** **interest payments (largest)**, defence, **subsidies** (food, fertiliser), salaries, pensions, loans to States/UTs/PSUs.
[102:2:3] - Plan = asset-creating, productive; non-plan = consumptive, committed. **Maintenance of completed Plan assets** was shifted to the **non-plan (non-developmental)** side.
[102:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.10, p.40; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 02 p.11; app notes 3:102 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Developmental vs Non-developmental
[102:3:0] TABLE head: Developmental | Non-developmental
  [102:3:0.0] Education, sports, art, culture | Defence, border roads
  [102:3:0.1] Medical and public health | Interest payments
  [102:3:0.2] Irrigation and flood control | Pensions
  [102:3:0.3] Rural development, power, railways | Administrative and fiscal services, law and order (police)
[102:3:1] - Development expenditure of the Centre **does not include defence**.
[102:3:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:102 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Subsidies
[102:4:0] - **2026-27:** **₹4,54,773 crore**; **food ₹2,27,629 crore (largest) + fertiliser ₹1,70,799 crore = 87%**.
[102:4:1] - Major subsidies (food, fertiliser, petroleum) **₹4.11 lakh crore = 1.0% of GDP**; Q1 2026-27 up 37.4% (crude, West Asia).
[102:4:2] - **2002-03:** Central subsidies about **1.6% of GDP** (never above 2% since 1991).
[102:4:3] TABLE head: Explicit | Hidden (implicit)
  [102:4:3.0] Budget line: food, fertiliser, LPG, export incentives, interest subvention | Under-pricing of public services: higher education in public universities, health, irrigation water
[102:4:4] - **Oil Pool Account** under the **Administered Pricing Mechanism** closed **1 April 2002** (FM **Yashwant Sinha**); under-recoveries later paid through **oil bonds**.
[102:4:5] - **NBS:** from **1 April 2010**; fixed subsidy per kg of **N, P, K, S**; **22 grades** of decontrolled P&K; **urea outside NBS**.
[102:4:6] - **16th FC:** well-targeted subsidies, **exclusion criteria, sunset clauses**, no off-budget financing.
[102:4:7] - **Rationalising subsidies** and cutting revenue expenditure reduce the deficit.
[102:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.10; RBI Annual Report (web search); app notes 3:102 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Expenditure Reform Bodies

  [102:5:0.0] Expenditure Reforms Commission | 28 Feb 2000 | K.P. Geethakrishnan
  [102:5:0.1] High Level Expert Committee on public expenditure | 2011 | C. Rangarajan
  [102:5:0.2] Expenditure Management Commission | 2014 | Bimal Jalan
  [102:5:0.3] RBI Economic Capital Framework committee | 2018-19 | Bimal Jalan

## SUB 6 | Capital Expenditure Push
[102:6:0] - Capex 2026-27: **₹12,21,821 crore** (+11.5%, **3.1% of GDP**) = capital outlay **₹9,43,042 crore** + loans **₹2,78,780 crore**.
[102:6:1] - **Effective capex** = capex + **grants-in-aid for capital assets**: **₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP)**; grants ₹4.93 lakh crore.
[102:6:2] - **SASCI:** **50-year interest-free** loans to States for capex; **₹1.85 lakh crore** (2026-27).
[102:6:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:102 sub 5
## SUB 7 | Laws of Expenditure Growth
[102:7:0] TABLE head: Law | Statement
  [102:7:0.0] Wagner's law (Adolph Wagner) | Spending rises faster than national income as an economy industrialises = law of increasing state activity
  [102:7:0.1] Peacock-Wiseman (1961, UK data) | Spending rises in steps; wars/crises raise the tolerable tax level = displacement effect
[102:7:1] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:102 sub 3
## SUB 8 | State and Andhra Pradesh Expenditure
[102:8:0] - **RBI "State Finances: A Study of Budgets" (2018):** States' capital outlay was highest on **rural development**, then water supply and sanitation, urban development, education.

=== NOTES 3:103 | Public Debt - Internal and External, Debt-gdp Ratio, Sustainability, State Debt and Off-budget Borrowing
## SUB 0 | External Debt
[103:0:0] - **Size:** end-Dec 2025 **US$ 765.5 bn = 20.4% of GDP**. History: US$ 98.2 bn (Mar 2000) → 100.2 bn (Mar 2001, rise from **commercial borrowings and NRI deposits**); about **US$ 300 bn** around end-2010 (297.5 bn Dec 2010, 305.9 bn Mar 2011); ratio ~**21%** of GDP (Mar 2002), **23.7%** (Mar 2016).
[103:0:1] - **Who owes it:** mostly **non-sovereign** (companies, banks); government external debt ~2.6% of GDP.
[103:0:2] - **Largest component:** **commercial borrowings** (about 38% till 2017; still largest end-Dec 2025). **ADB** = largest multilateral lender (32.8%).
[103:0:3] - **Currency (Dec 2025):** **US dollar 54.8%**, rupee 30.1%, yen 6.3% – not all in dollars.
[103:0:4] - **ECBs** are regulated by the **RBI** (FEMA).
[103:0:5] - **World Bank:** India a **less indebted** country. **GDF 2010** most indebted: **Russia, China, Turkey, Brazil, India**; around 2000 **Brazil** was the top developing-country debtor; India ranked about **10th** of the top fifteen (GDF, ES 2001-02).
[103:0:6] - **Grants 2005-06:** the largest source was the **United Kingdom** (DFID).
[103:0:7] - "India's External Debt: A Status Report" – **DEA, Ministry of Finance**; RBI compiles quarterly data.
[103:0:8] > Exam angle: UPSC 2019 – "most debt is governmental" and "all in dollars" are both false.
[103:0:9] ~~ Sources: MoF external debt release 31 Mar 2011 (web search); app notes 3:103 sub 2
## SUB 1 | Components of Public Debt and Government Funds
[103:1:0] - **Art. 292:** the Union borrows on the security of the **Consolidated Fund of India**. Internal debt = **96.7%** of public debt; **G-Secs** over 90% of Central debt. Internal vs external is by **source** of borrowing.
[103:1:1] TABLE head: Head | Items
  [103:1:1.0] Internal – marketable | Market loans (dated G-Secs), Treasury Bills (91/182/364-day), Cash Management Bills
  [103:1:1.1] Internal – non-marketable | Special securities to NSSF and RBI, 14-day intermediate T-Bills, securities to international institutions
  [103:1:1.2] Other liabilities (Public Account) | Small savings (NSC, post-office deposits), provident funds, reserve funds
  [103:1:1.3] External | Loans from foreign governments and multilaterals
[103:1:2] - **Consolidated Fund (Art. 266)** = main account: **all revenues, loans raised and loan repayments**. **Public Account** = money held **in trust** (State Provident Fund credited here). **Contingency Fund** = urgent needs.
[103:1:3] - **Provident fund = contractual savings.** **Life insurance policies** are insurers' liabilities – **not** national (government) debt; NSCs and PF are.
[103:1:4] - **T-Bills** = short-term debt instruments; dated securities at market-related rates in auctions = the largest part of internal debt.
[103:1:5] - **Non-financial(-sector) debt** covers households (**housing loans, credit-card dues**), non-financial firms and government (**Treasury Bills**).
[103:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.22; app notes 3:103 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Debt Sustainability and Debt Trap
[103:2:0] - **Debt trap:** a country has to **borrow to pay interest** on its outstanding loans.
[103:2:1] - **Zero primary deficit** = fresh borrowing only for interest payments.
[103:2:2] - **r − g:** if g > r the debt-GDP ratio falls; if **r > g a primary surplus** is needed.
[103:2:3] - Interest ≈ **40% of revenue receipts** → high interest **squeezes other spending**; a **rising debt-GDP ratio hampers** good fiscal administration.
[103:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.54; app notes 3:103 sub 3
## SUB 3 | Market Borrowings and Savings
[103:3:0] - **Market borrowings = largest source of capital receipts**; borrowings gave the maximum resources for plan expenditure.
[103:3:1] - 2026-27: gross **₹17.20 lakh crore**, net ₹11.73 lakh crore.
[103:3:2] - Household savings reach government via bank deposits (**SLR** holdings), small savings/NSSF, insurance and PF.
[103:3:3] - **Per capita (Union) debt:** ₹53,796 at end-March 2016 (₹49,270 a year earlier).
[103:3:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:103 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Debt-GDP Targets
[103:4:0] TABLE head: Measure | Value
  [103:4:0.0] Centre BE 2026-27 | 55.6% (peak about 61%, 2020-21)
  [103:4:0.1] New anchor (Budget 2026-27) | 50 ± 1% by 31 March 2031; debt-GDP replaces fiscal deficit as the anchor
  [103:4:0.2] FRBM (2018) / N.K. Singh Review Committee (2017) | General government 60% = Centre 40% + States 20% (Centre 40% by 2024-25)
[103:4:1] ~~ Sources: Union Budget 2026-27 Speech p.22; app notes 3:103 sub 4
## SUB 5 | State Debt
[103:5:0] - **Art. 293:** States borrow **only within India** on the security of their Consolidated Fund, via **SDLs**; a State **owing the Centre** needs its **consent** to borrow; the Centre may lend to States (Art. 293(2)). External loans to States are **routed through the Centre** since **2005-06**.
[103:5:1] - **Net borrowing ceiling:** **4% of GSDP in 2021-22** (+0.5% for power reforms); **16th FC: 3% of GSDP** (2026-31). Key ratios: debt-GSDP, interest/revenue receipts.
[103:5:2] TABLE head: State (2023-24) | Debt % GSDP
  [103:5:2.0] Punjab | 42.9
  [103:5:2.1] West Bengal | 38.3
  [103:5:2.2] Rajasthan | 37.9
  [103:5:2.3] Andhra Pradesh | 34.6
[103:5:3] - **AP** 2025-26 RE: **₹6,35,177 crore = 36.04% of GSDP**; **market borrowing** (₹4,83,093 crore) largest; crosses ₹7 lakh crore (BE 2026-27).
[103:5:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:103 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Off-budget Borrowing and Debt Management
[103:6:0] - Off-budget: PSU/SPV loans **serviced from the budget but kept outside the deficit** → hides true debt (makes it look lower), hurts ratings.
[103:6:1] - **FCI borrowing from NSSF** for food subsidy – ended in **Budget 2021-22**. FRBM: new Central guarantees ≤ **0.5% of GDP** a year.
[103:6:2] - **AP** off-budget **₹1.28 lakh crore** (9.7% of GSDP, March 2023). **16th FC:** stop it and bring existing debt **on-budget**.
[103:6:3] - **RBI** manages government debt (RBI Act 1934). **PDMC** (2016) is in the **DEA**, not the RBI. A statutory **PDMA** was proposed (2015-16) but **not created**.

=== NOTES 3:104 | Deficit Financing - Meaning, Methods and Consequences
## SUB 0 | Meaning and Purpose of Deficit Financing
[104:0:0] # Meaning
[104:0:1] TABLE head: Usage | Meaning
  [104:0:1.0] Indian | Budget gap met by borrowing from the RBI; RBI creates new money – the government "buys money" from the RBI
  [104:0:1.1] Western | Any financing of a budget deficit, mainly borrowing from the public/market
  [104:0:1.2] Effect | Increase in money supply; creates extra paper currency
[104:0:2] - **Deficit financing** = the act of financing a **deficit budget** – **spending in excess of revenue** (total expenditure > total receipts) and sustaining that gap (APPSC G1 1999).
[104:0:3] - In India, deficit financing = borrowing from the **RBI** (money creation), not from the public (APPSC AD Economics).
[104:0:4] - **Fiscal deficit** (Union Budget) = budgetary deficit + net increase in internal and external borrowings and other liabilities.
[104:0:5] - An economic unit that **spends more than it receives** in a period is a **deficit unit** (APPSC Degree Lecturers 2017).
[104:0:6] # Purpose in Indian Planning
[104:0:7] - Purpose: **raising resources for economic development** – not redemption of public debt, BoP adjustment or cutting foreign debt (UPSC 2013 ×2); a "pragmatic tool" to finance the **Five Year Plans**.
[104:0:8] - **Small doses** of deficit financing for productive investment need not be inflationary, and it is an **often-used tool** for financing budget deficits (CDS 2011: both true).
[104:0:9] - Needed after 1947 because of a **low tax base**, poor compliance, weak private banking and **low domestic savings** (not a high savings rate).
[104:0:10] - NextGen objectives: remedy for depression, raise aggregate demand, subsidies, anti-poverty programmes, PSU losses.
[104:0:11] - Independence to **late 1960s**: little use, to fund plans. **Second Plan**: about **₹1,100 crore** against ₹1,200 crore planned. **Third Plan**: reliance to be **strictly limited**.
[104:0:12] - **1970s onwards** (NextGen: "period of deficit financing 1970-1991"): heavy reliance (oil shocks, welfare spending) led to debt and inflation.
[104:0:13] > Exam angle: "In India deficit financing is used for" = **economic development**.
[104:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.1-2 (deficit financing, monetised deficit, period 1970-1991, objectives, effects); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 06 p.18.10 (definition, India from 1969/1970s); app notes 3:104 sub 0, 1
## SUB 1 | Methods and Their Inflationary Effect
[104:1:0] # Methods (NextGen)
[104:1:1] - Running down **cash balances** with the RBI; **issue of new currency**; **borrowing from the RBI** (RBI prints notes); also internal and external borrowing, external aid and grants.
[104:1:2] - Ramesh Singh's order of preference: external aid/grants → external borrowing → internal borrowing → **printing currency (last resort, most inflationary)**.
[104:1:3] - **Monetised deficit**: borrowing from the RBI through fresh currency (**high-powered money**); the FRBM Act disallows it in normal times.
[104:1:4] # Inflationary Ranking
[104:1:5] TABLE head: Mode | Effect
  [104:1:5.0] Creation of new money | Most inflationary (UPSC 2013, 2021; State PSC)
  [104:1:5.1] Borrowing from banks | High
  [104:1:5.2] Borrowing from public | Lower – uses existing savings
  [104:1:5.3] Repayment of public debt | Not inflationary – withdraws money
[104:1:6] - Deficit financing is **inflationary in character** (APPSC G1); it **increases the money supply** (UPPSC 2016); if it fails to raise output it **generates inflation**, not deflation (UPPSC 1993).
[104:1:7] # Control and Phase-out
[104:1:8] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [104:1:8.0] Mid-1950s | Ad hoc Treasury Bills – automatic RBI financing of the government begins
  [104:1:8.1] Sep 1994 | RBI-Government agreement begins phasing out ad hoc T-bills (₹6,000 crore cap for 1994-95)
  [104:1:8.2] 31 Mar 1997 | Ad hoc T-bills abolished; Ways and Means Advances (WMA) from 1 April 1997
  [104:1:8.3] 2003 | FRBM Act
  [104:1:8.4] 1 Apr 2006 | RBI barred from subscribing to primary issues of G-Secs
  [104:1:8.5] 2018 | Monetised borrowing only on escape-clause grounds; deviation cap 0.5% of GDP a year
[104:1:9] - Market borrowing; liquidity is managed by **OMOs**: **sale** of G-Secs **drains** liquidity, **purchase adds** it.
[104:1:10] - **15 Sep 2026**: RBI announced **OMO sales of ₹1 lakh crore** with 91/182/364-day T-bill auctions.
[104:1:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.1-2 (methods, monetised deficit); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 06 p.18.11-18.12 (means of deficit financing, printing currency), p.18.18-18.20 (WMA, RBI primary bar 2006-07, 1994 agreement ₹6,000 crore); app notes 3:104 sub 3, 4
## SUB 2 | Consequences – Inflation, Debt Trap, Crowding Out
[104:2:0] TABLE head: Effect | Mechanism
  [104:2:0.0] Demand-pull inflation | Money supply and demand rise without more goods and services; hurts the poor most
  [104:2:0.1] Crowding out | Market borrowing raises interest rates, cuts private investment
  [104:2:0.2] Debt trap | Government borrows to make interest payments (APPSC G2); little room for health, education
  [104:2:0.3] Others (NextGen) | Adverse effect on savings and investment, rising inequality, BoP deficit, higher cost of production
  [104:2:0.4] Rating downgrades | Higher borrowing cost for government and firms
[104:2:1] # Public Debt Heads
[104:2:2] TABLE head: Head | Items
  [104:2:2.0] Internal debt | Market loans, Treasury Bills, special securities to NSSF
  [104:2:2.1] Other liabilities (Public Account) | Small savings, State Provident Funds, reserve funds and deposits
  [104:2:2.2] External debt | Loans from foreign sources
[104:2:3] # Current Data
[104:2:4] - Interest = **20 paise** of every rupee spent (Budget 2026-27); about **40% of revenue receipts**.
[104:2:5] - States borrowed **₹5.23 trillion** till Oct 2025 (**62%** of FY26 plan); RBI wants a shift from **subsidies to capital expenditure**.
[104:2:6] - **AP** fiscal deficit 2024-25: **5.05%** of GSDP vs 4% limit; **market loans ≈ 75% of AP's debt** – after bifurcation AP met its heavy deficit mainly through **market loans** (APPSC AD Economics).
[104:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 10 p.2 (effects); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 06 p.18.12 (printing currency, wage-price spiral); app notes 3:104 sub 2, 5 (2025-26 data)
